en: Salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Now begins the fifth maṇḍala.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
In the fifth maṇḍala dedicated to Agni, there are six anuvākas.
Therein, in the first anuvāka, there are fourteen sūktas.
Among them, the first sūkta, consisting of twelve ṛcs, begins with “abodhy agniḥ.”
Here is the table of contents (anukramaṇikā): "Abodhi [is the hymn] of Budha and Vasiṣṭharas, [belonging to] the twelve [verses].

Since it has been established by the general rule (*paribhāṣā*) that in the fifth maṇḍala one should know those whose lineage (*gotra*) is not mentioned as being Ātreyas, Budha and Vasiṣṭharas are both Ātreyas.
By the rule regarding the absence of specific instruction (*anādeśa-paribhāṣā*), the metre is Triṣṭubh.
By the technical convention of the *maṇḍala* and so forth, Agni is the deity.
These four hymns beginning with this one belong to the *prātaranuvāka*, the *āgneya* sacrifice, the *triṣṭubh* metre, and the *āśvina* recitation.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "The four [beginning] with 'abodhyagniḥ samidhā'. (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
Regarding the rites of the conclusion and commencement of the term (*adhyāyotsarjana* and *upākaraṇa*), it has been stated that the verse beginning with "dhāmante viśvam" is to be employed as a *ṛc*.
The fire of the people has been awakened by their fuel, facing the Dawn as she approaches like a milch-cow; like birds flying up to a branch, the rays of light stream forth toward the firmament.
Agni, awakened by the kindling-sticks of men, goes forth toward them like a cow approaching her calf; like birds rising up to their branches, his rays stream upward toward the firmament.

This Agni of the people— the officiants and others— has been awakened by the fuel-sticks (*samidh*). Just as one rouses a milch-cow for the sake of the *agnihotra* sacrifice in the morning, so too has he awakened toward the approaching *uṣas*.
The meaning is "at the time of dawn.

Now, the rays—the flames—of the awakened fire, which are great like branches (*vayāṃsi*) rising up, just as trees rising up (*projihānāḥ*) leave their own foundations, flow forth (*prasistrte*) toward the sky (*nākam*), that is, toward the intermediate space (*antarikṣam*).
Purified for the sacrifice to the gods, Agni has risen erect and well-disposed at dawn.
The radiant splendor of the kindled one has been seen; the great god has been released from the darkness.

The Hotṛ has awakened the gods for the sacrifice. Agni, well-disposed, has risen erect in the morning. The brilliant luster of the kindled one has been seen; the great god has been released from the darkness. 2.

The Hotṛ has awakened the gods for the sacrifice. Agni, well-disposed, has risen erect in the morning. The radiant luster of the kindled one has been seen; the great god has been released from the darkness. 2.
1. The manuscript kha-ca-pha lacks the word *āgneye*.
2. The manuscripts kha-ga-ca-ṇa-ma-la-sa lack the word *prātaranuvāke*. 3. The manuscripts kha-ga-ca-ṇa-na-ma-la-sa read *prabuddho 'bhūt*.
4. na-la-sa— or alternatively, 5.

kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-na-ma-la-sa: This Agni, awakened by the Prabhūtas, is the Hotṛ, the performer of the oblation; he has been awakened (abodhi)—that is, he awakens—to sacrifice (yajathāya) for the sake of worshipping the gods who are to be worshipped.
That Agni, being well-disposed—possessing a beautiful mind and an intention to favor the sacrificers—rises up from here at the time of dawn.
Of him, once kindled, the radiant, shining strength characterized by flames is seen;
such is the great deity who has been released from the darkness of gloom.
When he has awakened the tether of the quality, the pure one anoints himself with pure, radiant rays;
the impelling [sacrifice] is joined with the sacrificial fee, and the upright one has sucked the outstretched [milk] with his ladles.

When he has awakened the tether of the sacrificial quality, the pure Agni anoints himself with pure rays of light; then the prize-seeking Dakṣiṇā is yoked, and standing upright, he has sucked her as she lies extended by means of the sacrificial ladles.
Whenever this Agni has awakened— the *namas* (reverence), which is like a tethering rope (*raśanā*) that binds the activity of the gathered multitude of the world—
he swallows it or seizes it;
the meaning is that he becomes fully kindled.

Then the pure, blazing Agni anoints—that is, he manifests—the entire world with pure, radiant rays. Immediately thereafter, the increasing *dakṣiṇā*—the stream of clarified butter (*ājya*) seeking nourishment (*vājayantī*)—is yoked; that is, it becomes joined. Or rather, the increasing *dakṣiṇā*, the stream of clarified butter, is yoked.
And he, being upright and elevated, drank—that is, consumed with his sacrificial ladles—that stream which was spread out flat, extended upward, and wide above.
The minds of those seeking the gods turn toward Agni, just as eyes converge upon the sun;
when the two Dawns of different forms have given birth, the white steed is born at the beginning of the days.
Toward Agni, the minds of those seeking the gods turn together, as eyes turn toward the sun. When the two Dawns of different forms give birth to him, the white steed is born at the beginning of days.
The minds of the sacrificers—who are *devayantaḥ*, desiring the gods for themselves—move together toward Agni.
This means that the gods, who are to be worshipped, reflect upon him, thinking, "When will he increase?
Just as the eyes of all living beings move together toward the sun, so it is here.

Whenever the two worlds, Heaven and Earth—dissimilar in form, that is, possessing diverse forms—bring forth this Agni with their creative power (*upās*), then at that time the white, endowed with excellent color, the vigorous (*vājī*) and impetuous Agni is born at the beginning of the days, that is, at the time of sunrise; the meaning is that he comes into being.

1. [The variants] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, and la read *abudhyata*. 2. [The variants] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and sa do not have the word *asan*. 3. [The variants] na and la read *atha tathābhūtaḥ*. 4. [The variant] la reads *saṃghātātmakasya*. 5. [The variants] na and la read *rajjum iva*. 6. [The variant] ta reads *yadā ca*. 7. [The variants] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, and bha read *agniḥ*; [the commentary explains] "by the waters" means by those that consume or burn. 8. [The variants] kha, ga, ca, ṇa, and sa do not have the word *anānārūpe*. 9. [The variants] ta and pa read *prātaḥkāle*. 10. [The variant] la reads *jāyate utpadyate*. [The verse:
"For the one worthy of being born was born at the beginning of the days; he, the red-hued, was placed in the woods for the sake of what is beneficial."
Bestowing the seven treasures upon the tamed and the untamed, Agni, the most excellent sacrificer, has sat down as the invoker.

For he has been born, the one to be praised, at the beginning of the days; the ruddy one has been placed among the well-disposed woods. Bestowing seven treasures in every house, Agni, the most excellent sacrificer, has sat down as the Hotṛ priest. 5.

This Agni, worthy of being generated, was born—that is, he became manifest—at the beginning of the days, at the time of sunrise. Afterwards, shining brightly within the woods—that is, within the pieces of wood placed there—he was established. Then, in every house, he maintained the seven jewels, that is, the seven beautiful flames.
Alternatively, Agni—the Hotṛ, the performer of the oblation—bestowing the seven kinds of jewels upon the sacrificers, being most worthy of sacrifice, has sat down in his place.
If the word "dead" should be uttered while the sacrificer is actually living, then the *Surabhimatī* sacrifice must be performed.
In this regard, the following is the *anuvākyā*:
it is stated in the Sūtra—“Agni, the Hotṛ, the most excellent sacrificer, has sat down today for our auspicious feast of the gods” (*Ai. Brā.* 7.9).
The Agni, the Hotṛ, the most worthy of sacrifice, has sat down upon the mother’s lap in her fragrant place;
he is the youthful sage, established in many places, the observer of Truth, the sustainer of the peoples, kindled in the midst of the world.

Agni, the most excellent sacrificer, has sat down as the Hotṛ-priest in the fragrant lap of his mother, in her place; he is the young sage, established in many places, the observer of Truth, the sustainer of the peoples, kindled in their midst. 6.
This Agni, being the *hotṛ*—the performer of the oblation—and being the most worthy of sacrifice (*yajīyān*), has sat down (*nyasīdat*).
Where? That is stated:
in the lap (*upasthe*) of the Mother—the Earth, the creator of all—and there specifically in the fragrant (*surabhau*) place, the altar characterized by all that is desirable for sacrifice.

Moreover, he who is ever-youthful, or who is everywhere mingled; who is a seer (kavi), wise, established in many places, faithful to the cosmic order (ṛtāvā), possessed of sacrifice, and the sustainer of all—being such, he remains kindled and fully enkindled in the midst of the people, that is, among the officiating priests and the sacrificers.
(The verb "remains" is to be supplied.)
Now they indeed praise with salutations this inspired sage, effective at the sacrifices, as the Hotṛ-priest;
he who has spread across both worlds by the Eternal Law (Ṛta), him they constantly groom with clarity like a prize-winning steed with ghee.

Now they praise with homages that inspired sage, the effective Hotṛ Agni, at the sacrifices—he who has spread across the two worlds by the Eternal Law (ṛta). They groom the vigorous one constantly with clarified butter. 7.
They quickly praise with obeisances—that is, with hymns of praise—that Agni;
how is he?
He is the wise one, the one who is effective (*sādhu*) in the sacrifices, the accomplisher of results, the Hotṛ, the performer of the oblation.
The god who illumines the two worlds, heaven and earth—
[this is] the remainder [of the text] according to the recensions designated as Ta, Pa, La, Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṇa, Pa, Pha, and Bha.
U-pūraṇaḥ (the filler).
Ṛgveda 2.91:
"By ṛta, [meaning] by water, he has spread it out."

Because the oblation cast into the fire produces rain by means of the sun, [he pervades both]. Alternatively, with the *ṛta*—that is, with the sacrificial offering which has become Truth—he has stretched across the sky (*divam*), and likewise with such a fruit as rain, he has stretched across the earth (*bhuvam*).
The sacrificers constantly adorn—that is, they serve—the vigorous, food-possessing God with *ghṛta*, meaning either water or clarified butter.
The son of Mārjālya is cleansed in his own dwelling, the one who brings happiness, praised by sages, our auspicious guest;
that bull with a thousand horns, possessing such vigor, O Agni, shall by thy power surpass all others.

The purifier; he who is cleansed; in his own [dwelling]; the destroyer of enemies; praised by sages; the guest; auspicious to us; the thousand-horned bull; born of that power; O Agni, you surpass all others by your might. 8.
"This fire is to be cleansed; it is being wiped clean, that is, it is being served.
It is in its own place.
Of what nature is it?"

O Agni, youngest one, those who are free from debt, whose minds are intent on giving, or whose minds are subdued— those humans, the sacrificers praised by the sages, the wise— bring and accomplish for you,
O most youthful one, what? [They bring offerings.]
Accept from near at hand, and also from afar, the offering characterized by oblations;
moreover, take note of—the word "ā" serving as a conjunction—the hymn of praise from the most excellent praiser. Know it well.
O Agni, let your protection—great, auspicious, and worthy of praise—be granted to us.
O Agni, mount your radiant chariot together with the worshipful ones;
knowing the paths through the wide mid-air, bring the gods here to receive the oblation.
Now, O radiant Agni, mount the shining chariot together with those worthy of sacrifice; you who know the paths, bring the gods here to this oblation across the wide mid-air. 11.
O radiant Agni, today on this day of sacrifice, mount—ascend—the shining, luminous, and all-encompassing chariot together with the gods who are to be worshipped;
you, being wise and possessing full knowledge of the deities to be honored, [mount] toward the paths that lead to the world of the gods.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
O Agni, you bring hither—the gods who are to be worshipped—to this sacrifice here, across the wide mid-air, for the sake of the offering, that they may partake of the oblation.
We have spoken a word of praise to the wise and holy sage, to the bull, the vigorous one.
With reverence, I have fashioned this hymn for the foremost [god], as one who gazes upon the firmament beholds the broad golden disk in heaven.

We have spoken a reverent word for the sage, the worthy one; for the bull, the vigorous one. Gaviṣṭhira, with homage, has offered a hymn of praise to the foremost one—he who is far-famed like a golden ornament set in the sky. 12.

We, the descendants of Atri, have uttered a hymn of praise—a song of adoration—to the seer, the wise one, the worthy of sacrifice, the fit recipient of wisdom, the showerer of fruits, the bull, the vigorous one, and the youth.
Now, the seer, referring to himself in the third person, concludes the hymn:
this Gaviṣṭhira also has offered, or fixed, this hymn of praise—endowed with reverence or oblation—upon the foremost [Agni].
Like the shining golden disk in heaven, the far-reaching Āditya who traverses the wide expanse.

The second hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with “*kumāraṃ mātā*,” has as its seers Kumāra, the son of Atri, and Jananānna’s son Vṛṣa; both are the seers here. However, for the two verses beginning with “*kam etaṃ tvam*” and “*vi jyotiṣā*,” Vṛṣa alone is the seer, and not both [Kumāra and Vṛṣa].
Another *śakvarī* consists of six *dvādaśākṣara* (twelve-syllable) feet; it is a *triṣṭubh* derived from the *śiśu*. Agni is its deity.
The *Anukramaṇikā* on food states: “The *kumāra*, the *kumāra*, the *vṛśa*, or both; they may be capable, or let the *vīthi* be the *vṛśa* itself.”
The application of this hymn, along with the preceding one, has been stated for both the Prātaranuvāka and the Āśvina-śastra.
1. "The worlds—human beings—are not for you; *la-sa-tu* are for you. 2. "O Kha Ga Gha Ca Ṇa Pa Pha Bha Ma! May there be great auspiciousness.
3. "Na La Sa: in this sacrifice, there is no [fault]."
4. [The syllables] kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, ta, pa, pha, bha, la, and sa belong to Jarā. 5. Both kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, pha, bha, and la belong to Jarā.
The youthful mother carries the boy hidden in her secret place; she does not give him to the father.
Those who possess unerring knowledge behold the arrayed host and the citadels laid down for the mortal.

The Mother bears the youth; the young woman carries him closely hidden in her secret cave. She does not yield him to his father. O people, you do not see his face; it is placed within the fire-drill, yet it does not diminish.
The history recounted in the Śāṭyāyanabrāhmaṇa is told here: King Traivṛṣṇa, a descendant of Ikṣvāku, was the son of Vyaṅku. He had a son named Varuṇa.
At that time, Vṛśa Jāna was indeed the family priest (purohita) and the seer (ṛṣi).
The priests gather the chariots for the protection of the kings.
The family priest seized the reins of Vṛṣa, the son of Varuṇa;
while playing on the road, the prince was then struck down by a wheel.
The prince was struck down by a wheel and died, as did the family priest;
the priest cursed the king, saying, "May you be torn apart by your own hands," and the king likewise cursed the priest.
Then Khaṇḍāraka said, "It was not I;
since you were the driver of the chariot's speed, it was by you that he was slain."
"O King, since you are the owner of the chariot, you are therefore its slayer.
While they were thus disputing, those two arrived at the presence of the Ikṣvāku king.
The two of them asked the Ikṣvākus, "By whom was that twice-born man slain?
They pointed out the one named Vṛśa as the slayer who had strung the bow.
That sage, by means of the Vārṣaṇa [mantra], restored that boy to life;
having related this, he then spoke another matter right there.
Because the Ikṣvākus, out of passion, spoke even of a slayer [of their own kin],
therefore the splendor departed from their houses and entered into these [trees].
In our home, there were no longer any cooked foods or such things, for we had not considered the cause;
it was because of what we said regarding the slayer of the boy.
Thinking, "We shall go to see the one who is free from fear of the fire," they respectfully called out to that sage.
"Having arrived there quickly, he shall become the leader among them.
Thus, with gentle words, he made his request as before.
Singing thus, that seer Hastyāhavya took away the wife of King Trasadasyu,
who had been born from [his] wife and was disguised as a *piśāca*, and having seized her, he placed her upon his bed.
Having seen this correctly and having pacified his chest, he subsequently joined him with the Sāman;
thereupon, he became endowed with splendor, and his digestion and other functions returned to their former state.
Thus it was spoken by Śāṭyāyana; now that which was spoken in the Tāṇḍaka is being stated:
Vṛśa became the domestic priest (purodhā) of King Tadsadyu.
As the king was driving the chariot, he accidentally cut off the young son of a brahmin with a chariot wheel; at that, the boy spoke these words.
"While you are acting as my domestic priest, she has come here to kill me;
she must be removed by you," the sage said to the seer Māṇḍakarṇi.
That seer, by means of his ascetic power, restored that boy to life.

The mother, the progenitor of the prince, a young woman endowed with youth, while traveling on the path with the prince, [saw him] struck by a wheel that had become stuck; she carried and sustained him in a cave within a cave, and did not give him back to his father, his progenitor.
Or else:
The Mother, the creator of all, the Earth, bears him well-concealed and securely hidden in her cave; she does not give him to the Father.
O people, you do not see this boy’s face or his form, for it is harmed [by being hidden].
But in a place of non-delight (*aratau*), they see him situated before them in the front region (*puraḥ*).
Alternatively, this prince, having been restored to life by the physician, speaks of himself through direct perception;
or, knowing him [the physician], he speaks after having had him restore [himself] to life.
Or else:
Because the hymn belongs to Agni, he is addressed as "the youth" (kumāra).
His mother, seeking him out in the forest, carries him—bound up and hidden within a secret cave—and does not give him to his father, the progenitor who performs the sacrifice.
For people do not see his face, his consuming brilliance, nor his heat.
But in the wilderness, they perceive what is base.

1. Kha, ga, ca, pha, bha: Ikṣvāku. 2. Only ca, pha, and tra: Matha spoke. 3. Kha, ga, ṇa, ta, na, bha, la: Jāra. 4. Taṃ, likewise (tathā). 5. La is dropped (pātita). 6. Ṇa, bha, ma: Dvijāḥ. 7. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, pha, bha: By force (vegāt); ta, la: From contact (saṃgāt). 8. Ta, la: Having determined (niścitya). 9. Ta, na, la, rā: Having come (āgatya). 10. Ta’s wife (ta-bhāryā) was born. 11. Kha, ga, ṇa, ta, na, na, la, sa: Establishing (sthāpayantī). 12. Kha, ga, ca, pha: Having seen (dṛṣṭvā) the eyes (dṛśaḥ), having satisfied on the bed (saṃstare); having seen ṇa, having satisfied on the bed (saṃstare); having seen bha, having satisfied on one's own bed (svakastare); having seen la, having satisfied on one's own bed (svakastadaratoṣayitvā); having seen sa, having satisfied on one's own bed (sakastare?). 13. Oṃ, na: Thus it has come (itihāgata). 14. In the cave (guhāyām) of la. 15. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, bha: "In front of the region" (purodeśe) does not exist. 16. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ta, na, pha, ma, la: Jāra. 17. Hidden in la (la-nihitam).

Whom, O young woman, do you carry as this boy? A mother has given birth to him; for the embryo grew through many autumns, since the mother brought forth the one who was born. Who? This one. You. O young woman. The boy. As a fetus. You carry. A mother has given birth to him. For many. Indeed. Autumns. The embryo grew. Since the mother brought forth the one who was born. 2.
Because fire is being brought forth from fire, it is designated by the word "boy" (*kumāra*).
O young woman, you carry this boy; for you are a *peśī*, a female demon (*piśācikā*) who causes harm.
Thus, the great seer named Vṛśa speaks of the power of Agni concealed within Kaśipu.
The meaning is that because he was not produced from the womb, his being supported [as a son] is improper.
The queen—the great, worshipful one—bore him; she gave birth to him.
He states this very point as follows:
The embryo is the grasper of the child; for the embryo belonging to the fire-drill (araṇi) indeed grew—increased—through many past autumns, through numerous years that have passed.
And I saw him born from that, since the mother, the fire-drill, gave birth to him, brought him forth.
In the context of the prince: O young woman, O Goddess of the Earth, whom do you, being a *peśī* (embryonic mass), bear—this prince?
The remainder [of the verse] is to be construed with reference to the intent of the prince’s birth.
Likewise, in the subsequent passages as well, the meaning should be explained appropriately with reference to the delight in the prince.

I beheld from afar, near the field, one with golden teeth and pure luster, fashioning weapons; giving him immortality, the violator—what can those who lack Indra and are devoid of hymns do to me? 3. With golden teeth, of pure color, from nearby, from the field, I saw him fashioning weapons; giving him immortality, the violator—what can those who lack Indra and are devoid of hymns do to me? 3.

I beheld—that is, may I behold—near at hand, in every region and field, the fire being fashioned: one with golden teeth, possessed of flames corresponding to those golden teeth, pure in color, blazing in hue, and measuring out—that is, creating—the weapons, meaning sparks or flames that serve as its instruments.
Thus does the seeker desire:
"May I be the giver of the oblation or the hymn of praise, which is immortal, indestructible, or the means to immortality, and which is distributed and pervading everywhere, unto this Agni."
"Indraless me":
Indra is Agni, who possesses supreme sovereignty;
those devoid of him are "indraless."
The meaning is that they sacrificed to Indra; and being "without hymns" (anukthāḥ), that is, not praising Indra, what could they have done? What would they have accomplished?

From the field I saw him wandering far away, like a well-fed herd, shining intensely. They did not seize him, for he has come into being; the grey-haired women indeed become young again. 4. From the field. I saw. Far away. Wandering. Well-fed. The herd. Like. Intensely. Shining. Not. Them. Seized. For. He. Has come into being. Grey-haired. Indeed. Young women. Become. 4.

1. Covered by Taḷakaśipu. 2. Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṇa, Bha, and Sa say that very thing; La says they say that very thing. 3. La [says] "the princes" (rājakumārāḥ) in the sense of "possessing glory" (śriyapakṣe). 4. Ta [says] "on account of devotion to the mother of the prince" (kumāramātṛparatayā). 5. Ta [says] "in the region of the field" (kṣetradeśe). "I am now a bull from field to field"—this is a name for what is hidden (antarhita).
I see him moving secretly in the forest like a herd of cattle, himself shining brightly and abundantly.
Formerly, at the time of the Piśācī’s assault, men did not seize those flames; they were powerless. Now, indeed, that Agni has become manifest.
Indeed, they have manifested through his fiery power (*haras*).
For this very reason, those who were once grey-haired and aged (*palitāḥ*) now become young women, being nothing other than flames (*jvālāḥ*).
May those who have driven away the sun with their cattle, whose guardian was not even a stranger—may they who have seized him surrender the cattle;
may he who knows us come to our livestock.

Who are they? They have separated my cattle by driving them away with their own; those whose protector was not even a stranger—may they who seized them release them. May he, the wise one, drive our cattle back to us.
Who have separated my *maryaka*—my middle assembly, the kingdom—along with the cattle? They have deprived us even of our servants.
Those whose guardians were once our protectors, yet who have become like strangers, no longer appearing before us.
This is that Agni.
Those haters who have seized—indeed, seize—this host of people, this kingdom, let them be released; let them perish.
Furthermore, Agni, who is healing, conscious, and possesses knowledge regarding our domain, approaches—goes toward—our cattle.

The bull, the king of men, the immortal one, has been established among mortals as their dwelling. May the priests release him from the oppressor; may those who revile become themselves objects of reproach.

The swift ones have established the Bull, the King, the dwelling-place of people, among mortals. Let them release him here for the sake of the sacred word (brahman); let those who revile become objects of reproach. 6.

The enemies have hidden away—the sovereign lord of living beings who dwell therein, the abode of people, the fire characterized by freedom from strife—or they have concealed him among mortals in the worlds.
May the sacred prayers (*brahmāṇi*), the mantras or hymns of Atri, of the lineage of Atri, release that youth, or Agni;
or alternatively, may the sacred prayers [release] the youth of Atri, of the lineage of Atri.
Alternatively, Vṛśasya is the Brahman of Atri; [this refers to] the Atri lineage.
The sixth case ending is used in the sense of the object.
Let them release that youth; let them let him go.
Let those who revile us become objects of our reviling, and let the revilers themselves be subject to our reproach.
On the basis of the statement "the sacred hymns of Atri," they also call Vṛśan Ātreya.
According to the view that [the son] is Ātreya Kumāra, he himself hopes: "May he release this very self consisting of breath."
1. *ta-āraṇyam* | 2. *pa-śobhamānamim* | 3. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, *bha*, *la*, and *sa*, the word “*jīrṇāḥ*” is absent.
4. He separated the cowherds from Kha, Ga, Gha, Ca, Ṇa, Ta, Bha, La, and Sa; he also separated Na from the cowherds. 5. Na, Bha, La, and Sa were protectors. 6. Kha, Pa, Pha, and Bha did not exist.
7. la-na do not see;
8. in kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha, "vyaraṇa... vā" is absent; 9. ta—in mortals belonging to him.

10. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, and bha, the phrase “or hymns” (*stotrāṇi vā*) is absent. 11. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, pa, pha, and bha, it reads: “the death of a youth is an unfavorable omen. 12. In the manuscripts kha, ga, ca, ṇa, bha, la, and sa, it reads: “of Atri” (*atreḥ*), [referring to] Atri.
13. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ta, na, bha, la, sa—these constitute the Brahmāṇī [section].
14. Kha, ga, ca, ṇa, ta, na, bha, la, sa—the Śāṇa-megha (?).
At the Ājya-śastra, during the worship of the Āhavanīya fire, this verse beginning with "aśunaścicchepam" is used.
"He caused him to stand near the Āhavanīya fire with the words: *śunaścicchepaṃ niditaṃ sahasrāt* (AiB 7.17)," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"Śunaḥśepa, who was bound by a thousand [cows], has indeed climbed up the lofty sacrificial post.
Even so, O Agni, loosen our bonds; O wise Hotṛ, having sat down here, [release us]."

Even Śunaḥśepa, who was bound, you released from that sacrificial post among the thousands; for he indeed [was so]. O Agni, release the bonds from us as well, O wise one, having sat down here as the Hotṛ priest. 7.
O Agni, you released the seer Śunaḥśepa, who was firmly bound, from that thousandfold sacrificial post of various forms.
The particle *cit* is a filler.
In the compound word *śunaḥśepam*, the internal word has been placed out of its regular order due to the requirements of *saṃhitā*.
This Agni shines forth intensely with his vast splendor and brilliance;
being thus, by means of his own greatness, he makes manifest all classes of existing things.
Having grown so, he overcomes and subdues the godless, evil-acting, and sorrowful illusions of the Asuras.
Furthermore, "śiṇīte" means he sharpens;
"śṛṅge" means horns;
or rather, he sharpens the flames, which are like horns, acting as destroyers.
For what purpose? "To destroy" means for the destruction of the *rakṣas*.
Yāska says: "'He drives away the two horns of the *rakṣas* for its destruction'" (Nirukta 4.18).
And indeed, those who dwell in heaven, wielding sharp weapons, shall slay the Rakṣasa.
Even in his exhilaration, his splendors shatter [the foe]; the godless obstructors do not hold him back.
And let the roarings of Agni be in heaven;
two bulls with sharp and powerful necks, growing strong, who, being without an enemy, shall win the prize.
Thus have the immortals spoken to this Agni: may he grant protection to the man who spreads the sacrificial grass; may he grant protection to the man who offers oblations.

"Strong-necked, the bull, growing mighty, without an enemy, the noble one, shall gather together the wealth"—thus have the immortals spoken of this Agni. May he grant protection to the man who spreads the sacrificial grass; may he grant protection to the man who offers oblations. 12.

The bull—mighty-necked, possessing many flames, or rather having a vast neck—the Agni who is increasing and growing, bestows wealth that is free from enemies and without thorns upon the enemy’s property; he unites it [with the sacrificer]. Regarding this matter, the other immortal gods have spoken thus to Agni.
Therefore, may he grant protection and happiness to the human being, the sacrificer, who possesses the sacrificial grass.
And may he grant protection to the one who offers the oblation.
The third hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with “*tvam agne varuṇaḥ*,” is the seerly composition of Atri Vasuśruta; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and is addressed to Agni.
It is cataloged as “*tvam agne vasuśrutaḥ*.
Its application (*viniyoga*) is in the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra*, as stated in the section beginning with “*abodhy agniḥ*.”
O Agni, you are born as Varuṇa; when kindled, you become Mitra.
In you, O son of strength, dwell all the gods; you are Indra for the mortal who offers oblations.
O Agni, you are Varuṇa when you are born; you become Mitra when you are kindled. In you, O Son of Strength, all the gods abide; you are Indra for the mortal who offers oblations. 1.
O Agni, you are indeed Varuṇa—the deity presiding over sovereignty who wards off darkness—whenever you are born.

Furthermore, you are Mitra—the deity presiding over the day and the protector of those who have perished—whenever you are kindled. The meaning is that as soon as you are born, you dispel the darkness, and once fully grown, you become the benefactor.
In you, all the gods indeed abide, for they live by means of the oblation offered to you; for so says the Śruti: "Those gods, being afraid, entered into Agni" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 6.2.2.6).
He is the Son of Strength (*sahasaputra*), because he is pressed by force. Furthermore, you, O Indra, are the Lord for the mortal sacrificer who offers oblations.
At the marriage ceremony, during the fourth oblation of clarified butter, this verse "Thou art Aryaman" is used.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "In the marriage rite, at the fourth [oblation], [the verse] 'Thou art Aryaman when [it concerns] young maidens' (Āśvalāyana Gṛhyasūtra 1.4.7)."

1. *pa-manave* (for the sake of Manu). 2. *sa-vasuśrutaḥ*; the first [verse] is Virāṭ, the third is Mārutarādvāvaiṣṇavī. 3. *kha-gha-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha-san* [these phonemes] become [the result]. 4. *la—śrutiḥ* (the hearing of *la*). 5. *ca-martyāya manudhyāya* (for the mortal, for the human being). Ṛgveda 2.1.2:
"You become Aryaman when you bear the secret, self-sustaining name of the *kūnīs*.
They anoint you like a well-placed Mitra with [milk from] cows, when you make the husband and wife of one mind."

You are Aryaman; O possessor of self-sustaining power, you bear the secret name of the Kūnīs. They anoint you like a well-established friend with oblations of milk, when you bring the two spouses into harmony of mind.
O Agni, you become Aryaman;
you are the restrainer of all. When—whenever—you are connected with the maidens, the young girls.

Furthermore, O *svadhāvan* (possessor of the sacrificial food), you indeed bear a secret name worthy of concealment, namely "Vaiśvānara. Like a well-placed friend (*mitra*), you are [honored] with "cows"—
the word for the material cause being used here for its effect.

They anoint [the couple] with products of the cow, such as milk and the like, because you make the husband and wife— *dampatī*, *jāyāpatī*— of one mind (*samanasā*), that is, possessing a common intention.
The Maruts groom you for glory, O Rudra, for that birth of yours is beautiful and wondrous.
That supreme station of Viṣṇu which has been established—by means of it, you guard the secret name of the cows.

For glory, O Maruts, you have adorned yourselves; O Rudra, that birth of yours which is beautiful and wondrous, that footprint of Viṣṇu which was established in the highest place—by that you guard the secret name of the cows. 3.
By this [verse], the form of the Madhyamikā is described.
O Agni, for the sake of your glory (*śriye*), that is, for your manifestation (*śrayaṇāya*), the Maruts—the waters and the intermediate spaces—purify (*marjayanta*) you; they cleanse you.

O Rudra, that birth (*janima*) of yours, characterized by lightning, which is beautiful (*cāru*), worthy of being traversed (*caraṇīya*), wonderful (*citram*), and worthy of being admired (*cāyanīyam*), is increased by rain (*rudravardhitam*). 4 *vṛṣṭyā* emended from *vṛṣṭyāḥ*. 5 *rudravardhitarame* emended from *rudravardhitaram*. 6 *caraṇīyaṃ* emended from *caranīyaṃ*. 7 *cāyanīyaṃ ca* emended from *cāyanīyañca*.
If it is asked how that is so, it is said:
the secret, inaccessible station of Viṣṇu—the god whose nature is all-pervading—which was established;
by this, the intermediate space (antarikṣa) is indicated.

"Like the middle station of Viṣṇu, they do not see the intermediate space (antarikṣa)," so says the Brāhmaṇa. By that [power], you guard and protect the secret names, the names of the cows and of the waters.
O God, the gods, bestowing much upon you who are beautiful with splendor, have served the immortal nectar.
Men have established Agni as the Hotṛ-priest; desiring his favor, the yearning ones have seated themselves before him to praise the one who brings well-being.

You, O God, with your splendor, [make] the two well-looking ones; the gods, bestowing much, have served immortality. Men have established Agni as the Hotṛ-priest, the desiring seers (uśijaḥ) honoring him, the praise of the living one. 4.

1. In manuscripts kha, ca, ṇa, na, pa, pha, bha, and la, the word *suṣṭhu nihitam* is absent. 2. In manuscripts kha, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, and bha, the word *govikāraiḥ* is absent. 3. In manuscript ta, the word *apaḥ* is absent. 4. In manuscript la, it is *dṛṣṭyā*; in manuscript sa, it is *dhiṣṇyā*. 5. In manuscripts ca and na, it is *rudravardhitām*; in manuscript ta, it is *rudravibhitām*. 6. In manuscript ca, it is *ramaṇīyam*. 7. In manuscript ca, it is *śobhanam*.

O divine Agni, O wise one, by means of your splendor—that is, your abundance—the gods, Indra and the others, placing [it] abundantly within you and maintaining their affection for you, touch the immortal nectar (*amṛta*).

The human priests perform the service for Agni, the invoker who accomplishes the sacrifice; what do they do? Bestowing gifts, offering oblations, and desiring the praise—that is, the fruit—for the sake of Vāyu, the wind, and for the human sacrificer who desires it.
O Agni, no one before you has been a better sacrificer through his poetic wisdom, O self-dependent one;
and whatever mortal you become the guest of, he shall win through sacrifice as if with a boat.

No priest before thee, O Agni, has been more skilled in sacrifice; none excels thee in wisdom, O self-sustaining one. And whosoever thou dost become the guest of, that mortal, O God, shall win through sacrifice. 5.
There is no other Hotṛ priest before you—none more ancient, none more excellent, nor even one more skillful in his office.

He is to be praised with poetic wisdom and hymns; there is no one else superior to you, even in the most distant time. O God, O Lord of self-sustaining power, you are the guest of this people—their assembly and their sovereign—and like a venerable guest, you are worthy of honor.
He would harm mortals through his lack of discernment; he would be hostile, he would strike down, and he would destroy.
Or rather, he would harm—that is, he would favor—mortals, namely, his attendants.
O Agni, may we, protected by you, victorious and seeking wealth, be awakened by our oblation;
may we, O Son of Strength, be masters of the assembly and of the sacrifice, and may we, O Mortal, be masters of riches through your power.

May we, O Agni, protected by you, victorious, seeking wealth, and awakening with our oblation, overcome [our enemies] in the three-day battles; may we, O Son of Strength, overcome mortals through riches. 6.
O Vayu, being protected by you, guarded by you, and favored by you, may we—acting as sacrificers—overcome our enemies, crush them, or enjoy their wealth.
Of what sort are we? [We are those who...]
Desiring wealth, seeking wealth, awakening you with oblations while being awakened ourselves, may we conquer our enemies in the encounter, in the assembly—this is the sense.
May we obtain strength in the contests for booty, that is, in the raids. Or rather: [the rest follows].

The phrase "may we win" (vvanuyāma) is supplied here. On all days (vsarveṣvahaḥsu), O Agni— O son of strength (vsahasaputra), O protector (vpālaka)— may we, together with wealth (vrāyā dhanena), obtain mortals (vmartan), such as sons, servants, and so forth.

1. The instigator. 2. O Agni, [protect us] from foodlessness. 3. He who is to be honored like a guest—[this is not found in some versions]. 4. You. 5. You indeed act in vain; you cause harm (according to *pa*: you will harm). 6. We are the virtuous ones. 7. Those desiring wealth. 8. O protector of strength. 9. [Not for] mortals.
He who brings against us one who is hostile, place him under the curse of the reviler.
O wise Agni, strike down this very calumny. Slay him who seeks to crush us with duplicity.
Whoever brings guilt and sin against us, let him bear the evil upon himself; O wise Agni, strike down this curse of the one who intends harm. Slay him who seeks to crush us with duplicity.
Whatever mortal brings against us—whether it be transgression, offense, sin, or evil—and inflicts it upon us from all sides, upon that evildoer let Agni bestow misfortune and evil; let him give it.
(The word *it* is a filler.)
The meaning is: "May this fire strike back at that very mortal who commits this offense against one who is innocent. Now, it is recited directly:
"O Agni, destroy this malevolent spell!"
Since the word *yaccha* (restrain) is heard later on, it is explained here in accordance with that [later sense] as "one who accuses" (*abhiśaṃsaka*).
He who is the accuser (*abhiśāstā*) harms or oppresses us—meaning "us"—with the twofold offense or sin mentioned; him [we restrain].
At the dawning of this [light], O God, the ancients, making you their messenger, worshipped you with oblations;
when, O Agni, you proceed to the assembly of riches, you, the god, are impelled by the mortals along with the Vasus.

The ancients, O God, making you their messenger for this [sacrifice], worshipped you with oblations, since you, O Agni, are impelled toward the assembly of riches, a god kindled by mortals and by the Vasus. 8.
O Agni, at the dawning of this night—

that is, when it has dawned— those ancient sacrificers of old, making you their messenger who impels the gods, worshipped you with oblations as their means, when the presentation of the offerings characterized by wealth had been completed; O Agni, whenever you go forth to your journey.
The god, shining, being praised by wise men, by the *vibhus*, and by the *vasus* who provide dwellings, is being kindled while he himself is already fully ignited.
Release the father; as one who knows, O Son of Strength, let your son bear you up.
When, O wise Agni, will you look upon us? When will you, through your sacred rite, extend yourself to us?

Release the father; fight as one who knows, O Son of Strength, for he is the son who honors you. When, O wise Agni, will you look upon us? When, O knower of the seasons, will you take heed of our offerings? 9.

O Agni, you who are powerful, O son of strength, protect him; release him and carry him across. Fight for him and deliver him from evil. He who is your son, or one who stands in the place of a son—that sacrificer who, knowing you as his father, protector, and fatherly being, carries you [as an offering].
1. *pa-aghāśaṃse pāpakāriṇe* (to the one who intends evil and performs wicked deeds).
2. *ca-pha- he agne cikitvaḥ cetanāvann etām abhiśastim*; *pa-he cikitvaḥ cetanāvann me etām abhiśastim mābhiśaṃsakam*. 3. *pa-he deva*.
4. In the manuscript *pa*, the word "devaḥ" is present;
5. in the manuscripts *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *pa*, *pha*, and *bha*, the word "samidhyamānaḥ" is absent; 6. in the manuscript *pa*, [the scribe] has separated the words.
7. There is no *putraḥ* (son) [in the words] *kha-ga-gha-ṇa-na-pa-pha-bha-la-sa*. 8. Or rather, there is *ta-putratā* (the state of having *ta* as a son).
These *yāmāsaḥ* (journeys/steps), which are the *stomāḥ* (hymns/praises), have become, or are, *śvadrik*, i.e., directed toward the dogs (*śvan*).

Or rather, I spoke—that is, I uttered—that offense in the form of a request, namely "Give this," to Agni, who is the Vasu (the dweller) or the abode; for such a petition itself constitutes an offense. The word "itaḥ" is used as a filler.
Or rather:
this offense committed by our enemies has been spoken of, which is about to be described.
Furthermore, may this Agni, growing strong—that is, increasing through praise—not indeed deliver us over to censure or reproach.
Likewise, one should never give [anything] to a harmful enemy.
The fourth hymn, consisting of eleven verses beginning with “tvām agne,” is addressed to Agni; it is composed by Atri Vasuśruta and is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
It is cataloged as: “‘tvām agne,’ eleven [verses].
Its application is in the Prātaranuvāka and the Āgnimāruta Śastra.
This was stated in the verse beginning with "abodhyagniḥ."

O Agni, King, I exult in you, the lord of riches among all treasures, during the sacrifices. Through you, seeking booty, may we win booty; may we overcome the hostile attacks of mortals. tvām agne vasupatim vasūnām abhi pra mande adhvareṣu rājan | tvayā vājaṃ vājayanto jayemābhi ṣyāma pṛtanā martyānām || 1 ||

"O Agni, [I praise] you, the lord of riches among the Vasus. By means of "acquisition" (*vṛtti*) and "non-acquisition" (*avṛtti*), both the capacity for acquiring wealth and the status of its ownership are expressed. O King, I exult in you—the master of abundant treasures—facing you with praise during the *adhvara* sacrifices.
Moreover, being impelled by you, we who desire food (*anna*) may win booty (*vāja*);
furthermore, we shall overcome the armies (*pṛtanāḥ*) of mortals, those subject to death.
In the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifice, during the *patnīsaṃyāja*, this is the *yājyā* for the householder.
It is stated in the Sūtra: "The *patnīsaṃyājas* are performed with [the verses] beginning 'havyavāḍ agnirajaraḥ pitā naḥ' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.10).
In the oblations of the *devasū* sacrifice as well, the *yājyā* belongs specifically to Agni.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The bearer of oblations, the ageless father, and the men—the Soma is our desire" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.11).

The bearer of oblations, ageless, our father, pervasive, radiant, beautiful to behold—O Agni, with a good household-fire, shine forth upon our fuel; bestowing upon us, measure out for us glorious renown. Bearer of oblations, Agni, ageless, our father, pervasive, radiant, beautiful to behold—for us! With a good household-fire, shine forth upon our fuel; bestowing upon us, measure out for us glorious renown.
This Agni, the carrier of oblations, being undecaying and unaging, becomes our father—this is the ellipsis.
Furthermore, may he who is all-pervading (*vibhu*), radiant (*vibhāvā*), luminous (*sudṛśīka*), and beautiful to behold (*sudṛśīka*) be with us (*asme*). Now follows the direct address.
O you who possess a beautiful household fire, bestow these sacrificial oblations for perfect illumination;
and toward us, mete out and grant us renown and wisdom.

1. The syllables kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pha, bha, and dha denote "dwelling" (vāsaka); gha, pa, and dha denote "for the sake of wealth" (dhanārtham). 2. The syllables ta, ta, ditta, and ta [denote this]. 3. The syllable kha and pha denote "I have spoken" (ūktavān asmi). 4. In the versions kha, ga, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and sa, the phrase "the offense committed was told" (kṛtamāgo 'vāci) is absent. 5. In the versions kha, ga, ca, ṇa, and bha, it occurs elsewhere.

You have established him—the seer of the clans, the lord of all human tribes, the pure, the purifier, Agni with the ghee-backed back—as the all-knowing Hotṛ priest. He wins desirable treasures among the gods. [The Seer of] the clans, the Lord of all human tribes, the wise, the pure, the radiant, the purifier, Agni whose back is sprinkled with ghee—him, the all-knowing Hotṛ, you have established. He, among the gods, wins for himself desirable riches; or [he wins] for us those desirable oblations.

O Agni, take pleasure [in our praise] with the *iḷā* (the sacrificial food, the altar, or speech), being well-pleased; striving together with the rays of the Sun, take pleasure in our fuel, O Jātavedas, and bring the gods here for the consumption of the oblation. O Agni, take pleasure—enjoy—the hymn of praise, being well-pleased (*sajoṣāḥ*) through the *iḷā* (characterized by the altar, the earth, or speech). Likewise, at the time of dawn, making effort with the rays of the Sun. Furthermore, O Jātavedas—O Agni, knower of all that is born—take pleasure in our fuel. And bring the gods here for the eating of the oblation (*havirdhāya*); having brought them, you carry that oblation.
Now, regarding the *pavitra* sacrifice, there is an invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*juṣṭo damūnā agne śardha mahate saubhagaye* shall be the two *saṃyājyā* verses” (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.12).
This same invitatory verse for the *sviṣṭakṛt* applies here as well to the cake on seven potsherds for the Maruts.
"The Maruts who are not seated, who move at their own will, the beloved householders" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.18).

This Agni—indeed, this Agni—bestows upon the people (*viśe*) or upon the sacrificer (*yajamānāya*) a vigorous son, or one possessing horses, or a horse; he who is "belonging to all people" (*viśvacarṣaṇiḥ*), meaning he whose protectors or worshippers are all the people (*carṣaṇayaḥ*) or humans. Or rather, this is a word for "seeing": Agni is the seer of everything. For the sake of wealth (*rāye*); or else, the dative case is used in the sense of the accusative: he goes toward, or restrains, wealth that is self-existent, well-pervading everywhere, or desirable by all, being pleased [to give it]. To you, O Agni, with a verse of praise, an oblation is offered—O Lord of bright radiance, O resplendent one, O wonder-worker, O Lord of all, bearer of the sacrificial offerings! To you it is poured; bring nourishment to those who sing your praises. || 5 ||
1. Kha-ga-ṇa-pha-bha—this fire does not exist. 2. Pa-iṣamacaṃ—bring food and strength to us, the singers. 3. Na—in the third pressing, at the Maitrāvaruṇa recitation.
4. O Lord of light (*śociṣ-pati*), for you, the foremost (*agra*), the oblation (*havis*) is offered together with the *ṛc*—the sacred hymn—to you who are bright and radiant (*śukra*).
O most delightful one (*suśrand*), O possessor of beautiful gold, O destroyer of enemies (*dasma*), O Lord of the people (*viś-pati*), O bearer of the oblation (*havyavāt*).
"Food" has already been explained.

For you, the fires nourish every desirable thing within the fires. They are urged forward; they are incited; they strive in succession. Bring food to those who praise you! 6. *Pro* | *te* | *agnayaḥ* | *agniṣu* | *viśvam* | *puṣyanti* | *vāryam* | *te* | *hinvire* | *te* | *invire* | *te* | *ipaṇyanti* | *ānuṣak* | *iṣam* | *stotṛbhyaḥ* | *ā* | *bhara* || 6 ||
For indeed, those fires of yours— the *ghisnyas* (the sacrificial fires) within the *āhavanīya*, *gārhapatya*,
and other hearths— or rather, the worldly fires as the substance of brilliance— cause all desirable wealth to flourish within the Vedic fires.
Those Agnis are urged forward; they satisfy, they impel, and they pervade;
they desire food.
*Ānuṣak* means "continuously connected" (*sarvatrānuṣakta*). In this context, the singular number is used with the intention of expressing a general sense.

O Agni, those flames of yours, possessing great strength, exert themselves like prize-winning steeds; they who with their joints break open the stalls of the hoofed cattle—bring nourishment to your worshippers! 7. Your... those... O Agni... flames... great... exert... prize-winners... who... with joints... of hooves... stalls... of cows... food... to the singers... bring! 7.

O Agni, those rays of yours—your own flames—possessing great strength (*vājinaḥ*), meaning either full of vigor or possessing horses, increase even more than the vast (*mahi*). Or rather, it is an elliptical simile:
like horses that possess vigor (*vājinaḥ*).
Those rays which, with their joints— that is, their falls— seek out the stalls, the herds of cows; that is to say,
they desire the extended flames for the oblation—
they increase.

O Agni, bring to us, your praisers, nourishment and secure dwellings. May we be those who have proclaimed you as their messenger in every house; bring nourishment to your praisers! 8 O Agni, bring to us, your praisers, nourishment and secure dwellings. May we be those who have proclaimed you as their messenger in every house; bring nourishment to your praisers! 8
O Agni, bring—that is, bestow—upon us, your praisers, new songs of praise or, alternatively, fresh dwellings, excellent offspring, and such provisions as food.

We, who [reside] in every house—that is, in all sacrificial halls—[are yours]. (Note: Regarding the variants, the reading "tava" (your) is supported by the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa, na, bha, while the manuscript sa omits "tubhyam" (to you).)
2. *kha-ga-gha-ca-ṇa-bha-saha* read *tubhyam*.
3. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-bha-sa* do not have "in the *gārhapatya* and other [fires]". 4. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-na-bha-sa* read *te 'vardhanta*.
5. [The suffixes] kha, ga, ca, and ṇa are optionally used after the root *iṣ*. [Examples:
‘ānucuḥ’ (they have sought) and ‘arcayanti’ (they worship).
‘Te vayam tvābhūtāsaḥ’—meaning "we, having obtained you as our messenger who indicates the fruit, may we be prosperous."
Or rather, one should apply [the verse] as "dame dame syāma.
Among the Ābhiplavika days, when the *tṛṇata* hymn is optionally employed at the third pressing, this verse "ubhe sucandra" is the third.
This has been stated in the Sūtra.
O resplendent one, you cook both ladles of clarified butter in your mouth;
therefore, fill them up for us when we have uttered our prayers, O Lord of Might, and bring nourishment to those who praise you.
O you of beautiful splendor, you mix both [substances]—clarified butter and the ladle—in your mouth. And so, O Lord of Strength, may you fill us up; bring nourishment to those who praise you. 9.

O thou who art well-luminous (*asuścandra*), O giver of beautiful joy (*śobhanāhlādana*), or possessor of beautiful gold (*śobhanahiraṇya*); in both vessels, the *dhruvā* and the *upabhṛt*, which are full of clarified butter (*sarpiṣaḥ pūrṇe*), thou mixest, thou placest, or thou cookest within the mouth (*āsani*)—that is, the opening (*āsye*).
And furthermore (*uto*), do thou fill us (*naḥ*) with fruits in the sacrifices mentioned;
O Lord of Strength (*śavasaspate*), protector of power!
Thus they have anointed him in succession with hymns and sacrifices.
Bestowing upon us excellent heroic strength and that very wealth of horses, bring it for the nourishment of the singers.

Thus, with hymns and sacrifices in due order, we have generated Agni; may he bestow upon us great heroic strength and that famous wealth of swift horses. Bring nourishment to those who praise you! 10.

Thus, with *utkarīyā* (elevated songs), they have driven the *agni* (fire) with *gīrbhiḥ* (praises) and *yajñebhiḥ* (sacrifices) or by means of the oblations used in those sacrifices, *ānuṣak* (continuously, in succession). Having done so, they *ajuḥ* (have gone toward it); that is, they have restrained it, established it, and sacrificed with oblations.
In this way, the Ātreyas refer to themselves in the third person.
In the phrase *ajuryamuru*, there is a compound formed according to Pāṇini’s rule 2.1.72 (*ga.*): "A verb may be compounded with another verb when there is continuity of action.
Furthermore, *asme* means "in us"; *suvīryam* means "excellent heroic power," such as fine sons and so forth; and *uta* means "also"; *tyat* refers to that which is *āśvyam*.
One who possesses horses (*aśvāḥ*) is called *āśvaḥ*.
The state of that is "āśvyam. That too "dadhat" means it maintains or sustains.

The seventh hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "sakhāyaḥ saṃ vaḥ," has Ātreya iṣa as its seer (ṛṣi). The first verse is a Paṅkti; the remaining verses are Anuṣṭubhs according to the rule governing those ending in Paṅkti.
And thus it has been prescribed in the Prātaranuvāka: "The *sakhāyaḥ*, *iṣaḥ*, ending with the *paṅkti*."

O friends, you who have become companions—the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*)—prepare him thoroughly. Because of the presence of the prefix *sam-*, the verb "to join" (*yunakti*) is to be supplied. Furthermore, prepare for Agni—who is most excellent (*varṣiṣṭha*), meaning preeminently increased—for the sake of the dwellers (*kṣitīnām*), that is, the sacrificers; for the most excellent one, the greatest among those who have increased; for the grandson of strength (*ūrjaḥ naptre*), that is, the son of strength or its protector; for the powerful one (*sahasvate*), the mighty one. Prepare him thus.

In whose gathering, wherever it may be, men are joyful in the assembly of heroes; whom even those worthy of honor kindle, and whom all living beings bring forth together. 2. Wherever—in whose gathering—men are joyful in the assembly of heroes; whom even those worthy of honor kindle, and whom all living beings bring forth together. 2.
That Agni exists somewhere—this is the ellipsis. Where does he abide?
[He is where] at the encounter (saṃmṛti) or arrival of that Agni, the leaders—the officiating priests (ṛtvij)—are joyful (raṇvāḥ), that is, taking delight.
In the dwelling of men, that is, in the sacrificial hall—even the Arhats;
*cit* is used here for honor.
Being Arhats, worthy of worship, or indeed performing worship themselves, they kindle him, that is, they illuminate him.
And for that purpose, living beings and creatures produce it in the forest; "where is that?"—this is the connection [of the sentence].

When we choose together the nourishments and the oblations of men, then by the power of splendor I have seized the rein of Cosmic Order (ṛta). When we choose together the nourishments and the oblations of men, then by the power of splendor I have seized the rein of Cosmic Order (ṛta).

Whenever we gather together the *iṣas*, the foods—that is, when Agni partakes of our oblations, the sacrificial offerings belonging to us humans—then indeed, by the power and strength of this resplendent one, [he shines]. (Note: The word "saṃ" is absent in the Na-La-Sa recensions.)
2. *na-la-sa* "of men" does not exist.
Ṛgveda 2.94:
Agni takes up—that is, he seizes—the ray that grasps the *sāmadheya*, [meaning] the water of *ṛta*.
The meaning is that he has accepted the fire that produces the fruit.
Alternatively, he takes up— that is, accepts— the praise which is like a ray of *ṛta*, the sacrifice, being as it were a ray that grasps it.

He makes a signal even by night, though far away, when the purifier, the ageless one, has reached the pressed juice and consumes the lords of the forest. He makes a signal even by night, though far away, when the purifier, the ageless one, has reached the pressed juice and consumes the lords of the forest.
He—that very Agni—indeed makes a banner, that is, he provides knowledge, on all sides.
Of whom? It is said:
even of a conscious being (cit).
Even at night, even when he is far away—
*ā* being used here in the sense of "also"—
to the man who remains even at a distance.
When?
When this purifying Agni, being undecaying, unaging, and invincible, utterly consumes—burns away—the lords of the forest, the trees.
The particle *smā* is a filler.

In whose service they indeed offer up sweat upon the broad [altars], him indeed his own kinsmen have ascended from the earth as if upon the backs [of horses]. 5. ava | sma | yasya | veṣaṇe | svedam | pṛthiṣu | juhvati | abhi | īm | aha | sva-janyam | bhūma | pṛṣṭhaiḥ-iva | ruruhuḥ || 5 ||

In the service—that is, the ritual attendance—of that Agni, upon the broad paths of oblation, [and] upon the rays, the Adhvaryus pour down their sweat, [that is,] their own clarified butter (ājya), with faces turned downward; at that time, they indeed mount him, this Agni.
The streams of clarified butter truly ascend toward him.
The particle *aha* is used here for the purpose of emphasis.
Her own offspring is her own form; it is called *bhūmāpatya* because it becomes manifold (*bahu*). From that, "as from the back of the father" means as if from the region of the father's back.
Just as sons climb onto their father's lap, so it is in that manner.

That which mortals have found as much-desired for the sustenance of the universe—him, the self-enjoyer of nourishments, even the dwelling-place [of light], for the sake of the living man. 6. *yaṃ martyaiḥ puruspṛhaṃ vidad viśvasya dhāyase pra svārdanaṃ pitūnām astārtāti cid āyave* 6. [He] whom mortals have found as much-desired for the support of the whole world—him, the self-enjoyer of foods, even the place of rest, for the sake of the living man. 6.

1. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pha: "The state of producing a fruit [is] not; [it is] not the state of producing a fruit; [it is] by way of producing a fruit. 2. Ga, Ca, Ta, Na, Bha, Sa: "I accept. 3. Kha, Ga, Ṇa, Ta, Bha, Sa: "Of this. 4. Ta: "In the fires of the oblation. 5. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Bha: "One's own clarified butter, this one, [and] the *īma*. 6. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Pha, Bha: "The Adhvaryus. [This is] the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). 7. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Bha, La, Sa: The word "*īma*" does not exist. 8. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Na, Bha: The word "much" (*bahu*) does not exist. 9. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Bha: "On the back part. 10. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Bha: "A son. 11. Kha, Ga, Ca, Ṇa, Bha: "He ascends."

The mortal sacrificer knows— that Agni who is much-desired, sought after by many— for the sake of the sustenance of all, as one who makes things exceedingly sweet through the consumption of the offerings of the ancestors (the ignorant ones), who dwells in the house of the sacrificer, and who provides food for the living man (or for the sacrificer). *Cit* is a filler.
For he indeed cuts through the desert like a beast that bestows;
golden-bearded, pure-toothed, with unabated power.
For he, like a beast, shaves the desert land that has been worn away; golden-bearded, pure-toothed, a skillful artisan of undiminished vigor. 7.
For indeed, that fire consumes—that is, it cuts apart and burns on all sides—a parched desert region devoid of water, which is strewn with grass, shrubs, and the like;
it is a "consumer," one who cuts up grass and such, yet "not like a beast.
Just as a beast gradually devours a mass of grass, so does he.
With golden beard and golden mustache, pure-toothed with shining teeth, the *Ṛbhu*— meaning the vast,
the great—
one whose vital power (*taviṣi*) is unimpaired and whose strength is uncrushed.
He is indeed pure, from whom he flows like an axe, as Atri did;
the Mother has brought him forth, when she, performing the rite, attained her portion.
Pure indeed is he for whom [the sacrifice] flows forth like an axe, as with Atri; the well-bearing mother has brought him forth, when she, acting, attained her portion.
This Agni is indeed pure and radiant;
for which Agni the sacrificer, like Atri, goes forth to offer the oblation (haviḥ).
Or rather:
*Smā* is a filler word (*pūraṇa*).
*Śuci*, for whom—here the dative case is used in the sense of the nominative.
*Dyota* is one who is like Atri.
"He eats grass" is the etymology of *atri*; he is like a beast.
Just as a beast goes along eating grass, so too does he burn; such is the meaning.

Like an axe or a hatchet, cutting [through obstacles], the well-bearing, well-procreating Mother gave birth [to Him]. The *araṇi* (the fire-drill wood) produced Him who is active (*krāṇā*), performing what is beneficial for the world—
He from whom [all things arise], or He who is "ya" (the one).
The Agni who has attained, who enjoys, the portion which is food— O Agni, you to whom clarified butter is poured, may there be peace for you as you are maintained;
bestow upon these mortals glory, renown, and wisdom.
O Agni, that blessing which belongs to you when the clarified butter is poured, and for which you are maintained—bestow upon these mortals splendor, renown, and wisdom. 9.

1. *ta*-spr̥haṇīyam ārmam. 2. *na-la-sa* for the sense of pervasion (*vyāpyartha*). 3. *sa* for the sense of "with a friend" (*sāmitra*). 4. *na-la-sa*—the phrase "*'cit pūraṇaḥ'" does not exist. 5. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-sma*. 6. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-ma-ṛbhumahān*. 7. *kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pha-ma*—*atra*; *pa*—*annam*. 8. *ta*—*jagadupakāram*.

O Agni, you whose mouth is anointed with ghee (*sarpirāsuta*) and whose food is clarified butter (*ghr̥tāsyānna*), to you who exist everywhere (*ā bhavasi*) and who are the sustainer (*dhāyase*) of all, there is well-being (*śamasti*) from the act of praise. To you, such as you are, there is happiness. From the source of hymn.
If it be so, bestow— place within— glory that destroys [enemies] upon these mortal worshippers, the sons of Atri;
and furthermore, bestow food,
and bestow also the thought of your favoring mind.
Thus the self-born Cinmanyu seized the sacrificial animal;
from the offering of Agni, Atri overcame the Dasyus and overcame the weapons.

Thus [he spoke]. Citra, the conqueror, gave thee his fury; he took thee as his cattle. Then, O Agni, from the attackers Atri shall overcome the Dasyus; he shall overcome the men who seek our food. 10.
Thus, indeed, in this manner, the seer— whether he be one born from Agni, or one distinct from him, or his progenitor— having produced with his mind the hymn that is the means of wrath (*manyu*),
takes for himself, or may take,
the cattle that is to be given by you.
Immediately thereafter, Atri—that is, Tṛta—shall utterly overcome the Dasyus who do not bow before Agni; he shall overcome those who withhold the sacrificial oblations (*iṣ*).
He shall also overcome the men who oppose him from behind. The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.
"O Agni, your own..."—this eighth hymn, consisting of eleven verses, is the seer's own composition; it is in the Jagatī meter and addressed to Agni.
According to the Anukramaṇikā: "‘svāmagne matta’ [is] in the Jagatī meter.
This hymn is used in the Prātaranuvāka during the Āgneya rite, in the Jagatī meter, and in the Āśvina Śastra.
Likewise, there is a Sūtra: "O protector and lord of people, [we who] desire the Truth... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.13).
Thee, O Agni, those seeking the *ṛta* have kindled—thee, the ancient one, the ancients for their protection, O thou who art made by strength;
thee, the many-glittering, the worshipful, the all-sustaining, the friend of the house, the lord of the home, the most excellent.

Thee, O Agni, those seeking the *ṛta* have kindled—thee, the ancient one, the ancients for their protection—O thou who art made of strength, the many-shining, the holy, the all-sustaining, the friend of the house, the lord of the home, the most excellent. 1.
O Agni, you who are created by strength and are the maker of power—the ancient seers of old, seekers of *ṛta* and desirous of sacrifice, have kindled you thoroughly for protection.
Of what sort are you?

You are many-glittering (possessing abundant wealth or exceedingly delightful), worthy of worship, all-sustaining, domestic-minded (intent on giving), the master of the house (the protector of the sacrificer’s home), and most excellent (to be chosen).

1. Food smeared with ghee (pha-ghṛtāktānna). 2. O Agni, [beginning] with the syllables kha, ga, ca, ṇa, pa, pha, bha, and ha (kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pa-pha-bha-he agne). 3. No ghee was held (kha-ga-ca-ṇa-pha-na dhṛtam).

O Agni, the people have established you as a guest upon the earth, the flame-haired lord of the household—the one with the lofty banner, of many forms, the winner of wealth, the provider of good protection, and the consumer of the aged.

Thee, O Agni, the people have established as their guest upon the earth—the flame-haired lord of the house, the banner of greatness, multiform, the one who contends with the bow, the provider of good protection, whose vital power endures. 2.
O Agni, the people who sacrifice have established you as the lord of the household, the master of the house;
that is to say, they have installed you in the form of the Gārhapatya fire. Of what kind are you?

[We worship] the guest, whose nature is that of a guest, the ancient one from of old, with hair of flame—that is, a mass of blazing light—and a great banner—that is, abundant wisdom; he who possesses many forms, appearing in various forms such as the Āhavanīya fire and others; the winner of wealth, the protector of riches; the one who provides excellent refuge and beautiful happiness; the one who grants good protection; the one who pervades the decaying trees (or the dried-up waters); and the one who consumes his enemies.
Regarding the mutual contact of the fires, a certain [verse] has been prescribed for Agni:
"O Agni, your own human... as the *yājyā*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'svāmagne mānuṣīrīḷate viśo'ma āyāhi vītaye'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.13).
O Agni, the human tribes praise you—the Hotṛ-priest, the finder, the discerning one, the bestower of treasures beyond measure;
you who, though dwelling in secret, are fortunate, visible to all, possessing abundant splendor, worthy of excellent sacrifice, and adorned with clarified butter.

O Agni, the human tribes praise you—the Hotṛ-priest who has found the discerning one, the bestower of the most excellent treasure, who dwells in secret yet is auspicious and visible to all, possessing great splendor, a perfect sacrificer, and radiant with ghee. 3.
O Agni, O fortunate one, possessor of splendid wealth, all the human clans—that is, all the human communities—praise you; they laud you.
Of what kind are you?

[We worship] him who knows this—the Hotṛ of the Hotṛ-offices, the offerer of oblations, or the knower of the rites accompanied by the Hotṛs; the discerning one, the separator of the eternal from the transient; the best bestower of jewels, the most excellent giver of delightful riches; dwelling in the secret place, in the wilderness, or within the hearts, existing at all times; visible to all, worthy of being beheld by everyone; possessing abundant luster, loud-sounding; the excellent sacrificer, well-performing the sacrifice; and having the splendor of clarified butter, resting in the clarified butter.
O Agni, we have approached you, the sustainer, with songs from every side and with homage;
as such, being kindled, O Aṅgiras, take pleasure in us—a god among mortals—with glory and with splendid lights.

O Agni, you who are the sustainer, we have approached you from every side, praising you with songs and with homage. As such, O Aṅgiras, being kindled, as a god, take pleasure in us—mortals—with your glory and your beautiful splendors. 4.
O Agni, we—the descendants of Atri—praising you, the sustainer of all, in many ways with our songs, have approached you with reverence; may we remain seated near you.
As such, do you graciously accept us and favor us.

O most youthful Agni, the gods have made you—the carrier of oblations (*havyavāhana*), who are being properly kindled—into their messenger.
Among the three fires, Havyavāhana was indeed formerly appointed as the messenger by the gods for the purpose of carrying the offerings;
for the Śruti says: "Havyavāhana is [the messenger] of the gods" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.8.6).
Furthermore, [I praise] you who possess vast speed and abundant force, whose source is clarified butter—
that is, he for whom clarified butter is the cause—
invoking you as one impelled by the intellect.

The gods and humans established him as "Codayanmati," one whose intellect impels [them]; having made his "tveṣa" (splendid) and "dīpta" (blazing) "cakṣus" (eye)— the eye that is characterized by excellence and illuminates all things— the very seat of sight—
[they did so] for it is through the intellect that the eye is impelled.

O Agni, from of old you have been invoked with offerings of clarified butter; those seeking favor have kindled you with excellent fuel. Growing strong, nourished by the plants, you spread abroad over the earthly expanses. O Agni, from of old you have been invoked with offerings of clarified butter; those seeking favor have kindled you with excellent fuel. Growing strong, nourished by the plants, you spread abroad over the earthly expanses.

1. *kha*, *ga*, and *bha* are the new [letters]; *gha*, *pa*, and *la* are the old; *ca* and *pha* are the ancient.
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa!

In the first section of the fifth maṇḍala, the first eight hymns have already been explained.
The seventh and ninth hymns, beginning with "tvām agne haviṣmantaḥ," are the work of Gaya Ātreya.
The seventh and fifth verses are *paṅkti* meters; the remaining verses are *anuṣṭubh*.
The deity is Agni.
Thus it is enumerated: “*tvām agne gayaḥ*, *amyak*, and the two *paṅkti*s [beginning with] the fifth [verse].
These two hymns beginning with this [first one] are to be recited in the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra*.
Likewise, it is stated in the Sūtra: "In the hymn beginning with 'O Agni, you who possess the oblation'... (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.13).
O Agni, mortals bearing oblations praise you, the god;
I deem you to be Jātavedas, for you shall carry the offerings in due succession.
O Agni, mortals possessing oblations praise you, the god; I deem you to be Jātavedas. As such, carry the offerings in due order. 1.

O Agni, these mortals—possessing oblations (*haviṣmantaḥ*), meaning those who have the materials for sacrifice as their wealth—*īḷate*, that is, they praise you, the radiant god (*devam*). And I too [praise] Jātavedas. He is called *Jātavedas* because he knows (*veda*) all that is born (*jātam*), both moving and unmoving, the entire multitude of beings; or else, because all beings, whether stationary or moving, know him, he is *Jātavedas*. Or again, *veda* is a name for wealth; he whose wealth (*veda*) is all that is born (*jātam*) is *Jātavedas*. Such as you are, I honor (*manye*) and praise you. Here the root *man* is used in the sense of praising, since verbal roots can have multiple meanings. You, being such, *vakṣi*, that is, you carry (*vahasi*) the *havyā*, the offerings which are the means of sacrifice, *ānuṣak*, that is, continuously and without interruption. Regarding the word *haviṣmantaḥ*: the word *havis* ends in the *uṇādi* suffix *has*; by the accent of the suffix, it is oxytone (accent on the final syllable). The possessive suffix *matup* is added according to the rule "that which belongs to this" (*tadasyāsti*). Because this is an exception to the technical designation of a *pada*, the designation of *bha* applies by the rule "in the sense of a possessive suffix, *tas* and *sas* [become *t* and *s*]" (*tasau matvarthe*), and thus there is no change to *ru*. Since the suffixes *matup* and *jas* are anudātta, the accent of the suffix alone remains. Regarding *devam*: because it ends in the suffix *ac*, the word *deva* is oxytone. Regarding *martāsaḥ*: from the root *mṛṅ* (to die), the suffix *tan* is applied by the rule "asi, hasi, mṛṅ... etc. There is *guṇa* substitution. From *marta-* comes *martāsaḥ* by adding *jas* with the augment *asuk*. It is anudātta at the beginning and udātta at the end. Regarding *īḷate*: from the root *īḍ* (to praise). Because it belongs to the *adādi* class, there is elision of the *śap* suffix. By the rule "in the ātmanepada endings, [the *a* of] *anataḥ* [is elided]," the *ṭe* ending becomes *e*.

In the case of *dvitīyāyāṃ ca* (Pāṇini Sūtra 7.2.87), the vowel *ā* is substituted. According to the rule *ekādeśa udāttenodāttaḥ*, the single substitute (*ekādeśa*) is also necessarily acute (*udātta*).

Since it is a *piś* suffix, the rule for initial acute (*ādyudātta*) by the accent of the verbal root (*dhātusvara*) would have applied; however, the *nighāta* (elision of accent) takes effect. [The form] *ānupak*:
