Like the sun in the sky, in the intermediate space.
The fourteenth hymn, consisting of six verses, begins with “samiddho agniḥ.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: “samiddho; [the seer is] Viśvavārā of the Atri lineage; [the meters are] Triṣṭubh, Jagatī, Triṣṭubh, Anuṣṭubh, and two Gāyatrīs.
The seer (ṛṣi) of this hymn is the one named Viśvavārā, born of the Atri lineage.
The first and third verses are *triṣṭubh*, the second is *jagatī*, the fourth is *anuṣṭubh*, and the others are *gāyatrī*.
Agni is the deity.
The application (*viniyoga*) of the hymn is indicated by its internal characteristics (*laiṅgika*).
Kindled, Agni has sent his luster to heaven; facing the Dawn, he shines far and wide.
Rich in all boons, the butter-dripping ladle goes forward with homage, praising the gods with the oblation.

Enkindled, Agni has sent his flame to heaven; he shines far and wide, facing the Dawn. Rich in all boons, she goes forward toward the east, praising the gods with homage, anointing herself with the oblation of ghee. 1.
The well-kindled, perfectly blazing Agni has established his radiance—his brilliance—in the sky, the shining mid-air;
likewise, facing toward the Dawn, he shines forth widely and pre-eminently.

Praising the gods, Indra and the others, with hymns of homage, she who is joined with the oblation consisting of sacrificial cakes and the like, accompanied by the ghee-dripping ladle, and named Viśvavārā because she wards off every enemy in the form of evil—she goes forward, facing the east.
Thus transformed, he goes toward the fire.
Being kindled, you reign as the king of immortality; you accompany the one who prepares the oblation for his well-being.
He who you favor gains all wealth; O Agni, place him in front as our protector.

Being kindled, you reign over the nectar of immortality. You attend to the one who prepares the oblation for his well-being. He whom you impel gains all wealth; O Agni, he indeed places himself before [the enemy] as one to be overcome. 2.
O Agni, being properly kindled, you rule over the immortal water;
likewise, you attend to—that is, you serve—the sacrificer who prepares the oblation, such as the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), for his well-being and non-destruction.
Furthermore, that sacrificer whom I approach and favor shall possess and maintain all wealth, characterized by cattle and other riches.
Moreover, O Agni, one places and establishes before you—that is, in front of you—the oblation (havis) which is suitable for you, whose form is that of a guest (atithi).
In the Pavitreṣṭi, the *yājyā* for the Sviṣṭakṛt offering is "O Agni, be strong" (*agne śardha*).
For it is stated: "The two *saṃyājyās* are 'O Agni, beloved of the house,' and 'Be strong for great good fortune'" (*juṣṭo damūnā agne śardha mahate saubhagāya*) (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.12).
In the Mākamedha sacrifices, regarding the cake on eight potsherds for the Marut host, the *krīḍins*, this same [verse] is also the *yājyā* for the Sviṣṭakṛt.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The two concluding offering verses (*saṃyājye*) are: 'O Agni, being pleased with our self-restraint, bestow strength for great good fortune'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.18).
O Agni, be bold for great good fortune; may your splendors be most excellent. Bestow upon us a well-governed household lordship, and trample down the powers of those who act as enemies.
O Agni, be bold for great good fortune; may thy splendors be most excellent. Win for us a well-governed household lordship; trample down the powers of those who act as enemies. 3.
O Agni, you, for our great abundance—that is, for our possession of excellent wealth—overpower the enemies with your might!
Likewise, may your glories—your riches or splendors—be most excellent and preeminent.
Furthermore, O Agni, you [attain] the lordship over progeny.
The wife and the husband are "jāyāpatī";
their joint activity is "jāspatyam. That [activity] is "suyama," meaning well-restrained.

1. The definition of *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *bha*, *va*, *śva*, etc. 2. And that which is formulated (*sūtrita*) by *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *bha*. 3. Regarding *ja*: "After *anu* and *upa*, [the suffix] *cu* is applied; this very [verse] is the *yājyā* for the *Sviṣṭakṛt* offering. It is formulated in the same way. 4. *Śa*-sam. Ka. 2-100, section (*peṭa*).
The meaning is "mutually joined" (*anyonyasaṃśliṣṭa*).
Bring them together; make them perfectly united.
Furthermore, trample upon and overcome the splendors and powers of those who act as enemies—that is, those who desire you as their foe and harbor hostility toward you.
I praise the splendor of you, Agni, the kindled one of great majesty;
you are a radiant bull, and you are impelled at the sacrifices.
Of this [verse] beginning with "samiddha": "O Agni, I praise the splendor of thee, the mighty one; thou art a bull, full of light; thou art kindled at the sacrifices. (4)

I, the sacrificer, praise—that is, extol—the splendor, the radiance, belonging to you who are "vagne" (O Agni), "vsamiddhasya" (well-kindled), "pravṛddhasya" (fully grown), and "vpramahasaḥ" (possessing supreme luster). You are "vṛṣabhaḥ," the showerer of desires; O Agni, you are "vdyumnān," the possessor of wealth.
In the sacrifices of the seekers of the bridegroom, you are pierced through; you shine forth perfectly.
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there are two *sāmidhenī* verses beginning with "samiddho agna āhuta.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The two [verses] beginning with 'samiddho agna āhuta'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.2).
O Agni, kindled and invoked with oblations, perform the sacrifice to the gods in this well-conducted rite;
for you are the bearer of the sacrificial offerings.
Of the verse beginning with "samiddha": O Agni, invoked with oblations, worship the gods; you are a skilled performer of the sacrifice, for you are the bearer of the offerings. 5.

O you who are invoked on all sides by the sacrificers (*vāhuta*), O you who possess a beautiful sacrifice (*svadhvara*), O Agni, being well-kindled (*samiddhaḥ*) and perfectly radiant, do you worship (*yakṣi*) the luminous gods (*devān*), Indra and the others. For, O Agni, because you are the carrier of oblations (*havyavāṭ*), the bearer of offerings;
therefore, for that reason, worship the gods—this is the connection [of the words].
Offer oblations and serve Agni as the sacrifice proceeds;
choose him as the bearer of the sacrificial offerings.
O, offer oblations; pay homage to Agni at the advancing sacrifice; choose him as the bearer of the offerings. 6.

O officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), when our sacrifice has commenced and is proceeding, offer oblations into Agni—the bearer of offerings (*havyavāhana*)—who bears the name of that very deity; offer them completely.
Likewise, serve him and worship the bearer of offerings. Choose him and partake of him.

The connection of the one named Havyavāhana with the deities, as well as his being chosen by the sacrificers, is clearly recorded in the Taittirīya: "There are indeed three fires: Havyavāhana belongs to the gods, Kavyavāhana to the ancestors, and Saharakṣas to the Asuras.
They vie for this [office], each saying, 'Let me be chosen, let me be chosen! [The officiant] says, 'Choose Havyavāhana!'; he chooses him who belongs to the gods" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.5.8.6).

The fifteenth hymn, consisting of fifteen verses, begins with "vyayamā. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "vyayamā; five less [than sixteen]; Gaurivīti, son of Śākya; addressed to Indra; or the first quarter-verse belongs to Uśanas, the son of Uśanas. The seer (ṛṣi) is named Gaurivīti, a descendant of the Śakti lineage.
Because it has not been mentioned [elsewhere]:
1. for the sake of the *pa-pha-ba* [consonant groups] and the perfect flame (*samyagiddha*).

Furthermore, O *brahmāṇaḥ* (O great ones), O *marutaḥ* (O Maruts), and you, O *indra*, [partake] of this *soma* of mine, of this *soma* that is well-pressed (*susutasya*), beautifully extracted by the pressers.
The genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
Drink the gruels.
The singular form of the second person plural of the benedictive (āśīr-liṅ) of the root *pā* (to drink).

For indeed, that sacrificial offering consisting of Soma which was drunk by you is truly glorious; it "found" (avindan)—that is, it makes known or provides—cows, meaning waters characterized by rain, for the human sacrificer.
The sense is that it causes the sacrificer to obtain cows.
Furthermore, Indra, having drunk this Soma, slew—that is, struck down—Ahi, Vṛtra.
He made the two worlds, heaven and earth, tremble far and wide; enveloping himself, he struck down the beast that was fleeing in fear.
Indra, casting away the devourer, struck down the Dānava who was panting against him.
He propped apart the two worlds, heaven and earth, more widely; though he was already clothed [in them], he caused the wild beast to fear.

Who made the bay mares—the swift ones moving forward, belonging to Sūrya—slower, for the sake of the seer Etaśa? Who did this? *Note: This passage is from Ṛgveda Maṇḍala 5, Anuvāka 2, Sūkta 29, Verse 4.*
That is to say, Etaśa indeed engaged in a contest with Sūrya, his own son;
and so it is said in another Vedic hymn: "Indra [assisted] the presser of Soma, Sauvīrya, who was contending against Etaśa in the presence of Sūrya" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.61.15).

When Maghavan shattered his ninety-nine fortresses together with the thunderbolt, the Maruts sang praises to Indra at the place of assembly; with the splendor of the Triṣṭubh meter, he drove away the sky.
Nine-and-ninety were his possessions which Maghavan shattered together with the thunderbolt; the Maruts praise Indra at the assembly, and with Trishtubh splendor he drives away the sky. 6.
When the bountiful and wealthy Indra—
by the word "of him" (asya), Śambara is meant— [took] the nine,
meaning nine in number, and the ninety, meaning ninety in number, enjoyments, that is, the cities belonging to this Śambara.
The word *bhogān* is oxytone and denotes cities.

Simultaneously (*sākam*), as if with a thunderbolt (*vajreṇa*), Indra cut them down (*vivṛścan*), hewed them apart, and shattered them. Then, while the Maruts stood in their common abode (*sadhasthe*)—that is, in the battle—Indra praised him with the *traiṣṭubha*, that is, with speech in the *triṣṭubh* meter, in the form of hymns of praise. Thus praised, O Indra, you repelled (*bādhata*) the blazing Asura named Śambara by means of the mantra being employed by the Maruts at the Vipāś river.
The friend has prepared the fourfold [oblation] for the friend; by his wisdom, the great lord [has bestowed] three hundred [gifts].
Indra, together with Manu, drank the pressed Soma from the three lakes for the slaying of Vṛtra.

The friend; for friendship; he cooked; the musical instrument; Agni; by his wisdom; the great protector; three hundred; three together; Indra; of Manu; the lakes; drink the pressed Soma for the slaying of Vṛtra. 7.

Agni, the friend and ally of Indra—the great protector of great cattle—cooked that [victim] quickly by means of the ritual act (*kratu*) of this Indra, his friend and ally, for three hundred [cattle].
Furthermore, Indra, endowed with supreme sovereignty, [prepared] three lakes—that is, three vessels belonging to Manu;
here, by the word "lake" (*saras*), the vessels known as the *pūtabhṛt*, *ādhavanīya*, and *droṇakalaśa* are meant.
He drank—indeed, he drank up—the Soma juice that was situated within them, well-pressed, all at once, for the sake of slaying Vṛtra, that is, for the destruction of Vṛtra.
He restrained three hundred buffalo; Maghavan drank the Soma juices from the lakes.
All the gods acclaimed it like a song of praise, because he had slain Ahi for Indra’s sake.
Three hundred buffaloes were the price; three lakes of Soma-draughts did Maghavan drink. All the gods approved his deed as he bore it away, when he slew the serpent for Indra’s sake. 8.
1. *Kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-ma* is well-spoken.
O Indra, when (*yat*) you ate (*aghas*) the flesh (*māḥ*) of three hundred (*trī śatā*) buffaloes (*mahiṣāṇām*), that is, animals numbering three hundred.
The form [of the word] is like that of *ghasira*.
And when you, O Maghavan, possessed of wealth, drank from the three vessels—those three lakes consisting of Soma, O Somya;
and when Indra slew the serpent Vṛtra, then all the gods, having filled [the vessels] with Soma-drinks and other offerings, called upon Indra for the sake of battle.
In this regard, there is an illustration:
Just as one does not act for the sake of a master [but rather for oneself], so it is with that.
In the *Uśanas-stoma*, the *marutvatīya* hymn begins with "O Uśanas, come with the *rasahasyas*.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "One who considers himself as if swallowed by poison should sacrifice with the *Uśanas-stoma*, [reciting] 'O Uśanas, come with the *rasahasyas*' (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.5)."

When Uśanas and you, O Indra, went to the house of the powerful one with swift, speeding horses—there, winning the prize, you came on the same chariot with Kutsa; with the gods as your allies, you struck down Śuṣṇa.
The hymns of Gaurivīti strengthened you, as the nourishing draughts did for Pipru at Vaidathina;
Ṛjiśvan brought you forth for the sake of the *sarūpa* rite; cooking the *paktis*, you drank his Soma.
The hymns of Gaurivīti strengthened you; you brought Pipru to subjection for Vaidathina. R̥jiśvan made you his ally for Saryu; cooking the sacrificial cakes, he drank the soma of this man.
O Indra, may these hymns of praise belonging to Gaurivīti—the seer of this mantra—strengthen you, the one named thus.
For Vaidathina, the son of Vidathin, you, O Ṛjiśvan, subdued Pipru, the asura of that name, and brought him under your control.

O Indra, Ṛjiśvan, a certain person indeed, for the sake of your friendship (*sakhitvāya*), while cooking sacrificial cakes and other offerings (*paktīḥ*) until they were baked, turned you toward himself.
Furthermore, you drank—you did drink—the Soma belonging to this Ṛjiśvan.

On the tenth day, during the Marutvatīya Śastra, after reciting the hymn beginning with "navagvāmaḥ," it is stated in the Sūtra: "navagvāmaḥ sutasomāsa indraṃ sakhā ha yatra sakhibhirnavagvābhir iti nividdhānayorāśa" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.3).
The Navagvas, having pressed the Soma, and the Daśagvas, worship Indra with hymns;
even the stall of cattle that was enclosed, the men, performing their rites, have opened.
The Navagvas, having pressed the Soma, and the Daśagvas, praise Indra with hymns. Even the stall of cattle, though it be closed up, the heroes, performing their service, have opened.
The Navagvas are those who, performing the sacrificial session continuously, departed after completing it in nine months;
those who departed after completing it in ten months are the Daśagvas.
Both these types of Aṅgirases, having pressed the Soma (*sutasomāsaḥ*), worship and praise Indra with hymns (*arkaiḥ*) worthy of praise.

Likewise, the Aṅgirasas—men who were leaders, striving and praising—opened up that very *ūrva*, a multitude of cattle belonging to the Asuras, which was hidden by their power and well-known in many places. They disclosed it.
In the one-day sacrifice named *parikrī*, for the *marutvatīya* and *niṣkevalya* liturgies, the two verses beginning with "katho nu te" constitute the *sūktavāk*.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The two [verses] beginning with 'katho nu te pari carāṇi vidvān'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 9.5).

1. Those connected with *ta*. 2. *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, *śa*, and *tvā* [represent] you (*tvām*). 3. *pa*, *pha*, *ba*, and *daśagvāsaḥ* [represent] by means of ten months (*darśirmāsaiḥ*). 4. In many places, [the letters] *kha*, *ca*, and *ṇa* [are used].

How indeed may I, as one who knows, perform service for you, O Maghavan, regarding those heroic deeds which you have performed? And those new ones which you shall now perform, O Most Powerful—those very deeds of yours we shall proclaim in the assemblies. 13. How indeed... for you... around... may I proceed... knowing... the heroic deeds... O Bounteous One... which you have done... and those... new ones... which you shall now do... O Most Powerful... forth... indeed... those... of yours... in the assemblies... we shall speak. 13.

O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, whatever heroic deeds you have performed and whatever heroic deeds you have yet to perform—I, knowing and being aware of those heroic deeds of yours, how indeed, how indeed, shall I attend upon you? How shall I perform service for you? O most powerful Indra, whatever new and ever-newer heroic deeds you shall swiftly perform, those very heroic deeds of yours we shall proclaim aloud in the assemblies and at the sacrifices.

O Indra, possessor of the wheel, all these [powers] are yours by birth and by heroic might; they are not surpassed. O wielder of the thunderbolt, whatever you shall now perform for those who have offered [oblations], there is no one who can withstand your power. 14. O Indra, possessor of the wheel, all these are yours by birth and by heroic might; they are not surpassed. O wielder of the thunderbolt, whatever you shall now perform for those who have offered [oblations], there is no one who can withstand your power. 14.

O Indra, you who are unassailed by enemies and unapproached by foes, from birth—by your own innate heroism and power—you have brought into being, as they are perceived before our eyes, all these vast and manifold worlds.

O wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra, having taken up your position, quickly subdue your rivals! Whatever things you may do, there is no one whatsoever who can obstruct that majesty of yours, that power of yours.

O Indra, most powerful one, graciously accept the prayer being performed for you, this new hymn which we have fashioned for you. Like a well-crafted, auspicious thunderbolt, I, seeking wealth, have skillfully wrought it as a wise craftsman fashions a chariot. 15. O Indra! Prayer! Being performed! Accept! Which! For you! Most powerful! New! Hymn! Like a thunderbolt! Auspicious! Well-fashioned! Seeking wealth! As a chariot! Like a wise man! Skillful-handed! I have wrought! 15.

O most powerful, most mighty, or most heroic Indra, whatever new hymns—fresh and belonging to this very day—we have fashioned for you, O Indra, those *brahmāṇi* (sacred prayers) being performed by us, do thou accept and enjoy them. (Note: Regarding the variants, *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-bha-ra* read "kṛtavān"; *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra* read "indra"; *śa* reads "indra"; and *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra* read "brahma" as the citation.)

I, being wise (*dhīraḥ*), intelligent (*dhīmān*), skillful in my own work (*svapāḥ*), and desiring wealth (*vasūyuḥ*), have fashioned—just as one fashions *vajras* (thunderbolts)—these auspicious (*bhadrā*) and well-made (*sukṛtā*) hymns of praise, like a chariot (*ratha na ratham*).
The comparison with *vajras* is stated with the intention that the hymns are to be grasped like offerings;
the illustration of the chariot, however, is for the purpose of demonstrating them as the means for [the gods'] arrival.
The meaning is: "Having accepted my hymns of praise, bestow wealth upon me.
"Ka sya vīraḥ" is the fifteenth hymn, the sixteenth [in this section]. Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "Ka sya babhruḥ; Ṛṇacya also praises the King here.
The seer is Babhru.
The meters are Anuṣṭubh and Triṣṭubh;
Indra is the deity. A certain king named Ṛṇañcaya is also praised.
Therefore, he too is a deity.
In the *marutvatīya* śastra of the one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*) called Tīvrasoma, this hymn (*sūkta*) is the insertion (*nivid*).
And it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "With the Tīvrasoma [rite], one desiring food [recites] 'ka sya vīraḥ'? (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.7).

Who is that hero? Who has beheld Indra, as he speeds along on his easy-rolling chariot with his two bay steeds—he, the wielder of the thunderbolt, who, seeking the one who presses the Soma with wealth, comes as a protector to the one invoked by many?

Who is the hero? Who has seen Indra as he approaches on his easy-rolling chariot with his two bay horses—he, the wielder of the thunderbolt, who, desiring the one who has pressed the Soma, comes as a guest to that dwelling with wealth and for the sake of aid, being invoked by many? 1.

The wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), possessed of the *vajra*, Indra who is invoked by many (*puruhūta*), seeking with wealth (*rāyā*)—that is, with desirable riches—the one who has pressed the Soma, seeking the sacrificer who has offered the libation, comes as protection (*ūtī*) for the sake of defense; he reaches and attains that dwelling (*okaḥ*), the home of that sacrificer. Where is that hero (*vīraḥ*), that Indra, to be found? He is "one whose chariot has beautiful wheels" (*sukharatha*); he is called *sukha* because his chariot has beautiful axles and fellies, or because he digs well and furrows the earth.
"Such as that. Regarding the word *kham*, Yāska says: "It is well-situated (*suhitam*) in the cavities (*khebhyaḥ*); moreover, it is derived from the root *khan*" (Nirukta 3.13).
Who saw Indra—him who was going, being carried by the two bay horses (*haribhyām*) that are worthy of sacrifice (*svāhanābhyām*)? And who beheld him?
Seeking his footprint, which turns hitherward and is easy to find, I followed the track of the one who deposited it.
We questioned others, and they said to me, "May we, as men awakened, attain Indra."
I have seen his footprint; I have followed the fierce track of the one who laid it down. Seeking him, I questioned others, and they said to me: "May we, as men awakened, attain Indra. 2.
I have proclaimed the station, the place of this Indra—
what kind?
Hidden within, yet fierce and exalted.
Furthermore, desiring Indra—seeking him—I followed the track of this Indra, the establisher of his own station. Moreover, I questioned other wise ones on the way regarding Indra;
they, being questioned, told me of Indra.
What did they say? It is said:
"The *naras*, the leaders of sacrifices, being awakened... [Note: Variants 1–6 regarding specific words and readings are provided here for philological reference]. (Ṛgveda 2.101)
"Desiring to know, we have attained Indra.

Although Indra exists, if he were difficult to obtain, he would not be approached; thus, desiring to know his nature, [the seer] asked, and being told by those questioned that he was easy to attain, he recited the remainder of the hymn for the purpose of reaching Indra—this is the meaning.
Now, O Indra, let us proclaim at this libation those deeds of yours which we have performed and which you have graciously accepted.
Let the Knower know them; let the Wise One hear them. Here comes Maghavan with his entire host.

Now, O Indra, let us proclaim those deeds of yours performed at the soma-pressing which you have accepted from us. May he who does not know learn, and may he who knows listen; here comes Maghavan with his entire host.
O Indra, those deeds of yours which are most sweet and well-performed—now today, we who are your praisers, when the Soma has been pressed, shall proclaim those deeds with excellence.
And you, for our sake, whatever deeds you have enjoyed—that is, performed—we pray that a person who previously did not know them may come to know them;
and let one who knows them hear them.
Or rather, the wise man who knows should listen;

he should also cause even those who do not know to hear. Endowed with all armies, the wealthy Maghavan—this Indra, both knowing and listening toward those people—carries them away; that is, he attains them.
The agentive suffix is used by way of transposition.
It causes to reach.
O Indra, once born, you made your mind firm; you went forth alone to fight even against many.
With your power, you shattered even the rock with your lightning-flash and found the stall of the ruddy cows.

Firm was the mind you made when born, O Indra; you went forth alone to battle even against the many. With your might, you shattered even the rock with your lightning-flash, and found the stall of the lowing cows.
O Indra, as soon as you were born, you drew forth the steady, unwavering mind (citta)— the thought,
"I shall conquer all who are most powerful. Likewise, O Indra, even though you were alone and without a companion, you went forth to battle against many more, even against the Rākṣasas and others.
Furthermore, with your might (*śarvasā*), you shattered even the stone—the mountain that obstructed the cattle.
Moreover, you found (*vidaḥ*) and released (*alambhayaḥ*) the herd (*ūrvaṃ*) of the cows, the milch-cows that were driving away the milk of the female camels.

When you, the supreme one, first went forth to the distant realm, bearing a name renowned afar—from that very Indra the gods were struck with fear; he conquered all the waters that had their rivals as lords.

When you were born as the supreme one in the far distance, bearing a name worthy of being heard, even from that Indra the gods were struck with fear; he conquered all the waters that had the Dāsas as their masters. ||5||
1. *pa-pha-ba-gacchasi*:

O Indra, when you—being *paraḥ*, situated beyond the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the most excellent (*paramaḥ*)—were born (*ājaniṣṭhāḥ*), having been manifested everywhere, bearing (*bibhrat*) a name (*nāma*) worthy of being heard (*śrutham*) in the far distance (*parāvati*). The remainder [of the verse] is expressed in the remote past tense (*parokṣakṛtaḥ*).
From that very moment on, the gods—the shining ones such as Agni and others—were afraid of Indra.
Indra conquered all the waters; he brought them under his control.
Of what kind were they?
*Dāsaparṇā*:
those whose lord, protector, and master is Vṛtra, the Dāsa.
For you these Maruts, most gracious, sing their hymn and press the Soma juice;
Indra, with his wondrous powers, overcame the serpent Ahi, the deceiver, and the waters that were difficult to reach.

To you indeed these Maruts, most gracious, sing their hymn; they press the Soma juice. Indra overcame the serpent Ahi, who had swallowed the waters, and by his wondrous powers he subdued the magician.
These are the Maruts;
they are called Maruts because they run greatly and speak; they are the ones who cause delight; they are very gracious.
"Śevam" is a name for happiness;
[the word] "śobhana" means excellent.
The meaning is that they, being excellent, produce happiness through their hearing.
O Indra, for you alone they sing the *arka*, meaning they offer praise, they laud, they perform it;
they press the *andhas*, the food characterized by Soma, that is, they perform its extraction.

Indra, endowed with supreme sovereignty, overcame—that is, surpassed—the serpent Vṛtra by means of his own illusory powers (*māyābhiḥ*). Of what sort was he? One who was *ohāna*, harassing the gods; one who was lying in wait for the waters, having obstructed them and making his bed there; and one who was *māyin*, possessed of guile.
From birth you have scattered the mockers, O Maghavan, displaying your power and desiring to gather wealth;
there you struck off the head of the Dāsa Namuci, seeking a path for Manu.
O Maghavan, from birth impelling the gift, you struck down the Gṛvas, desiring to gather them; there you rolled off the head of the Dāsa Namuci, seeking a path for Manu. 7.
O Maghavan, possessor of wealth, you who delight in the moon-like splendor, being praised by us—[you are] you.
The root *kā* preceded by the prefix *sam* has "sound" as its object; the form [of the verb] is that of the perfect tense (*liṭ*) in the sense of the present tense (*laṭ*).

The gift [of the Vajra] was the obstructor of the gods; driving away—that is, striking and destroying—the Asura Vṛtra with the Vajra, you have thoroughly struck down, that is, utterly conquered, the enemies such as Rākṣasas who follow him, the "oppressors" (mṛdhaḥ) by their very birth.
The meaning is that for Indra, the Asuras have been enemies from the moment of his birth.

O Indra, you—desiring and longing for a path, that is, for my well-being, for me, the human whose cattle-wealth had been carried off by Namuci in this battle—then crushed, that is, shattered, the head of that Dāsa, the Asura named Namuci, the oppressor; thus [the sentence] connects with the preceding: "thereby you were victorious over the enemies."
1. [The letters] ga, gha, ja, ta, pa, pha, ba, and śa are present.
2. For the word *adāsasya*, the letter ra is not present. 3. For the word *acūrṇayaḥ*, the letters kha, na, jha, ṇa, na, bha, and ra are not present.

For you have indeed made me your ally, O Indra; then, while crushing the head of the Dāsa Namuci, you, the one who delights in the Maruts, cast forth both heaven and earth like two wheels, as if hurling a whirling stone that roars through the air. yujam | hi | mām | akṛthāḥ | āt | it | indra | śiraḥ | dāsasya | namuceḥ | mathāyan | aśmānam | cit | svaryam | vartamānam | pra | cakriyā'iva | rodasī iti | murudryaḥ || 8 ||

O Indra, you, crushing—that is, pulverizing—the head of the Dāsa Namuci, the Asura who oppresses, which was resonant with sound, whirling, and standing like a cloud of stone; immediately thereafter, you indeed made me your companion, for you have truly acted for my sake.
Then, for the Maruts who are your companions, heaven and earth (*rodasī*) bent down like a wheel.
Because of the hearing of a prefix (upasarga), there is the ellipsis-supplementation (adhyāhāra) of a verb-root (yoga) and its action (kriyā).

For the Dāsa made women his weapons; what could his weak armies do to me? For Indra hid both of his milch-cows within [the cave], and then he went forth against the Dasyu to fight him. For the Dāsa made women his weapons; what could his weak armies do to me? For Indra hid both of his milch-cows within [the cave], and then he went forth against the Dasyu to fight him.
The *dāsa*, the Asura Namuci, who was intent on destruction, indeed made the women his weapons—the instruments of war—and dispatched them;
this is the meaning: he sent them forth to fight with Indra.
What can those weak forces of this Asura, consisting of women, do to me?
Thinking, "What shall they do?", Indra placed two women—the two wives (*dhenī*) of that Asura, who were pleasing in form—within his house; indeed, he deposited them in the middle of the dwelling.
Then, immediately after that, Indra approached the Dasyu Namuci for the sake of battle, that is, for combat.
There, on every side, the cows lowed together, here and there separated from their calves; Indra reunited them by his powers when the well-pressed Soma juices exhilarated him. 10.

1. In the versions *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *bha-ra*, the word "crushing" (*cūrṇayan*) is absent. 2. In the versions *kha*, *ca*, and *ṇa*, the reading is "streams of women" (*strīrṣāṇi*). When the cows were separated from their calves—that is, when they became separated—at that time, the cows, having been struck down on all sides by Namuci, lowed together here and there, everywhere, and went away completely.

Whenever the well-purified, tawny-hued Soma juices, flowing with excellent praise, exhilarated this Indra and made him rejoice, then Indra, together with his powers and his abilities, released those cows belonging to this tawny one that had been stolen by Namuci; he reunited them with their calves.

When the Soma juices, shaken by Babhru, exhilarated him, the Bull bellowed at the gatherings. Having drunk of this, Indra, the breaker of forts, gave back the cattle, the lowing cows. When the Soma juices, shaken by Babhru, exhilarated him, the Bull bellowed at the gatherings. Having drunk of this, Indra, the breaker of forts, gave back the cattle, the lowing cows.

Whenever the brown Soma juices, shaken and poured by the brown [priest], exhilarated and intoxicated this Indra, then the bull Indra, the showerer of desires, roared loudly in the dwellings and in battles; he made a sound for his own purpose. Having drunk this Soma, Indra, the destroyer of forts, gave back to Babhru the cows that yield milk—the milch-cows of the cattle. He bestowed them upon Babhru.

This was auspicious: the Ruśamas first performed this deed; he who bestows gifts has given four thousand cattle. We have accepted the proffered riches of Ṛṇañcaya, the most heroic among men. Auspicious! This! O Ruśamas! In the beginning! They did! Of cows! Four! Giving! Thousands! Of Ṛṇañcaya! Proffered! Riches! Back! We have accepted! Most heroic! Of men! 12.
*Ruśama* is a particular region;
here, by the word *ruśama*, the people dwelling there are meant.
The *ruśamas* were the servants of the king named *Ṛṇacyut*. O Agni, they performed this auspicious and beneficial deed.
Of what sort?
Giving—that is, bestowing upon me—four thousand, meaning four times one thousand, of cows, that is, milch-cows.
For the implication is that it is indeed the king’s men who deliver the riches being given by the king.
Among the leaders of men, from the most excellent leader, the one called Ṛṇacya, we have accepted—received—the gifts consisting of cattle and wealth that were offered by him with devotion;
the plural number is used for honor.

The Ruśamas have sent me home well-adorned with thousands of cattle; the strong, exhilarating pressed juices [have sent] Indra at the dawning of the night that was to be passed away. They send me home well-adorned with thousands of cattle, the Ruśamas first; the strong, exhilarating pressed juices [have sent] Indra at the dawning of the night that was to be passed away.

1. In the versions kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra, and śa, the word *ayat* does not exist. 2. In the versions ga, gha, ja, pa, pha, and ba, [the reading is] *yajñagāvaḥ*. 3. In the versions ta and sādana, [the reading is as follows]. 4. In the versions kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, bha, ra, and śa, [the reading is] *narām*.

Those bright Ruśamas, the servants of Ṛṇañcaya, sent me—well-adorned and beautifully formed, refined by ornaments, clothing, and the like—to my home at sunset, together with thousands of cows and milch-kine.
Immediately thereafter, the intense and flavorful pressed juices—the Soma drops obtained through much wealth and pressed by me—are "paritakmyā.
That which spreads around and reaches all beings is *paritakmyā*;
at the dawning, that is, the breaking forth of that night.
The meaning is "at the time of dawn.
They "exhilarated" (amādayan) Indra; that is, they gladdened him. The meaning is that Babhru, immediately after receiving the cows, sacrificed with Soma without delay.
She chose that night, which was to be sought out, when Ṛṇaṃcaya was king of the Ruśamas;
like a swift prize-winning steed urged on, Babhru won four thousand.
She shone forth—the Night that was to be passed away—at the gathering of the Ruśamas under King Ṛṇaṃcaya. Like a noble steed urged forward in a race, the tawny one won four thousand.

In the presence of the sovereign, the powerful lord named Vr̥ṇacya, belonging to the people known by the name of the Ruśamas—right there, the night which was *paritakmyā*, moving all around, that very night *auccat*, it became dawning.
Like a swift horse that always moves forward, the rishi named Babhru—being urged on and driven forth—obtained four thousand cattle as his wealth.
We accepted four thousand head of cattle from the Ruśamas at the beginning; the heated offering was prepared for the Pravargya rite, and the wise ones took up the golden ladle.
Four thousand head of cattle we have received as our share from among the Ruśamas; even the iron cauldron that was used for the Pravargya rite, that very one the sages have taken up. 15.

O Agni, among these people known as the Ruśamas, we have received four thousand—that is, four thousand head—of cattle, horses, and livestock; "paśvaḥ" is used in the singular to denote the class. We have accepted them.

For the sake of offering, we have taken—that which was a beautiful-colored vessel, like a *gharma* or great sacrificial ladle made of iron (*ayasmaya*), and one made of gold (*hiraṇmaya*)—that very vessel for milking, O wise ones (*viprāḥ*), we have received among the Ruśamas.
The hymn beginning with “*indra rathāya*” consists of thirteen verses; it is the seventeenth [hymn] in the collection. The seer is Avasyu Ātreya;
the meter is *triṣṭubh*.
Indra is the deity.
For the two verses beginning with “upamayātam” and “saṃ ha yadvām,” Kuru and Śunaḥ are respectively the deities by way of option.
For the verse “indrākutsā vahamānā,” Indra and Kuru are the deities.

And thus it has been indexed: “‘Indro rathāya vāmam,’ ‘sasunvate’ [and] ‘avasyum’—these two quarters belong to Kautsa or to Uśanas; the rest belongs to Indra and Kautsa. The application [of these verses] is based on their indicative marks (liṅga).
1. Perfected by *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, *śa*, and *sa*.
2. Being filled by *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *bha*, *pūryamāṇa*.
3. Having the name *avaśyu* by means of *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ja*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *śa*.
This is a name for wealth. *Dediṣṭe*:
he bestows it upon the sacrificers.
Within the mountain that obstructs the thunderbolt, he drove forth by his might the well-yielding cows that were confined therein;
with his light and splendor, he dispelled the darkness that was habituated to enveloping.
May Arṇava fashion a chariot for your horse, and Tvaṣṭṛ, O much-invoked one, a radiant thunderbolt.
The Brahmins, magnifying Indra with hymns, strengthened him so that he might slay the dragons.

The ocean [brought] them; they fashioned a chariot for the sake of the horses. Tvaṣṭṛ fashioned the brilliant thunderbolt, O much-invoked one. The priests, magnifying Indra with hymns, strengthened him for the slaying of Ahi. Om! 4.

O Indra, invoked by many (*puruhūta*), the *anavas*— the *anavas* being humans— the *Ṛbhus* fashioned (*atakṣan*), that is, they made, your chariot (*ratha*) suitable for yoking to the horse (*aśvāya*).
O Indra, I proclaim aloud your ancient deeds— those most savory acts of old;
I also proclaim your ever-new deeds.
The connection is as follows: "O Maghavan, O wealthy Indra, those various deeds which you have performed—those I shall proclaim. "Ha" is an interjection. "Śaktīvaḥ" means "possessing power";
"śakti" refers either to a spear or to action.
O Indra, when you, as the subduer, conquering both heaven and earth,
brought forth and distributed the waters for Manu, for mankind—
of what kind were they?
Those of wonderful gifts, whose gifts are wonderful.

That indeed was your deed, O wondrous sage, when you measured forth your power against the serpent; even the magic arts of Śuṣṇa you seized, and advancing in your course, you drove away the Dasyus. That indeed was your deed, O wondrous sage, when you measured forth your power against the serpent; even the magic arts of Śuṣṇa you seized, and advancing in your course, you drove away the Dasyus.

O wise and intelligent Indra, you, the seer, who are beautiful to behold, have indeed destroyed Vṛtra, the Asura, in this world; that power and strength which you manifested—that is truly your own most excellent deed.
Moreover, you have completely seized the magical powers and insights belonging even to the Asura named Śuṣṇa.
O Indra, when you were approaching the *prapitva*—the battle or its vicinity—you drove away the Dasyus, the Asuras.

You, O Indra, stayed the well-flowing waters for Yadu and Turvaśa on the far shore; you brought Kutsa when you went against Ugra. Indeed, when the gods and Uśanas were in harmony with you both. 8. You [stayed] the waters for Yadu and Turvaśa; you stayed the well-flowing [waters], O Indra, on the far shore. You went against the fierce one; you indeed brought Kutsa. For when the gods and Uśanas were in harmony with you both. 8.

O Indra, on the further shore of the rivers— that is, on the bank— you caused the well-yielding plants and trees to flourish, and you made the waters flow for King Yadu, named Yadu, and for King Turvaśa, named Turvaśa. You have brought them to rest.
O Indra and you [Indra], "you" and "Kutsa"— this is the ellipsis—
went to the fierce, upraised, and swelling [Soma].
Immediately after that, having slain Śuṣṇa, you indeed carried Kutsa away; you brought him to your own home.
For when both of you, Indra and Kutsa, and Uśanas Bhārgava, as well as the gods, came together in assembly.

1. In the recensions kha, ca, jha, ṇa, bha, and ra, the word *udakāni* is absent. 2. In the recensions ga, dha, ja, pha, and ba, the form is *pāraḥ*. 3. In the recensions ga, dha, ja, and śa, the form is *pravṛddhaḥ*. 4. In the recensions ga, dha, and ja, the form is *āgacchatam*. Ṛgveda 2.102:
O Indra and Ākutsa, being carried by the chariot, let the two steeds bring you even to our ears.
Drive away the darkness from the dwellings of these wealthy patrons and from their seats. Drive it away from their hearts.

O Indra and Aṅgiras, being carried by your chariot, let your coursers bring you even to our ear. You drive away the darkness from the waters, from the dwelling place, and from the heart of the patron; you dispel the gloom. 9.

O Indra and Kutsa—Indra and Kutsa—you two, being carried by the chariot (*rathena*), whether you are carrying [us] or being carried yourselves, the *atyas* (swift horses) have brought you even to the ear (*karṇe*).
"Ear" (*karṇa*) refers to the one who performs the praises (*kṛṇoti*), that is, the singer or the sacrificer;
it means "even in the presence of him."
"Let them bring [him]; let the carriers come from all sides.
You two also, from the waters—that is, having entered into the waters—blow him out; you have driven away this Śuṣṇa Asura.
The word "him" (sīm) refers to Śuṣṇa Asura who is present in the mind.
From his own dwelling place, he formerly made Etaśa cease from his activity;
[he did this] for Etaśa.
The case endings are used according to their respective meanings.
Indra formerly took away one wheel of the two-wheeled chariot;
with that wheel, he Indra utterly destroys and slays the Asuras.
Moreover, placing us in front, setting us at the head, he shall win and enjoy our *ṛtu*, our sacrifice.
The noble one has come into view; Indra has gone for friendship, desiring the one who has pressed the soma.
Speaking loudly, he hastens to the altar with splendor—the one whose swift movements the Adhvaryu priests perform.

This Indra has come into view, O people, seeking friendship with the one who has pressed the Soma; speaking, the pressing-stone descends toward the altar, and the Adhvaryu priests move swiftly about him for his glory. 12.

O people, this Indra has come—indeed, he is coming—to behold you; desiring and longing for friendship with you, he seeks the praiser who has pressed the *soma*, the sacrificer who has purified the *soma*.

O Adhvaryus, as you perform the swift casting and impelling of the sacrificial ladle, that pressing-stone—the stone for crushing the *soma*—making a sound as it speaks, shall descend upon the altar and split [the offering].
Those mortals who have desired you, O Immortal One, and those who still desire—you do not lead them into distress.
Increase our sacrifices and bestow vigor upon those people among whom we may be numbered.
Those mortals who have desired you, O Immortal One—may they not fall into distress. Accept our sacrifice and bestow vigor upon those people among whom we may be numbered. 13.

O Indra, those people who, seeking wealth, have longed for you and desired you—let them now indeed long for you again quickly, O immortal, deathless Indra! Let those mortal beings, subject to death, not go (*āran*) into distress (*aṃhaḥ*), that is, into misfortune; the particle *mā u* is used in the sense of the single prohibitive particle *mā*. And furthermore, favor (*vavṛndhi*) and cherish the sacrificers.
Among those people, in the midst of whom we are singers, may we be yours; O Indra, bestow strength and power upon those people.

The eighteenth hymn, consisting of twelve verses beginning with “adardahat,” has Gātu as its seer (ṛṣi), who is a descendant of Atri; Triṣṭubh is the meter; and Indra is the deity. Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: “Adardat, twelve verses; Gātu. Its application (viniyoga) is according to the ritual context.

1. [The letters] kha, va, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra come [here]; śa goes [there]. 2. In ga, dha, ja, the word ‘kurvanti’ is not found. 3. In kha, a, ra, there is the pressing of Soma. 4. In ga, dha, ja, [the word] ‘dhanādham’. 5. In kha, va, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra, śa, they desire the endless speech.
Thou hast rent asunder the wellspring in the waters; thou didst delight in the boundless oceans.
O Indra, when thou didst split the great mountain, thou didst release the streams and slay the Dānava.
You pierced the spring; you released the channels. You set at rest the obstructed floods. O Indra, when you rent asunder the great mountain, you released the streams; you struck down the Dānava. 1.

O Indra, you shattered the overflowing spring— the cloud— and thereafter you opened wide the channels, the outlets for the water’s exit from the cloud. Furthermore, you released the obstructing, surging oceans— the watery clouds— meaning that you let them flow forth.
In this context, the ritual action consists of the dismissal of the one who has enjoyed [the offering].
O Indra, "yat" (which) refers to you;
"yat" is used for both genders.
Mahānirjaghāna struck down the weapon that Śakra had discharged at Vṛtra;
it was the great asura who had manifested from another part of Vṛtra’s body.
Having first slain Vṛtra, Indra then slew the second one named Śuṣṇa;
thus he is celebrated by others as "Indra the slayer again."

Indra, with his own powers (*taviṣībhiḥ*), utterly destroyed (*niḥ...jaghāna*) the weapon of that very Vṛtra—of the great, sovereign beast who moved swiftly like a wild animal. He alone, without a companion, being "unopposed" (*apratir*), meaning he considered himself to be "he who exists" (without a rival); at that time, another Asura, Śuṣṇa, who was even more swift than Vṛtra, was born from him.

The wielder of the thunderbolt, the bull-like one, struck down Śuṣṇa— the son of Mūhu, the increaser of darkness who delighted in these [waters] by his own power— with his bolt, crushing the fury of the Dānava.

The wielder of the thunderbolt, with his bull-like strength, struck down with his bolt that very one among them who rejoiced in his own power—the offspring of the mist, the well-increasing one who had gone into the darkness, the fury of the Dānava Śuṣṇa. 4.

[We worship] him who rejoices—that is, who takes delight—by means of *svadhā*, the food of these living beings; who himself consumes the food of all creatures; and who is the *napāt*—the protector and guardian—of the rain-cloud (*mihaḥ*), which is capable of pouring down water.
Here, the word *napāt* refers to a protector. As the Brāhmaṇa states: "Tanūnapāt is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for it protects the body" (AiB 2.4).

He struck down Vṛtra—who was well-grown, fully developed, and who had entered into the darkness (*tamas*)—that very one; this is the sense of the remainder of the verse. Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*), the hurler of the cloud that possesses beautiful color, by means of his own weapon, the *vajra*, [struck] the fury (*bhāma*) of Vṛtra, the Dānava, the son of Danu.
Here, by the word *bhāma*, which denotes anger, the Asura Śuṣṇa, who arose from that anger, is indicated.
He struck down—that is, he killed—that asura Śuṣṇa.

By his very powers of will, he pierced the vitals of that one who was shielded by armor and had no weak spot; for when you, O Lord of good dominion, were exhilarated by the intoxicating drink, you placed him who sought to fight within the darkness of the dwelling.

Even him who had turned away from his purposes, though he was invulnerable, he found his vital spot; for when you, O Lord of Good Dominion, at the offering of the exhilarating draught, placed him—though he sought to fight—in the darkness within the house.
Of this Vṛtra, who considers himself free from vital points (*amarmāṇaḥ*)—that is, one who imagines himself devoid of vital spots—the *nipatam* is that which has fallen;
*yam ca* is a deviation in gender (referring to *marma*).
*Marma* is the seat of the vital breaths (*prāṇasthāna*).
The spot where one who is pierced dies is called a *marman* (vital point).
O Indra, by means of the *kratus*—that is, by your insights—you indeed knew (*vidadidat*) this Vṛtra.

When, O you of good dominion (*sukṣatra*), O powerful Indra, at the offering (*prabhṛtā*)—the preparation—of the exhilarating Soma, you placed (*dhāḥ*) this Vṛtra, who desired to fight (*yuyutsantam*), within the *harmya*, the snaring darkness.
The meaning is that Vṛtra entered into darkness out of fear of Indra.
1. [The letter] *kha* is devoid of *ca*, *ṇa*, and *pra*. 2. [The letter] *kha* is free from opposition to *jha*, *ra*, *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *pa*, *ka*, and *ba*.
3. In *kha*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra*, the term "dry" (*śuṣṇa*) does not exist.
4. [The syllables] ga, gha, ja, śa, and ' do not exist in the word *vṛtra*.
5. [The syllables] kha, na, pa, ta, na, bha, ra, śa, and śu exist in the words *śuṣṇam asuram*, *tyam*, *cit*, *tithā*, *katpayam*, *śaryāṇam*, *asūrye*, and *tamasi vāvṛdhānam*.
Intoxicated by that pressed juice, Indra, the bull, raised his arm aloft and struck him down.
Even him, thus, the son of Katpa, Śaryāna, who had grown strong in sunless darkness—him even Indra, exhilarated by the pressed juice, having raised his voice aloud, struck down like a bull. 6.
Intoxicated and rejoicing with the pressed Soma, Indra—the bull, the showerer of desires—having raised his thunderbolt aloft and high, struck and slew even that very Vṛtra. Of what sort was he?
One who was thus fashioning the world of the atmosphere.
Him whose milk is the maker of happiness; him who makes his bed upon the waters; him who has grown, increasing, in the sunless darkness;
[the repetition] "him indeed" is for the sake of completion.
For the Taittirīyaka [text] states: "The rising Indra for the sake of great giving" (Tai. Saṃ. 2.5.2.2).

The mantra immediately following that says: "In the difficult battle, with great power, with the weapon—the thunderbolt—he [struck] the footless, measureless vessel; the one of hostile speech, whose faculty of speech was destroyed."
The meaning is that he was overcome by yawning. "He struck down Vṛtra; he utterly destroyed him.
From him, as he was yawning, Soma and Agni departed; indeed, the out-breath and in-breath abandoned him," so says the Taittirīya Saṃhitā (2.5.2.4).
Who can withstand his impetuous might? He alone, unopposed, carries off the spoils of wealth.
Even these two goddesses, Heaven and Earth, ageless ones, bow down in fear before the power of Indra’s strength.

Who shall withstand his impetuous force and might? He alone, unopposed, wins the spoils of wealth. Even these two goddesses, Heaven and Earth, out of fear of this Indra’s power, bow down before him who is ever victorious.
Who could restrain the vigor, the drying power, the majesty, and the strength of this Indra? Who would ward it off?
Although the word *śuṣma* functions as a feminine qualifier, it retains its masculine gender because it is a term with a fixed gender.
"Unopposed by anyone, unapproached, Indra—alone, indeed without a companion—'bharate' (bears or seizes) 'dhanā' (the riches), the wealth of his enemies.
These two divine, shining ones, Heaven and Earth, out of fear produced by the force of this Indra's impetuous power, 'nu' (quickly) 'jihāte', they depart;
that is to say, they move away."
May the divine axe yield for him; for Indra it has opened a path like a swift stream.
When he unites all vigor with these [powers], the peoples bow down before his self-sustaining nature.

To him the divine axe bows down; for Indra, the path has yielded like one who desires it. When he unites all his power with these [fingers], the peoples bow down in accordance with his self-sovereignty. 10.

The *svadhiti* (the axe), which is self-sustained (*svadhṛti*) and held by itself, and the goddess *dyauḥ* (Heaven), who is shining, bow down before this Indra; that is, she goes downward. The *gātuḥ* (the Earth), like a desiring woman, has restrained herself for Indra;
the meaning is that she becomes fit to employ herself as he desires.
Whatever "total" (*viśvam*) "strength" (*ojas*) Indra "unites" (*saṃ yuvate*) "with these creatures"—
the meaning is that Indra has deposited his own power within all living beings—
"the people" (*kṣitayaḥ*), that is, human beings, exist "in accordance with" (*anu*) it, following its favor.
"Kṣitayaḥ" is a term for humans.
"They bow down"—they bend together, they prostrate themselves—to the powerful Indra, toward his own domain.
1. *ga-gha-ja-ta-pa-pha-ba-atrama* | 2. *sva-ca-jha-ṇa-bha-ra-jambhābhibhūta* | 3. *jha-ra-tadajahitām*; *ta-tadajahitām*.

4. *kha*, *ṇa*, *bha*—these are for drying (*śoṣaṇam*); *na* and *śa*—for the head (*śīrṣiṇīm*); *bha*—for drying (*śoṣaṇam*). 5. *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *ta*, *pa*, *pha*, *ba*, *ra*—these; *śa*—these very ones. 6.
*ma* and *ca*—to be joined with *ṇa* (*niyoktum*); *jha*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*—to be separated from it (*viyoktum*).
7. [The syllables] *sa-ca-jha-ṇa-bha-ra* belong to their own domain (*svadhāma*) by virtue of their own nature (*svadhāja*).

8. Immediately after the word *na-pustakam*, the following reading is observed: "In the *Ekatrikanāman* one-day sacrifice (*ekāha*), when there is no *nidhana* and no *śastra*, the hymn beginning with *ekaṃ nu tvā* is the principal [hymn]. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Of me alone, O Vibhvan... for us, O Satapatis, you alone are the protector of all people."

I hear of you alone as the true lord, known among all peoples, the Pañcajanya, renowned among men. Him, the most heroic Indra, my prayers have grasped; seeking him, we invoke Indra at evening and at dawn. ekaṃ nu tvā satpatiṃ pāścajanyaṃ jñātaṃ śṛṇomi yaśasaṃ janeṣu | taṃ me jagṛbhre āśaso narviṣṭhaṃ doṣā vastorhavamānāsa indram || 11 || Now I hear of you alone as the true lord, known among all peoples, the Pañcajanya, renowned among men. Him, the most heroic Indra, my prayers have grasped; seeking him, we invoke Indra at evening and at dawn.
O Indra, I—the seer of the mantra—hear you alone as the preeminent one among all people, among all human beings, from the foremost of sages. Of what kind?
The protector of the virtuous (*satpati*), beneficial to the five classes of men (*pāñcajanya*), known, arisen, and endowed with glory (*yaśas*).

During the night and during the day, calling upon him, praising him, and proclaiming their hopes and desires, my subjects have seized—that is, they should take possession of—that Indra who is most worthy of praise, the most excellent among men.

Thus indeed I hear of you, as you bestow gifts in due season upon the inspired poets; what is withheld from you, O Indra, by those friends who, through their sacred prayer (*brahman*), have fulfilled your desire? Thus indeed I hear of you, as you bestow gifts in due season upon the inspired poets; what is withheld from you, O Indra, by those friends who, through their sacred prayer, have fulfilled your desire?
Indeed, in this very manner, I hear you, O Indra, bestowing and granting riches (*maghā*) to the inspired singers (*viprebhyaḥ*), you who impel living beings at the proper times (*ṛtuthā*).
This appears as if it were so.

O Indra, what do those singers—who have placed their desire (*kāma*) in you, having cast it down within you—receive from you? For they are the friends of yours, the destroyers of men (*brahmaṇaḥ nṛhantaḥ*), the singers of praise. What do they take for themselves from you?
The sage, having spoken thus because of the delay in obtaining his own desired object, meant "no."
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of ignorance,
may Vidyātīrtha Maheśvara bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the first chapter of the Fourth Aṣṭaka in the Commentary on the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial authority of the illustrious King Vīrabuka—the glorious sovereign over kings, supreme lord, and promoter of the Vedic path—under the patronage of Mādhava.
1. The word *anu* does not exist [in manuscript *śa*].

2. In manuscripts *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *bha*: *prajānāḥ*; in *jha*, *ra*: *prajanāḥ*; in *na*: *janāḥ*. 3. In manuscripts *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, *śa*: *tvā* [is read as] *tvām*.
4. In the manuscripts Kha, Ga, Gha, Ña, Pa, Pha, and Ba, the passage beginning with "vedārthasya" and ending with "maheśvaraḥ" is absent. Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa!
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose very breath is the Vedas and who fashioned the entire universe from the Vedas.
Having explained the first chapter in the fourth [book],
the wise Śrī Sāyaṇācārya, who is capable of exposition, now desires to explain the second.

In this regard, there are twelve hymns in the third section (anuvāka) of the fifth book (maṇḍala) of Atri. Among them, the first hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "mahi maha," has Saṃvaraṇa—the son of Prajāpati—as its seer (ṛṣi). Its meter (chandas) is Triṣṭubh, and its deity (devatā) is Indra. Thus it is stated in the Anukramaṇī: "mahi daśa; [the seer] is Saṃvaraṇa, the son of Prajāpati. The application (viniyoga) is determined by the indicative marks of the text.
I meditate upon the great [earth] for the sake of the great, powerful lord of men, as one who is invincible;
he who, when the prize is won, has bestowed favor upon this people and has been mindful of him in the battle.

I meditate upon the great, the mighty one for the sake of men—for Indra, the powerful, in this manner, for the sake of the unassailable. He who, when the soma is pressed among the people in the struggle for booty, grants him favor;

O Indra, let those [steeds] of yours not be withheld from us, as they were once unyoked due to a lack of prayer. Mount that chariot with the thunderbolt in hand; O God, you who possess noble horses, you hold the reins.

Not so! O Indra, lofty one, let those [horses] of yours not be unyoked from us due to a lack of prayer. Mount that chariot, O wielder of the thunderbolt; O God, you who possess noble horses, take up the reins.
O lofty Indra, those who are other than we—those who are unyoked by you, not joined with you, and devoid of *manas*—have become lacking in *brahman*.
*Brahman* is the sovereign power;
because they are destitute of it, those men do not belong to you.
Therefore, mount that well-known chariot in order to come to our sacrifice.
O Indra, wielder of the thunderbolt, god of noble steeds, mount that chariot which you grasp and control by its reins.
O Indra, you have exerted yourself greatly; fighting for cattle among the fertile lands, you have performed many deeds of truth.
You, the bull, have carved out a dwelling even for the sun in its own place, and you have struck down the very name of the Dāsa in battles—you who are by nature prone to slaying.

Furthermore, O you who are like a serpent (ahi-sūpama)— so called because of moving everywhere— O Lord whose power pervades all directions, by your grace may our noble follower (cāruḥ satvā), whether a servant or another, come to us (ā jambhāt) in great battles or sacrifices; one who is worthy of praise (havyaḥ), or one who may be challenged by adversaries (pratibhaṭaiḥ āhvātavyaḥ).
Like Bhaga, the one who partakes of the oblation;
the meaning is that the servant and others should come just as the god Bhaga comes with his horses.
O Indra, you have filled yourself with nourishment, for in you is the might and the most recent manly powers, O immortal one.
As such, O possessor of wealth, grant us riches; I praise the gift of the one of abundant bounty as if it were a constant stream.

O Indra, you are to be propitiated; for in you indeed is power and most recent manly deeds, you the immortal one. As such, O possessor of wealth, grant us enduring riches. I praise the gift of the noble one, the giver of much bounty.
O Indra, you have [attained] that strength—power worthy of being filled or worthy of being honored—for indeed, it is in you;
the meaning is that it is dependent upon you.
Dancing, immortal—that is, possessing the nature of immortality—you, O Vasavāna, clothing the world with your own splendor, [bestow] manly powers, that is, riches.
The word *ca* (and) is used in reference to the wealth (*rayi*) that is about to be mentioned.
Grant (*dāḥ*) us this wealth (*rayim*), which is of the color of *etá*, meaning white-colored; give it.
And I praise (*pra stuṣe*) the gift of the noble Lord (*aryaḥ īśvarasya*), who possesses abundant riches (*tuvimaghasya prabhūtadhanasya*).
Thus, O Hero, with your protections, guard us, the singers and poets;
and as you rend the skin in the contest for booty, be pleased with the sweet, well-prepared, and delightful soma.
Thus, O Indra, protect us with your aids; O Hero, favor the singers and the poets who rend the skin in the struggle for booty. Be pleased with the well-pressed, beautiful, and sweet soma. 7.
O heroic Indra, protect us thus—us who are singers, praisers, makers, and officiating priests—with your aids and guardianships.
Moreover, in the battle for booty, satisfy yourself with the soma—the sweet, delightful drink, well-pressed and beautifully poured—which bestows a covering form (or skin) upon the giver.
(The genitive case is used here in the sense of the accusative.)
The meaning is: "Drink the Soma characterized by longing.
Alternatively, the genitive case is used in the sense of the instrumental:
"Delight [me] by means of drinking the Soma characterized by longing."
And may these ten white horses of the son of Purukutsa, Suresadas, the possessor of gold, carrying me as gifts, convey me hither; they have been praised according to the wills of Gairikṣita.

And indeed, may those ten white horses of the liberal Trasadasyu, son of Purukutsa, who possesses golden wealth, carry me hither; may they bear me by the wills of Gairikṣita, for now the hymn has been recited. 8.

1. Those ending in *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *ga*; those joined with *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, and *sa*; and those joined with *ra* and *śa*. 2. *Ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *pa*, *pha*, *ba*, and *ava*: protect! 3.
*Kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *bha*, *ra*, and *sūkta*.
Trasadasyu, Vidatha, and Dhvanya— these three kings gave horses, wealth,
and cows to the sage Radasyu for his poetic composition.
Moreover, "ye te mā":
the accusative case is used in the sense of the dative;
it means "to me."
They have rejoiced.
This is the form of the *liṭ* (perfect tense) with the suffix *kānac*, derived from the root *rāti*, which has the meaning "to give," used in the sense of the object (*karman*).
The meaning is "given.

May the ten horses of beautiful color belonging to this Trasadasyu—named after a royal seer, the son of Purukutsa (the offspring of Purukutsa), the impeller Sureḥ, the possessor of gold (Hiraṇinaḥ), and born of the Gairikṣita lineage (Girikṣitagotra)—carry me, that is, bring me [to my goal].
And may I quickly go forth with sacrificial rites (Kratubhiḥ), such as the yoking of chariots or other sacrifices.

And those Maruts, the givers of wealth through their wisdom at the distribution of the sacrifice—Cyavatana, giving with greatness, has come to me; like a noble youth, he has approached for the sake of beauty.

And indeed, those crimson steeds of Mārutāśva—magnificent in their power at the distribution of the assembly—Cyavatāna gave me as thousands. The noble man sang forth, as it were, for the sake of beauty. 9.

Furthermore, those horses of his—belonging to Vidatha, the king of that name, who is the son of Marutāśva (so called because his horses are like the Maruts in speed)—are ruddy in color and worthy of praise through their skillful action characterized by swift movement; they carry me, being employed for the purpose of giving as a gift. This is the sense of the remainder.

Furthermore, with his greatness—bestowing immeasurable riches—he, the one who causes [them] to move away, giving and bestowing them upon me, the worshipful one (where the genitive *me* is used in the sense of the dative), gave him ornaments for his body as adornment for his person; he indeed offered them.
The particle *na* is used here in the sense of *ca* (and).
And indeed, those well-pleasing, radiant, and disciplined steeds of Dhvanya’s son Lakṣmaṇya have come toward me with great wealth, like cows entering the stall of the seer Saṃvaraṇa.

And indeed, those well-pleasing, brilliant, and self-controlled [rays] of Dhvanya Lakṣmaṇya have come toward me, like cows entering the stall of the seer Suvaraṇa, by means of the greatness of his wealth. 10.

Moreover, those horses of his—which are about to be described—belonging to King Dhvanya (the son of Lakṣmaṇa), who was the son of Lakṣmaṇa: they are *juṣṭāḥ*, having come to me; *surucaḥ*, possessing beautiful luster; *yatānāḥ*, striving for the purpose of carrying [me];
and being endowed with the greatness (*mahnā*) of wealth, these horses, once offered as gifts, have also gone to the seer Saṃvaraṇa;
"to me" is the ellipsis.
Like cows to their stall— meaning, as cows enter my pen—
or alternatively, "na" has the sense of "and," meaning the cows have entered my pen.

Having stated in the *Anuvyākhyāna* (2.22), "In the *Atraindra* hymn, there are generally praises of Indra, the Maruts, and kings for their gifts," praise of kings for their gifts is not contradictory.

1. [The variant] *ta-avidathasyaitannāmakasya* does not exist. 2. [The variants] *ga-gha-ja-ta-pa-pha-ba-śa* read *aśvāḥ*; [the variant] *vidathasya* means "of the means of knowledge. 3. [The variants] *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra* do not have the word *arātām*. 4. [The variants] *ga-gha-ja-pa-pha-ba* read *ābhūṣe*. 5. [The variants] *ga-gha-ja* read *mā*. 6. [The variants] *kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-ṇa-pa-pha-ba-śa* read *vahamānā*; *ra* reads *vahamānāya*. 7. [The variants] *ga-gha-ja-pa-pha-ba* read *rāyo dhanāni*.
The second hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "ajātaśatrum," is addressed to Indra and is the seerical composition (*ārṣam*) of Saṃvaraṇa, the son of Prajāpati.
The ninth [verse] is a *triṣṭubh*; the remaining verses are *jagatīs* according to the rule that those ending in *anuṣṭubh* are so designated.
The *Anukramaṇikā* states: “‘Ajātaśatru’: nine [verses], ending in *triṣṭubh*.
The application (*viniyoga*) is based on indicative marks (*laiṅgika*).
"Unborn is the foe; ageless and full of light, she moves toward her own nature according to her will.
Press the soma, cook the oblation, and offer a most ample gift to the one who is borne by prayer and invoked by many."

To Ajātaśatru, to the ageless, to the one possessing light, follows the immeasurable, self-sustaining power; it moves with heat. Press the juice! Cook the offering! For him who is borne by prayer, for the one praised by many, bestow gifts ever more abundantly.
Against him who has no enemy born after him— that is, one whose followers are his slayers—

against the *vadasman*, the enemy who brings about destruction; [the oblation] which is undecaying (*vajrā*), possessing light (*svarvatī*), measured out (*vamitā*), and unlimited (*aparimitā*), [and] which is the food (*svadhā*) and the sacrificial offering (*havis*), goes forth and reaches its goal.
For that purpose, O officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), press out [the Soma];
cook the sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) and other offerings;
[perform] the ritual action.
The sacrificer who [offers] to this Indra for *ghaṃsa*—
this is a name for a day; it is called *ghaṃsa* because essences (*rasa*) are gathered (*gṛhyante*) within it.

In that [context]: *uta vā* (or else), *yaḥ* (who) is the sacrificer (*yajamānaḥ*). *Ūdhani* refers to the night, understood as "that which is raised up" (*uddhatataram bhavati*) or "that which has been lifted up" (*ud-dham iti bodhaḥ*).
Because of the two [actions] of bestowing moisture (*sneha-pradāna*) and [shining], it is called "night" (*rātri*) due to its equality [with day];
for it pours forth the *soma* during both day and night, and thus it becomes luminous (*dyumān*), that is, radiant.
The particle *aha* is used here in the sense of distribution (*viniyoga*).
Furthermore: *Śakra* means this powerful Indra.
*Tatanuṣṭi*: he who impels (*nudati*) the extended continuity of Dharma (*tataṃ dharmasaṃtatiṃ*) and desires (*kāmayate*) rain and objects of desire (*kāmān*) is *tatanuṣṭi*.
*Tanmuśubhram*: him who is exceedingly brilliant (*suśubhram*).
"Tan" means that which is beautiful (*śubhā*), to be adorned with ornaments and the like;
he drives away such a nourisher who does not perform sacrifices.
Another "apa" is an expletive used for metrical completion.
He who is wealthy like Madhava and possesses the strength of Kava-Asva drives away that [enemy] who has base men as his companions.
He whose father he has slain, whose mother he has slain—he from whom even Śakra flees in distress;
he knows his way around, for he does not shrink from the sin of the Kuru, being a mine of wealth.

He whose father Śakra slew, whose mother he slew, and whose brother he slew—he, though distressed, does not flee nor shrink from him; for he is the one who acts with purpose, the source of wealth who does not shrink from sin. 4.
Śakra said: "This Śakra has slain the father of this non-sacrificer, and he has slain his mother;
furthermore, he does not flee from his brother—therefore, [he flees] from this non-sacrificer."
He neither fears nor flees;
rather, he simply desires that his offerings, when presented with devotion, be accepted.
The meaning is that, having instructed one who has not sacrificed, he compels him to do so.

The one who brings about the end (*yantakara*); the one who effects the restraint (*yamanakartā*); the one who brings forth wealth (*vasvaḥ*), that is, the bringer of riches (*ākara*) by facing them; he who does not shrink (*na īṣate*), does not waver, or does not fear from *kilbiṣa*, which consists of the killing of his father and others.

He is the slayer of those who do not drink (*amnonām*) of Indra—famous in such Vedic passages as: "Indra gave the *yatīs* to the *sālāvṛkas*; in the intermediate space he gave the *paulomas*, and on earth he gave the *kālakāñjas*—the foremost of the *yatīs*—to the *sālāvṛkas*."
He does not concern himself with five or ten, nor with rain, nor with one who does not press the soma, even if that person is prosperous.
The shaker conquers through his own power, he slays or strikes down the one who does not seek the gods; he bestows [wealth] upon the one who seeks the gods in a stall full of cattle.

Not with five, not with ten; he seizes the rain. He does not associate with the one who presses no Soma, even though that one prospers. Or rather, by such means he conquers, or the Shaker slays him. He shall cause the seeker of the gods to share in a stall full of cattle.
1. By means of the ornaments and so forth of *kha*, *ca*, *jña*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *bha*;
*ga*, *gha*, and *ja* are the ornaments. 2. *Kha*, *ca*, *jña*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *ma*, *ra*, and *yajvānam*.
3. [The letter] *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *bha*, or *ā* is elided; *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *pa*, *pha*, or *ba* elides the vowel *a*.
4. [The letters] *kha*, *ca*, *jña*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, or *ra* do not exist [in the word] "wealthy" (*dhanavān*). 5. [The letters] *a*, *ta*, *ra*, or *yajvan*: [are elided].
6. He desires Kha and Jha. 7. Those given by Ga, Gha, Ja, and Śa. 8. Ta is the maker of restraint; Ya is the maker of binding.

9. [The syllables] *kha*, *ca*, *jña*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra* are associated with wealth from one’s father and others; *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *pa*, *pha*, and *ba* are like one’s father and others; *śa* is associated with slaughter by one’s father and others. 10. [The syllables] *kha*, *ca*, *jña*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, and *bha* belong to those who offer praise.

This Indra, together with five divine beings as his allies, does not desire *ārambham*—that is, he does not require assistance—as a support for the undertaking (*ārambha*) of slaying the enemy. This is the meaning.
Or rather:
he does not desire—that is, he does not wish—to undertake, to apply effort toward this Indra by means other than sacrifice, such as by [using] five or ten [fingers].
He does not associate with—that is, he does not join with—one who is non-pressing, who does not perform the extraction [of soma], even if that person prospers or nourishes his kinsmen and so forth.
The meaning is that he does not reach one who does not press [the soma], who does not perform the purification, who does not sacrifice, and who is impotent.
It is not merely a matter of non-attainment; rather, he "conquers" (jināti) him. The word "vā" is used in the sense of "and."
And he conquers; he afflicts. "Hence" is a filler [of the verse].
Or indeed, by that [means], the shaker, the one who causes trembling, slays that sacrificer; let him hear.
He bestows upon the god-seeking sacrificer—who desires the divine Indra—the possession of a stall full of cattle; that is to say, he yokes [him] thereto.

Destroying the moment of battle, he hurls his wheel against the one who does not press the soma; he is the adversary of the non-presser and the strengthener of the presser. Indra, the terrifier of all, the subduer, leads [the enemy] according to his will for the sake of the liberal giver.
Destroying the eyes, at the proper season, he fixed the wheel. Of him who does not press the soma, he is the adversary; of him who presses it, he is the strengthener.
Indra, the tamer of all, the terrifying one, the Āryan leads the Dāsa according to his will. 6.

In battle, he who is tireless and especially the slayer of enemies, for that purpose set his wheel in motion; Indra, the non-stirrer of the wheel of the chariot for the one who does not press the soma, who does not sacrifice, and who is hostile—yet he is the prosperer of the one who presses the soma and sacrifices, the subduer of all, the instructor, the terrifying one who causes fear, the noble master who leads the servile folk, whose work is to tame, according to his will and desire, into his own power.
He drives away the food of the stingy man, but bestows noble wealth upon the donor.
Not even in a difficult place does he remain steadfast, for many people provoke his powerful might.
He drives away the food of the niggard to seize it; he distributes excellent wealth to the donor. Not even in a narrow place does every man stand firm who has provoked his wrath. ||7||
This Indra goes forth to seize— the food, wealth, or sustenance of the stingy non-giver, like a hunter seizing the prey of a merchant—
and having gone there, he takes it and distributes excellent, noble wealth to the donor, the sacrificer who offers oblations; that is to say,
he draws away from the one who does not sacrifice and bestows it upon the one who sacrifices.
It is not merely the giving of wealth to a merchant; rather, even in many difficult places that must be traversed with hardship, every single donor is supported—that is, established—by him.

As for the person who has not provoked the *tarviṣī* (the power) of this Indra by failing to perform his duties and so forth, [he is the one] "of whom the merchant does not pay," as is understood from the preceding context.
Or alternatively:
Whosoever provoked his wrath, every such person was held back by Indra even in a place of difficulty.
The word "caneti" is obtained through the tradition of those who study it.

1. [The variant] *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-bha-ra-janaṃ* does not exist. 2. [The variant] *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-bha-ra-vaṇijāmava*. 3. [The variant] *ma-ca-ṇa-vaṇikapradāna*. 4. [The variant] *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-bha-cana duḥkhena*; [the variant] *ra-ca duḥkhena na*. 5. [The variant] *jha-na-bha-ra-janaḥ* does not exist.
O Indra, you two who are worthy of sacrifice, possessors of great wealth, and masters of all strength—both of you, the bountiful lords, are present among the radiant cattle.
For you have made one of your companions tremble; indeed, the shaker releases the herd of cattle along with his warriors.

When the two people, both wealthy and possessing all strength, came together, Indra the Bounteous went forth among the beautiful cattle; for he made the other his ally through his shattering power, and the Shaker releases the herd of kine with his warriors. ||8||

When Indra, the bountiful lord of wealth, who possesses great strength, vast power, and immense energy—having become the rival of two other wealthy men of splendid riches and great force—made Vyañjana his driver and Vyuja his companion amidst beautiful cattle;
he, the shaker of enemies, together with the Maruts, the warriors, released for him that herd of cattle, shaking the clouds.
The meaning is that Indra, knowing whether a person is performing a sacrifice or not, and having ascertained that it is for the sake of cattle, bestows a herd of cows upon the sacrificer.
I praise Agniveśi, the son of Sahasra, Śatri, the peerless banner of manhood.
May the waters swell for him as he strives; may sovereign power be firmly established in him.
I praise the descendant of Agniveśa, Sahasrāsāṃ Śatri, O Agni. May the waters nourish this banner of the noble one with their united flows; may there be in him powerful and brilliant dominion. 9.
The wise sage, the son of Prajāpati, honored Agniveśi’s son Śaunaka— who bestows wealth—
and offered him this blessing with another verse.

O Agni, endowed with qualities such as being anointing and so forth, I praise—that is, I extol—the royal seer (rājarṣi) named Śatri, the son of Agniveśi, who bestows a thousandfold and immeasurable wealth.
How is he? [The text continues: "He who is... [etc.]
To him who is like a standard (*vupamām*), that is, one who has become a point of comparison,
a guide, meaning one who is renowned— to him, the waters (*vapaḥ*) moving together (*vsamyataḥ*), that is, flowing properly, may they swell (*vpīpayanta*), meaning may they cause him to overflow.
In that king, let there be *vkṣatram*, wealth, accompanied by *vamavat*, strength, and *tveṣam*, that which is brilliant.
‘yaste sādhiṣṭhaḥ’—this is the third hymn;
the seer is named Prabhavasu, belonging to the Aṅgiras lineage;
the meter is Paṅkti.
By the rule regarding the end of a *paṅkti* [verse], the remaining verses are *anuṣṭubhs*.
Indra is the deity. This is indicated by the metrical index (*anukramaṇī*) which states: "The eight [verses] beginning with 'yaste' are by Prabhava Āṅgirasa; [the last] is a *paṅkti*."
The application of the hymn (*sūkta*) is based on its indicative marks (*laiṅgika*).

Among the *ābhilāvika* rites, at the third pressing, the verse beginning with ‘*yaste sābhiṣṭo’vase purāṃ bhinduryuvā kaviḥ*’ (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8) serves as an optional counterpart (*anurūpa*) for the Ādhvaryu. This is also stated in the Sūtra.
For the second and third [stotras], which are attained by their own inherent force, the two *ṛcas* beginning with *ā ca* are the *anurūpas*;
for it is stated in the Sūtra: "The six *anuṣṭubh*s beginning with 'yaste sāmiṣṭo'vasa' [are the stotriyas]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.5).

1. Kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra, and no are without *nimitta* (indicatory marks). 2. Ga, gha, ja, pa, pha, ba, and artha signify the master (*svāmī*). 3. Ga, gha, ja, pa, pha, ba, and puṣyantu. 4. Ga, gha, ja, pa, pha, ba, and *balamavat* joined with *gṛha*.
O Indra, bestow upon us that most effective will and power which subdues the people and is invincible in these battles.
