O Indra, bring forth for our protection that most effective will of yours which overcomes the people, so that it may be invincible in these battles.
O Indra, that most effective *kratu*—whether it be the ritual action characterized by hymns (*uktha*) or wisdom—that you possess, bring that *kratu* to us for our protection; bring it to us!
Of what nature is it?
It is one that overcomes all people (*carṣaṇīsaha*), one that is resolute or pure, and one that is invincible in battles (*vāja*), being unassailable by others.
O Indra, if you have four, or if you, O Hero, have three,
or if you have [the wealth] of the five peoples, bring that down to us for our aid.
O Indra, whatever four [helps] are yours, O Hero, or whatever three there are, or whatever aid belongs to the five peoples—that favor, bring it well to us. 2.
O Indra, whatever aids (*ūtayaḥ*) of yours there are— those which reside in the four castes (*caturṣu varṇeṣu*), or those, O Hero, which exist in the three worlds,
or indeed (*vā*) those which belong to the five peoples (*pañca kṣitīnām*)— bring all that protection (*avaḥ*) most excellently (*su*) to us; bring it hither!
We invoke from you that most desirable and virile power, for you were born with the impulse of a bull; O Indra, you are victorious through your manifestations.
We invoke your most excellent protection, O you who are full of manly vigor; for you were born with a rush like a bull, O Indra, victorious through your powers of assistance.
O Indra, we invoke for ourselves your excellent, desirable protection (*avaḥ*), which is the bestowing of fruits upon the showerer [of rain].
O Indra, you whose impetus is virile, who moves swiftly, and who is the overcomer or the destroyer—along with those who are all-pervading and powerful, you indeed bring forth this protection;
we invoke that protection of yours.
Or rather:
since you, moving as a bull, have come to the sacrifice and produced fruit, therefore we invoke your protection.

1. In the four [mantras] beginning with *kha*, *jha*; in the four beginning with *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *pa*, *pha*, *ba*, there are the four *rakṣās*; in the four beginning with *ta* and *ra*, there are four [mantras]. 2.
In the versions *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, the word "yat" does not exist.
3. In the versions *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, the phrase "yadvā" does not exist.
4. Kha, va, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra—may all that be protected. 5. Kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra, yāhi.

For you are a bull; you were born for the sake of bounty. Bullish is your strength, O Śarva; steadfast is your own dominion, and firm is your mind, O Indra, ever-conquering the enemy. 4. For you are a bull; you were born for the sake of bounty. Bullish is your strength, O Śarva; steadfast is your own dominion, and firm is your mind, O Indra, ever-conquering the enemy. 4.
O Indra, you are indeed for the sake of bestowing gifts upon the sacrificers and for their prosperity; for you are a bull (*vṛṣan*), that is, you are truly the showerer of fruit.
Or rather, you are a bull in your own nature.
For the sake of prosperity and wealth, you are born; you arise.
Your strength (*śavas*) is that of a showerer (*vṛṣṇi*).
Your mind is self-dependent in power (*svakṣatra*); it rains down upon the adversary who is a showerer of hostility.
O Indra, may your ancient manly power truly overcome all [enemies].

O Indra, O lord of the stone-weaponed bolt, O lord of a hundred powers, O master of might, come down with your entire chariot against that mortal who acts as an enemy, O friend of the Madras. 5. You, O Indra, [against] that mortal, [who] acts as an enemy, O lord of the stone-weaponed bolt, with your whole chariot, O lord of a hundred powers, come down, O lord of might. 5.
O Indra, you— O Indra— protect that enemy who acts with hostility, and protect our chariot, or our son whose nature is to move;
what kind of chariot?

[The one] difficult to overcome, who is to be crossed with difficulty; [the one] who goes at the head in battles, the mingler who stands in front; [the one] full of guile, who goes along with his followers; [the one] who, in every instance of wealth, seeks booty or wealth in battle.

O Indra, come to us; protect our chariot with your wisdom. O Most Powerful One, may we establish desirable glory in heaven; in heaven we fashion our hymn of praise. asmākam | indra | ā | ihi | naḥ | ratham | ava | puramdhyā | vayam | śaviṣṭha | vāryam | divi | śravaḥ | dadhīmahi | divi | stomam | manāmahe || 8 ||
O Indra, being ours, come hither to us!
Having arrived, protect our chariot with your *puraṃdhī*—your auspicious wisdom.
And we, O most powerful one (*śaviṣṭha*), through your favor, may establish in heaven—that which shines—the desirable food or glory that is to be chosen.
Likewise, in heaven, we meditate upon—that is, we shall perform—the praise, the hymn of praise.

The fourth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “sa ā gamat,” has Prabhūvasu Āṅgirasa as its seer. The third verse is a Jagatī; the remaining verses are Anuṣṭubhs and Triṣṭubhs. Indra is the deity. It is described [in the Anukramaṇī] thus: “sa ā gamat, six verses; the third is a Jagatī. The application [of the hymn] is indicated by its internal characteristics (liṅga).

May that Indra come, he who knows how to bestow a portion of treasures and the granting of riches. Like a bull roaming in the desert, thirsty and longing, let him drink the pressed stalk. He, Indra, shall come—he who knows how to grant a portion of treasures and the bestowing of riches. Like a bull wandering in the desert, satisfied and desiring, let him drink the milked stalk.
May that Indra come toward our sacrifice; may he, the god who [is the master] of riches, come hither.
The genitive case is used for the object of an action.
He knows—that is, he understands how—to bestow riches and wealth.
Of what nature is he?
He is a giver, or one whose mind is intent on giving, of treasures and riches.
There is an illustration regarding his movement:

like an archer moving with his bow, a *vaṃsaga*—one whose gait is desirable—being exceedingly thirsty (*tṛpāṇaḥ*) and desiring (*cakamānaḥ*), let him drink the Soma, the stalk that has been milked and purified.

O Lord of the bay horses, O Hero, may Soma ascend your jaws and your two cheeks, as if upon the back of a mountain. O King, invoked by many, may we all rejoice with songs of praise, urging you on like swift steeds. 2.
O Indra, O possessor of wealth, with your two bay horses, O hero, let that [Soma] reach you, O slayer, by means of your two arms which accomplish the slaughter.
Although this word *śiprā* refers to the jaws, nevertheless, because it is mentioned again here, it should be understood figuratively.
Let Soma, in his excellent form, or gathered together, ascend or reach our two joined jaws.
He does not mount the back of the mountain;
that is to say, he does not stay there.
Or else:
The word *na* (not), though placed at the beginning, has here the sense of a comparison (*upamā*).
It means "like the moon on the back—that is, the upper region—of a mountain.
Just as [the moon] spreads there with confidence, so too [does he].
O radiant Indra, let him go forth, seeking you as his own, desiring you along with your host.
By the rule "in the sense of the third case," these two [words] possess the status of *karmapravacanīya*.
O Puruhūta (Indra, invoked by many), may we all, like those who tend to horses with grass and other fodder, gladdening you— that is, pleasing you— with our words and hymns of praise,
rejoice and exult.
O Puruhūta, my wheel does not turn; it trembles from fear of the lack of intelligence within my mind, even from heaven.
O ever-increasing Maghavan, will the singer, who possesses many riches, indeed praise you from his chariot?

The wheel does not turn, O much-invoked one; my mind trembles with fear of indigence, O wielder of the stone. Will not the singer, O Maghavan, possessor of many riches and ever-increasing, praise you from the chariot? ||3||

O you who are invoked by many (*puruhūta*), O wielder of the thunderbolt (*vadrivaḥ*), O Indra, my mind (*manaḥ*) trembles with fear (*bhīyā*) from poverty (*dāridryāt*) or from the presence of the non-praiser (*astotuḥ*).
Like a wheel (*cakraṃ na*) rolling upon the ground, it quivers.

Therefore, O ever-increasing (*sadāvṛdha*) Maghavan Indra, standing above me like a chariot (*rathāt adhi*), may the praiser (*jaritā*), rich in wealth (*puruvasuḥ*), quickly (*kuvit nu*) offer praise to you. May he indeed sing your hymns.
In this case, even though there is a connection with *ku* and *vicchanda*, the verb receives the *nighāta* accent because of the inclusion of the term "many" (*bahu*) in the rule.
Like a pressing-stone, this singer raises his voice to you, O Indra, offering it up with great fervor.
O Maghavan, bestow wealth upon us through your favor; O Dariman, grant us riches from the right hand and do not let our spirit fail.

This singer here, O Indra, like a pressing-stone, utters a lofty voice to you, aspiring for strength. O Maghavan, bestow upon us wealth with your right hand; O Lord of the Bay Steeds, do not turn away from us. 4.

The singer, the praiser, the one who lauds you—like a pressing-stone, like a loud voice—he generates the essence [of praise]. In that same way, O Indra, this speech (vāc) impels a hymn of praise toward you;
it means "it sends forth. O Maghavan, bestowing abundant and great fruit, with my capable hand, I offer wealth to you. I present it to you.
The remainder [of the sentence] is: "He bestows even with the right hand from the right.
Do not make me devoid of desire (*vigata-kāma*).
With the sounds *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *la*, you possess abundant strength.
May the bull-like heaven increase you, the bull; as a bull, you are borne by two bull-like bay horses.
O bull with a beautiful helmet, O bull of mighty will, O possessor of power, may you, the bull, bestow upon us wealth through your bull-like chariot.

May the Bull Heaven cause you, the Bull, to grow strong. As a Bull, you are borne by your two tawny Bulls. Thus, O Bull with the Bull-chariot, fair-jawed one of Bull-like wisdom, O Bull, bringer of strength, bestow wealth upon us.
O Indra, you—[you whom] the heaven, the showerer, and the illuminating hymn [invoke].
Or rather, this form [of "dyota"] belongs to the root *div*, in the sense of praising.
May you, the showerer of desires, cause yourself to increase;
may you, the bull, be carried by the two tawny steeds, the bulls who sprinkle [rain], as you are driven toward the sacrifice.
O you with beautiful jaws, O Indra of bull-like power, wielder of the thunderbolt—being both a bull and possessing a bull-chariot, do you support us in battle or establish us in the sacrifice.

O Maruts, may the people bow down before this youth Śrutaratha with offerings, he who, rich in horses, has bestowed two ruddy steeds accompanied by three hundred [cows]. May all the settlements submit themselves to him.
May the people bow down before this youth, Śrutaratha, who is accompanied by three hundred steeds—two ruddy, vigorous horses that bring abundance; O Maruts, grant him your service. 6.
This is a praise of the gift of King Śrutaratha:

that King Śrutaratha, possessed of steeds and rich in food, bestowed two ruddy, reddish-colored horses—vigorous and spirited—along with three hundred cattle or wealth, accompanying them as they were presented.
This is the form of the root *dadāti* or *diśati* in the *luṅ* tense.

To this youth, the mixer of all things, or to him who is eternally young, Śrutaratha—to him all the peoples, all creatures, offer worship; *duvoyā* is the substitute for the third case singular ending.
"By means of service, let them bow down; let them become prostrate"—this means "let them serve.
"O Maruts! is an address to the Maruts who have become the companions of Indra.

The fifth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “saṃ bhānunā,” is addressed to Indra and is composed in the Triṣṭubh meter. The Anukramaṇī states: “saṃ bhānunā; [the seer is] Atri; [the deity is] Indra.
The application [of the hymn] is determined by its internal characteristics (liṅga).

He vies with the radiance of the sun, being invoked, he whose back is sprinkled with ghee and who possesses fine horses. For him, may the unerring dawns shine forth; "Let us press the soma for Indra," so he says.

He strives with the radiance of the sun, being invoked, his back anointed with ghee, possessing noble horses; for him may the unceasing dawns shine forth—he who says, "Let us press the Soma for Indra. || 1 ||
1. [The syllables] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra, vṛṣa;
2. [the syllables] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra, śa, from the root dā (to give).
Together with the *bhānu*, the light of the Sun, he is *ājuhvānaḥ*, being invoked everywhere.
In the case of the object (karman), there is the suffix denoting the agent (kartṛ-pratyaya).

Ghṛtapṛṣṭhaḥ—having a back sprinkled with ghee, or having a region of the back joined with ghee; svapnāḥ—the fire that is sleep (or the fire of the dream-state); saṃ yatate—he exerts himself properly.
For at the time of sunrise, the fires are kindled.

For that reason, for that sacrificer who says "Let us press [the Soma] for Indra," speaking thus to the Adhvaryu, for that sacrificer may the unassailable (amṛdhāḥ) dawns (uṣasaḥ) break forth (vyucchān).
The meaning is that for one who says, "Since the fire has been kindled at the time of sunrise, let us perform the Soma sacrifice," his days become auspicious.
With the fire kindled, the sacrificial grass strewn, and the pressing-stones yoked, he whose Soma has been pressed shall sing praise;
while the pressing-stones speak aloud for him, the Adhvaryu priest offers the oblation across the river.
"That king does not tremble; he does not become distressed.
In that king's sacrifice, Indra drinks the potent *soma* which produces intoxication—the friend of the cow.
[This refers to] the word for the cause (*prakṛti*) being applied to the effect (*vikāra*)."
[He is] mixed with milk and other [substances].
That king, together with his followers—both non-beings and beings—goes forth and moves everywhere;
and he slays Vṛtra, that is, evil or the enemy.
He dwells and moves; he has protected the subjects. Or rather, he dwells in the *kṣitis*, that is, in dwellings.
"Subhaga" means having a beautiful face. "Nāman" refers to the name, wealth, or the hymn of praise for Indra. "Puṣyan" means nourishing.
May he prosper in security and prevail in battle; may he conquer both armies when they meet.
He who offers the pressed Soma to Indra shall be dear to Sūrya and dear to Agni.

May he prosper; may there be security for him in the pursuit of his goal. He shall conquer both opposing armies when they clash. May he be dear to Sūrya, may he be dear to Agni—he who has pressed the Soma for Indra.
(Ṛgveda 8.32)
O most powerful Indra, you who possess exceeding strength, you hold or bestow from all sides that food which is worthy of being heard and celebrated.
The word *iṣas* also exists as a neuter gender.
O golden-hued Indra, that food has spread forth— it extends—
how?
Most far-famed, most worthy of being heard even from the greatest distance.
The meaning is that it must be performed everywhere.
That which is difficult to overcome, unassailable, and characterized by its own nature becomes manifest.
O wielder of the stone, those impetuous ones of yours who move at will by the power of your banner—
both you gods, as lords of heaven and earth, rule for our protection.
O wielder of the stone, those two impetuous ones who hasten at your signal—both gods, you rule over heaven and earth for our protection. 3.
O wielder of the thunderbolt, O lord of the mountain, those Maruts who are your own—your very breaths of power—are present.
Of what nature are they?
They are *mehanā*, worthy of praise; they are *ketusāpaḥ*, touching the intermediate space which is the indicator of action or the source of wisdom.

O you two gods—both yourself and the host of Maruts—you two rule over both the heaven from the celestial world and the earth from the ground, for the sake of our protection and for our approach. You possess sovereign power.
And of whatever such power there may be, O Vṛtra-slayer, bring manly strength to us; for you desire to show manly favor toward us.
Or indeed, O Vṛtrahan, from whatever power of yours it may be, bring us manly strength; you who take pleasure in manly deeds, bestow it upon us. 4.

Furthermore, O Vṛtra-slayer Indra, bring to us—those who belong to you—whatever power (*dakṣa*) is unassignable and increased, or whatever wealth (*nṛmṇa*) belongs to you; bring it, for the sake of us who are your own.
The repetition [of "to us"] is for the sake of emphasis.
Bring it! Bring it!
O Indra, since you desire manly-mindedness for us, you seek wealth for us.
O Indra, Lord of a hundred powers, may we now be under your protection with these aids; O Hero, may we have you as our good guardian, may we have you as our good guardian.
Now, O Śatakratu, through these aids of thine, may we be well-protected under thy shelter, O Indra; O Hero, may we be well-protected. 5.
1. [The syllables] *sva-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra* do not exist [in this context]. 2. And [the syllable] *śa* is followed by *marudga*.
O *śatakrato*, O Indra, through these *ābhiṣṭibhiḥ*—that is, through your approaches—we may quickly become prosperous; this is the ellipsis.
O Indra, under your protection—under your shelter and in your blissful thought—may we be well-guarded; may we become so.
O Hero, under your protection, may we be well-guarded, possessing excellent defense.
The repetition is for the sake of emphasis.

The seventh hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with "yad indra citra," has Atri as its seer and is addressed to Indra. One verse is in the *paṅkti* meter; the remaining verses are *anuṣṭubh*s according to the technical rule regarding those ending in *paṅkti*.
This is stated in the *Anukramaṇikā*: "yad indra [is] a hymn ending in *paṅkti*."
Among the Ābhilāvika hymns, the first triplet at the third pressing is an optional *stotriya* for the Acchāvāka.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Indra, [the hymn] beginning with 'yad indra citra mehanā yate sādhiṣṭhā'vase' (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.8)."
O Indra, whatever wonderful wealth you have to bestow, O wielder of the thunderbolt,
O possessor of riches, bring that to us with both your hands.
O Indra, whatever wonderful and bountiful gift is yours to bestow, O wielder of the stone, bring that to us, O finder of wealth, with both your hands! 1.

O *citra*, wondrous one; O *adrivaḥ*, wielder of the thunderbolt; O *indra*, since there is wealth (*rādhaḥ*) to be given by you for greatness, indeed, that wealth—O *vidadvaso*, Indra who has found riches—bring it to us with both hands! Regarding this, the Nirukta passage beginning with "O Indra, O wondrous one, since there is wealth to be admired for greatness" (Nirukta 4.4) should be consulted.
O Indra, bring that which you deem most excellent and celestial;
may we know it from you as you bestow the boundless [treasure].
O Indra, bring that which you deem most excellent and celestial; may we know it from you, as you bestow that which is boundless.
O Indra, bring to us that celestial food which you consider most desirable; may we be the ones to find— that is, to obtain—
the gift of such food from you,
which is like an unfathomable ocean whose further shore is beyond reproach.
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, during the *atiriktoktha*, this verse beginning with “*yatte diśaḥ*” is used.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*yatte diśaḥ parādhya svāmicchavasaḥ pate*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 9.9).

1. *ra* and *he*: *indra he*. 2. *ta*, *śa*, and *‘indra’*: these do not exist. 3. *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*: *asmabhyam ābhara*; *śa*: *asmabhyam ābhara āhara*. 4. *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *pa*, *pha*, *ba*: *dyumnasya*. 5. *ta*: *atiriktaukthye*. (Ṛgveda 2.105)

With that renowned and exalted mind of yours, which is intent on giving and successful in its aims—O wielder of the stone, with that very mind, rend even the firmest obstacles for us to win the prize of booty.

O Indra, with that mind of yours which is desirous of giving, most excellent, highly praiseworthy, renowned, vast, and great—with that mind, O wielder of the thunderbolt, you rend even the firmest food (vāja) for our enjoyment or gain.

For the sake of praise, I have offered many songs to Indra, the most bountiful of you wealthy ones, the king of the peoples. || 4 || [The most bountiful] of you [wealthy ones], the king of the [peoples], Indra—for the sake of praise—I have [offered] many [songs]. || 4 ||

Approaching Indra—the most worshipful among all, the king of men (carṣaṇīnām)—who possesses the wealth characterized by the oblations of you (maghonām) who are most bountiful (maṃhiṣṭham), the singers (girah) serve him with ancient words (vāgbhiḥ) for the sake of his praise (praśastaye). They enjoy him with their songs.

To him indeed belongs poetic splendor; for Indra, the hymn is to be recited. To him, the bearer of the sacred word (*brahman*), the Atris increase their songs; the Atris beautify their songs. asmā it kāvyaṃ varca uktham indrāya śaṃsyam | tasmai u brahmavāhase giro vardhanty atrayo giraḥ śumbhanty atrayaḥ || 5 || To him alone belongs the splendor of inspired poetry; for Indra, the hymn is to be recited. For him, who is borne by the sacred word, the Atris augment their songs; the Atris adorn their songs.
To this very Indra, the poetic work (kāvya) belonging to the sage (kavi), that is, the singer;
or alternatively,
[from the root] *ku* "to sound."

That which is to be sounded is speech; that which is of the nature of voice is the *uktha*, the sacrificial recitation (*śastra*), and that which is to be praised is the hymn (*śaṃsya*) to be recited.

Because it is so, therefore, to him—to Indra alone, who carries the sacred formulation (*brahma-vāhas*), the carrier of the powerful hymn—the *Atris* (those of the Atri lineage) increase and magnify their songs of praise. The *Atris* beautify and illuminate those songs.
Furthermore, it is from within the meaning.
“*Ā yāhy adribhiḥ*”: this is the eighth hymn, consisting of nine verses.

Regarding this, the *Anukramaṇikā* states: “*Ā yāhi* [has] nine [verses]; [the first] three are *uṣṇih*, the middle one is an *anuṣṭubh*, and that [verse] is dedicated to Sūrya; because it begins with an *itihāsa* and consists of acts of praise, its deity is the pressing-stones (*adri*) themselves.
[The seer of] the entire [hymn] is...
1. [The letters] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra, and śa do not exist [in this context].
2. By the paribhāṣā rule "śrāmyasmāt" (Anuvāka 12.2), the seer here is Atri.

The first three verses are *uṣṇih*s; the fifth and ninth are *anuṣṭubh*s; and the remaining four are *triṣṭubh*s. Because Atri is being praised here, the sixth verse and those following have Atri as their deity (*atridevatāka*); the fifth is addressed to Āditya (*ādityeya*); the one concerning the Sun (*sūryadevatyā*) is the fifth [of the second group]; and the remaining verses are addressed to Indra (*aindrī*). In the *prauga-śastra* on the third day of the ten-day rite (*daśarātra*), the first triplet is addressed to Indra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Come with the stones to the pressed [juice], in harmony with the Viśvedevas" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.10).
This triplet of verses is also used in the Mahāvrata, in the Auṣṇiha-Cārśāta ritual.
Come hither with the stones to the pressed juice; O Indra, Lord of Soma, drink it, O Bull, most mighty slayer of Vṛtra!
Come! To the Soma pressed by the stones, O Lord of Soma, drink, O Bull Indra, most excellent slayer of Vṛtra, with your bulls! 1.
O Indra, come to our sacrifice;
having arrived, O Lord of Soma, O Indra, drink the pressed Soma extracted by the stones.
O Showerer of benefits, O greatest slayer of Vṛtra, come with the rain-giving Maruts and drink!
The pressing-stone is a bull, the exhilaration is a bull; this pressed Soma is a bull, O Indra, most mighty slayer of Vṛtra, come as a bull to us who are bulls.
The pressing-stone is a bull; the exhilaration is a bull; this pressed Soma is a bull. O Bull Indra, best slayer of Vṛtra, [drink] with the bulls. 2.
The pressing-stone is the means of purification; it is a stone, a bull, a showerer [of rain].
Intoxication is that which is produced by the drinking of Soma; it is a bull, a showerer.
This pressed, purified Soma is a bull.
Drink that Soma together with the bulls.
As a bull, I call upon you, the bull, O wielder of the thunderbolt, with your wondrous aids;
O Indra, bull among bulls, greatest slayer of Vṛtra.
O Bull, I call upon you, the bull, O wielder of the thunderbolt, with your wondrous aids; O Indra, Bull, most excellent slayer of Vṛtra, [I call] with the bulls. 3.
O Vajrin, wielder of the thunderbolt, Indra, bull, you who pour forth the Soma—I, the bull, call upon you, I invoke you.
For what purpose?
For the sake of wondrous, praiseworthy aids (ūtibhiḥ) serving as the means of protection.
The rest has been explained.
"Ṛjīṣī vajrī"—this is the *ājya* offering verse for the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin's *śastra*;
for it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "Ṛjīṣā vajrī vṛṣabhas turāpāṭ" is the *yājyā* (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.16).
1. O most excellent slayer of Vṛtra, O bull-like Indra, [the syllables] ga, gha, ja, pa, pha, ba, and he [are present].

2. O wielder of the thunderbolt, [the syllables] kha, ga, gha, ca, ja, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra, and ' [are present]; "vajravan" does not exist [here]. 3. [The syllables] ga, gha, ja, pa, pha, ba, and tvā mean "you."
4. The *yājyā* for the *ra-śas* sacrifice.

The consumer of the *ṛjīṣa*, the Vṛtra-slayer, the bull, the overcomer of the swift, the impetuous king, the slayer of Vṛtra, the drinker of Soma—having yoked his two bay steeds, may Indra come hither; may he exhilarate himself at the midday libation. *Ṛjīṣī* (the consumer of the *ṛjīṣa*): that Soma which has lost its essence after being pressed at the two previous libations is the *ṛjīṣa*; that which remains of it is the *ṛjīṣin*. *Vṛtrī*: possessing the thunderbolt. *Vṛṣabhaḥ*: the showerer (of benefits). *Turāṣāṭ*: the endurer of the swift, that is, of the rushing enemies. *Śuṣmī*: powerful. *Rājā*: the sovereign lord of all. *Vṛtrahā*: the slayer of Vṛtra. *Somapāvā*: the drinker of the Soma juice. Indra, who is thus endowed with such majesty, having yoked his chariot with his two bay steeds (*haribhyām*), may he approach; may he come toward us. Having arrived, may Indra exhilarate himself with Soma at the midday libation (*mādhyaṃdine savane*).

When, O Sūrya, Svarbhānu, the son of the Asura, pierced you with darkness, all the worlds were bewildered, like one who is deluded and ignorant of his way. (5) With these four verses beginning here, the ritual act of the Atris is celebrated. O Sūrya, O impelling deity, when—*yat*—the son of the Asura, the life-taker, namely Svarbhānu, known by that name, pierced you with darkness created through *māyā*, the meaning being that he enveloped you; then all the worlds (*bhuvanāni*) were bewildered (*adīdhayuḥ*). Just as a mortal person there, not knowing his own place (*akṣetravit*) and being deluded (*mugdhaḥ*), becomes confused, so it was. (13)

Then, O Indra, you struck down the magical illusions of Svarbhānu which were operating below the shining sky; Atri discovered the sun hidden by the lawless darkness through the fourth sacred prayer (brahman). *adha*: then; *yat*: those which; *indra*: O Indra; *māyāḥ*: magical illusions; *avaḥ*: below; *divaḥ*: from the shining sky (the sun); *vartamānāḥ*: operating; *ava-ahan*: you struck down; *gūḷham*: hidden; *sūryam*: the sun; *tamasā*: by darkness; *apavratena*: lawless; *turīyeṇa*: by the fourth; *brahmaṇā*: through the sacred prayer; *avindat*: he discovered; *atriḥ*: Atri. *adha*: then, after the delusion of the world [had occurred]; *svarbhānoḥ*: of the Asura Svarbhānu; *yat*: those which; *māyāḥ*: magical illusions exist. Of what kind? *divaḥ*: from the shining Āditya (the sun); *avaḥ*: below; *vartamānāḥ*: operating. The sense is that they were capable of obscuring it from above.

1. Of the Soma whose essence has gone to *kha*, *ca*, and *ṇa*; of the Soma gone to *jha* and *bha*; of the Soma whose essence has gone to *ta*; [and] of the essence of the Soma. 2. Not swelling (*na-āpyāyamāna*), it is pressed out (*abhiṣuta*). 3. And having come (*āgatya*) to *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, and *śa*, it does not exist.
4. [The letters] ga, gha, ja, pa, pha, and ba are not seen.
5. [The letters] ga, gha, ja, jha, na, bha, and ra [are present] due to the power of concealment; pa, pha, and ba [are present] due to the lack of power for concealment.
O Indra, you have carried, you carry, all of them.

Now, in this very context, there is an indirect mode of expression (*parokṣavāda*). [The verse speaks of] the sun hidden by darkness—that is, by obscurity which has "departed" from its activity; for darkness, being of the nature of an obstruction, is said to have "departed."
Atri found—that is, he obtained—such [a state] through the fourth Brahman, by means of the mantra "Breath is Brahman.
This refers to the sun that is unobscured and pure, which is the means for the removal of veils.
Its status as the "fourth" (turīya) is in relation to the preceding mantras.
The meaning is that having impelled each individual portion of illusion with its respective mantra, he also dispels the latent darkness with the fourth mantra.
Let him not, driven by envy and consumed by fear, swallow up this hymn of mine here;
you are Mitra, whose bounty is directed toward mortals—may you two, along with King Varuṇa, protect me.

Do not! Let him not, having been milked by you through envy while he was still mine, O Atri, fall down out of fear. You are Mitra, whose gifts are true; those two [Mitra and Varuṇa] saw me here, established in splendor, free from concealment—this is the meaning.

The obstruction of the sun by the illusion of Svarbhānu is recorded in the Hāridravika [portion of the Veda]: “The Asura Svarbhānu pierced the sun with darkness; the gods sought an expiation for him. That first darkness they struck away became a black ewe; that second became a Phālgunī ewe; that third became a white ewe; and what was stuck fast to him, they cut off,” and so forth.
When the Asura Svarbhānu pierced the sun with darkness, Atri found it; others were not able to do so.
The son of the Asuras, Svarbhānu, pierced the sun with darkness; the Atris found him, for no others were able. 9.
The text restates the inherent capacity not created by Atri with the words, “The Atris indeed found that sun. This is explained by the nature of the *nigada* (recited mantra) itself:

the meaning is that the Atris, for the sake of Indra, found that sun by gradually illuminating it through praises and salutations to the deities of the Soma sacrifice, thereby dispelling the darkness.
‘By others,’ ‘indeed not,’ ‘being unable, they certainly did not obtain.’
The ninth hymn, consisting of twenty verses beginning with “*ko nu vām*,” has Bhauma Ātreya as its seer (*ṛṣi*).
The sixteenth verse is an *ati-jagatī*, the twentieth is a *virāṭ* with one foot, and the remaining seventeen are *triṣṭubh*s.
The Viśvedevas are the deity (*devatā*).
And thus it has been listed: "What indeed [is] twenty? That belongs to the Viśvedevas; it is with the Ṣoḍaśī, beginning with the Atijagatī, ending with the one-footed verse.
The application is based on indicative marks (liṅga).
Who indeed, O Mitra and Varuṇa, would turn you away from the great heaven or from the earth?
Or in the seat of Truth, may you protect us; or grant us strengths, like those who sacrifice for cattle.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, who among you two, following the cosmic order (*ṛta*), shall protect us from the great heaven or from the earth, or in the seat of the cosmic order, for the one who offers sacrifice, as a provider of cattle, bestows strengths? 1.
"O gods Mitra and Varuṇa, what sacrificer indeed—what person seeking sacrifice while striving for cosmic order (*ṛta*)—could possibly [accomplish this]? (the remainder of the sense is supplied).
Therefore, by their very form: "in the seat of heaven," that is, in the place connected with the celestial world; "in the seat of the great earthly [realm]";
and "in the seat of *ṛta*," that is, of the atmosphere which produces [all things].
And it is called *chadya* because it is the cause of that [protection].
In the three places, the word *naḥ* means "us"; *trāsīthām* means "protect.
The word *vā* has the sense of *ca* ("and").
Furthermore: "He who desires sacrifice, he who seeks sacrifice," and "To the gods and to the giver of the oblation.
[Note: 1. Variant readings kha, ca, ṇa, śa include *nivāraṇam*;
2. Variant readings kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, bha, ra, śa include *prāyaścittam*.]

3. This is the explanation for what is stated in *kha*, *ca*, and *ṇa*; this is the explanation for *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, and *ya*, where the Asura Svarbhānu pierced the sun with darkness, yet he did indeed release it; this is the explanation for what is stated in *jha*, *bha*, and *ra*; this is the explanation for what is stated in *ta*; or this is the explanation for what is stated in *na*. 4. In *ga*, *gha*, and *ja*, "darkness" (*tamaḥ*) is contradictory. 5.
In *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *bha*, *ra*, and *śa*, the phrase "others... indeed" (*anye... khalu*) does not exist.

6. After *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, and *devānām*, [the suffix] *tum* is used for the second person dual (*yuvābhyām*); after *jha*, *bha*, *ra*, and *śa*, [the suffix] *tum* is used for the second person dual (*vām*), or [the suffix] *dātum* is used for the third person singular (*dadātu*).
7. After *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and *śa*, [the suffix] *śaknuvān* is used; after *ra*, [the suffix] *śaknuvan* is used. 8. Also, when *na* follows *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *pa*, *pha*, and *ba*.
9. In the manuscripts ga, gha, ja, pa, pha, and ba, the word “sadasi” is present.
10. In the manuscripts ga, gha, ja, pa, pha, and ba, the word “sadasi” is absent. 11. In the manuscripts kha, va, jha, ṇa, ta, bha, and ra, the phrase “yajñamicchate” is absent.

12. [In the variants] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, bha, ra, śa, the word ‘ca’ is absent. "O you two who possess cattle (paśupaḥ), give us the *vājās*—the *vājās* which sit within the cattle, like milk, curd, and so forth. Grant them to us just as you do. Or rather, it has the sense of the negative particle *na*: "O you two who possess cattle, give us cattle and *vājās*."
May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Āyu, Indra, Ṛbhukṣan, and the Maruts take pleasure in us;
or those who, being of one mind, offer with prostrations a well-fashioned hymn and a praise-song to the bounteous Rudra.

May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Āyu, Indra, R̥bhukṣan, and the Maruts take pleasure in us—whether they are those who, in harmony, offer salutations, or those who present a well-fashioned hymn of praise to the bounteous Rudra. 2.

May those gods, Mitra and the others, accept—through our well-fashioned hymns (*suvṛkti*) or through our offerings (*havirbhiḥ*)—our *stoma*, that is, our praise characterized by the avoidance of evil and so forth, along with our salutations (*namobhiḥ*). Those gods who maintain the aforementioned praise are of two kinds: those who partake of the *stotra* and...
The celestial Sukṣaṇa, Kaṇva the Hotṛ, Trita of heaven, Mujoṣas, Vāta, and Agni;
Pūṣan, Bharga, and Viśvamojas—like horses most excellent in the race, they have hastened forth at the offering.
Sukṣana, Divya, Kaṇvahotṛ, Trita, Sujoṣas of heaven, Vāta, Agni, Pūṣan, Bharga—possessing all power at the offering, they have come like racers to the contest with their swiftest steeds. || 4 ||
Here, the deity is indicated by the gender of the word:
the connection is with the phrase "they went forth.
1. *Sukṣaṇa*: one who favors the sacrifice, or one who endures enemies. 2. *Divya*: celestial, existing in heaven (*divi*). 3. *Kaṇvahotā*: he for whom Kaṇva is the Hotṛ-priest.
He is so described as one whose invokers—the wise seers Kaṇvas—are the Hotṛ priests who offer praise.

4. Trita: extending through the three abodes, beginning with the dwelling place. 5. Of heaven: together with the sun. 6. Well-pleased: having a common course or common delight. 7. Vāta: characterized by upward motion. 8. Vāyu: the wind. 9. Agni: fire. 10. Pūṣan: the nourisher, one who has this name. 11. And Bharga: splendor. 12. At the offering: in this sacrifice where there is the act of bestowing, all the gods are mentioned. 13. Viśvabhojas: the nourishers of all, the protectors of all, or the deliverers of all. 14. Most swift: those possessing the excellence of rapid movement; the most excellent ones. 15. Like a race: as if toward a battle. 16. They have gone forth: they proceed forward.
Bring forth wealth with harnessed horses for you; let the prayer be offered for the seeking of riches and for protection.
May the Hotar-priest of Auśija be very gracious through his rites—those who are your ways, O swift Maruts.

Bring forth wealth with yoked horses for you! Let the prayer be established for the sake of seeking riches and for protection. May the Hotṛ-priest of Auśija be most gracious through his movements—those movements of yours, O swift Maruts. || 5 ||

O Maruts, you indeed must bring forth— accomplish and bestow— wealth, riches, a son fit for horses or accompanied by horses (yuktāśvam). For the sake of attaining (eṣe) riches characterized by cattle, horses, and the like, and for protection (avase)— desiring to protect us— we invoke you.
For the sake of obtaining food or for the protection of wealth, the wise man should offer praise;
he, Agni—the invoker of Kakṣīvat, the son of Uśij—being most gracious (suśeva), [is present] with his steeds, which are means for reaching desires and destinations. *Śeva* is a name for happiness.
May it be very pleasant!
O Maruts, by means of those very desires or horses which belong to you, the swift ones who are crying out.
‘Pra vo vāyum’ is the *yājyā* for the oblation in the sixth animal sacrifice dedicated to Vāyu;
it is prescribed in the Sūtra: “Pra vo vāyuṃ rathayujaṃ kṛṇudhvam uta svām adite mahi” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
Bring forward Vāyu, who yokes his chariot; bring forward the divine sage, the praiser with hymns.
Seeking nourishment, you who follow the cosmic order (*ṛta*), O wise ones, bring hither the wealthy wives here for our prayer.

Bring forth Vāyu, who yokes his chariot; bring forth the god, the inspired singer, who praises with hymns. Seeking [your favor], you who uphold the cosmic order and possess abundant wisdom—may the excellent wives here bestow upon us for our prayer what is necessary for our success. 6.

1. The deities are indicated by the consonants *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *la*. 2. [The syllables] *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, and *na* are to be led [together]. 3. [The syllables] *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *na* express the qualities. 4. [The syllables] *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, and *bha* do not contain the word ‘agni’.
O my priests (*ṛtvij*), you—*vaḥ*—must make Vāyu the god *rathayujam*, yoked to the chariot for the purpose of the sacrifice;
[you must] praise the shining god, the inspired one (*vipram*) who especially fulfills desires, or who is worthy of worship by the best of sages.
The agentive suffix occurs in the sense of the object.
The meaning is "worthy of praise.
Or rather, praise with *arkas*—that is, with hymns that are the means of worship—the giver of rewards.

Furthermore, let the *iṣudhyavas*, the *gandhyas*, the *ṛtasāpas* (those who touch the sacrifice), the *purandhīs* (the wise ones, or those possessing beautiful forms), the *vambīs* (the praiseworthy), the *patnīs* (the wives of the gods) come here to this sacrifice and bestow upon us their favor for our ritual action and for our prayer. They have arrived.

I approach you with these manly, vigorous hymns; come forth from heaven with your enlightening songs! Dawn and Night, like two wise women, bring all things hither for the mortal’s sacrifice. upa | vaḥ | eṣe | vṛṣṇyebhiḥ | śuṣmaiḥ | pra | yāhi | divaḥ | citayadbhiḥ | arkaiḥ | uṣāsānaktā | viduṣī-iva | viśvam | ā | ha | vahataḥ | martyāya | yajñam || 7 ||

O Upas and Naktā—the two deities presiding over day and night—great ones, together with the other gods worthy of praise, I bring forth and offer to you from the sky, that is, from the intermediate region, oblations to every part; for the root *iṣ* signifies "to cause to reach," here joined with the prefix *upa-pra*. With hymns (*arkaiḥ*) that are refreshing, bliss-bestowing, and enlightening, I offer this great oblation.
O you two deities thus described, like two who know all that is to be done, like two kinsmen, you bring the sacrifice toward the mortal sacrificer;
this completes the sense.
Or alternatively:
Some say that words such as *arpis*, ending in the third case plural, are qualifiers of the word *vahnibhiḥ*.

I sing forth to you, the nourishers of the strong steed and the men; to Tvaṣṭṛ, the Lord of the Dwelling, offering gifts. With reverent salutations, may the bountiful and well-pleased Dhiṣaṇā [the Goddess of Inspiration] grant us the lords of the forest and the plants for the seeking of wealth. 8. I sing forth to you, the nourishers of the strong steed and the men; to Tvaṣṭṛ, the Lord of the Dwelling, offering gifts. With reverent salutations, may the bountiful and well-pleased Dhiṣaṇā [the Goddess of Inspiration] grant us the lords of the forest and the plants for the seeking of wealth. 8.
I praise—that is, I extol—you, the leaders of action, who possess nourishment and are joined with many people to be supported.
But who are you?
It is said:
I, rejoicing—either playing with hymns of praise and the like, or bestowing the oblation—[address] Vāstoṣpati and Tvaṣṭṛ.
May Dhiṣaṇā, the goddess of speech, who brings wealth (dhanyā), who goes in harmony with the other gods (sajoṣāḥ), and who gratifies them, [accept] this from me. [Dhiṣaṇā is] Speech.
These nominative cases are used in the sense of the accusative.
The connection is: "I praise with reverential salutations (namobhiḥ) the speech characterized by longing (utkalakṣaṇām vāṇīm), the lords of the forest (vanampatīn), and the plants (oṣadhīḥ).
For what purpose?
"For the seeking of wealth" (rāya eṣe)—that is, in order to obtain riches.

1. *ga-gha-ja-vāyudevam*. 2. *kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-jha-ṇa-śa-rathasaṃbandham*. 3. *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-bha-striyāḥ*. 4. *ta-praśaṃsthāḥ*. 5. *kha-ca-ṇa-bha-asmadīye dhiye*; *ga-gha-ja-asmadīyā dhiye*; *jha-na-2-śa-asmadīyādhāya*. 6. *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-ma-ra-śa-arka haviḥ*. 7. *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-bha-ra-nṛn karmanetṝn* [is not present]. 8. *jha-na-bha-tvaṣṭāraṃ ca*. (Ka. 2.106)

The *parvatas* are those possessing joints (*parvan*) or those possessing fullness; they are clouds. In the sense of "extension" (*tane*) or "giving" (*tuje*). Or else, *tanā* is a name for a son.
The dative case is used in the sense of the genitive.
The meaning is "for the gift of a son.
Alternatively: "May they be *svaitavaḥ*—possessing beautiful movement—for our *tuje*, that is, for our son, and for *tane*, that is, for his son as well.
Of what nature are they?

Those Vasus, the dwellers of the world, who are like heroes—moreover, the Aditya, who is praised, worthy of being approached by all, and worshipful—may he, the god beneficial to men, ever increase our hymn of praise at our invocation or our approach. May he, increasing [our devotion], cause it to prosper.

I have praised the embryo of the mighty one on earth; Trita praises the offspring of the waters with a well-fashioned hymn. Agni, like a hero rushing forward with his companions, he whose hair is flame consumes the forests. I have praised the embryo of the mighty one on earth; Trita praises the offspring of the waters with a well-fashioned hymn. Agni is celebrated like a hero with his followers; he whose hair is flame utterly destroys the woods.
Of the one belonging to the earth; "earth" is the intermediate space (antarikṣa);
[this is] for that which is worthy of it.
Of such a *vṛṣṇi*, the showerer Parjanya; or rather,
of the *vāha* (carrier) of the earth (*bhūmi*), because he bestows appropriate growth upon it—
of such a cloud, [I praise] with a well-fashioned hymn (*suvṛkti*) the *apām napāt*, the lightning-fire which is like the embryo (*garbha*) situated within it and is its protector.
This is an act of praise.
With a hymn that avoids both good and evil, I have praised (astopi) you.

That Trita—the most excellent ford, who is extended across three places or three supports—is Agni. Toward me, the one who goes (etari), he does not roar (gṛṇīte)—that is, he does not make a noise of anger; he does not become wrathful. He does so with his "heroic" (śūraiḥ) rays, which are sources of happiness.
But he, having flaming locks and blazing rays, destroys—that is, consumes—the forests, forest after forest.

What shall we speak as a hymn to the great Rudriya? What to Bhaga, the wise one, for the sake of wealth? May the waters and the plants protect us; may the heaven and the mountains with trees for their hair protect us. 11. What shall we speak as a hymn to the great Rudriya? What to Bhaga, the wise one, for the sake of wealth? May the waters and the plants protect us; may the heaven and the mountains with trees for their hair protect us. 11.
How, in what manner, shall we three speak praises to the great Rudriya, the son of Rudra, the host of Maruts?
And what hymn shall we speak to Bhaga, the god of that name who knows all, for the sake of attaining wealth?
1. ḷ-va-śa-ta-na-bha-2-bhūmam.
2. The fire of *kṣa-va-śa-ta-na-bha-ra*, and furthermore, the fire of the earth;

both those belonging to the gods (*daivyāni*) and those belonging to the earth (*pārthivāni*), as well as births (*janmāni*) and the waters (*apaḥ*)—I shall speak toward these for the sake of the Maruts, who are of noble sacrifice (*sumakhāya*).
May my songs of praise (*giraḥ*) increase.
May such verses increase— those which are radiant, illuminating the meaning of their own words, possessing the brilliance of the moon, and which bring joy or gold to the one who attains them.
May the waves and the rivers, joined by the Maruts and filled with water, swell and become prosperous.

At every step, my old age has been laid down by Varūtrī, or by Śakrā, and by her protections. May the great mother Rasā attend upon us, together with the wise ones—she who is straight-handed and whose path is upright. 15. At every step; for me; old age; has been laid down; by Varūtrī; or; by Śakrā; she who; with protections; may she; attend; the mother; the great; Rasā; us; together with; the wise ones; straight-handed; straight-pathed. 15.
My old age—at every step, at each moment—is laid down upon the earth; that is to say, it is deposited, established, or made to cease.
And she who, being capable (*śakrā*), through her protections (*pāyubhiḥ*) becomes our *varūtrī*, the warder-off of calamities—*vā* being used in the sense of "and."
May the Mother, the creator of all, the great and vast Earth worthy of worship, the delightful one who is the very essence, the ground—may she attend to us, may she favor our praise;
or rather, being praised, may she attend to us.
The word *smat* is a term denoting excellence.
By the praiseworthy sages,
the wise ones who are the causes of praise;
for the sake of pleasing them through their service.
May she who has straight hands, who has hands that are favorable to others, and who possesses a straight path,
be a bestower of auspiciousness.

How may we worship with homage the Maruts, the bounteous givers? O Maruts, come toward our invocation! O Maruts, you of great renown, come toward our invocation! May Ahi Budhnya not deliver us to harm; may he be a winner of superior favor for us. How may we worship with homage the bounteous givers? O Maruts, come toward our invocation! O Maruts, you of great renown, come toward our invocation! May Ahi Budhnya not deliver us to harm; may he be a winner of superior favor for us.

In what manner (*kena prakāreṇa*) might we serve (*dāśema*) or attend upon (*paricarema*) with reverence (*namasā*), with praise (*stotreṇa*), or with fire (*agninā*)—the Maruts, who are of beautiful bounty (*sudānūn*, those whose giving is excellent)?
When there is the occasion of speaking directly (*acchaukau*) toward them in this manner (*evayā*), how indeed (*eva*) might we serve those Maruts?
The sense is that they are difficult to propitiate.
How so?
Those who possess excellent hearing become possessed of superior knowledge;
they are free from doubt.
*Abhigantṛyukti*: [The compound means] "in me who am such as to be praised," or alternatively,
"for the sake of praise directed toward me, who am preeminent (*praśastaḥ*) and excellent (*prakṛṣṭasya*)."

1. I said that to him. 2. [The variants] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, and ra read "because of being difficult to propitiate" (*durārādhyatvāt*); ga, gha, and ja read "difficult to propitiate" (*durārādhyām*).
3. [The variants] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, and ra read "even the vital point" (*marmāpi*).
O Maruts, how may we serve you?
(The repetition is for the sake of emphasis. May the god Ahirbudhnya not deliver us over to the injurer; may he not place us in harm's way.
May that god be our protector; may he be one who bestows superior wealth and is the slayer of enemies.
Thus, O gods, does the mortal man win you for the sake of offspring rich in cattle; O gods, the mortal man wins you.
May Nirṛti swallow even my old age, so that she may consume this auspicious nourishment of my body here.

Thus, O Gods, may you favor this prayer for the sake of offspring rich in cattle; O Gods, may you favor this prayer of mine. Here, grant me a nourishing portion of this auspicious body; let not Destruction swallow even my old age. 17.

O gods, indeed, even thus, may you—the gods—quickly grant [favor] for the sake of offspring consisting of cattle, that is, for progeny accompanied by livestock; so does the mortal, the human sacrificer, entreat you.

The repetition "O gods" is for the sake of emphasis. In this sacrifice, may Nirṛti, the deity, provide auspicious nourishment—that is, food—for me, for this body of my son who has been favored by the gods.
O you who have accumulated old age, swallow old age; let it be swallowed.
O Gods, may we obtain from you that benevolent favor which bestows strengthening nourishment, O Vasus, through the praise of the cow.
May that Goddess, being gracious and bounteous, come swiftly toward us for our well-being.

O gods, may we obtain that benevolence of yours, which bestows strength and nourishment; O Vasus, through the praise of the cow. May she, the goddess of liberal gifts, being gracious, hastening toward us, come for our well-being. 18.

O gods, O Vasus, the dwellers, may we obtain through praise—that is, by means of hymns—from the cow that well-known, auspicious favor (*sumati*) which belongs to you and is the instrument of noble thought;
for as it is said in such passages as "The mind, my dear, consists of food" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.5.4), it is well known [to be so].
And may we obtain from the cow, through praise, *iṣ*, the means of food—namely, food characterized by autumnal curds and the like—which bestows strength and nourishes us.

May she, the goddess, come toward us for our well-being and happiness; may she approach and draw near. That deity is further specified as *sudānuḥ*, one who gives beautiful gifts; *mṛḷayantī*, one who bestows comfort; and *dravantī*, one who comes running toward us.
1. [The letters] kha, ca, ṇa, bha are for beautiful means (*sādhanā*); [the letters] ga, gha, ja are for those possessing beautiful minds (*manas*).
2. One should go to [the letters] ga, gha, ja. 3. Na and śa are the deities (*devatā*).

May Iḷā, the mother of the herd, together with the rivers, or Urvaśī, praise us; or may Urvaśī, praised as dwelling in the great heaven, come toward us, bestowing wide spaces upon the active man. 19. Abhi | naḥ | iḷā | yūthasya | mātā | smat | nadībhiḥ | urvaśī | vā | gṛṇātu | urvaśī | vā | bṛhaddivā | gṛṇānā | abhyūrvānā | prabhūtasya | āyoḥ || 19 ||
May Iḷā, the mother (the creator) of the herd—the multitude of cows—protect us.

Or rather, they say that Iḷā is the daughter of Manu who sustains the cattle. Or else, Iḷā is the speech of the intermediate region (mādhyamikī vāk), the creator of the herd, that is, the host of Maruts.
Alternatively, Urvaśī is the intermediate speech (*mādhyamikā vāk*).
Let her sing together with the rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and others.
It has been said that "one who covers the truth" (*saccchadaḥ*) means one whose speech is praiseworthy.
Let her proclaim its excellence.
Or rather, let Urvaśī—of vast splendor, praising my deed by uttering sounds, and covering [me] over—proclaim it. Whom?
[He bestows] life upon the life of the human sacrificer.
By what means? By the gift of sovereign splendor or of water.
"Nirukta (11.49) states: 'Of the lordly splendor, or of the water.
Alternatively, [it means] of the lordly one—that is, the possessor of power—who, by means of *āyu* (vitality), covers over the sacrifice."
May we partake of the nourishment of the strengthening food.
May he drive away our scabies;
may the one rich in nourishment [drive it away].
Of nourishment.
May she who belongs to King Ūrjavya—so named—and to Puṣṭi, the Nourisher, protect (sirṣaktu) us;
by implication, it is understood that this refers to the host of gods (devasaṃgha).
Alternatively, Urvaśī or the Marut host may be intended, because they are the subject under discussion.
The eighteenth hymn, the tenth, beginning with "pra śatamā," consists of eighteen verses; it belongs to Bhauvana Ātreya and is in the Triṣṭubh meter.
Since the preceding hymn ends with "vai tat," this one is also Vaiśvadeva. The eleventh verse, "tamu ṭuhi," has Rudra as its deity.
The seventeenth [verse] consists of single-footed lines; because of the statement "of these two, the subsequent one consists of single-footed lines," it is not possible to enumerate them further.
Here is the index: "The eleventh, consisting of two fewer than a hundred, is dedicated to Rudra.
The application [of the verses] is based on their indicative marks (*liṅga*).

May the most peaceful song, through our devotion, now reach Varuṇa, Mitra, Bhaga, and Aditi; may they be worthy of our praise. May the Asura, whose source is the back of heaven, who is the invoker of cattle, whose path is unassailable, and who brings bliss, hear us. pra śamtamā varuṇaṃ dīdhitī gīrmitraṃ bhagamaditiṃ nūnamaṃśyāḥ | pṛṣṭhayoniḥ paśvahotā śṛṇotvatṛtapanthā asuro mayobhuḥ || 1 ||

May the most peaceful (śaṃtamā), that is, exceedingly blissful (atyantaṃ sukhakarī) speech (gīḥ)—speech in the form of praise—reach (pra aṃśyāḥ) Varuṇa, Mitra, Bhaga, and Aditi, together with devotion (dīdhitī), that is, through the act of offering oblations (haviṣprakṣepaṇātmakena karmaṇā), now (nūnam) as something unfailing (avitatham).
Furthermore, [may it reach] him whose source is the back (pṛṣṭhayoniḥ).
(Note: The variants *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra* do not contain the word "vāk" [speech], which is absent from the manuscript.)
2. Ga, gha, ja, na, śa, pra: Śatamā. 3. Kha, ca, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra: Prāpnotu.
Vāyu, situated in the intermediate space behind the debts (*pṛṣṭharṇa*), is the fivefold *Pañcahotṛ*, the accomplisher of the fivefold oblation of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth.
Alternatively, "Pañcahotṛ" is a name for Vāyu, for the Śruti states: "Vāyu is Pañcahotṛ; he is Prāṇa."
And may that Vātūthapatha— whose course is unharmed, who is a bestower of wealth, the giver of life, and the abode of bliss— may Vāyu,
characterized in this way, hear our hymn of praise.
May Aditi accept my hymn of praise, as a mother her dear son, like a heart that is most auspicious—
the beloved prayer ordained by the gods, which brings delight to Mitra and Varuṇa.
May Aditi accept my hymn of praise, as a mother her own dear and most gracious son; may I possess that beloved prayer established by the gods, which brings delight to Mitra and Varuṇa. 2.
May Vāc, the goddess, accept—literally "seize"—my hymn, my song of praise;
just as a mother receives her own son, so may she receive it with delight, embracing it as her own offspring. This is the meaning.
Of what nature is it? It is *hṛdayaṅgama*, reaching the heart, and *suśeva*, producing excellent happiness.
This heart is common [to all].

Furthermore, whatever *brahman*—the collection of mantras, that which is dear, that which brings pleasure, that which is beneficial to the gods (*devahita*), and that which is attained by the gods—and whatever *brahman* is *mayobhu*, a means of happiness—that I bestow upon Mitra and Varuṇa; this is the ellipsis.
Or alternatively:
for Mitra and Varuṇa—the deities presiding over day and night—I maintain that aforementioned *brahman*, the sovereign power consisting of rituals such as sacrifice.
"Recite [the verse] 'udīraya'"; this is for the omentum-offering in the eleven-animal sacrifice dedicated to Savitṛ.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Recite the two verses beginning with 'udīraya kavitamaṃ kavīnām' and 'bhagaṃ dhiyaṃ vājayantaḥ purandhim'" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.7).
Proclaim this most excellent hymn for the sages; exalt him with honey and clarified butter.
May the divine Savitar impel toward us the bestowed treasures, the well-disposed and resplendent gifts.
Urge forth the most wise among the sages; let him drink of this with honey and ghee. May the god Savitar bestow upon us excellent, well-presented, and brilliant treasures. 3.
By this [verse], Savitṛ is also praised:

"O officiating priests (ṛtvijaḥ), awaken—meaning, cause to rise upward—the one present before you, Agni or Savitṛ, who is 'the most wise among the wise' (kavīnāṃ kavitamaṃ) and possesses far-reaching vision; [awaken him] with longing.
Anoint—that is, sprinkle—the god Vena with honey, meaning with the sweet juice of Soma and with clarified butter.
The meaning is "may he satisfy.

*Saḥ* (He), the god *Savitṛ*, may *naḥ* (to us) bestow *vasūni* (riches)—such as cattle and other wealth fit for dwelling—*prayatāni* (extended/ready), *hitāni* (beneficial), and *candrāṇi* (delightful) *hiraṇyāni* (gold). The meaning is: "May he grant [these]."

O Indra, Lord of the Bay Steeds, lead us together with the mind, together with cattle, together with wise patrons, and together with well-being; lead us together with the sacred prayer bestowed by the gods, and together with the benevolent favor of the gods worthy of sacrifice.

O Indra, Lord of the Bay Steeds, lead us together with a well-disposed mind, with cattle, with wise patrons, and with well-being; bring us together with the sacred prayer that is ordained by the gods, and with the benevolent favor of the deities worthy of sacrifice. 4.
1. [The sequence] kha-ca-ṇa-na-bha-ra has transcended vision;
[the sequence] kha-ca-ṇa-na-ra lacks the word “*asaḥ*”.
O Indra, with your *manas*, your preeminent mind, you lead us (*naḥ*) together with cattle (*gobhiḥ*). You lead us on.
The meaning is: "Lead us to the cattle.
This applies everywhere [in similar contexts].
O *haṃ*, O *harivaḥ* (possessor of bay horses), like those two bay horses, O *indra*, lead us together with the *sūribhiḥ*—the wise ones, the sons, or the wealthy ones.
Likewise, you lead us with blessings— by means of auspiciousness and security— and you lead us with *brahman*, that is, with abundant food;
by means of that food which is ordained by the gods.
Furthermore, lead us together with the benevolent thought—that is, with the mind of grace—of the gods who are worthy of sacrifice.
May the divine Bharga, Savitar, the portion of wealth, Indra, the conqueror of Vṛtra and the winner of riches,
R̥bhukṣan, Vāja, and Purandhi— the immortal and impetuous ones— protect us.
May the god Bharga, Savitṛ, Aṃśa who bestows wealth, Indra the conqueror of Vṛtra, the winner of riches, Ṛbhukṣan, Vāja, and also Purandhi—may these immortal, swift ones protect us. 5.
In this context, the deities are indicated by their characteristic marks:

Bhaga, the god Savitṛ, Aṃśa—the lord of wealth (*rāyaḥ*)—Tvaṣṭṛ, and Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra; these gods are the complete conquerors (*saṃjitaḥ*) of riches. Furthermore, Ṛbhukṣan, Ṛbhu, Vāja, and also Purandhi, who is called "the many-bestowing" (*bahudhā vibhū*).
And these immortal ones—the gods, such as Bhaga and others, whose nature is deathlessness—being swift and hastening toward our sacrifice, may they protect and guard us.
Let us proclaim the deeds of the one accompanied by the Maruts, the unconquered victor who advances with might.
O Maghavan, neither those of old nor those of later times, nor anyone of the present day, has equaled your heroic power.

O you who are accompanied by the Maruts, let us proclaim the deeds of this unconquered, victorious one as he rises up. Neither those of old, O Maghavan, nor those of later times, nor anyone at present has attained your heroic power.
We, the sacrificers, shall proclaim—that is, make known—the deeds performed by Indra accompanied by the Maruts.
Of what sort is he?
He is "unyielding," meaning he does not retreat or flee in battle.
It is not merely that much;
[it belongs] to the victorious one (*jiṣṇu*), who is ever-conquering and *ūrdyataḥ*, meaning "not aging," that is to say,
eternally youthful.
Now it is stated by direct perception:
"O Maghavan Indra, the men of old, those of ancient times, did not attain your heroic prowess; nor did those of later times attain it."
In short, there is no one at all, however new or marvelous, who has not attained— or does not attain— valor.
Praise Bṛhaspati, the first bestower of jewels, the winner of riches—
he who is most beneficent to him who recites and praises, the possessor of abundant wealth who comes to the one who calls upon him.

Praise Bṛhaspati, the first bestower of jewels, the winner of riches—he who, most beneficent and possessing abundant wealth, comes to the one who calls upon him, for the sake of the one who recites and praises. 7.
1. In the manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra, and śa, the word "saṃ" is absent.
2. In the manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra, and śa, the reading is "asmabhyam".
3. In the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ja, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra, the word "svastibhiḥ" is absent.
4. [The reading] *kha-ca-ga* has *ajīryamāṇasya*.
5. [The reading] *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra* has *kaśca āścaryabhūtaḥ*. [End of] the fourth Aṣṭaka, Chapter 5, Section 3, Sūtra 42; [page] 849.

O Inner Self, you are the first—that is, the primary, most excellent, and unsurpassed one. You are the bestower of delightful wealth, the gatherer and distributor of riches characterized by oblations.
Alternatively, here the word *ratna* refers to gems, pearls, and the like, while the word *dhana* refers to cattle and other such assets.
Praise Bṛhaspati, the lord and master of the great mantra, the divine one who brings across [the seeker] like a cow;
that god who, being most conducive to happiness (*śambhaviṣṭha*), becomes the greatest bringer of bliss for the sacrificer of the Aṅgiras clan who praises him with hymns;
and who, possessing abundant wealth (*purūvasu*), comes to the sacrificer who calls upon him—praise him.
O Bṛhaspati, through your protections, may we be true, unharmed, and possessed of brave sons;
among those who bestow horses or cattle, and those who grant wealth, may there be auspicious riches for us.

O Bṛhaspati, accompanied by your protections, may we be unharmed, possessing liberal patrons and brave sons. Among those who give horses, or those who give cattle, or those who give garments—among those fortunate ones, let there be riches. 8.
O Bṛhaspati, those who associate with your protections— that is, who come together under your guardianship— become unharmed, uninjured, wealthy, possessing excellent heroes (fine sons),
and those favored by you become givers of many horses; or indeed, they become givers of cattle.
And those who are "vakṣadāḥ" (bestowers of vigor) and "subhagāḥ" (fortunate ones) possessing beautiful wealth—in all of them, "rāyaḥ" (riches) may abound; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Render their wealth useless for those who enjoy it while withholding offerings from us with their hymns;
deprive of light from the sun those haters of sacred knowledge who grow strong in their lawlessness during the creative impulse.

Make their wealth perish—those who enjoy it without offering hymns of praise! Those who are lawless, who have grown strong in their own way, and who hate sacred prayer: deprive them of the light of the sun! 9.
O Brahmaṇaspati, make the wealth of these—who are about to be mentioned—disperse, that is, make it prone to scattering away.
To whom does "of these" refer? He says:
those who consume [the offerings] while not giving, that is, while not bestowing gifts.
From whom?
From those distinguished by *ukthas*—the *śastras* that set forth praises—from us.

Separate from the sun those haters of prayer (*brahmadviṣaḥ*), who have abandoned their proper duties (*apavratān*) and are increasing in the world of men which is characterized by birth (*prasave*). Keep them far away.
The meaning is: "Place [it] in darkness."

O Maruts, strike down those two Rākṣasas who, at the divine feast, have acted as obstructors; he who reviles the protection of you who are performing your service shall have his empty desires fulfilled, even though he knows better.

O Maruts, come down upon that Rakshasa at the feast of the gods with your wheelless [missiles]—upon him who reviles the protection of you who are striving, and who, though knowing better, makes empty desires for himself. 10.
1. The gift of wealth through *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *ra*, and *śa*.
2. Through *jha*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *rakṣaṇa*.
3. The praise of well-being through *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, *śa*, and *sva*.
The sacrificer (*yajamāna*) drives away the powerful *rakṣasa*s (demons) to the feast of the gods (*devavīti*).
That which is called *devavīti* is where there is the eating or the enjoyment of the gods.
In that sacrifice,
by means of performing it otherwise [than prescribed] and so forth, they make it demonic;
O Maruts, go down— that is, lead— that sacrificer into darkness with wheelless chariots.
Alternatively,
the word "acakrebhiḥ" connects with what precedes;
by the word "cakra," those lacking wisdom (ajñānin) are meant.
Again and again, with the principal [sacrifices] alone, devoid of their constituent parts (*aṅga*), he ascends—that is, he attains [the goal].
For a ritual action accompanied by its constituent parts (*sāṅga*) reaches the gods.

And as for your ritual action characterized by praise, which belongs to me who am reciting it—[he] censures it; having censured the ritual action consisting of the Jyotiṣṭoma and other such forms, he himself creates trivial and perishable desires, the enjoyments produced by gambling and the like, while tormenting his own self.
Or else, he renders the desirable enjoyments among you worthless.
Praise him who is well-armed among women, he who rules over all healing medicine.
Worship Rudra for his great goodwill; honor the divine Asura with prostrations.

Praise him with "Ūm!"—him who possesses the excellent arrow and the excellent bow, he who rules over every healing medicine. Worship Rudra for his great goodwill; honor the divine Asura with prostrations. 11.
O Ātman, praise— that very Rudra— perform a hymn of praise to him who is well-armed with arrows and possesses a beautiful bow,
being excellent because he is the slayer of adversaries.
And He is the master (*īśvara*) who will cause the healing of every medicine and remedy;
because there is no medicine other than God for the pacification of bodily and worldly calamities, or because He is God Himself, He possesses the nature of being the supreme medicine.
This is supported by such scriptural passages as: "I hear of You as the best of physicians among physicians" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 2.33.4).
Furthermore, we invoke and worship that very god Rudra, the deliverer from suffering or from sin caused by its means, for the sake of great *saumanasa*—that is, for a well-disposed mind;
for it is well known that peace of mind results from the propitiation of the Lord.
Moreover, with obeisances (*namas*), oblations (*havis*), or salutations, [we worship] the shining god, the bestower of wealth (*vasu*), who is present here.
The meaning is "the powerful one. Alternatively, it means "he worships," that is, he serves Rudra, the giver of life.
May those who are skillful-handed, active, and destroyers of enemies; the wives of the Bull, established on all sides in heaven;
Sarasvatī, Bṛhaddivā, and Rākā—may these radiant goddesses, looking upon us, grant us wide space and prosperity.
The skillful workers, deft-handed, the wives of the bull, the all-fashioning nymphs—Sarasvatī, Bṛhaddivā, and Rākā—may these radiant ones, looking upon us, grant us wide space. 12.
Here, the deities are indicated by their names:

the *vadmūnasas*—those whose minds are intent on giving, or whose minds are self-controlled; the *vapasaḥ*, who possess beautiful deeds such as [the making of] ladles, cups, horses, chariots, and so forth.
The sacrifice is cut off.
Therefore, those Ṛbhus are indeed "well-handed," meaning they possess skillful hands.
The wives (patnīs) of Vṛṣṇi, the showerer Indra—wives meaning protectresses.
Others are the roaring rivers, such as the Gaṅgā and so forth.
Fashioned on all sides by Viśvakarman, they were made by the Ribhus with their middle [hand].
Sarasvatī is either the river of that name, or the goddess of speech; Vṛhaddivā means "possessing abundant radiance."
And furthermore, the goddesses Vrākās, who bestow desires, are gazing upon [the practitioner].
May those bright and radiant ones grant us prosperity; may they desire wealth for us.

1. Kha, ca, ṇa: the meaning is "he makes [it] demonic" (āsurīkaroti); jha, ta, ra: the meaning is "he makes [it] quick/easy" (āsukarā karoti). 2. Ga, gha, ja, śa: the word "of one praising" (śaṃsamānasya) is absent. 3. Jha, śa: "of a Lord who is distinct" (īśvarasya vyatiriktasya); ta, ra: "or of a Lord who is non-distinct" (īśvarasya vātiriktasya).
I offer this newest, newly-born hymn of wisdom to the Great One, the excellent refuge— He who,
fashioning forms within the breasts of his daughters, has brought forth this light for us.

To the great one, the excellent refuge, I bring forth this newest prayer, a song of wisdom now being born—[the song] of him who, impetuous, fashioning forms within the womb of his daughter, brought forth this for us. 13.

7. *Su* (well), *pra* (forth), *bhare* (I offer)—I accomplish with excellence—for *maha* (the great), *suśaraṇāya* (for the one who is a beautiful protector), for *Indra*, for *Parjanya*, or for *Sukha* (Happiness).
What?
*Medhām* (wisdom), that which is placed in the mind, and *giram* (speech), that is, praise.
Of what kind? "Navyasīm" means newer, more recent, or exceedingly praiseworthy; "jāyamānām" means being born, currently arising, or fresh—this is the meaning.

May he who is Indra or Parjanya, the striker, the slayer, the pourer, for the benefit of the daughter—that is, the earth who occupies the position of a daughter—making various forms in the channels, that is, the rivers, create this water for us. May he do so.
O singer, may your excellent praise now reach the Lord of Refreshment (*iḷaspati*), who thunders and roars— he who,
possessing waters and possessing the clouds, sends forth rain with lightning, drenching both heaven and earth.

O singer, may your excellent praise now reach the Lord of nourishment, who thunders and roars—the one who, possessing waters and possessing the clouds, impels the two worlds with his triple lightning as he pours forth rain.

Here Parjanya is praised. 7. *Suṣṭutiḥ* means an excellent hymn of praise. 7. *Stanayantam* means roaring; 7. *ruvantam* means making a sound produced by his own color. 7. *Iḷaḥ* means of food or of water; 7. *patim* means the lord or master. 7. O 7. *jaritar*, O singer, may your hymn of praise 7. *nunam* 7. *pra* 7. *aśyāt*—may it pervade him thoroughly.
7. And that Parjanya who is 7. *abdimān* (possessed of water).
The cloud is the year-long container of waters;
it possesses that. 7.
Possessing rain, 7. possessing water, 7. with lightning—that is, with the flash—7. sprinkling the two worlds, heaven and earth, 7. it 7. sends forth; it moves forward.
This hymn is directed toward the Marut host, the sons of Rudra, who are eager for the sacrifice and swift in their onset.
Desire for wealth calls out to me for well-being; praise the tireless ones who have spotted deer as their steeds!

This hymn has reached the host of Maruts; may it go forth toward the youthful sons of Rudra. Desire calls me for wealth; may there be well-being for me. Praise the tireless ones who have spotted deer as their steeds! 15.
May this hymn (stoma), which is a song of praise (stotra) addressed to the Maruts—the host (śardhaḥ), the strength of the Maruts—reach them (accha), that is, attain them face-to-face.
Having praised them as a collective group, he speaks of them again as a collective group:
"the sons of Rudra."
This [speech] was uttered once by Rudra, who conceived of them as his sons:
"O mind, you who desire to mix with young men, rise up— be uplifted and exceedingly expansive."
Desire, which is volition, calls me—me, the imperishable (*svarit*)—for the sake of wealth (*rāye*), meaning it impels me;
since this is so, therefore, having approached (*upa*), praise the *pṛṣadaśvas* (those with spotted horses), who are the *ayāsas* (the unwearied ones) that go to the sacrifice.
May my praise reach the earth, the mid-air, the forest trees, and the plants for the sake of wealth.
May every god be easy for me to invoke; may Mother Earth not grant us evil thoughts.

May this hymn of praise reach forth to the earth, to the mid-air, to the trees, and to the plants, so that we may attain wealth. May every god be easy for me to invoke. May Mother Earth not deliver us over to ill-will. 16.
May this hymn—this praise—reach the deities such as Earth and the others.
For what purpose?
For the sake of wealth.
May every god be easy to invoke for me—that is, may he become one who is easily summoned. May she, the Mother—the creator of all—be [favorable] toward us in our evil thoughts;
or alternatively: [may she protect us].
May the Earth, who is the mother of Atri through her remainder consisting of Bhīmaratva and the rest, establish me as such— may she place me [therein].
May we be free from oppression in the wide space granted by the gods.
O gods,
in the wide, unoppressed [space].
May we be.
O gods, may we, your kin, abide in that vast, great, and unobstructed happiness which is entirely free from affliction. May we, the three of us, become such.
May we go forth under the newest, bliss-bestowing protection of the Aśvins, with their excellent guidance.
Bring to us wealth and heroic sons, and all forms of immortal happiness.
O Aśvins, through your newest protection, which brings about well-being, may we proceed with excellent guidance. Bring to us wealth, and also heroic sons, and all immortal blessings, O Immortals. 18.

May we come together with the Aśvins through their newest protection—newer than those experienced by others—which is bliss-bestowing, a bringer of happiness, and characterized by excellent guidance. O immortal Aśvins, bring wealth to us;
bring also heroic sons endowed with great valor.
Bring hither all auspicious fortunes as well.
The hymn beginning with “ā dhenavaḥ” consists of seventeen verses; it is composed by Atri, is in the Triṣṭubh meter, and is addressed to the Viśvedevas.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇī states: “ā dhenavaḥ—[these] two [verses] are in the Cyūṣṇik meter; the next is an ekapadā.
The application [of the hymn] is determined by its indicative marks (liṅga).
The *ādhānuvacanīyā* [verse] is recited when the waters for the *aponaptrīya* rite and the *ekadhanā* vessels are being led toward the *havirdhāna* shed.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "‘The milch-cows come with their milk, eager for the goal; some come together, others approach’" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 5.1).
1. The meaning is "that which causes fear" (āhayati) [is derived from the letters] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, and bha.
2. [The word] netrī [is derived from the letters] kha, ca, and ṇa. 3. [The word] vayamatraya [is derived from the letter] na.

May the milch-cows, their purpose fulfilled by their milk, come toward us with sweetness, never failing. For the sake of great wealth, the inspired singer loudly calls upon the seven mighty ones who bring bliss. ā dhenavaḥ payasā tūṇyarthā amardhantīrupa no yantu madhvā | maho rāye bṛhatīḥ sapta vipro mayobhuvo jaritā johavīti || 1 || May the milch-cows, whose aim is the udder, come to us with milk, unceasingly, with sweetness. For the sake of great wealth, the inspired singer—the chanter—loudly invokes the seven mighty ones who are sources of bliss.

May the cows—the nourishing rivers—accompanied by sweet, honey-like milk and essence, moving swiftly for the sake of the water-vessels (tūṇī), as Yāska says in the Nirukta (1.14): "They are 'adhorthaiḥ'";
may they, being non-injurious and not causing harm, come toward us and approach us.

For that purpose—for great wealth—he, the inspired singer (*vipra*), the one who especially gladdens, the chanter (*jaritṛ*), repeatedly calls upon the great ones, the vast seven rivers whose nature is to flow, or rather the Gaṅgā and others mentioned in the mantra "This [water] of mine, O Gaṅgā... (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.75.5); for there, seven are primarily enumerated. These are the "blessers," the bringers of happiness. The inspired singer, the one who especially gladdens, the chanter, repeatedly calls upon them.

May Heaven and Earth, the bountiful ones, be brought hither by our fair praise and our homage for the sake of strength. Father and Mother, sweet of speech and skillful-handed, may you two, glorious ones, protect us in every battle. ā suṣṭutī namasā vartyadhyai dyāvā vājāya pṛthivī amṛdhre | pitā mātā madhuvacāḥ suhastā bharebhare no yaśasāvaviṣṭhām || 2 ||

With excellent praise, with beautiful hymns, with reverence, and with oblations, I desire to turn hither the two worlds, Heaven and Earth, which are unfailing and free from harm, for the sake of strength—that is, for the attainment of food;
for the Śruti says, "Strength (*vāja*) is indeed food" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.3.6.6).

May the Father, the protecting Heaven, and the Mother, the fashioning Earth, who possess sweet speech, speak kindly, and have beautiful hands through the granting of desired gifts, [turn them hither].
These two are qualified by both [epithets]. O you two glorious ones, endowed with fame, Heaven and Earth, protect us—*aviṣṭam*—in every battle or sacrifice.

O Adhvaryus, having prepared the sweet juices, bring forth the lovely, bright [Soma] for Vāyu. O God, drink of this first portion of our honeyed [Soma] like a Hotṛ-priest; we have offered it to you for your exhilaration. 3. O Adhvaryus! Having prepared the sweet juices! Bring forth! For Vāyu! The lovely! The bright! Like a Hotṛ-priest! For us! First! Drink! Of this! O God! Of the honey! We have offered! To you! For exhilaration! 3.

1. Either those numbering seven: *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *bha*, *sa*; or those numbering seven: *ta*, *ra*, *sa*. 2. He offers with *kha*, *jha*, *bha*, and *ā*. 3.
