In *kha*, *ca*, and *ṇa*, the phrase "the two unimpaired ones... earth" is absent; in *jha*, *na*, *ma*, and *ra*, it is "heaven and earth."

4. [Regarding the variants: In the *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, and *bha* recensions, the reading "śobhanahastā" (having beautiful hands) due to the granting of desired objects is absent; in the *ga*, *gha*, and *ja* recensions, it is "śobhanahastā.

O *adhvaryu*s, you who are engaged in the sacrifice (*adhvara*), having prepared (*cakṛvāṃsaḥ*) the sweet juices (*madhūni*)—the soma, clarified butter, and so forth—bring forward (*pra bharata*) first for Vāyu the beautiful (*cāru*), the excellent (*caraṇīya*), and the bright (*śukra*) soma.
O Vāyu, like a *hotṛ* priest—just as the *hotṛ* drinks first—drink this Soma for our sake; drink it first, before the other gods.
O divine Vāyu, we have offered the sweet Soma juice to you for your exhilaration.
Vāyu’s priority in drinking is well-established.
The two arms, the ten fingers, and the two well-skilled preparers of Soma join together the pressing-stone;
with skillful hands, the mountain-dweller has milked the bright, pure ray of the honeyed juice from the plant.

The ten fingers join the arms; they are the two skillful-handed preparers of the Soma. With beautiful hands, he has extracted the mountain-dwelling essence of the honeyed juice; the stalk has yielded the bright, pure sap. 4.
Since the pressing is being performed here, Soma is the deity;
or alternatively, it is Indra.
They join—that is, they take hold of—the *adr̥*, the pressing-stone, with the ten fingers, which are the ten countable digits.
Or rather:
they become joined with one another;
the two arms belonging to the Adhvaryu join the pressing-stone.
Those two arms, which have beautiful hands—that is, excellent striking instruments—and which are the preparers and pressers of the soma, they employ.

The Adhvaryu, with beautiful fingers (*sugabhasti*), causes the sweet juice of the soma—which dwells on the mountain (*giriṣṭhām*), meaning it stays upon the mountain or is situated in a place of descent like a mountain—to flow forth, gladdening [the gods].

The word *cadi* is a Vedic form derived from the root *cad* meaning "to delight," with the suffix *luṅ* elided. *Duduhe* means "he milks. And that *aṃśu* (soma-stalk) "milks," that is, yields, the *śukram*, the pure essence.
When there is a single sentence:
*aṃśuḥ* (the stalk), *vyāsaḥ* (extended), *sugabhastiḥ* (having beautiful rays), *suhastaḥ* (having good hands)—the *adhvaryu* priest milks, that is, he draws out, the sweet juice (*madho rasaṃ*).

The Soma has been pressed for you who take pleasure in it, for the sake of will, for skill, and for great exhilaration. Being invoked, bring Indra hither with his two bay steeds, well-yoked to the chariot at the time of the rite, making them dear to him.

The Soma has been pressed for you who enjoy it, for the sake of will, for great skill, and for exhilaration. When you are being invoked, bring the two bay horses, well-yoked to the chariot, toward us at the time of harnessing; make Indra dear to you. 5.
O Indra, for you who take pleasure in it, the Soma has been pressed.
For what purpose?
For every purposeful action such as the slaying of Vṛtra, for strength, for great exhilaration, and for intoxication.

Since this is so, therefore, O Indra, being invoked, having yoked to the chariot your two beloved bay horses, *harī*, which are well-yoked—that is, appointed to the beautiful pole—or rather, already harnessed for the occasion of the yoke, turn that chariot toward us, making it face our direction.

1. Not delightful. 2. O God, [the syllables] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra, and vā are missing. 3. Hands that are not beautiful. 4. In the manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, and ra, the word "śamitārī" is absent. 5. In the manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, and śa, the word "tau" is absent. 6. Pervading: kha, ca, ṇa, and bha. [Maṇḍala 5, Anuvāka 5, Adhyāya 3, Sūtra 43; Fourth Aṣṭaka, Verse 855]

Bring hither to us, O Agni, the great Aramati, who is well-disposed, the goddess who is honored with reverence and to whom offerings are presented; bring her, the lofty one who knows the eternal Law (Ṛta), for the exhilaration of the sweet mead, by means of the many paths traveled by the gods. 6.
In this context, having addressed Agni prior to the invocation of the deity, Agni himself is the deity.
O Agni, being "asajoṣāḥ"—that is, rejoicing together with us—you [should approach] "mā," the goddess who is to be reached by all and who makes this known;
as Yāska says: "‘Menā mā’ means ‘the exhausted one’" (Nirukta 3.21).
"Bring [them] hither toward us, for our sake, by means of the paths—the ways to be traveled by the gods—along the god-going routes.
How so? Let our song of praise go forth toward the Aśvins to call them, like a messenger, as it were, to summon them."
The speech is distinguished [as follows]:
"Mahī" means worshipful; "bṛhatī" means great; "śantamā" means most blissful.
O Aśvins, "mayobhuvā," you two who bring about happiness, being "marathā," that is, riding on a single chariot, "arvāk yātam"—come toward us—to the "nidhim," the deposited Soma.
The *dhura* is that which bears the burden; the *nābhi* is the central pivot, like a pin.

Just as a chariot whose pivot is not firmly fixed cannot function, so too Soma, when separated from you two, cannot carry out the sacrifice—it is for the sake of making this known that this simile is employed.
"I have directed my prayer toward the most powerful Pūṣan, and also toward the swift Vāyu."
Those two who, by their bounty, are the inspirers of prayers, who are the givers of wealth and of strength, even by their own nature.

I have proclaimed the hymn of homage to the most powerful and swift Pūṣan, and also to Vāyu—those two who are the impellers of thoughts through their bounty, who are the bestowers of strength and wealth, and who do so by their own inherent power. 9.

I, the seer, offer forth a word of praise—the utterance "namas," a hymn—to Pūṣan, the nourisher, the god who possesses the aforementioned qualities, who is most excellent, of preeminent strength, swift, and hasting; and also to Vāyu, who likewise possesses those characteristics. I offer this praise to those two, Pūṣan and Vāyu, who, by means of the sacrificial offering characterized as *rādhas*, are the impellers and stimulators of our thoughts.
Alternatively,
the instrumental case in *rādhasā* expresses the sense of the genitive; thus,
they are the two who impel both wealth (*rādhas*) and thoughts (*matī*).

And you two gods, who are the impellers of *vāja*—whether it be food or battle—even by yourselves (*ātman*), without being prompted by another, may you both become bestowers of wealth (*draviṇodas*). O Jātavedas, being invoked, bring hither all [the gods] with their various forms through our songs; O Maruts, come all of you to the sacrifice, to the singer’s well-spoken praise, with all your aids.

O Jātavedas, being invoked, bring hither all the Maruts with their names and with their forms; come all you Maruts to the sacrifice, to the songs and the beautiful praise of the singer, all of you with your aids. 10.

O Jātavedas, being invoked by us—meaning one whose wisdom has been born and who is being summoned by us—you bring hither all the Maruts, as well as all the gods who partake of hymns and oblations, by their names characterized as Indra, Varuṇa, and so forth;
and you bring the sacrifice by their forms characterized by having a thousand eyes, holding the thunderbolt in hand, and so on.

Furthermore, O Maruts, all of you [accept] our sacrifice, or the oblation related to the sacrifice; [accept] the songs—the words of praise—belonging to the singer, the praiser; and [accept] the "good praise" (suṣṭuti), the praise accomplished by those [songs] which yields auspicious fruit. The singular number is used for the praise as a whole (the composite), while the plural number is used for its constituent parts.
The praise of the sacrifice having been uttered, come hither;
and you all, O Viśve, come with *ūti*—that is, with protection.
‘Ā no divaḥ’ is the eleventh [verse]; in the expanded ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), on the ninth day, it is the second [verse] in the *prauga* recitation when the deity is Sarasvatī.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: ‘Ā no divo bṛhataḥ parvatād ā sarasvatībhyo no neṣi vasyaḥ’ (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 8.11).

1. Not illustrated by an example; therefore, you two, come, approach. 2. To the one possessing the qualities mentioned in the versions kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, and ra; in version ta, "to the one possessing the mentioned qualities. 3. In version ta, "the two who are impelled. 4. In versions ga, gha, ja, and śa, "by the very act of impelling. 5. In versions kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, and ra, the word "yajñam" (sacrifice) is absent. 6. In versions kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, and ra, the reading is "avayavyāḥ" (of the composite whole). 7. In versions kha, ca, and ṇa, it says "ganta āgacchata" (O goer, come); in version bha, it says "ganta eta" (O goer, come here).

May Sarasvatī, the worshipful goddess, come from the great heaven and from the mountain to our sacrifice. May she, the divine one, delighting in the oblation and dripping with clarity, graciously hear our effective word as she desires it. 11. From the great heaven, from the mountain, may the worshipful Sarasvatī come to our sacrifice. May the goddess, rejoicing in the offering, dripping with clarity, desiring it, graciously hear our effective word. 11.
May the goddess Sarasvatī, who is to be worshipped (*yajñīyā*), come from the shining sky (*divaḥ*) to our sacrifice (*yajñam*);

likewise, may Sarasvatī come from the great mountain (*bṛhataḥ parvatāt*)—that is, from the atmosphere which possesses mountains, or which is full, or which delights—or from the cloud. By this, the intermediate speech (*mādhyamikī vāk*) is expressed.
Alternatively, this is an adjective qualifying *divaḥ*.
For there are indeed three joints (*parvan*) of the heavenly world, according to such Vedic revelation as, "Three are the heavens, [and] the earths.
In this view, the second vowel *ā* is a filler (*pūraṇa*).

For that purpose, may the goddess Sarasvatī, graciously accepting our invocation and enjoying our praise, she who is *ghṛtācī*—anointing herself with *ghṛta*, which is water—listening with desire to our effective and bliss-bestowing speech of praise, may she hear us.

Seat in the sacred place the ordainer, the blue-backed, the great Bṛhaspati. May we serve him who shines within the home of the two worlds, the golden-hued and ruddy one. 12. Seat in the sacred place the ordainer, the blue-backed, the great Bṛhaspati. May we serve him who shines within the home of the two worlds, the golden-hued and ruddy one. 12.
This verse belongs to Bṛhaspati.
O officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), you must seat—that is, establish—in our sacrificial hall (*sadana*) the god Bṛhaspati, the lord of the great mantra (*bṛhat*).
What kind of god?
We, manifesting ourselves, shall serve— that is, we shall attend upon— the ordainer, the maker of various things, the blue-backed one with smooth limbs, the vast and great;
he who exists in such a manner is further specified.

Seated in the womb of the two good ones, in the house—that is, in the sacrificial hall—shining brightly on all sides, golden-hued (meaning of a color that is pleasingly beautiful), ruddy—that is, ascending;
or rather, this [verse] pertains to Agni.
Bṛhaspati is designated as the master of the extensive, encompassing ritual act.

Likewise, by such signs as his dark-blue color, his back being like smoke, his abode, his sound, and his golden hue, he is indeed Bṛhaspati. "May the one who supports the vast heaven come, bestowing gifts, with all his swift movements, being invoked; clothing himself in plants, the bull with three-layered horns, the giver of vigor. (RV 2.23.13) May the supporter of the great heaven come, bestowing gifts, with all his swift movements, being invoked; clothing himself in the plants, the unassailable one, the bull with three-layered horns, the bestower of vitality. (13)
1. [The syllables] *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, and *ha* are pleasing (*ramaṇīya*). In the versions *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, and *ra*, the term "*hita-ramaṇīya-varṇa*" (of pleasing color) does not exist.
According to *ka* 2-1-8, this is improper; this is thus.
May Agni come; may he approach our sacrifice—he who maintains all things, possessing vast radiance, rejoicing, or bestowing desires, being invoked together with all protective powers.

He who fills the quarters with his flames and clothes himself in plants, who is unassailable, unhindered, and possesses a threefold luster—his flames appearing in three ways as blue, red, white, and black—he is the bull, the showerer of benefits, the bestower of vital strength, or the sustainer of the oblation.
At the highest station of the Mother, in the pure light, the two praising ones have come, breathing forth their song;
with reverence, they who have offered oblations approach the most gracious one, as living beings bathe a child for its clothing.
At the mother’s highest, radiant station, the Āyus, longing for praise, have come to the most gracious one, offering oblations with their hymns. Like men for clothing, the Āyus bathe the infant. 14.
O you who are worthy of praise, this is the life-span of the human sacrificer;
it belongs to the praisers—
the Hotṛ and the others— who are full of resonant speech.
*Rā* refers to wealth characterized by the oblation (*havis*). Those [vessels] such as the *juhū* touch that [wealth]; therefore, it possesses *rā*, and thus is called *rāsvī*.
Those who possess that are the Rāspiras.

The officiating priests (ṛtvijas), described as above, went to— that is, they approached and attend upon— the Son of the Mother, the Fashioner, who stands upon the radiant, supreme station, the high altar (uttaravedi). For that purpose, having offered oblations (rātahavyāḥ) with reverence and praise, they cleanse and purify the Child, who is most auspicious (suśevya) for the sake of happiness and who has just been born, for the sake of his dwelling (vāse).
In this regard, there is an illustration:
"like Āyavas" means like ordinary worldly men;
just as they immerse a child in water for the sake of bathing, so it is here.
O Agni of vast power, for you who are great, the two pairs that offer praise through their devotion attend upon you.
May every god be easy for me to invoke; may Mother Earth not grant us evil thoughts.

Great is your power, O Agni; for you, the great one, the couples, long-lived through their devotion, attend upon you. May every god be easy for me to invoke; may Mother Earth not set us in an evil state of mind. 15.
O Agni, [those] who have grown old through age (*dhiyāja*)—that is, worn out by ritual action (*karman*)—serve you, the great and abundant food (*vayaḥ*), as couples accompanied by their wives.
This is based on such injunctions as, "The husband and wife should establish the sacred fire" (*jāyāpatī agnimādadhīyātām*).

For it is established in the sixth chapter on qualification (*adhikārādhyāya*) that women also possess the right to perform rites, and that this right is shared with the husband (Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra 6.1.24).
The remainder has been explained.
1. In manuscripts Kha, Kṣa, Na, Bha, and Ra, "abhiḥ" is absent.
2. In manuscripts Ga, Gha, and Ja, "vā" is absent.
3. In manuscripts Kha, Ca, Kṣa, Na, Bha, and Ra, it is "kṛṣṇajvālaḥ"; in manuscript Śa, it is "kṛṣṇabahujvālaḥ".
4. In the manuscripts kha, ca, ṇa, and na, "abhajante" is absent; in jha, ta, bha, and ra, it is read as "ajñate.

5. In kha, ca, jha, ṇa, and bha, it is "susukhā"; in na and ra, it is "susukhāya. 6. In kha, ca, ṇa, and dā, it is "dātahavyā haviṣkāḥ"; in jha, bha, and ra, it is "dātavyahaviṣkāḥ"; in śa, it is "dātavyahaviṣkāḥ."
7. [The vowel *i* is substituted] for *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, and *ma* when followed by a heavy syllable (*mahate*).
8. [The vowel *u* is substituted] for *kha*, *ca*, *kṣa*, *na*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *da* when followed by a short vowel (*patibhiḥ*).

O Gods, may we abide in a wide space, free from oppression. (16) May we go forth together with the newest, joy-bestowing protection of the Aśvins, under their excellent guidance. O Immortals, bring to us wealth, and heroes, and all auspicious blessings. (17)
The explanation is concluded.
The twelfth hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with "taṃ pratnathā," has an *ṛṣi* named Avatsāra, who belongs to the Kaśyapa lineage.
In those verses where Sadāpraṇa, Bāhu, Vṛktabarhiṣ, and others are mentioned, they too are included therein.

The fourteenth and fifteenth verses are *triṣṭubh*s; the remaining verses are *jagatī*s according to the rule regarding those ending in *triṣṭubh*. The deities are the Viśvedevas. And it has been recorded: “‘Taṃ pratnathā’—consisting of five fewer [verses]—is by Kāśyapa Avasāra; other seers are also seen here as indicators; it ends in *triṣṭubh*.”
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, when there is an excess [of verses], the Āditya hymn consisting of thirteen ṛcs is to be recited.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “Of the thirteen [verses] beginning with ‘taṃ pratnatha,’ having left out one, he should ascend the *dūrohaṇa*. (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.9).

As of old, as formerly, as always, as now—him, the most excellent, seated upon the sacred grass, the finder of light; him who turns toward us, the enclosure, you milk with your song—the swift one, the conqueror, whom you strengthen in these [praises]. 1. As of old, as formerly, as always, as now—him, the most excellent, seated upon the sacred grass, the finder of light; him who turns toward us, the enclosure, you milk with your song—the swift one, the conqueror, whom you strengthen in these [praises].
They say that these two, *iyam* and *uttarā*, belong to Indra and Viṣṇu.
Regarding this, they state the following justification:
the verse beginning with *taṃ pratnathā* is employed for the *śukra* and *manthin* cups.
The Śukra and Manthin cups belong to Indra.
For the Brāhmaṇa states: "In that he recites [the hymn] for Indra, by that the Śukra and Manthin become possessed of the Uktha" (AiB 3.1). There is also a direction from the Adhvaryu.
"Having sent forth [the call] for the Soma juices dedicated to Indra, which are offered at every morning pressing, bright, and dripping with honey" (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 4.2.1.23).
There is also the *praśāstṛ*-directive: "Let the Hotṛ worship Indra at the morning pressing" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.5), and so forth.
And the *yājyā* verse dedicated to Indra is: "The Somas have been presented for Indra; this is your honeyed [draught], O Soma-drinker" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.5).
Therefore, they belong to Indra.
To that Indra, as of old— O gods, may we, the Atris, abide in that broad, great, and unobstructed happiness which is connected with you, being entirely free from affliction.

May we be united with the protection of the Aśvins— protection that is new, experienced through ancient hymns, bliss-bestowing, the bringer of happiness, and characterized by excellent guidance. O immortal Aśvins, bring to us wealth that brings prosperity,
and also bring sons who are heroes endowed with great valor.
Bringing hither all auspicious fortunes.
2. [The syllables] *jha*, *ta*, *na*—[these are] not in excess; 3. *jha*, *ta*, *bha*, *ra*—thus it is *ba*.

Just like our ancient sacrificers (*yajamāna*), so "in the former manner" (*pūrvathā*) means as our ancestors did; "in every way" (*viśvathā*) means as all living beings do; and "in this manner" (*imathā*) means as these present-day sacrificers do.

Just as they obtained the fruit through the praise of Indra, so too, O Inner Self (antarātman), you also— through song (girā) as the means— should milk [the cow] for all desires at all times: Indra, who possesses the *jyeṣṭhatāti* (supremacy), who sits upon the *barhis* (barhipada), who knows himself (*svavit*), who is all-knowing or the bestower of everything, who is turned toward us (*pratīcīna*), who possesses the thunderbolt (*vajrin*)— for the word *vajra* occurs here in the sense of strength (*balavat*)— who is powerful (*āśu*, moving swiftly or pervasive), and who conquers (*jayant*) by overcoming all.

In those praises through which you grow—that is, you become increased—and through which you cause Indra to grow; "in those" is used in the plural by way of grammatical substitution (vyatyaya). Furthermore, [the verse] is a *preṣa* for the *antarātman*. Just as [Indra] grows through praise, so too do you.
Thus, "in those" is a plural form used by transposition (*vyatyayena*).
For the sake of glory, he has impelled those beautiful ones of the highest heaven who shine in the sky;
you are a good guardian for the doers of good, so that no harm may come to them. You have overcome the illusions with your wondrous power; "Māyābhikṛt" is your name.

For glory, [behold] the beautiful ones of the upper realm, which shine like the sun. Illuminating the quarters of the sky, you are a good guardian; you cannot be deceived. You are far beyond the wiles of the doers of evil; even by means of *ṛta*, your name remains unassailable. 2.
O Indra, shining in the light of heaven, you who are manifesting yourself, you [are the one] for the one who impels, even for the one who does not impel.
The dative case is used in the sense of "for the sake of" (padyarthe).

"Of the waters belonging to the upper cloud, which are beautiful and radiant—among all those waters, in the midst of all the quarters (kakubhaḥ), may you be the impeller for the prosperity (śriye) of living beings; this is the ellipsis.

O Indra, O performer of good deeds (sukṛtaḥ)—that is, one who performs the excellent work of bestowing rain and so forth—you are a good protector (sugopāḥ) of living beings. Therefore, you do not exist (na asi) for the sake of harming (dabhāya), that is, for the destruction of living beings."
And you, surpassing all illusions by means of your own asuric powers— being superior to all deceits—
your name, that is, your essential form, abides in the realm of truth (*ṛta*).
The oblation accompanies the horse and bestows wealth; he is the Hotṛ-priest who provides a secure path and brings strength.
Lying upon the sacrificial grass like a child, yet placed in the midst as a youth, he is established among the two aged ones as one who bestows wide-reaching power.

The oblation attends upon him who is both Truth and the Ordainer; he whose path is unharmed is the Hotṛ-priest, the bringer of strength. The bull, the infant, the youth, the ageless one, established among the people, has spread himself across the sacred grass as he sits down. 3.

This [offering] belongs to Agni by virtue of its being the office of the Hotṛ, its youthfulness, and so forth. This Agni constantly (*athyaṃ*) attends to (*sacate*) the *havis*, such as clarified butter (*ājya*) and the like. Of what nature is the *havis*? It is *sat* (real/true); because it is the means to a fruitful result, the *havis* itself is also *sat*. And it is a *dhātu*—a sustainer of all; for the *havis* that is offered becomes the means for rain through the medium of the Sun, and through that rain, since creatures are produced, it possesses the quality of a sustainer. For instance: (Note: The variants marked 1. kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra omit the phrase "ity antarātmanaḥ preṣaḥ"; variant 2. kha-jha-na-ma-ra reads "yathā".)

3. kha-ca-jha-ṇa: shining toward heaven; na: shining forth toward heaven; bha-ra: shining forth in heaven. 4. kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-jha-ṇa-bha-ra-śa: Śakra, lord of karma. 5. kha-ga-gha-va-ja-ṇa-na-bha: worthy of constant resort.
‘An oblation properly cast into the fire reaches the sun;
from the sun rain is born, from rain comes food, and from that, living beings’ (Manu Smṛti 3.76). *Ariṣṭagātuḥ* means one whose movement is unhindered or unharmed.
If he goes, the sacrifice will be accomplished, and through that accomplishment, the fruit will be attained; thus, his departure is not a cause for misfortune. This very point he expresses:

He, indeed, the Hotṛ—the performer of the oblation—is the sustainer of strength with his powers. Following the sacrificial grass (*barhis*), he flows forth with clear waves. A bull, a showerer of rain, like a child who is to be protected or a youth not yet fully matured, he is a mixer everywhere, undecaying and free from old age. Among the plants that have spread out, he is placed, established, and set down; being such as this, he accompanies [the sacrifice].
These well-yoked ones of yours I shall urge forward; for him, O increasers of Truth, you must descend.
With well-guided, all-controlling reins, Krivi steals away their names upon the slope.

These well-yoked [steeds] of yours go forward for the journey, for the sake of nourishment; downward for that one, they are yoked by the Law, increasing the Truth, with well-guided reins that control all. The active one steals away their names in the descent.
This is the solar [chariot].

These rays are well-yoked, meaning they are perfectly joined with one another; for the journey—that is, for the movement toward the sacrifice—they go downward, as is understood from the word *nīcīḥ*. They are "yummyaḥ," meaning fit for the journey, for the sake of this sacrificer.
Alternatively, *yamaḥ* refers to the one who restrains the sun;
[the gods] are connected to him.
And they are the *ṛtāvṛdhaḥ*, the increasers of the sacrifice.

This Āditya, with his well-guiding, easy-to-traverse reins—reins that govern all, being the controllers of everything—the active creator (*kriviḥ*) steals away, that is, he takes up, the names, meaning the waters, in the downward slope, the low-lying region of the earth.
Or alternatively: when the two horses are yoked at the front of the chariot for the journey to the sacrifice, they proceed well-yoked on the path of desire;
the rest is the same.
The Krivi, Agni who is like the Krivi, in the downward slope [of the earth], by means of the nets characterized by the names and oblations, seizes—that is, takes—this [victim].

O Soma, shimmering with your stalks, you have entered the womb of the plants like a bird that seizes its prey; you, of beautiful voice, shine forth with straight songs as the one who holds the vessel. Increase in strength at the sacrifice, O living one, for the sake of your consorts.

Moving swiftly with the swift ones, grasping that which is poured out, possessing branches, within those pregnant with thought—O you of beautiful sacrificial post, you shine among the reciters of the *dhāravāka* hymns; O singer of straight songs, prosper! Over the wives, as a living being, advance toward the sacrifice. 5.

O Agni, you who possess straight songs and beautiful praise, with the trees—that is, with the large products derived from trees—[you take] the *vayākinam*, [the Soma] seized by the pressed juice. *Vayākinam* refers to that which possesses *vayās*, meaning wretched branches or creepers (*latās*). Grasping and seizing the Soma within the *cittagarbhāsu*—that is, within the praises that capture the mind—you, possessing a beautiful ladle (*susvaruḥ*), having a beautiful movement, or having beautiful praise, [act] amidst the utterances of the *dhāravākas*.
Those who maintain the words of praise are the *dhāravākās*, namely the officiating priests and the sacrificer;
among them you shine.
Moreover, O Living One (*jīva*), the vivifier of all, the protector of the wives and the plants, or the flame, grow forth toward them; cause them to increase.

1. Kha, Ca, Ṇa, Ya: "In the completion of the sacrifice. 2. Kha, Ca, Jha, Ṇa: "These are yours. 3. Ta: "The waters. 4. Kha, Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Bha: "Desiring beautiful praise"; Śa: "Possessing beautiful praise. 5. Kha, Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Ta, Bha, Ra, Śa: "Alā" (or "alpa": small? branches. 82. The Ṛgveda.

Just as it appears, so it is described. Together with their shadow and their power, they have established themselves within the waters. For us, [grant] the great earth, wide space, vast victory, mighty strength, excellent heroes, and unshakable power. This verse belongs to all the gods (*vaiśvadevā*). "Just as it appears" means exactly in whatever form it is seen, "so it is described," meaning it is described in that very same form. It is praised exactly as it was perceived, and not through reliance on the testimony of others. Because, together with their shadow—that is, their radiance—and their power, which is effective, they have fully established (*sam dadhire*) their own form or their praise within the waters, that is, within the pervasive hymns, or indeed within the waters themselves. Those gods [grant] the great (*mahīṃ*), worshipful, wide-extending (*uruṣām*) wealth; vast (*uru*) victory, that is, impetus; mighty (*bṛhat*) strength; excellent heroic offspring (*suvīram*); and unshakable (*anapacyutam*) power.
The sacrificer approaches, goes toward, and worships you, the Lord of Sages, who are to be praised by the sages. By what means? [By the sacrificial offering.]
The meaning is: by means of those "vāsu" [praises], that is, by means of your own praises, your name—which is either the act of bowing or the name itself—or your form exists.
Alternatively:
he moves toward you, who are distinguished by the "ketu" (banner/sign) of this "yatuna" (one who moves), namely by your activity such as the removal of darkness.
In whatever manner, in whatever desire, it was placed, so does it maintain [it].
The affix *ciṇ* occurs in the sense of the agent.
By implication, it is understood that the mind is [the subject].
The meaning should be known as follows: just as a substitute substance is similar to the original, so too is the object to be understood.
One finds such a desire through the service of the household, by means of ritual action characterized by oblations, hymns of praise, and the like.
He who, being himself unimpelled by another, carries—that is, maintains—the fruit by his own intellect alone, he indeed makes it sufficient;
or rather, he who carries it himself, who performs it by himself, he too shall then accomplish it.
For that which is caused to be done by another does not bear fruit.

He who stands firm like the flesh of the ocean does not suffer harm from fire; he in whom all nourishment is contained, in whom the heart of the one who acts is established as food, and where the thought that binds the purified exists.

To the ocean; of these, the swift one has stood near. Agni does not harm him in whom food is placed; he does not fail the heart’s desire of the one who bestows wealth. Wherein exists the thought that is bound to the pure [sacrifice]. 9.
This [hymn] also belongs to Sūrya.

Among these praises, our own praise—which is like the ocean, having the sun as its ultimate source—has reached Agni; that is, it has come to rest in him as the most excellent. Alternatively, the connection may be understood as "the praise of these people, the priests."
*Savana*:
That in which Soma is pressed is a *savana*, meaning a sacrificial hall.
It does not perish; it is not destroyed.

But the meaning is that it increases. That sacrifice (*savana*) in which the hymns of praise (*stotra*) are long and extensive— in this very house of the sacrificer, the heart’s desire (*hārdi*), the desirable fruit residing in the heart of the one who performs the praise (*kṛvaṇa*), does not waver (*na retate*).
It does not become false.
In whatever house of praise there exists a hymn of praise (*mati*) that is "bound to the pure"—that is, one which follows after the pure Sun—it is not so that "the food does not flow."

For he, through the intentions of Kṣatramanasa, with the companions of Evāvada the sacrificer—may we win the wealth of Avatsāra along with our debts; may we obtain the most powerful strength, even that which is sought by the wise.

For he, through the intentions of Kṣatramanas, with the companions of Evāvada, the sacrificer—may we discharge the debts of Avatsāra; may we win the most powerful prize, even that which is sought by the wise. 10.
This too belongs to the Sun. For he indeed is that god Savitṛ, who is to be praised by all;
the meaning is that he is the fulfiller of all desires.
The word *hi* indicates what is well-known in both worldly and Vedic usage. From that source;
here, other sages as well have perceived the signs.
Having said this, here today the seers—
of Kṣatra, Manasa, Avada, Yajata, Sadhri, Vatsāra, and Vaiṣa— fill and satisfy ourselves with the delightful thoughts of us, the seers, by means of our prayers. What?
The most powerful one (śaviṣṭham).

1. In the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, ca, ja, ṇa, na, bha, the phrase "or... becomes" is absent. 2. In manuscript kha, it reads "he approaches" (abhigacchati); in ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra, it reads "he approaches" (abhigacchati).
3. [The letters] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra, and śa follow [the preceding].
4. [The letters] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, bha, and ra indicate what is well-known.
*Vāja* is food that is exceedingly powerful.

According to the Vedic scripture, "Food indeed is strength" (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.3.6.6). We—the Kṣatriyas and others—shall spread out that which is to be honored and sustained by even a learned and wise man; such is the connection [of the words].

The falcon is their mouth; Aditi is the belly of the exhilarating drink of the all-desirable, worshipful, and wondrous one. They strive for one after another in your service; they know the horn; they drink from the vessel all around.

The falcon [has come] to these; Aditi is their womb. The exhilaration of the all-bounteous, worshipful, and wondrous one—[the drops] seek one another to flow together. Threefold is your drinking-vessel and your draught nearby. 11.

This [verse] has the intoxication of the waters as its deity. The *mada* (intoxication) belonging to these three [gods], beginning with Viśvavāra—namely, of these waters characterized by the essence of Soma—is the *śyena*, one whose movement is praiseworthy, who goes swiftly to the presence of the drinker;
it is *aditi*, undepressed and exceedingly abundant.
The phrase "the bellies" implies that they also become fillers of the bellies;
those [Maruts], beginning with Viśvavāra, have engaged in the sacrificial session (sattra) in order to go—
that is, to reach the Soma for its consumption.
They mutually entreat one another, requesting permission;
they know, or obtain, the *vipāṇam*—the special giver of exhilaration—as their *paripānam*, being close to it.
Sadāpṛṇa, the sacrificer, has slain his enemies; Bāhuvṛkta and Śrutavit have been with you.
He attains both boons and shines when he partakes of the offering with well-prepared oblations.

Ever bestowing gifts, the worshipful one has struck down his enemies. Bāhu-vṛkta, the knower of sacred lore, is with you; he approaches both boons and shines forth when he partakes in the praise-song with those who are well-disposed toward him. 12.

Sadāpṛṇa—always giving, one whose nature is charity, and who bears this name; Yajata—the sacrificer; Bāhuvṛkta—one who has gathered [the clouds] with his arms; Śrutavit—a knower of sacred learning; and Tarya. Regarding these five, each is put in the singular in relation to the others. He, that very R̥ṣi, shall strike down (vi vadhīt) the enemies (dvipaḥ). Together with you (sacā)—meaning accompanied by you—that R̥ṣi attains both excellent (varā) desires (ubhā), pertaining to this world and the next. And he shines (bhāti). Because he honors (bhajate) this host (gaṇam)—the assembly of gods—with well-uttered (suprayāvābhiḥ) hymns that thoroughly and excellently intermingle [with them], therefore he becomes so.

1. Kha, Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Bha, Ra, Ma, Da, Devatya; Na, Ma, Da, Ya, Ja. 2. Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Ta, Bha, Ra, Mā, Tu, Ma, Kā, Śa, Gāṃ, Mām; Na, Mā, Tu, Ma, Kā, Śa, Gāmī. 3. Kha, Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Bha, Ra—“Sam” does not exist.
4. In the versions kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, and bha, the word *ca* does not exist. 5. In the versions ca, ta, bha, and ra, the word *saḥ* does not exist.
6. In the version gha, ja, and śa, it says *bhāti*.
The supporter of the one who has heard [the hymns], the sacrificer, the protector of the people, he is the sweetener of all; he is the anointer of our prayers.
He brings the cows full of essence for the sake of glory; reciting the milk, he studies, not sleeping.

The sustainer of what is heard; belonging to the sacrificer; the protector of beings; of all [the people]; upright; he; of prayers; the anointer; he brought; the milch-cow; full of essence; she has yielded; the milk; reciting after; he goes beyond; not sleeping. 13.
For me, the sacrificer who has descended into the pit, there is the seer named Sutaṃbhara, the performer of the sacrifice.

Satvati means one who protects the existing fruits; the sense is that he becomes the *hotṛ*. Furthermore, he is the one who brings forth—meaning the one who causes to rise upward and bestows—the most exalted fruit, the udder of all thoughts and all ritual actions.
The cow is a milch-cow;
she brought milk that was flavorful and substantial;
therein the milk rested and, by implication, continues to rest for him.

Proclaiming all that in due order, he has disclosed the secret of heaven with his hymns; the radiant singers have come forth from the dawns. The god has opened the doors of the human world, having unbarred the gates of the enclosure and the celestial realms.

They have split the mountain of heaven with their hymns; the singers of the approaching Dawn have come. He has opened the cow-stalls; the Sun has risen. The God has thrown open the doors for mankind. Thus [it is said]. 1.
In this [hymn], Indra and the others are the deities indicated by their characteristic marks.
Here, the release by Indra of the cows—which had been carried away by the Paṇis and placed below a mountain by the Aṅgirases—is set forth.
*Vidāt*: Indra made it known.
What? The meaning of the mantra is "the cows are hidden.
What is he doing?
With *ukthas*— that is, with the hymns of the Aṅgirases serving as the cause—
he hurled the *adri*, the thunderbolt;
he hurled it both upon the guardians and for the purpose of splitting the mountains.

The radiant rays belonging to the approaching dawn have gone forth; they have spread everywhere. Opening up the nights that possess masses of darkness, the Sun, who is by nature luminous, has indeed risen.
Having done so, the divine Sūrya opened wide the human doors—that is, the gates belonging to mankind;
the meaning is that by dispelling the darkness, he made them available for the activities of humans and others.
Sūrya has spread his immortal splendor like a straight path; the two Mothers have come forth as they give birth.
The rivers flow with desert-like beds, their waters deep; the sky is firmly established like a well-constructed pillar.
Sūrya has won immortality and glory; from the vast enclosure, the Mother has come forth bringing the cow. The rivers flow with a desert-like flood; like a well-erected pillar, the sky stands firm.
The god Sūrya distributes—that is, he illuminates—*śriyam*, meaning splendor or light;
*amatiṃ na*:
this is a name for form (*rūpa*).
Substance is like form;
just as substances such as jars and cloths receive forms such as blue or yellow,

so too the dawns (*uṣas*), the measurers of the rays of light (*go*), coming from the vast mid-air (*urvāt*), approach— knowing that the sun will rise and that she herself must perform her shining forth.
Likewise, those whose color is like that of the desert.
"Dhanvartitakarmā" means one whose activity moves upon the desert. Those [waters] in which they move—that is, go—are so described.
The absence of the long vowel is Vedic.
The syllable *kha* is the first letter.
Those who have consumed the lineage-protectors (*kulodaka*)—
that is to say, those who have performed the piercing of the ear (*kṛtakarṇa*).
And the rivers likewise become such as these. Furthermore, the sky (*dyauḥ*) is well-measured (*sumitā*), firmly established like a pillar that supports a house; it stands firm (*dṛhata*).
The sense is that all this is to be known through the command of the Sun.
For this hymn of praise, the child of the mountain has grown for the prosperity of his great birth;
the mountains have opened wide, heaven has been perfected, and the earth has yielded as they displayed their power.

For this hymn, may the womb of the mountain [open] for the birth of the great ones, for their nourishment; let the mountains part asunder, while Heaven grants success, and they, revealing themselves, cause the earth to tremble.

1. One whose nature is to take refuge in *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *sa*. 2. The suppression of *ta* and *ra*. 3. Established in the house by *kha*, *ca*, and *ṇa*; established in the house by *jha*, *bha*, and *ra*. 4. Having become firm through *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, and *bha*. [Aṣṭaka IV, Adhyāya 4, Sūtra 45] 867:
For this, for me, for the hymn of praise (*uktha*), the water situated within the womb of the mountain—the cloud—flows forth; it moves.
And Indra moves [the chariot] for him—of what sort?
For the sake of the birth, that is, the production, of great and mighty hymns; for the ancient, primordial leader.
That very thing is stated again: "The mountain and the cloud shall give way;
and the sky shall accomplish, that is, bring about, the rain."
The Aṅgirases, not desiring to shine forth for themselves but serving from all sides, wander about excessively; being *dasyus*, they exhaust themselves through their ritual acts.
With these words of yours, which are pleasing to the gods, I shall now invoke Indra and Agni for our refreshment;
for the sages, skilled in sacrifice, desiring to win them over, worship the Maruts with hymns.

With well-spoken words, with splendors, those which are dear to the gods—O Indra and Agni, now call them hither for the sake of the worshiper; for indeed, the sages, skilled in sacrifice, seeking to win over the Maruts with hymns, [invoke] them.
(Rigveda 8.68)
O friends, let us fashion this prayer, by which our Mother opened the cow-pen;
by which Manu conquered the fiercely-shouting [foes], and by which the merchant dug up the soil with his spade.
Come, friends, let us fashion this prayer, by which the Mother opened the stall of the cow; by which Manu conquered Triśiśipa, and by which the merchant reached the winding water.
This is also a statement of the Aṅgirases:
"Come here!
Having come, let us perform—that is, we shall offer—*dhiyam*, which is praise."
O friends, those who have become mutual companions— this is the speech of the Aṅgirases—
the *dhī* (inspired thought) which is the mother, the creator of cows, opened up the enclosure of the cows that had been carried off by the Paṇis.
And by means of that [thought], Manu conquered the enemy Viśiśipa, whose jaws were shattered.
Or rather:
Manu is the lord of thought (mantendra) of all; Vṛtra was his adversary.
He conquered him by means of the *dhī* characterized as a hymn (*stoma*) composed by us.

And by that [power], just as the merchant Kakṣīvat—desiring great fruit through his trade as a merchant, and Vaṅku, who went to the forest out of a desire for water—obtained *purīyam*, the water that fills;
for it is heard in the Śruti: "With which [gifts] he gave honey to the merchant Auśija Dīrghaśravas from the cask" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.112.11).
There the pressing-stone did not fail the ten-month Navagvas as they strove with their hands;
Saramā, moving toward the *ṛta*, found the cows, and the Aṅgirases made the clans true.

He pressed [the juice] here; the stone was extended by the hand. They sang praises with which the Navagvas [attained] the ten months. Saramā, going toward *ṛta*, found the cows. Aṅgiras made all things true. 7.
In this sacrifice, the pressing-stone—the stone used for pressing—being held together by the hands, resounded;
here the verb *nau* (to praise) refers merely to sound;
it made a noise.
By means of that pressing, the Navagvas—
the Aṅgirases who, for the sake of cows, performed their rites for nine months or ten months—
praised Indra.
Alternatively:
the Aṅgirases, who performed the rites for ten months—meaning they were accompanied by a period of ten months—and these others, the Navagvas, all worship with that [sacrifice].
For there is a Vedic citation: “The Navagvas, having pressed the Soma, [worship] Indra” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.29.12).
Saramā—either the ever-moving speech in the form of praise, or the divine dog sent by Indra at the request of the Aṅgirases, seeking the cows—found the cows that had been carried off by the Paṇis;
and the Aṅgirases made all the truthful acts characterized by praise and other virtues come true.
When at the dawning of this mighty goddess, the Aṅgiras, rich in heroes, gathered together with the rays;
Saramā, finding the source of these [waters] in their highest dwelling-place, discovered it by the path of Eternal Order (Ṛta).
When at the dawning of this mighty goddess, all the Aṅgirases, together with the men, gathered the cows at their highest dwelling place; Saramā, the knower, found them by the path of Truth. 8.

1. [The syllables] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, and ga he pierced through; ta, ra, and apā he pierced through. 2. By means of the characteristic of Soma: kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra, and śa. 3. The others: ta. 4. In the versions kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra, and śa, the word “vā” does not exist.

When all the Aṅgirases had gathered together at the dawning of the light, when the darkness that concealed the cows was removed, and when they had come together with the cows, then the calf—the yielder of milk and other products—of those cows became employed in the highest, most excellent place of assembly, namely the sacrifice.
By the path of Ṛta (Truth), Saramā—the goddess of speech or the divine hound—found the cows that were held in confinement.
Or else:
In the supreme dwelling place, the common abode of these cows, in the secret enclosure of the pen, there exists a fountain—a spring of water;
that is to say, a cave.
By means of that, along the path and way of *ṛta*—of water—Saramā found the cows.

May Sūrya come with his seven horses to the field that he has made wide for his long journey. Like a swift falcon, he flies toward the soma-juice; the youth shines brightly as he goes among the people.

May Sūrya, drawn by his seven horses, come to the field that extends far for his long journey. Like a swift falcon swooping toward the food, may the youthful sage shine forth as he goes among the cattle.
May Sūrya—the god who impels all things, endowed with seven horses whose nature is to glide, or perhaps possessing seven forms—come toward us.
Because of his long journey, the field—that is, the region to be traversed—is wide and exceedingly vast.
That very god, moving swiftly like a falcon, comes flying toward the offered oblation, his flight being praiseworthy.
The all-pervading, wise, and far-seeing one, moving among the rays of light, shines forth as he proceeds through the midst of them;
or rather, like a falcon, the well-winged bird flies toward the food.
He went toward the moon situated in the celestial realm (*dyuloka*)—which bears the characteristic of *soma*—in order to bring it for the purpose of the gods' drinking assembly.
The remainder, beginning with "you two," is the same as before.
Sūrya has ascended to the bright realm; he has yoked his bay horses with their shining backs.
Like wise men launching a boat upon the waters, the listening waters have stood still for him as he comes hitherward.
The Sun has mounted the bright flood; he has yoked his bay horses with smooth backs. As the wise led a ship by means of water, so have the waters, hearing him, come hither and stood still. 10.
The divine Sūrya has appeared everywhere toward the bright, shining water.
When he yoked to his chariot the green horses with beautiful backs, the wise and thoughtful sacrificers and others then directed him with water as if with a boat.
Then the waters, granting permission from all sides, stood facing downward.
1. In the manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, and ra, the phrase "goṣu raśmiṣu gacchan" is absent.
2. In the manuscripts kha, ca, ṇa, na, bha, and ra, the phrase "madhye vartamānaiḥ" is absent.
3. In manuscript kha, ca, and ṇa, it reads "suṣṭhu andho apatayat"; in jha, bha, na, and ra, it reads "suandho apatayat"; and in śa, it reads "andho apatayat."

4. In manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, bha, the reading is *ayojata*; in manuscript ra, it is *ayojayata*. 5. In manuscripts kha, ca, ṇa, and na, the reading is *nāvam*; in manuscript jha, it is *nāvamita*; in manuscripts na and bha, the phrase "nāvaṃ na" is absent; in manuscript ra, it is *nāvamiva*. 6. In manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, and ra, the word "arvāk" is absent.
I place within the waters your self-sustaining wisdom, by which you made manifest the months for the Navagvas.
Through this wisdom may we have the gods as our guardians; through this wisdom may we overcome the day of distress.

I place this prayer for you among the waters, a prayer that wins the light of heaven, by which the Navagvas crossed over the ten months. Through this prayer may we have the gods as our guardians; through this prayer may we pass beyond the day. 11.
O gods, I maintain for you your "dhiyam"—your hymn of praise—which is established in the waters, self-sustaining, and the bestower of all things.
By means of meditation, the middling [attainment].

By this wisdom and action, the Aṅgirases, who were "not of the herd" (navagvāḥ), completed ten months while performing the sacrificial session (satra). By this very wisdom, may we be "protected by the gods" (devagopāḥ)—that is, guarded by the gods—and by this wisdom, may we cross over and transcend "distress" (aṃhaḥ), that is, sin.
The second hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "hayo na," has Pratikṣatra as its seer.
The eighth and the second verses are *triṣṭubh*s; the remaining six are *jagatī*s.
Regarding the deities: the first five have the goddesses as their subject, while the seventh and eighth have the wives of the gods as their deities.
And thus it has been listed: "The *haya*, the two *aśva*s, *pratikṣatra*, another [verse], *devapatnī*—these are in *dvipadā*; otherwise, the second [verse] is in *triṣṭubh*.
The application (*viniyoga*) of this hymn is based on its internal characteristics (*laiṅgika*).

Like a wise horse, I have yoked myself of my own accord to the pole; I bear that which carries us forward, seeking protection. I do not desire to unyoke from it nor turn back again; the wise leader, knowing the path, leads me straight.

I am no horse; I, the wise one, have yoked myself to the pole. I bear that which carries forward and seeks aid. I desire neither its unyoking nor its turning back again. The wise one, the leader upon the path, leads straight ahead. || 1 ||
Like a horse, the wise one, the omniscient one, the protector of the kingdom, being himself unimpelled by another, has yoked himself to the pole—that is, to the body of the sacrifice.
That pole, which is "prataraṇī" (one that carries across excellently) and "avasyuvam" (one that desires to protect), I carry;
that is, the Adhvaryu or the Hotṛ maintains it.

"I do not desire the unyoking"—that is, the release or abandonment—"of this yoke. Nor do I desire "the covering again"—that is, the re-covering or bearing [of it]. What my burden is, that alone is now stated.

The "wise one," the inner controller (antaryāmī) who knows the path, being the "leader" who goes before, "leads"—that is, causes one to reach—the "paths," the ways of sacrifice, "straight," meaning without crookedness.

1. The sequence "kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra-’vaḥ” is not present in manuscripts Kha, Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Ra. 2. The phrase “apsu agnim itām” is not present in manuscripts Kha, Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Na, Bha, and Ra. 3. Manuscripts Ga, Gha, and Ja read "samanutiṣṭhantaḥ"; manuscripts Ta and Ra read "sarvatra samanutiṣṭhantaḥ."
4. In the manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra, and śa, the word ‘ati’ is absent. 5. In the manuscripts kha, ca, ṇa, and bha, it is the twenty-third. 6. In the manuscript ta, it is ‘vidvān’.

7. In the versions *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra*, the word "again" (*punar*) does not exist. 8. In *kha*, *ca*, and *ṇa*, it is said: "What is the burden from another? In *jha*, *ta*, *bha*, and *ra*, it is said: "What is the burden that comes? In *na*, it is said: "The burden becomes. In *śa*, it is said: "The burden is called by the gods.
O Agni, Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, and gods, O Maruts and Viṣṇu, extend your strength!
May both the Nāsatyas, Rudra, Aditi, Pūṣan, Bhaga, and Sarasvatī be pleased with this offering.
O Agni, Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, O gods, and the host of Maruts, as well as Viṣṇu—may both Nāsatyas, Rudra, Aditi, Pūṣan, Bhaga, and Sarasvatī be pleased with us. 2.
O Agni, Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, O gods, you all extend—that is, bring forth—the strength and power of us.
In all these cases, because the preceding word is non-existent [as a separate entity], there is no elision of the *anunāsika* for each subsequent word at the beginning of the quarters (*pāda*), etc.;
however, the first word possesses the status of being at the beginning of a quarter by its very nature.
Moreover, O Maruts, you who possess the powers of the Maruts, and O Viṣṇu, you all go forth as a host;
[the word *viṣṇo* does not receive the *nighāta* accent because it is separated from *uta* by the word *iti*.]
Furthermore, may both the Nāsatyas, who are truly real, as well as Rudra, and moreover these women of the gods—Pūṣan, Bhaga, and Sarasvatī—enjoy and favor our sacrifice or our hymn of praise.
I invoke Indra and Agni, Mitra and Varuṇa, Aditi, the Sun, the Earth, the Sky, the Maruts, the Mountains, and the Waters;
I call upon Viṣṇu, Pūṣan, Brahmaṇaspati, Bhaga, Śaṃsa, and Savitṛ for our protection.

I invoke Indra and Agni; Mitra and Varuṇa; Aditi; Svar (the Sun); Pṛthivī (the Earth); Dyau (the Sky); the Maruts; the Mountains; the Waters; Viṣṇu; Pūṣan; Brahmaṇaspati; Bhaga; Śaṃsa; and Savitṛ for our protection. 3.
I invoke, or praise, the fourteen gods beginning with Indra and ending with Savitṛ for our protection.
The Āditya is called "Svasti" because he causes one to hear [the truth].
May Viṣṇu and Vāta, the Aśvins, and Draviṇodas, as well as Soma, grant us bliss;
and may the Ṛbhus, for the sake of wealth, the two Aśvins, Tvaṣṭṛ, and all the gods, be mindful of us.

May Viṣṇu grant us joy, and Vāta, and the Aśvins, and may Soma, the giver of wealth, grant us delight; and may the Ṛbhus, and the two Aśvins for our prosperity, and Tvaṣṭṛ, and all the gods, take heed of us. 4.
Moreover, may Viṣṇu, the pervasive God, grant us happiness; "maya" is a name for happiness—
may He make us happy.
Moreover, let Vāta, the wind, being harmless, bring us well-being;
and furthermore, let Soma, the giver of wealth, also bring us well-being.
Moreover, let the Ṛbhus grant their approval for our sake so that we may obtain riches.
And may the two Aśvins, and also the god Tvaṣṭṛ, and also any one among all the Viśvedevas, the Ṛbhus—may all these indeed grant their approval;
or rather: [the text continues].
The word "anumaṃsta" (approve) should be connected with each [item] individually.
1. In manuscripts ga, gha, ja, and jha, the word "he" does not exist.

2. In manuscripts ga, gha, and ja, "svaḥ" (the sun) appears; it is a praiseworthy epithet of Savitṛ, meaning "quickly. 3. In manuscripts kha, ca, kṣa, ṇa, na, bha, ra, and śa, the word "aśvinā" (the two Aśvins) does not exist.

And may that host of Maruts come hither, dwelling in heaven, to sit upon the sacred grass for our sacrifice. May Bṛhaspati and Pūṣan grant us protection; may Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman grant us secure shelter. And may that host of Maruts come hither, dwelling in heaven, to sit upon the sacred grass for our sacrifice. May Bṛhaspati and Pūṣan grant us protection; may Varuṇa, Mitra, and Aryaman grant us secure shelter.
Moreover, may that host, that Marut-force, the strength and assembly of the Maruts, come toward us; may it approach.
Of what nature is that host?
It dwells in heaven, existing in the celestial realm, and is worthy of worship.
The purpose of the arrival is stated as follows:
"Upon the sacrificial grass (*barhis*),
for the sake of sitting— that is, for the purpose of sitting down to accept the oblation."
Furthermore: May the god Bṛhaspati grant us (naḥ) protection (śarma), that is, happiness;
may Pūṣan also grant it to us. Of what kind is this protection?
7. *Varūdhyam*. It is called a *varūtha* because it wards off cold, wind, and so forth; that is, a house.
I am that *varūdhyam*.
Furthermore, may Varuṇa and the others also each grant protection.

And may those mountains, worthy of fine praise, and the brightly shining rivers, be our protectors. May Bhaga, the distributor, come with power and aid; may the far-reaching Aditi hear my invocation. 6. And may those mountains, worthy of fine praise, and the brightly shining rivers, be our protectors. May Bhaga, the distributor, come with power and aid; may the far-reaching Aditi hear my invocation. 6.

And also those mountains which possess mountain-like heights, the stones that are well-praised with beautiful hymns, and moreover, the rivers that are brightly shining and bountiful givers—may they all be for our protection and preservation.
May the god Bhaga, the distributor and giver of riches, come hither with strength, with food, and with protection.
And may Aditi, the vast-expanding and undepressed mother of the gods, hear my invocation, my praise, or my call.
At the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings, there are two invitatory and offering verses for the wives of the gods, beginning with "devānāṃ patnīḥ.
And the Sūtra states: "'devānāṃ patnīruśatīravahantu naḥ'—these two" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 1.10).
These [verses] are also [recited] at the Āgnimāruta Śastra:
"The wives of the gods, longing, shall bring [the sacrifice] for us"—these two [verses]; and "I [invoke] Rākā"—these two [verses] (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.20).

May the longing wives of the gods carry us forward; may they protect us for the sake of progeny and the winning of booty. Those who belong to the earth and those who abide in the domain of the waters—may those goddesses, who are easily invoked, grant us protection. (7) *devānām* | *patnīḥ* | *uśatīḥ* | *avantu* | *naḥ* | *pra* | *avantu* | *naḥ* | *tujaye* | *vājasātaye* | *yāḥ* | *pārthivāsaḥ* | *yāḥ* | *apām* | *api* | *vrate* | *tāḥ* | *naḥ* | *devīḥ* | *suhavāḥ* | *śarma* | *yacchata* || 7 ||

1. May she who bestows *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *bha*, *ya*, and *chatu*; may she who bestows *jha*, *ra*, and *yaccha*—the wives (*patnyaḥ*) of the gods, Indra and the others, desiring (*uśatīḥ*), that is, longing for our praise or our ritual act—protect (*avantu*) us.

Likewise, for the sake of our offspring (*tujaye*) or for the son (*vaddhavate*), for the winning of food (*vājasātaye*) or for battle (*saṃgrāmāya*), may they protect us preeminently (*prāvantu*), or may they go forth [to aid us].

O goddesses, you who belong to the earthly—that is, those connected to the earth—and you who abide within the domain of the waters in the intermediate space, O deities of auspicious invocation, grant us protection.
And may the wives of the gods come toward me: Indrāṇī, Prāṇī, Aśvinī, and Rāṭ;
may Rodasī and Varuṇānī hear me; may the goddesses who are the seasons of women come toward me.
And may the wives of the gods come hither: Indrāṇī, Agnāyī, Aśvinī, and Rāṭ; may Rodasī and Varuṇānī hear us; may the goddesses come, who are the season of women. 8.
Moreover, the eastern women— the wives of the gods (devapatnyaḥ), meaning those whose husbands are the gods—
let them enjoy, that is, consume the oblation. They are described individually as follows:

Indrāṇī is the wife of Indra; Agnyāyī is the wife of Agni; Aśvinī is the wife of the Aśvins; Rāṭ is the shining one. Furthermore, Rodasī—regarding whom Yāska stated, "the wife of Rudra" (Nirukta 11.49).
This being the case, just as in the verse "viṣitastukā rodasī" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.167.5), where neither the udātta accent nor the *pragṛhya* status occurs, so too should it be here.
Nevertheless, since the great seer Śākalya has stated it thus, it must be understood exactly in that way.
*Varuṇī*, the wife of Varuṇa, let her hear from every side, individually.
Furthermore, O Goddess: may the wives of the gods (*devyaḥ patnīsaṃyājadevyaḥ*) enjoy and consume the oblation.

May that deity who presides over the *ṛtu*—the proper time of the women, the wives of the gods—also hear and partake [of it]. In this regard, the *Nirukta* passage beginning with "And may the wives of the gods meditate upon me" (Nirukta 12.46) should be consulted.
By illuminating the meaning of the Vedas and dispelling the darkness of the heart,
may the Great Lord of Yati-tīrtha bestow the four aims of human life.

Thus ends the second chapter of the Fourth Aṣṭaka in the Commentary on the Ṛgveda-Saṃhitā, titled *Vedārthaprakāśa*, composed by Sāyaṇācārya, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabuka—the glorious Emperor, Supreme Lord, and promoter of the Vedic path—under the patronage of Mādhava.

1. *ca-ca-ṇa-bha* [may] grant; *jha-ta-na-ra* [may] grant. 2. *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-bha-na*; *na*—[this is not found in] *na-rta*. 1. *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-śa* [may] bestow; *ga-gha-ja* [may] give to oneself. 4. By *Ṇa-sāyaṇācārya*.
1. 2-110 Homage to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
I bow to that Great Lord Vidyātīrtha, whose very breath is the Vedas and who created the entire universe from the Vedas.
Now the third chapter begins.
Therein, the mantra "prayuñjatī" is the third; it is the seer's [verse] of Pratiratha, composed in the Triṣṭubh meter.
Since it was stated previously that "that indeed belongs to the Viśvedevas," this one also belongs to the Viśvedevas.
"‘Prayujatī sapta pratirathaḥ’—thus says the Anukramaṇikā. Its application is worldly."
Exerting herself, she goes toward heaven, speaking as the great mother awakening her daughter; manifesting herself as a youthful maiden, the inspired thought calls aloud from the seat of the fathers.
She goes forth from heaven, speaking as she proceeds—the great Mother, awakening her daughter, manifesting herself as a young woman, a wise thought, calling aloud to the Fathers at their seat.
This is the approach: "Employing living beings in the rites that have been commenced, she comes from heaven—that is, from the celestial world—speaking, meaning being praised."
The agentive suffix occurs in the sense of the object.

"Mahī" means great; she is the mother of light, or the creator of the gods. She is "awakening," meaning she brings about awakening. Her status as a daughter is figuratively attributed because she is dependent upon that [light].
Alternatively, the connection is with "the daughter of heaven" (duhitur divaḥ).
Uṣas’s status as the daughter of Heaven is well known from such passages as “Shine forth, O daughter of Heaven” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.48.1),
and elsewhere her status as daughter is declared in “Daughter of Heaven, mistress of the world” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 7.75.4). From this, the following is understood.

Sometimes, as in the case of the *aupaniṣada* [mantra], "The Upāṃśu [is] from the Upāṃśu; the Divākīrtya [is] from the Divākīrtya," it is heard in scripture: "'Prajāpati meditated upon his own daughter, thinking her to be the Sky,' so say some; 'the Dawn,' say others" (*Aitareya Brāhmaṇa* 2.33).
Furthermore, an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is seen in the reversal of the relation between cause and effect: "From Aditi was Dakṣa born; from Dakṣa was Aditi born" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 10.72.4).
Furthermore: "Manifest, dwelling, serving, youthful, mixing [all things], everywhere directed toward her goal, the inspired thought (manīṣā) is full of praise for the ancestors."
The ablative case is used in the sense of the instrumental.
Together with the Pitṛs, the divine Pālakas, being summoned from all sides in the *sadana*, the sacrificial hall; or alternatively,
being summoned for the sake of the Pitṛs— the sacrificers who protect through their rites— or for the sake of those who protect by granting what is desired.
Swift-moving, they have gone toward those waters, having reached the navel of immortality;
their paths go around heaven and earth on all sides, infinite and wide.
Swift-moving, they have traversed that; advancing, they have taken their stand at the navel of immortality. Endless and wide, on every side, the paths encompass heaven and earth. 2.
1. The status of being a daughter of Kha, Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Na, Bha, Ta, and Du;

2. [The status of] Kha, Ca, and Ṇa as belonging to Uṣas; Jha, Ta, Na, Bha, Ra, and Ca as belonging to Uṣas; 3. The status of being a daughter of Kha, Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Bha, Ra, and Du; and the status of being a daughter of Śa and Div.
4. *kha-ca-ṇa-bha-dakṣādaditiḥ pāra*.
*Ajirāsaḥ* means "those whose nature is to move.
The root *aji-* ends with the suffix *irac*, and it is established as such by the rule beginning with *ajiraśiśara* (Uṇādi Sūtra 1.53).

That very day, whose nature is action consisting of illumination—[the rays] moving toward it, reaching the *nābhi*, the encompassing orb of the immortal sun (or the *nābhi* of the immortal water, namely the intermediate space)—having ascended, being infinite, immeasurable, and vast, the paths—the rays characterized by flying—go all around heaven and earth, that is, across the sky, the earth, and the intermediate space on every side. The particle *sīm* is a filler.
The bull, the ocean, the ruddy one, the fair-winged bird, has entered the womb of the ancient father.
Placed in the midst of heaven, the speckled-hoofed one has strode across the two ends of the realm of space.

The bull, the ocean, the ruddy one, the fair-winged bird—has entered the womb of the ancient father. Hidden in the midst of heaven, the dappled stone has stepped forth; he guards the two ends of the space. 3.
This triplet belongs to Sūrya.
The *ukṣan* is the sprinkler of water or of desires; the *samudra* is the one who swells together (*samundana*).
Or else:
It is called *samudra* because the gods rejoice (*saṃmodante*) in it.
It is *arūpa*, meaning shining; *suparṇa*, meaning easy to traverse; and *pūrvamya*.
This is a derivative based on its constituent parts.
He entered—that is, he pervaded—the womb, the generative part, of the father who protects the eastern quarter, namely the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).
Afterwards, the dappled one (*pṛśni*) was placed in the midst of heaven;
for he whose color is heard from afar is the sun, the *pṛśni*.
The stone is pervading everywhere; or it is a metaphor with an elided comparison (*luptopamā*), meaning "like a stone.
He has stepped out across, that is, he strides through, the two ends—the eastern and western parts—of the *rajas*, the intermediate space.
And he protects the world;
the meaning is that he exerts himself for the sake of protecting the world.
The four, seeking security, support him; the ten suckle the embryo for its movement.
His supreme cows, of threefold nature, move from heaven around the boundaries of the seat.
Four [fingers] bear him up, seeking security; ten [breasts] suckle the embryo so that he may move. His supreme cows, possessing threefold natures, roam around the ends of the firmament from heaven.
The four officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), desiring security for themselves and seeking peace for him, support and maintain this Āditya with oblations and hymns.
Furthermore, the ten directions cause him—who has arisen within the womb—to move about, leading him forth for the sake of movement, that is, for the worldly activity of rising and setting.

The three realms are of three kinds, distinguished by cold, heat, and rain; the supreme, most excellent rays (gāvaḥ) of this sun move about, that is, they travel, all around the ends of the sky, the intermediate space, immediately after its rising.
1. In the manuscripts *sva*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, and *ma*, the word "pṛthivīm" is absent.
2. In the manuscript *a-na-ra*, the word "tasmin" is absent.
3. In the manuscripts *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, and *ma*, the phrase "havirbhiḥ stutibhiśca" is absent.

4. [The variants] *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-ma-ra* do not contain the word *caranti*. This form, O people, which is a secret name, moves about—that which mortals have established as the waters. When two others, born here and there from the mother, support it, they are twin siblings, close companions. 5. This. Form. Secret name. O people. They move about. Which. Mortals. Have established. Waters. Two. When. Him. Support. From the mother. Others. Here and there. Born. Twin. Close companions. (5)
O people, O officiating priests, know this body— the visible orb before you— to be worthy of praise;
that orb upon which you depend, which the rivers flow toward,
and over which the waters rest.

Because they are dependent upon the *maṇḍala*, this is its defining characteristic: that *maṇḍala* consists of two days and nights. From the "mother"—the creator who stands in the place of a mother—from the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), others are born here and there; that is, when the sun has been born and brought to completion, it is born and established here and there. These two, which are to be restrained (*yamyā*), which form a pair (*yamye*), or which are joined as a couple, are "of common kin" (*sabandhū*)—meaning they possess equal power and an identical bond. For both of them, the sun alone is the single binding axle (*bandhaka-akṣa*), by means of which their two ends are "sustained" (*vibhṛtaḥ*), that is, held together.

They extend their prayers for him; the mothers weave garments for their son. Rejoicing in the sprinkling of the seed, the virile ones go toward the brides by the path of heaven. They extend their prayers for him; the mothers weave garments for their son. Rejoicing in the sprinkling of the seed, the virile ones go toward the brides by the path of heaven.
For this Sūrya, the sacrificers extend their prayers, hymns of praise, and ritual deeds.
Like mothers for their son—or for one who stands in the place of a son—the Dawns, or the quarters of space, weave garments;
that is to say, they produce dense splendors resembling garments.

Rejoicing and exulting when there is the sprinkling, the pouring, and the union with the Sun—the showerer—those rays, standing in the place of a bride, go toward us, proceeding along the path of heaven belonging to the Sun.

May that be so, O Mitra and Varuṇa; may that be so, O Agni—peace and well-being for us. May this recited prayer come true. May we attain a firm footing and a secure standing. Homage to the lofty Heaven, the dwelling place! 7. May that be so, O Mitra and Varuṇa; may that be so, O Agni—peace and well-being for us. May this recited prayer come true. May we attain a firm footing and a secure standing. Homage to the lofty Heaven, the dwelling place! 7.
In this context, the deities are established by their indicative marks (*liṅga*).
O Mitra and Varuṇa, may this hymn (*sūkta*) be recited and praised for you.
O Agni, may that hymn be recited for you.
May this be praised for our *śam*, for happiness, and for *yoḥ*, for the non-mixture of sufferings.
And may we attain, may we reach the firm ground— the state of stability.
And furthermore, may we obtain a firm foundation, stability, and unbroken continuity.
I pay homage—*namas*—to the radiant *div*, to the great *sūrya*, the vast abode and support of the universe.
The fourth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “kadu priyāya,” has Pratibhānu Ātreya as its seer (ṛṣi) and Jagatī as its meter (chandaḥ).
The Viśvedevas are the deity.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇī states: "Kadu pañca... pratibhānuḥ; it is in the Jagatī meter.
This hymn is the insertion point for the Nivid in the Vaiśvadeva Śastra on the fifth day of the Abhiplava period.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The Vaiśvadeva [offering] is for 'kadu priyāya'? (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.7).
We meditate upon the beloved, great, and resplendent abode, which possesses excellent dominion and celestial glory;
for there, in the cloud of the mutable atmosphere, the creative power, choosing the waters, spreads them forth.

To him who is dear, to his own abode, we meditate; to him of his own sovereign power, of his own glorious fame, the great one. When the crafty one, choosing the waters, spreads them out across the cloud in the region of the atmosphere that is free from enemies. 1.
Here is a praise of the fire of lightning. *Kad* means "when";
*u* is a filler particle.
To the one who is dear to all, who has become the beloved of all;
for his being dear to all is well known because he is the cause of rain, oblations, and so forth.
To such a one, to the radiant light (*dhāman*), to the lightning-like splendor (*tejas*).
In the subsequent statement, "he spreads the waters upon the clouds," heaven (*div*) is understood, as it will be mentioned later.

For what kind [of one]? For one possessing his own sovereign power (*svakṣattra*), that is, for one possessing his own inherent strength; and furthermore, for one possessing his own glory (*svayaśas*), that is, for one possessing his own inherent authority.
Everything here belongs to him alone.
When shall we honor—that is, praise—the Great One, the Worshipful One? That...
Because of the feminine gender indication later on, the word "yā" (which) must be modified [to "yām"].
That which is the Āpreyī power— that is, the power belonging to the *āmenya*, the dust (*rajas*) of the atmosphere (*antarikṣa*) that is to be measured all around—
even though the sky is immeasurable, it is measured as being "this much."

Upon the cloud—the relative, the rain-bearing mass—he spreads out the waters, characterized by rain, above the cloud; [the waters] being chosen, covering, or being enjoyed, he who is possessed of *māyā*.
*Māyā* means wisdom (*prajñāna*);
thus, being one endowed with wisdom.
Or it may be construed as: "that speech which belongs to him is the Madhyamika."
They [the waters] possess infinite wisdom, nourishing heroes; with their uniform flow they traverse the entire space.
The person devoted to the gods pushes back the waters that flow away, and by means of the ancient ones, he presses forward.

These [streams], from there, [flow] toward the goal that provides nourishment for heroes, by a single common path through the entire mid-air. Away they drive the waters backward; away they flow. The man who seeks the gods prospers by means of the ancient [streams]. 2.

This is the approach. These Dawns spread out that which? Wisdom (*vayuna*). Of what kind? "Vīravakṣaṇam": to be carried by heroes, or rather, that by which the carriers of tasks (*vakṣaṇāḥ*) are impelled. Furthermore, with a common, uniform, and encompassing light (*dīdhyā*), they spread out the entire realm (*rajaḥ*), the whole world. This being so, the person who seeks the gods (*devayuḥ*), longing for the gods, [drives away] the western ones—those whose faces are turned back—the others, those yet to come.
(Note: *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra* manuscripts read *stutim*.)
2. To the one who lies like a worm (kīṭaśāya) for strength;

he drives away, he causes to move away from the dawn. Another "apa" is a filler [particle]. He extends forward with those former ones. In the word preceded by "pra," the sense is "to increase"; he increases his own debts, or he himself increases.
With these pressing-stones, through these nights, he hurls the shattered thunderbolt at the guileful one—
[the thunderbolt] whose hundred [edges] move within his own dwelling, as they roll it together and roll it apart day by day.
With these unassailable, never-failing pressing-stones, he hurls the most excellent thunderbolt at the guileful one.
He in whose own house a hundred [blows] go forth, he who, being worthy, both brings them together and casts them asunder. 3.

In this [verse], Indra is spoken of in the first half, while in the second half, Sūrya, who is the very self (ātman) of Indra, is addressed; the word "is invoked" (āhūyate) is to be supplied. By whom?
By these *ahnī*, meaning by the days accomplished [therein]; and by the *aktūbhiḥ*, meaning by the nights produced therein;
that is to say, by such *grāvabhiḥ* (stones).
The word "means" (sādhana) refers to that which is to be accomplished.
By means of the stones, the joints, and the instrumental causes,
having arrived here while Vṛtra— the possessor of illusion— is the objective, he brandishes— that is, he inflames on all sides— the most excellent, supreme thunderbolt.
Or furthermore:
the word *vā* has the sense of *ca* (and).
Of that Āditya who consists of Indra, whose hundred rays—numbering one hundred—move about (*pracaran*) in his own dwelling (*sve dame*), namely in his own abode, the sky.
Doing what? Causing [them] to perish, that is, destroying living beings;
or alternatively:
Turning the days—the days—forward, they cause them to proceed correctly; and turning them back, they cause the days to return, bringing back again those very days that have already passed.
This is because the exhaustion of the life-span of living beings and the conventional reckoning of day and night are dependent upon the movement of the sun.
This powerful one holds in his arm that form which is like the edge of an axe, irresistible to the enemy;
when he bestows treasure upon the people who call him to bear their burden, as if it were a dwelling-place filled with nourishment.

That stream of his—like ribs, I have set his countenance before me for my enjoyment; may he, the showerer of blessings, bestow treasure upon this people who call him to battle, as one provides a food-filled dwelling. 4.
This is the Āgneyī [verse]. I perceive that well-known *rīti*—the nature, disposition, or course—of this Agni as being like a *paraśu*; that is, like a representative axe.
The meaning is: just as an axe accomplishes what is desired by its owner, so does it [accomplish his will].
I shall describe for my own enjoyment the host—the multitude of rays—of this showering, beautiful Āditya.

For if that god, being our companion (*sacā*), bestows a delightful treasure (*ratnam*) upon the people (*viśe*) who invoke him in battle or at the sacrifice (*bharahūtaye*), [bestowing it] like a dwelling (*kṣayam*) full of food (*pitumantam*);
that is to say, he grants both.
1. Kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra, śa, and soma.
2. Kha, ca, ṇa; "vā" does not exist. 3. Ga, gha, na, ja, ṇa, śa; "parispandā".
4. *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, and *sva* belong to their respective owners (*svasvāmin*); *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *śa* are desired by their respective owners.
5. *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra*: "I shall tell the hymn"; *śa*: "If I tell the hymn.
6. *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*: "He gives"; *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*: "He places," "he holds," "he gives."

With his four-faced tongue, he strives on, clothed in beauty; Varuṇa, exerting himself, reaches out toward the enemy. We do not know him in his human form, from which Bhaga and Savitṛ bestow what is desirable. With his tongue, the four-faced one exerts himself, wearing what is beautiful; Varuṇa, striving, reaches toward the enemy. We do not know him in his human nature, from whom Bhaga and Savitṛ grant what is desirable.

Yama says: Agni, having four aspects (*catūrṇīka*) with flames extending in the four directions, "reaches" (*ṛñjate*)—that is, goes toward—the clarified butter and other offerings by means of his "tongue.
Alternatively, being four-faced, he "reaches"—that is, adorns—himself by means of his tongue.
Doing what?
