Wearing—that is, covering—his beautiful and charming splendor; being Varuṇa, the warder-off of darkness; uprooting—that is, destroying—the enemy, the adversary;
of him.

The meaning of this is as follows: "We do not know him," that is, we do not understand him as being endowed with "puruṣatva"—either by virtue of his being a Puruṣa or by his being the fulfiller of desires.
Another [instance of] a derivative suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*):
"Knowing the departure of the Asura toward fulfillment, worship the god Savitṛ with hymns;
let him who understands address him with homage—the one who distributes the supreme treasure to man."

At the departure of the Asura, may the one who knows worship the divine Savitṛ with well-spoken hymns. May he who knows the three births address him with reverence—the one who distributes the highest treasure to mankind. 2.
O inner self, knowing— the one who knows— the setting forth, the departure, of Savitṛ, the Asura who destroys his enemies, worship and serve the god Savitṛ with hymns.
Furthermore, [serve him] who distributes, that is, causes to arrive, the most excellent treasure for Āyu, for man.
"By means of *namas*," that is, by means of salutation or an oblation; the meaning is "cultivating [him] particularly. Alternatively, this [term] contains an implied sense of distress (*vyatha*).
May your honor inform, address, and praise [him].
With triple bounty he bestows desirable gifts: Pūṣan, Bhaga, Aditi, Vṛtra-slayer Uṣas, Indra, Viṣṇu, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni—these wondrous ones have generated auspicious days.
May they grant desirable boons through their triple gift: Pūṣan, Bhaga, Aditi, Dawn, Indra, Viṣṇu, Varuṇa, Mitra, and Agni—these wondrous ones have generated auspicious days. 3.

This Agni consumes (*adatrayā*) things that are edible (*adanīyāni*). The suffix *tra* is derived from the root *ad* by means of the *auṇādika* suffix *ap*. According to the rule *supāṃ suluk*, there is the substitution of the case-ending *yā*. Alternatively, *adatrā* refers to the tongue (*jihvā*), which is so called because it eats (*atti*). By means of that [tongue], he bestows (*dayate*) the desirable (*vāryāṇi*) pieces of wood. The root *day* is used here in the sense of burning, as its primary meaning is "to give" (*ekakarmārtha*); thus, it means "he burns. From the context, it is understood that this refers to Agni. Or else, he bestows the edible and desirable sacrificial offerings (*yajñāni*). He gives them to the sacrificer. [The root] *day* is used in the senses of giving, going, harming, and taking. What kind of Agni is he? He is *pūṣā* (the nourisher), *bhagaḥ* (the one worthy of being enjoyed), and *aditiḥ* (the indivisible). Or rather, each of these three—Pūṣan and the others—bestows the edible and desirable pieces of wood. *Usraḥ* (the sun) covers (*vastai*) [them]; by implication, this refers to his rays. Indra and the other five gods are *dasmāḥ* (wondrous/visible), and they generate all the coming days as auspicious (*bhadrā*) and beautiful. The auspiciousness of the days consists precisely in their being distinguished by sacrifices, gifts, and other such rites.
May that invincible Savitṛ grant us protection; in it may those who do evil follow after us.
When I, the Hotṛ-priest of the sacrifice, address you, may we be masters of wealth, having strength as our treasure.

May Savitṛ, the unassailable one, grant us that protection; may the rivers follow it, purifying it. When I, as the Hotṛ-priest of the sacrifice, address this prayer, may we become masters of wealth, possessing treasures of strength. 4.

1. [The syllables] kha, ca, ṇa, bha are to be turned back; 2. kha, ca, ṇa, bha are to be avoided; 3. kha, ca, ṇa are the deities; 4. ga, gha, ja, śa are to be beautified. That well-known, desirable, and chosen wealth—which we intend for ourselves—may the god Savitṛ, who is unassailable (anarvā), never falling away, and unopposed by anyone, bestow upon us; this is the sense of the remainder. May the rivers—the flowing, moving streams—follow along that wealth and go after it.
The meaning is: "Let them go to give wealth.
Since I am the *hotṛ*—the performer of the *homa*—of the *adhvara*, the sacrifice, and I speak thus having approached [them], the ellipsis is: "therefore, let him bestow that.
And may we, the Atris, become masters and lords of manifold riches (*rāyas*).
"Vājaratnāḥ" means delightful through food or through strength;
or alternatively, since I praise [him] (*doce*), therefore may Savitṛ come to our protection (*varūtham*).
And from that [protection], may they go toward our sacrifice (*yajñam anu gaman*); thus it should be construed.

Those who offer homage like wealth to the Vasus, and who speak well-spoken words to Mitra and Varuṇa—let the overwhelming power depart from here; let them make wide room for us. Through the protection of Heaven and Earth, may we rejoice. 5.
Those sacrificers who have offered food—consisting of the fivefold oblation—to the Vasus, the gods whose abode is the sacrifice, and who address auspicious hymns to the god Mitra and to Varuṇa;
may that great wealth or splendor reach them.
O gods, grant them a wider, more expansive happiness.
Through the protection of Heaven and Earth, may we rejoice with our oblation.
The hymn beginning with “viśvo devasya,” consisting of five verses, is a *sūkta* dedicated to the Viśvedevas; it is the seerly composition of the sage Svasti-Ātreya.
The fifth verse is in the *paṅkti* meter, while the first four are *anuṣṭubh*s. This is stated in the *Anukramaṇī*: “Viśva [is the seer], [the hymn belongs to] Svasti-Ātreya, ending in *paṅkti*.”

On the first day of the two Abhiplava Ṣaḍahas, the opening verse (*pratipad*) of the Vaiśvadeva Śastra should be "viśvo devasya... This is prescribed in the Sūtra: "The [verse] 'viśvo devasya netuḥ' is the one [for the first day]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.6). In the Abhiplava Ṣaḍahas, this same verse serves as the *pratipad* for the Vaiśvadeva Śastra on the second and fourth days of the Pṛṣṭhya period.
He has formulated the rule: "If it is thus in the *abhiplava* [sacrifice]" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 7.6).

May every mortal choose the friendship of the leading god; everyone strives for wealth; may he choose glory for his prosperity. Every mortal should choose the friendship of the leading god; everyone seeks after wealth; may he choose splendor for his nourishment.
"Viśvaḥ" means "all," referring to those led by the god Savitṛ; let him choose the friendship of the one worthy of homage. Every person strives for wealth, seeking riches.
The fifth mood.
O Ruler! By his grace, may every person choose glory—that is, wealth—for the sake of nourishment, that is, for abundant sustenance.
1. In the versions *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, and *ā*, [the word] “āgacchatu” is present.
2. In the versions *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *’*, the phrase “he devāḥ” is absent.
3. In the versions *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, *śa*, and *’*, the phrase “havyema” is absent.

4. The first triplet beginning with *jha*, *bha*, and *ra* should be the opening [verse] for the Vaiśvadeva; the first triplet beginning with *ta* is for the Vaiśvadeva. 5. *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, *śa*: "Savitṛ chose... (ka. 2-111).

O God, Leader, may we follow those whom you have instructed; for with wealth and with your companionships, may we associate with those who are worthy of being associated with. 2. O God, Leader, those whom you have instructed—may we follow them; for with wealth, indeed, may we associate with those who are worthy of being associated with. 2.
O Leader, those sacrificers who are yours by nature— namely we here—
and those others [indicated by the change of case-ending] such as these Hotṛ-priests and the rest who are capable of praising you, they too are yours.
Alternatively, the meaning is that these other deities, Indra and the rest, are capable of being praised in succession;
for it has been stated, "There is indeed only one Great Self, the deity, who is Sūrya, for he is the self of all beings," and thus these deities are included within him.
The meaning is that it is not only those who praise you; the connection is: "may both of us, we, be united with *rāya*, i.e., wealth.
For they indeed are your *āpṛcaḥ*, those worthy of being honored (*āparcanīyāḥ*).

The suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of "made" (*kṛta*). Because it ends in a long vowel (*ejanta*), it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*) according to the rule *kṛnmejantaḥ*; consequently, there is no appearance of case endings (*bhakti*).
May we be united with all our desires; may we come together.

Or, from here, show us men who are travelers; from here, show us our wives. May the Dispeller drive far away every enemy standing in our path. 3. From here, for us, [show] men, the travelers; from here, show us our wives. Far away, may the Dispeller drive off every enemy stationed on the road. 3.
Therefore, in this sacrifice.
The suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of all case endings.
Serve us—our officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), the leaders (*nṛn*), the guests, and likewise the gods who are worthy of honor—from all sides.
Therefore, in this sacrifice, serve also the wives of the gods (*patnīḥ*) by means of the offering of oblations and so forth;
or alternatively:
Grant us, O gods, men—sons, servants, and so forth—as well as guests and wives; show these to us through this mantra. Bestow them upon us!

Let the host of gods, or Savitṛ—the separator who keeps all things unmixed and distinct—drive far away, to a distance, every enemy standing in our path, and separate us from other haters and those who harbor enmity.

Where the beast of the troughs, urged forward, ran forth—the one who is mindful of men, whose home is heroes, like a wise man winning the waters. 4. Where the beast of the troughs, urged forward, ran forth—the one who is mindful of men, whose home is heroes, like a wise man winning the waters. 4.
In that sacrifice where Vahis, the bearer of the sacrifice, has been addressed and brought to the sacrificial post (*yūpa*),
and where the *droṇya*— the animal fit for the post— rushes toward it, there Savitṛ, whose mind is fixed on man (*nṛmaṇas*) and whose home is the heroes (*vīrapastya*),
[is present]. The heroes are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
1. In the manuscripts Kha, Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Bha, and Ra, the word "ubhaye" is absent.
2. In the manuscripts Kha, Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Bha, and Ra, the word "prayacchata" is absent. 3. In manuscript Ta, there is "yuyuviḥ". 4.
In the manuscripts Kha, Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Bha, and Ra, the word "pṛthakartā" is absent.

*Mānaḥ*: one whose house contains sons, servants, and so forth, situated in a noble form; or, "one whose house is impelled," meaning one who bestows a house accompanied by sons and others. *Sanitā*: he becomes a distributor or a possessor. *Arṇā*: like a woman skilled in running (*araṇa-kuśalā*) or like a wise (*dhīrā*) wife. Alternatively, he becomes a distributor with respect to the offerings (*arṇāni havīṃṣi*).

O God, may this leader of yours, the lord of the chariot, be auspicious wealth; may he be auspicious for our riches and auspicious for our well-being. We meditate upon the praise of food; we meditate upon the praise of the gods.

This, O God, is your chariot, the leader; it is the lord of wealth, a blessing for prosperity, a blessing for riches, and a blessing for well-being. We meditate upon you as one praised for food; we meditate upon you as one praised by the gods. 5.
O God Savitṛ, this chariot of yours is the lord— the protector of all—and it possesses wealth that is to be bestowed.
One's own welfare is destroyed.
"May he bring about welfare"—this is the ellipsis.
And may we [attain] welfare for wealth (*rāye*), that is, for the easy attainment of riches (*dhanasya*).
Or else:

For wealth, for riches, for happiness, and for well-being—that is, for non-destruction—O praised one, we who are the praisers of Savitṛ, the one worthy of being sought after, meditate upon you; we praise you.
O praised by the gods, we who are the praisers of the gods, or of the god Savitṛ, meditate upon you; we praise you.
“*agne sutasya*” is the seventh hymn, consisting of fifteen verses.
Regarding this, the *Anukramaṇikā* states: “*agne*: five less [than sixteen]; four are *gāyatrīs*, six are *bṛhatīs*, three are *jagatīs* or *triṣṭubhs*, and the others are *anuṣṭubhs*.
According to the metrical rule (*paribhāṣā*) that “the seer [of a hymn] is the one to whom it is addressed,” its seer is Atri himself.

The first four verses are *gāyatrīs*; the five beginning with the fifth are *bṛhatīs*; the three beginning with the eleventh are *jagatīs* or *triṣṭubhs*; the fourteenth and fifteenth are *anuṣṭubhs*; and the Viśvedevas are the deity. 18.
O Agni, come with all the gods for the drinking of the pressed juice, for the offering of the oblation.
O Agni, come with all your protecting helpers, with the gods, for the drinking of the pressed juice and for the offering of the oblation. 1.

O Agni, come hither for the drinking of the pressed [Soma], for the sake of the Soma-drinking, together with all the gods—Indra and the others—who are protectors possessing all forms, for the giving of our oblation, or for the sake of that sacrificer who offers it. Come! Approach!
May those of true insight and true laws come to the sacrifice;
drink with the tongue of Agni.
May those whose study is the *ṛta*, whose nature is truth, come to the sacrifice; drink [the soma] with the tongue of Agni. 2.
1. Or one whose house is occupied by sons and others;
2. [The syllables] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra, and dhīrā;
3. [The syllables] sa, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra—“śam ... for the sake of non-destruction” does not exist.
4. Not a deity. This hymn is to be recited during the Smārta Pratyavarohaṇa rite.
Having performed the fourth [rite], the Sūrya-hymns and the Svastyayana-hymns are to be recited; this is prescribed by the Sūtra with the words "apitvā."
When being consoled by the preceptor after the *sarvatobhaya* oblation has been performed, one should mutter the remainder of the hymn beginning with "svasti no mimītām.
Accordingly, the Sūtra states: "In this case, he mutters the remainder of the hymn starting with 'yata indra bhayāmahe' as [the verse] 'svastyātreyaṃ'.
This hymn is also to be muttered during the *śāntikarman* prescribed in the Smṛti.

Regarding the statement "embraced by the Guru," it is because of the Sūtra: "When the sun has risen in the section [of the ritual] that has been proclaimed, one should mutter the Saurya hymns and the Svastyayana prayers.
O Gods—those whose thoughts are fixed on the Ṛta, whose praises are true, and whose actions are inviolable—come hither, come to our sacrifice (*adhvara*).
Having arrived, O you who possess the nature of truth and are the sustainers of truth, drink the clarified butter, Soma, and other offerings with the tongue of Agni.
O wise one, come hither at dawn with your swift steeds and with the gods, O truthful sage, for the drinking of the Soma.
With these sages, O sage, with those who are present, come hither with the early-faring gods for the drinking of the Soma. 3.

O wise one, O fulfiller of various desires, O true and worshipful Agni, come hither together with the gods—the "wise ones" possessing the aforementioned characteristics who arrive as "morning-travelers" at the time of dawn.
For what purpose? For the drinking of Soma.
This daughter of Soma, having reached the further shore of the mantra, was cooked;
she was offered to Indra and Vāyu.

This Soma, pressed with the *cam* vessel, has been poured into the cup. O Indra and Vāyu, you two deserve to drink of these pressed juices; as those free from blemish, enjoy them along with the offerings. And you two, Indra and Vāyu, deserve to drink of these pressed juices; as those free from blemish, enjoy them along with the offerings.
O Vāyu and you, Indra, you two are worthy of the drinking—the consumption—of these pressed-out, extracted Soma juices taken from the front.
Since this is so, therefore, being stainless (*arepasau*) and non-violent (*ahiṃsako*), may you both enjoy and partake of those Soma juices;
for that purpose, come toward the food called Soma—this is the ellipsis.
Or rather:
*prayaḥ* means food in the form of nourishment.

The Soma juices, mixed with curds, have been pressed for Indra and Vāyu; they flow toward the offering like rivers descending to the lowlands. 7. Pressed for Indra and Vāyu are the Soma juices mixed with curds; they go toward the food like rivers to the lowland. 7.

For Indra and Vāyu, the Soma juices—pressed, purified, and prepared, mixed with curds as their base (*dadhyāśiraḥ*)—flow toward you both, O Indra and Vāyu, like rivers descending to the lowlands; they approach you as food (*prayaḥ*).
On the third day, at the Prauga-śastra, the Vaiśvadeva mantra is "sajūr viśvair devaiḥ";
and it is stated in the Mūlaka: "sajūr viśvair devair bhista naḥ priyā priyām" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.10).

Accompanied by all the gods, accompanied by the two Aśvins, accompanied by Uṣas—come hither first; rejoice in the pressed juice like Atri. 8. Accompanied by all the gods, accompanied by the two Aśvins, accompanied by Uṣas—come hither first; rejoice in the pressed juice like Atri. 8.
O Agni, come hither, united with all the gods, joined with the Aśvins and Uṣas, sharing their same delight; come as you did at the sacrifice of Atri— just as [you came] at Atri’s sacrifice—
or rather, [come] like Atri.
Just as you delight in sacrifice, so do you take pleasure in the pressed soma; rejoice therein!
The latter two, the ninth and tenth, are clear.
1. [The syllables] kha, ca, ṇa, bha, followed by any vowel (annarūpa); or jha, ta, na, ra, followed by any vowel (annarūpa). 2. Na—on the tenth day, on the third day.
3. Ma—jha, ta, na, bha, ra: "āyāhi āyāhi" is not present.
In harmony with Mitra and Varuṇa, in harmony with Soma and Viṣṇu, come hither, O Agni; like Atri, rejoice in the pressed juice.
In harmony with Mitra and Varuṇa, in harmony with Soma and Viṣṇu, come hither, O Agni; rejoice in the pressed juice as you did for Atri. 9.
In harmony with the Ādityas and the Vasus, in harmony with Indra and Vāyu, come hither, O Agni; as you did for Atri, take delight in the pressed juice.
In harmony with the Ādityas, in harmony with the Vasus, in harmony with Indra and Vāyu, come hither, O Agni; as you did for Atri, take delight in the pressed juice. 10. 6.
On the sixth day of the *pṛṣṭhya* [ṣaḍaha], in the *vaiśvadeva* *śastra*, there are three verses beginning with "svasti naḥ.
This is stated in the Sūtra: "The *vaiśvadeva* consists of the three verses: 'svasti no mimītām aśvinā bhagaḥ'" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 8.1).
Likewise, these three verses are intended for the purpose of identifying the *vaiśvadeva* at the *bṛhaspatisava*.
This is because it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "‘May the Aśvins and Bhaga grant us well-being’—this is for the Viśvedevas" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.5).
May the Aśvins and Bhaga grant us well-being; may the goddess Aditi, who is free from enemies, grant us well-being.
May Pūṣan, the Asura, bestow well-being upon us, and may Heaven and Earth, the wise ones, grant us well-being.

May Bhaga grant us well-being with his unceasing bounty; may the goddess Aditi, who is free from enemies, grant us well-being; may Pūṣan, the Asura, bestow well-being upon us; and may Heaven and Earth, the wise ones, grant us well-being. 11.
May the two Aśvins bestow upon us well-being— security and freedom from destruction— and may Bhaga also bestow well-being; likewise, may the goddess Aditi bestow well-being.
May Pūṣan, the unassailable, the unshakable, the Asura who drives away enemies and bestows life-breaths and strength, grant us well-being.
And may Heaven and Earth, distinguished by their excellent wisdom, measure out well-being for us.
For our well-being, let us invoke Vāyu; for our well-being, Soma, who is the lord of the world;
Bṛhaspati with his entire host for our well-being; may the Ādityas be for our well-being.
For well-being, let us address Vāyu; for well-being, Soma, who is the lord of the world; for well-being, Bṛhaspati with his entire host. May the Ādityas be for our well-being. 12.
1. Because it is not prescribed [in the Sūtra].
This triplet of verses is for the purpose of inserting [the *nivid*] when those who have been initiated suffer from illness.
And thus it is prescribed in the Sūtra: "One should insert the *nivid* in the *Svastyātreyī*."
"By nature it is a *nigada*.
On the sixth day of the ten-night rite (*daśarātra*), in the *vaiśvadeva-śastra*, there are three verses beginning with "May the Aśvins measure out well-being for us" (*svasti no mimītām*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The *vaiśvadeva* [śastra] consists of the three verses beginning 'May the Aśvins and Bhaga measure out well-being for us' (*svasti no mimītāmaśvinā bhagaḥ*)."
2. Kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra, magadha.
For the sake of well-being and security, let us address Vāyu—we mean that we shall praise him—and let us also address Soma.

And we praise for our well-being that Soma who is the lord and protector of the universe— for the life of all worlds depends upon Soma— as well as Bṛhaspati, the guardian of great rites and mantras, accompanied by the entire host of gods.
May the Ādityas—the sons of Aditi, all the gods, such as Aruṇa and the others, numbering twelve—be for our well-being.
If the consecrated sacrificer falls ill during the middle of a sacrificial session (*sattra*), this triplet of verses is to be inserted as the *nivid* at the *vaiśvadeva-śastra* on that day.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "One should place the *nivid* in the *svastyātreya*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra* 6.9).
It is explained there that by the word *svastyātreya*, this triplet of verses is intended.
Likewise, when fear and other such states are present, this triplet of verses is to be recited.
May all the gods today grant us well-being; may Agni Vaiśvānara, the Vasu, grant us well-being.
May the divine Bhavas protect us for our well-being; may Rudra preserve us from evil.
May all the gods grant us well-being today; may Agni Vaiśvānara, the Vasu, grant us well-being;
may the divine Ṛbhus protect us for our well-being; may Rudra guard us from distress for our well-being. 13.
May all the gods protect us today, on this day of sacrifice, for our well-being and security.
Vaiśvānara:
he is called Vaiśvānara because all men lead him [as fire].
Agni, the divine one, is the *vasu*, the dweller of all;
as Yāska states, "This very Agni is Viśvānara, according to Śākapūṇi" (Nirukta 7.23).
May he also protect us for our well-being.
May the divine Ṛbhus also protect us for our well-being;
and may Rudra, the god who drives away suffering, protect us from sin for our well-being.
May there be well-being from Mitra and Varuṇa; may there be well-being, O wealthy Pathyā Svasti.
May Indra and Agni grant us well-being; O Aditi, bestow well-being upon us.
Welfare! O Mitra and Varuṇa! Welfare! O wealthy Pathyā Svasti!
Welfare to us! May Indra and Agni grant us welfare! O Aditi, bestow welfare upon us! 14.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, the two deities presiding over day and night, grant us well-being!
O Pathyā! "Path" (panthāḥ) refers to the path of the intermediate space (antarikṣa).
In this context, the goddess Hitā is one who takes pride in the path.
O such ᵛRevatī, O wealthy goddess, ᵛbestow well-being!
And may both Indra and Agni each individually ᵛbestow well-being upon ᵛus.
O Goddess Aditi, grant us well-being; perform it for us.
1. *Kha-ca-ṇa-stuma* means "we praise.

2. *Kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra-panthāḥ*: "May there be well-being on the path; O God, may the path through the intermediate space be auspicious"; *śa-padhyā svasti devaṃ panyā antarikṣamārgaḥ*: "O God, may there be well-being on the path; may the path through the intermediate space be auspicious.
May we travel along the path with well-being, like the sun and the moon.
May we come together with you, who give again, who do not strike, and who protect the knees.
Hail! May we follow the path like the sun and the moon; may we go back again, giving, not harming, and bowing low before me. 15.
May we travel along every path with well-being and safety, like the sun and the moon;
just as those two move upon the supportless path unharmed by Rākṣasas and other dangers, so may we.

Furthermore, while we are away on our journey, may he—giving back what was desired, not harming us, free from anger due to long delay, non-violent, knowing us, and not forgetting—avoid the doubt, thinking, "Who is this person who has been gone for so long?"
The meaning is: "by one who perceives [the person] as 'this is mine'.
We shall meet, we shall come together, with kinsmen possessing the aforementioned characteristics.
Or else:
The first half [of the verse] is the speech of those traveling abroad; the second half is that of their kinsmen:

"We are your kinsmen; may we be reunited with you who are traveling abroad—giving what is desired, bestowing what has been acquired, not harming, not being angry at home, not injuring, knowing us, and possessing affection."

For they are the friends of steadfast power; with boldness, they protect all who are constant upon their path by their own daring might. 2. For they are the friends of steadfast power; with boldness, they protect all who are constant upon their path by their own daring might. 2.
Truly, those who are steadfast and immovable are my companions, possessing strength;
they are bold, being themselves courageous,
and they are present upon their journey.
The word "ā" is used here in the sense of "and.

Even in their movement, those who are "dharṣviṇaḥ"—possessing boldness—by "ātmanā," that is, by their very self through their grace alone, and without regard for our assistance, "śaśvataḥ"—many of us, such as sons, servants, and others—they "pānti," meaning they protect.

Like bounding bulls, they leap over the nights; indeed, we perceive the greatness of the Maruts both in heaven and upon the earth. 3. They, the leaping ones, like bulls, leap over the nights; then we perceive the majesty of the Maruts in heaven and on the earth. 3.
The seven great ones are the seven *spandrāsaḥ*, meaning those characterized by motion;
and the *ukṣaṇaḥ* are the sprinklers of water.
The particle *na* is used here in the sense of "and."
Because others are subject to movement (*spandana*), therefore [he creates] the nights (*śarvarīḥ*). "Nights" means *rātrayaḥ*;
that is to say, the divisions of time.
They transcend them; that is, they go beyond them.
The meaning is that they are eternal.
Since they are of such a nature, therefore we praise the great majesty (*mahaḥ*) of the Maruts, which exists both in the sky (*divi*) and upon the earth (*kṣamā*).
We boldly offer to you, O Maruts, this hymn and sacrifice—ye who are all protectors of mortals from harm throughout the ages of mankind. || 4 ||
O Adhvaryus, Hotṛs, and others, may we place you among the Maruts with boldness, among those who are courageous.
The last [word] is placed first by way of transposition.
Hold fast! What? The *stoma*, the hymn of praise, and the sacrifice.
That by which one sacrifices is the *yajña*, namely the oblation (*havis*). For what purpose are both of these given?
[It is for] those Maruts, all (*viśve*) without exception, who belong to the human ages (*mānuṣā yugā*).
The meaning is "at all times. They protect—that is, they guard—the mortal sacrificer, who is subject to death, from *riṣas*, that is, from the one who causes harm.

1. jha-ṇa-iha-ā; 2. ta-dha-ṣa-ṇa-va-ṣe-vantaḥ; 3. kha-ca-ṇa-asmat-upakārān-apekṣayā; 4. kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-bha-loke-'pi-atrārthe. Ka. 2-112: Worthy are they who are bounteous givers, heroes of unfailing strength. Proclaim the sacrifice to the Maruts, the worshipful ones of heaven. (5) Worthy; those; bounteous givers; heroes; of unfailing strength; proclaim; the sacrifice; to the worshipful ones; from heaven; sing; to the Maruts. (5)

O Soul, to those Maruts—who are worthy of sacrifice, who are Arhats (deserving of honor), who are Sudānavas (givers of beautiful gifts), who are Naras (leaders) of actions, who possess Asāmi-śavas (unfailing strength), who are fit for sacrifice, and who shine from heaven—to them [I offer praise].
There is an interchange of case and number;
or rather, the genitive case is used in the sense of the accusative.
"Offer the blazing sacrifice, the means of sacrifice, and the oblation; praise it, worship it, and present it"—this is the meaning.
Alternatively, it may be construed as "to those who have come from the sky, that is, from the intermediate space."

With their golden ornaments and with their weapons, the lofty heroes have hurled forth their spears. After them, indeed, the lightnings have followed like the Maruts as they are born; the radiance has spread abroad from heaven.
The men, the leaders, the lofty and great Maruts, shine with their golden ornaments—specifically, with shining breastplates; "they shine," is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Upon hearing a prefix (upasarga), there is the mental supply (adhyāhāra) of an action [of conjunction] associated with it.
Likewise, they shine with weapons— the instruments of combat—
as they hurl great spears (*ṛṣṭi*), specific types of missiles, for the purpose of splitting the clouds.
These Maruts are like lightning-flashes, or like waters that produce sound, as if they were being born.
‘When they are born, the waters become sound-makers’—thus says the Nirukta (6.16).
Indeed, they follow after [the Maruts].
The radiance, the light, of the shining host of Maruts has itself gone forth, extending far.

Those who have grown great upon the earth, those who [have grown] in the wide mid-air, or in the gathering-place of the rivers, or in the assembly of the great heaven. 7. Those who have grown great... upon the earth; those who [have grown] in the wide mid-air; or in the gathering-place of the rivers; or in the assembly of the great heaven. 7.
Those Maruts who, being earthly— that is, connected with the earth— have grown and continue to grow;
and those who have grown in the vast, great intermediate space (antarikṣa)—
the word "ā" is used in the sense of "and."
They increased in strength amidst the roar of the sounding rivers, or in the power of the great heaven. (In the yoga of the great strength.)
They have grown strong in the abode and common dwelling place of the heavenly world;
the word *vā* is used in both instances in the sense of "and.
Thus, the connection with the preceding [verse] is that the Maruts, growing in this manner everywhere, have released showers for the sake of rain.

Praise forth the host of Maruts, truly powerful and full of vigor; for indeed, those heroes, eager for glory, have themselves yoked their swift steeds. 8. Host; of Maruts; forth; praise; truly powerful; full of vigor; also; indeed; they; for glory; heroes; forward; swift; yoked; by themselves. 8.
O singer, praise the host of Maruts, their strength, their preeminent power; extol it!
What kind of host?
One with true vigor, with true speed, possessing great wealth, and exceedingly increased.

And indeed, O Maruts, you heroes are the protectors of the rain; for the sake of splendor and for the purpose of water, you have harnessed yourselves—you have exerted yourselves, you have joined yourselves together by your own names, that is, by your own forms—for my sake, you carry forth the sacrifice, being wide-extending. Or rather: with these names, namely the Rudras, you carry forth the sacrifice. 9.
Then the men draw near; then they draw near the team of horses.
Then there are those on the far side—wondrous forms worthy of being seen.
Then men are brought low; then the teams are brought low; then those from afar—thus his wondrous forms are visible. 11.
Now, furthermore, the heroes—the leaders who bring about desired rain and so forth—truly carry the world along.
Now, the *niyuts*—those who mix [with others] by their own accord—also carry it. Now, furthermore, they are those who are beyond [the reach of enemies].
"Parāvat" means a very distant place.
The meaning is that, being connected with that, they are seen—possessing clouds of rain and so forth—in a distant region such as Śrānta-śikṣā and other places.
"Iti" (thus) refers to the manner mentioned; their "forms" (rūpāṇi) are "variegated" (citram), meaning manifold.

O Ṛṣi, O Iyāvāśva, worship and serve with reverence; praise that host of Maruts with a delightful song of praise—those Maruts who are worthy of being seen through their hymns, who are impetuous, who flash with weapons, who are seers possessed of wisdom, ordainers, and the creators of all.
Come, O Rishi, to the host of Maruts; like a maiden to her lover, they seek to give.
Or rather, O bold ones, from heaven, impelled by your might and praised by our prayers, bestow nourishment upon us.
Come, O Sage, to the host of Maruts; like a woman to her lover, they come with gifts. Or rather, O bold ones, from heaven, incited by our prayers and hymns, hasten hither with your might. 14.

O Sage, [approach] the host of Maruts, the assembly of Maruts, like Mitra, the Āditya, with gifts—that is, through the offering of oblations. "Yoṣaṇā" is a form derived from the root *yu* (to join); it means "yoṣā," which is praise. And with that, the ellipsis is "approach" (*accha... abhigaccha*). From the sage's subsequent verse, there is a direct statement: "by might" (*ojasā*), meaning by strength; "the bold ones" (*dhṛṣṇavaḥ*), meaning the daring Maruts; "from heaven" (*divo vā*), that is, from the world of heaven—the word *vā* being heard here.

When there was a search for my great kinsmen—that is, when there was a quest for my own relatives—the wise ones, the impellers, proclaimed *gām*, the speech of the middle region, or the deity Gāyatrī.
This is an unadorned, polished statement;
the seer repeats the words of the Maruts.
Therefore, because the relative pronoun *yad* does not follow them, there is no suppression (*nighāta*) of the accent in the two subsequent verbs.
They called upon the mother cow with their prayers;
they spoke, as it is heard in the Śruti: "The Maruts were born from the milk of Pṛśni" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.11.4).
And then, they—the capable ones—called upon their own father, Rudra, who is impetuous, moving, or swift.
Rudra’s acceptance of the Maruts as his sons has been established on many occasions.
Seven hundred and seven powerful ones have each given me a hundred gifts.
On the Yamunā, I cleanse my fame; below the seal, I cleanse my wealth of cattle and my wealth of horses.
Seven [men], seven powerful ones, each gave me a hundred. On the Yamunā, I have displayed my renowned wealth in cattle; I have displayed my wealth in horses. 17.
There are forty-nine *saṃghas* (groups), for the Śruti states:

"The Maruts indeed consist of groups of seven" (*Taittirīya Saṃhitā* 2.2.11.1). It is well known in the Purāṇas that Indra, having entered Vāyu while he was in the womb of Aditi, divided him into seven parts, and then divided each of those seven parts again into seven; thus they became the forty-nine forms of the Maruts.
And those seven Śākinīs are capable of accomplishing everything.
Each one of them, as a single group, gave—or let it be hoped that they will give—to me hundreds, that is, groups numbering in the hundreds, of cattle and horses;
this was given upon the river Yamunā.

This is a restatement of the sevenfold meaning. Therein, *śrutam* means well-known; *gavyam* means consisting of a herd of cows or related to cows; *rādhaḥ* means wealth; *ut mṛje* means I cleanse upward. Likewise, *abhyam* means consisting of a herd of sheep or related to them; *rādhaḥ* means wealth; *vani mṛje* means I cleanse down.
"Ko veda jānate" is the ninth hymn, consisting of sixteen verses.
Śyāvāśva is the seer (ṛṣi). The first, fifth, tenth, eleventh, and fifteenth verses are in the Kakubh metre.

The sixth, seventh, ninth, thirteenth, fourteenth, and sixteenth verses are *satobṛhatīs*; the eighth and twelfth are *gāyatrīs*; the second is a *bṛhatī*; the third is an *anuṣṭubh*; and the fourth is a *purauṣṇih*. The Maruts are the deity.
Thus it has been enumerated: “*Ko veda*: sixteen [verses], consisting of *kakubh*, *bṛhatī*, *anuṣṭubh*, *purauṣṇih*, *kakubh*, *stobṛhatī*, *gāyatrī*, *satobṛhatī*, and *kakubhasatobṛhatī*.”
The application is based on indicative marks.
Who knows their origin, or who was the first among them in the past to dwell in prosperity?
If indeed the impetuous one has harnessed his team.
Who knows them? Who has understood these? Or who was formerly among the dwellings of the Maruts when the impetuous one harnessed his team? 1.
1. In *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *me*, [the vowel] is the *ṛṣi*.
2. In *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and the two [consonants] *n* and *gh*, [the vowel is the *ṛṣi*].
3. [The consonants] *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra* are seven in number; they are of this number.
4. [The letters] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, and ra signify the fifth case (pañcamī).
5. For these [letters], namely kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, and ra, the term ‘dhana’ does not exist.
Because the Maruts were introduced in the preceding hymn, they fall under the scope of an *anvādeśa* (subsequent reference), and thus the first syllable of *eṣām* is subject to the *nighāta* accent.
Who knows their origin? What man truly understands it?
Or who was there even in the past among these Maruts, who are so well-known—when they, indeed, were weary?
The meaning is "they were satisfied.
They "yoked" them, that is, they harnessed them to the chariot; the sense is: "Who then knows their station, their powers characterized as strength, or their comforts?
The intention is that in matters of speed, they are everywhere the standard of comparison for the wind.
Who has heard of those who stood upon these chariots, or who went forth with them? To which liberal giver did the flowing streams of rain, along with nourishing offerings, submit themselves?
Who has heard of these who have stood firm for the sake of wealth? How did they go? To whom did they submit? For Sudās, his kinsmen submitted along with the *iḷā* offerings and the rains. 2.
Who has heard— meaning, who could cause others to hear— the sound of these [beings] standing still amidst the great chariot-arrays?
Or rather,
who would hear the shouting and the rattling of their chariots?
How do they go? Who even knows that?
Or rather, how could the gods and others follow after them?
For which liberal donor, for the one who gives good gifts, have the kinsmen—the expansive, rain-showering clouds—come as allies?
This [suffix] *ktic* occurs in the sense of the agent.
Accompanied by offerings of various kinds of food, they descended in succession one after another.
They said to me:
"Praise these blameless heroes, the men who have come near with their steeds and intoxicating draughts, saying, 'Behold us!'"
They have told this to me: "The heroes, the men, the spotless youths who have come hither with their chariots and birds for our exhilaration—behold them and sing their praise! (3)
The seer, wishing to describe the manifestation of the Maruts with faltering speech, speaks while beholding those who have thus manifested:
"Those Maruts who have approached me—those who have come to me—said this to me as they arrived. By what means?"
With horses that shine with their manes and move swiftly;
for what purpose? For exhilaration—that intoxication produced by the drinking of soma.

"What do they say?"— referring to what was experienced there— "Men," that is, leaders, "martyas," meaning beneficial to mortals, "arepasas," meaning stainless; "O Seer, seeing us here, looking at us with your eye while we stand thus, praise us"— this is what they say.
Or rather:
"Beholding thus, in this manner, praise!"
Those who are self-luminous in their ointments, or in their axes, in their garlands, in their golden ornaments, and in their rings,
come for the sake of wealth from the chariots.
Those who are in the ointments, or those who are in the axes, self-radiant; those who are in the garlands, in the golden ornaments, in the rings, in the chariots, and in the bows. 4.

1. [The suffixes] following *kha*, *na*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra*; [those] following *śa*. 2. In the region of *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and *da*; not in the region of *na* and *deva*. 3.
*Kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *a* would descend into the *dhṛṣṭyajña*s; *ta*, *ra*, and *a* would descend into the *dhṛṣṭyajña* and others.
4. *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra-yathā*.
By this [verse], he describes the true nature of the Maruts:
"O Maruts, those well-known inherent natures of yours which reside (*śrayāḥ*)—that is, serve as the substratum (*āśrayabhūtāḥ*)—within the fires and within your ornaments."
And those who are in the axes and weapons;
and those who are in the garlands on the necks;
and those who are in the golden ornaments upon the chests.
And those who are in the eating-vessels, in the hands, feet, and bracelets—there are indeed two Vedic verses:
“He takes away both the eating-vessel and the work” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.168.3), and “The eating-vessels are in the feet” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.54.11).
And those self-luminous ones who are present in the chariots and in the bows.
The Vedic citations are: “sudhanvāna iṣumantaḥ” and “surathāḥ pṛṣṭhibhātaraḥ” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.57.2). The ellipsis to be supplied is: "we praise all of them.
Or alternatively: [the meaning of the citation is as follows].
Whatever our own nature may be, O Maruts, we shall become the refuge and support for you when you have fire as your ornament and when weapons are the instruments [of your action];
and likewise when axes are the instruments.
Thus it should be applied in all cases.
The rivers, bearing such gifts, have spread across the mid-air with their flood-waters like lowing cows; they rush forth like horses at the unyoking of their journey, as the bright streams disperse.

The rivers, gushing with their waters, have rushed forth across the mid-air like milch-cows; they spread out like well-trained horses at the unyoking of their journey, as the bright streams flow wide apart.

The Sindhu-like Maruts, rushing along, piercing the waters and rending the clouds with their force, have spread forth and are streaming through the *rajas*, the intermediate space, together with the *kṣoda*, the water—
just as cows that have recently calved, like milch-cows, pour out their milk. Furthermore, there is another simile.

Like swift-moving horses, like steeds at the release of the path, they move for the sake of humans' release from the road; such is the meaning. When—this refers to the rivers—they flow forth, they move in various ways.
Alternatively, they turn back;
that is to say, they increase. Thus, "acting in this way" connects with what precedes.
Come hither, O Maruts, from heaven, from the intermediate space, or from the exhilarating draught; do not remain far away in the distance.
Come, O Maruts, from heaven, from the intermediate space, or even from near at hand; do not stay far away. 8.
O Maruts, come from the far distance, from the highest realm of heaven;
likewise, come from the intermediate space;
and also, come from this world near us.
The same [interpretation] should also be applied here to the word *parāvataḥ*.
Do not cause me to stay, do not let me remain, in *parāvatam*—that is, in a distant place, such as the heavenly world (*dyuloka*) and so forth.
May the Rasā, Anitabhā, Kubhā, and Krumu not harm you; may the Sindhu not destroy you;
may the Purīṣiṇī Sarayū not stand around you; may your favor be with us alone.

May the Rasā with its unfailing waters, the Kubhā, and the Krumu not hold you back; may the Sindhu not cause you to sink; may the turbid Sarayu not stand in your way. May your favor be with us alone! 9.

O Maruts, may the Rasā—this is a name for rivers; according to the Nirukta (11.25), "Rasā means a river"—may she, who is full of moisture (*rasanavatī*) and full of sound (*śabdavatī*), not neglect us. May Anitabhā—she whose light (*bhā*) has not departed (*ita*)—not neglect us. Nor may Kubhā, she of inferior luster (*kutsitadīpti*), neglect us. May Sindhu, who traverses everywhere (*sarvatrakramaṇaḥ*), not neglect us. Likewise, may Purīṣiṇī—*purīṣa* meaning water—[and] Sarayū, who flows along, not stand around us [to harm us].
1. *kha-ca-ṇa-ma* ending in *taranta*; *jha* ending in *vitaranta*; *ta-na-ra* ending in *vitaranta*. 2. *sa-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra* ending in *nava-prasūtika*.
3. *ga-gha-ja-ra-śa* ending in *aśvāḥ* does not exist.

4. They proceed toward liberation through *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *bha*; they turn away from non-liberation. 5. It is exactly the same for *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *bha*, *ra*, *śa*. 6. In this regard, it is as follows: *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*.
7. [The syllables] kha, ca, ṇa, ta, na, bha, and ra are low-pitched; śa is also low-pitched.
Let it stand all around me; let it not obstruct me. (Ṛgveda 2.113)
May there be for us alone that well-being arising from your arrival—well-being belonging to you, originating from you.

After that host of yours, that brilliant throng of Maruts, the charioteers of the most heroic men, the rains follow forth. (10) After that host of yours, that brilliant throng of Maruts, the charioteers of the most heroic men, the rains follow forth. (10)
The word "that" (tam) is connected with the phrase "the Marut host.
The meaning is: "I praise that host of Maruts—your impelling force, the strength of your new chariots, which is brilliant and radiant.
Or alternatively: [the text continues].

"I praise your host—the multitude of you chariots that are swift by nature, which overcomes enemies"—such is the very meaning of the sentence. Now, [the following] is composed in the third person (*parokṣakṛta*):
"The rains go forth, proceeding excellently after you."
Or rather:
the rain-bringing Maruts proceed, that is, go, favorably and excellently.

Group by group, troop by troop, and company by company of these [Maruts], may we follow you with fair praises and with our prayers. 11. Group by group; of you; of these; troop by troop; company by company; with fair praises; may we follow; with prayers. 11.

O Maruts, we would follow—by means of excellent praises (*suśastibhiḥ*), by our thoughts (*dhītibhiḥ*), that is, by ritual acts characterized by the offering of oblations and so forth—the various hosts (*śardha-śardham*) of you all, each of those forces; the term *vrāta* here does not imply a specific numerical group, but refers to each such host—that very host of yours, each collective assembly (*gaṇa-gaṇam*) consisting of seven members. We would thus go after them.

To whom today have they gone forth with this course—the Maruts—to the well-born one to whom the oblation has been offered? ||12|| To whom? Today. To the well-born one. To whom the oblation has been offered. Forth. They have gone. With this course. The Maruts. ||12||
Today, on this very day, to which well-born one who has offered oblations—unto him who has presented the sacrificial gift—do the Maruts go forth pre-eminently by means of this journeying chariot?

That by which you carry grain and undecaying seed for your children and grandchildren—grant us that wealth for which we pray to you, along with all-encompassing prosperity and good fortune. 13. By which; for children; for grandchildren; grain; seed; you carry; undecaying; to us; that; grant; which; from you; we pray; wealth; all-encompassing; good fortune. 13.
1. *kha-ca-ṇa* take *vācchanti*; *bha* takes *vācchayanti*.

2. *ta-na-ra* is the group of syllables intended [for this meter]. O Maruts, with that same mind with which you swiftly carry and sustain for your child (*tokāya*), your grandson (*tanayāya*), or for wealth, imperishable (*akṣitam*) grain (*dhānyam*) or seed (*bījam*), bestow (*dhattana*) that grain and seed upon us with that very thought.

And whatever wealth (*rāghas*) we entreat from you—whether it be *viśāyu*, meaning endowed with all the senses or possessed of complete youthfulness—and also prosperity (*saubhagam*), grant that to us; such is the syntactic connection.
May we pass beyond reproach through blessings, leaving behind blame and hostilities;
O Maruts, may we be with you in rain, in peace, in well-being, in water, and in healing medicine.

May we pass beyond this censure with blessings, leaving behind disgrace and hostilities; O Maruts, may we be together with the waters, rain, health, and prosperity, and with the healing medicine of the dawn. 14.
O Maruts, having abandoned— having cast away— misfortune, evil, reproachers, and enemies who have cast us down,
or rather, those who are hidden (tiras),
may we pass beyond them; that is to say, may we go having transcended them, or may we overcome them.
By this [verse], the avoidance of the undesired is requested; by the following [verse], the attainment of the desired is stated:
"In the rains," that is, when the rains are sent forth by you, there is "śam" (happiness) and "yoḥ" (the warding off of evils), as well as "āpaḥ" (waters).
In place of *śas*, there is *jas*.
The camel is the medicine joined with cattle.
Although this is a name for water, nevertheless, because water has been mentioned separately, here its effect caused by it is being described.
Therefore, O Maruts, may we all together obtain [it].
Or rather:
O Waters, impelled by you, may you perform everything that has been said;
may we all together become one with you, existing as your very self.
O Maruts, that mortal man shall laugh with a goodly laugh and possess noble heroes, whom you protect; may we be such as he.
Sudeva! Truly! He shall be! Possessing noble heroes! O men, O Maruts, that mortal whom you protect—may we be such as he! 15.
The word *samaha* signifies a word of praise. O honored host of Maruts, that mortal shall indeed become *sudeva*, one endowed with gods known as "possessors of auspicious luster."
O *naras*, leaders; O *marutas*, that mortal shall be possessed of excellent sons and other blessings—he whom you protect and preserve. May we likewise become such as these, belonging to you.
Praise the liberal lords for the one who praises them; may they take delight in his path like cattle seeking pasture.
Therefore, with song, celebrate those who desire you, following them as one follows former friends.

Praise the liberal patrons for this singer; let them rejoice at his course like cattle seeking pasture. As of old, follow with your song those who desire you, even as you did yesterday for your friends. 16.
1. *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra-yam* | 2. *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra-yavam* | 3. *ga-gha-ja-ra-śa-‘sa martyaśca’ nāsti* | 4. *ga-gha-ja-sa martyaḥ* | 5. *ta-ya evam*:

O *ṛṣi*, praise the Maruts, the generous givers (*bhojān*), at the sacrifice (*yāmati*) of this sacrificer (*yajamānasya*) who offers praise (*stuvataḥ stutim kurvataḥ*). They are like cows in a pasture (*gāvo na yavase*).
Just as cows delight while going out to graze upon grass and other fodder, so may the Maruts also delight in their resonant play.
Therefore, call upon the Maruts as they go forth, as if toward ancient friends from days of old;
praise with your voice those Maruts who are full of desire and seek death [as their goal]. Praise them, celebrate them with hymns!
The tenth hymn, consisting of fifteen verses beginning with “pra śardhāya,” is the ṛṣi-verse of Śyāvāśva and has the Maruts as its deity.
The fourteenth verse is in the Triṣṭubh meter; the remaining verses are in the Jagatī meter.
It is cataloged [in the Anukramaṇī] thus: “‘pra śardhāya’: five short [verses], in the Jagatī meter; the penultimate is in the Triṣṭubh.”
The application of the hymn is based on its internal indicative marks (*liṅga*).
It serves as the *yājyā* for the principal offering to Agni-Indra-Marut.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Having recited the verse addressed to Indra, 'pra śardhāya mārutāya svabhānave,' one should sacrifice with the verse addressed to the Maruts" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.11).
To the Marut host, self-luminous, this speech is extended;
like a cloud, the Marut host—or rather, the individual Maruts—roars or sounds forth. In this latter case, it is a collective designation.
Then the waters, flowing all around with fragrance, roar upon the earth—their refuge—and fall downwards.
‘*Vidyunmahasaḥ*’ is the *yājyā* for the second *piṇḍī*, just as the third [verse] is for the *kārīrī*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*Vidyunmahaso naro'madidyavaḥ kṛṣṇaṃ niyānaṃ harayaḥ suparṇāḥ*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.13).

The Maruts, heroes of lightning-splendor, who strike with stones, flash like the wind, and shake the mountains; though they are clothed in water, they are repeatedly enveloped in thundering clouds, impetuous and of fierce might.

The Maruts, brilliant as lightning, men who shoot with stones, flashing like the wind, shakers of mountains; though they are from the clouds, they are repeatedly enveloped in thundering hail, roaring, impetuous, and exceeding in might.

The men who possess the brilliance of lightning, whose splendor is like that of lightning, who are leaders of rain and other benefits, whose weapons are stone-tipped or consist of the essence of stone, who have attained radiance through the wind, who cause mountains or clouds to fall, and who are the constant givers of water from the clouds.
The substitution of *yaja* [for *yajati*] occurs;
*cit* is an expletive.
"Roaring" (hādunīvṛtaḥ) means "roaring" (hādanyaḥ), meaning those that set [the rain] in motion with thunder;
the word *amā* expresses accompaniment.
The meaning is: "possessing hosts accompanied by sound."

The Maruts, "impetuous" (rabhasāḥ), meaning those who have yoked themselves for the sake of rain, and "of uplifted vigor" (udaujasaḥ), meaning those whose strength has arisen—this means they manifest themselves for the sake of rain.

The wise Maruts have pervaded the days with their brilliance; they have spread across the mid-air and the regions, O shakers. When you drive forth the sacrifices like ships, O Maruts, you do not suffer harm even through difficult passages.

O Rudras, you have pierced through the nights; O Śikasas, you have pierced through the days; O shakers, you have pierced through the mid-air and the regions. When you drive through the unknown places like a boat, O Maruts, you do not suffer harm even in difficult passages.
"O Rudras"—that is, the Maruts, the sons of Rudra—"you drive away the nights," this is connected with the word following in the subsequent line;
the same applies everywhere.
"You scatter them" is the meaning of that [verb].
O Śikasas, you who are capable of accomplishing all things, you have even driven away the days; you have driven away the mid-air,
and likewise you have driven away the regions.

O Maruts, you shakers, when you drive away the clouds of ignorance as one drives a boat across the ocean, you likewise drive away all difficulties and the fortresses of the enemy; indeed, O Maruts, you do not suffer harm, nor do you cause injury.

1. Kha, ca, ṇa, and sarva are *da*; jha, ta, bha, and sa are *saṃvāda*; na is *saṃpravāda*; śa and sa are *saṃviyutā*. 2. Ra, śa, and śama [are *saṃviyutā*]. 3. Kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, ma, and ra do not exist in ‘aśaneḥ’.
4. Those rich in *kha*, *ca*, and *ṇa*; those whose strength has arisen from *jha*, *na*, and *ra*; those possessing great strength through *bha*.
5. *Jha*, *ta*, *bha*, *ra*, and *vi*—you Maruts, that vigor of yours and that greatness of yours has extended far, like the sun across its course.
These [flames], whose brilliance is ungraspable, have not failed to reach the mountain as they strive toward the night.

That valor of yours, O Maruts, is great in its majesty; it has extended far like the sun across its course. Like coursers unrestrained in their flight, they whose splendor is ungraspable have cast down the mountain that withholds the waters.
O Maruts, that well-known heroic power, your capacity, and your greatness— your vastness— stretches out, extending exceedingly far,
like the sun’s radiance across the world for a *yojana*,
or like the brilliance of the gods.
Just as they extend a long distance of one *yojana* in their march during a watch of the night, such is the illustration for those intent on vigor (*vīrya*).
And they are "those whose brilliance is ungrasped" (*argṛbhītaśociṣaḥ*), meaning their splendor is not seized;
or rather, this is a specific epithet of the Maruts.

O Maruts, you who possess ungraspable splendor, whenever you struck down the mountain—the cloud, or the mountain that was the obstructer who had carried off the horses taken by the Paṇis, or the giver of those horses—you have indeed struck it down.
In this battle, O Maruts, you shattered the host like a tree, O wise ones, as if with a cleft;
now, being of one mind, lead our devotion to a good path, as if leading one who is already on the way.

In this battle, O Maruts, you who are wise, when you let loose the flood like a tree shaken by a woodpecker, then, being of one mind, lead our devotion along an easy path, just as one guides the eye. 6.

O Maruts, you who are the ordainers (*vedhasaḥ*) and the bestowers of rain—let your host (*śardhaḥ*) be victorious in this battle. For [you] strike down the "tree" (*vṛkṣaḥ*), which means the cloud, for it is that which is "split" (*vṛśyate*) or torn asunder; it is full of water (*arṇasam*). You strike it down like "shakers" (*kapanāḥ*); the particle *iva* here is meaningless, or rather, *kapanāḥ* refers to "scorpions" (*kramayaḥ*) or "gnats," just as they sting a tree, so do you. Furthermore, the particle *sma* is a filler. O you who are "united in joy" (*sajoṣasaḥ*), being of one mind with one another toward us—meaning toward me—lead on in succession (*anu nepatha*) him who goes toward *aramati*, that is, toward delight such as wealth and the like, along a "good path" (*sugam*) that is easy to travel. Therein lies the illustration: "like an eye. Just as a leader becomes one by showing the way, so do you.
1. In the manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra, and śa, the word ‘na’ is absent.

2. In kha, ca, and ṇa, it reads *yajanam*; in jha, na, bha, and me, it reads *yajanam*; in ra, it reads *yāme yajanam*; in śa, it reads *yāme gamanāya yojanam*. 3. In kha, ca, and ṇa, it reads *nihatavantaḥ sthāḥ*; in ga, gha, ja, and śa, it reads *nihatavantaḥ*.
4. Like those who are free from desire (ta-kapanā).
5. In the guidance of the path through the letters kha, ga, gha, ca, ja, ṇa, and ma, he is the leader; in the guidance of the path through the letter śa, he is the leader.
He is not conquered by the Maruts, nor is he slain; he does not waste away, he does not tremble, and he does not perish.
Neither his riches nor his protections fail him—him, whether he be a seer or a king, whom you two bring to perfection.

No, he is not conquered; O Maruts, he is neither slain nor does he fail; he does not tremble, he is not harmed, and his riches do not perish, nor do his aids. Whomever—whether a seer or a king—you bring to perfection. 7.

O Maruts, you who cause this seer—the seer being the composer of mantras, the Brahmin, or the king—to prosper, that is, to flow forth or be impelled toward virtuous deeds; he, whether seer or king, is not overcome by others;
he is not defeated by others.
This is either from the root *ji* in the sense of "to conquer" (*ji jaye*), or it is a form of the root *jyā* in the sense of "loss of vigor" (*jyā vayohānau*).
Like the Maruts, he is not struck down; he is not harmed; he is not deprived of his life-breaths;
he does not falter, nor does he decay.
He does not tremble; he is not afflicted.
He does not perish; he is not harmed.
Here, "harming" refers merely to injury.
His riches—that is, his wealths—do not fail him; they do not diminish.
Likewise, his protections (notayah) also do not fail him. For the Kārīrī sacrifice, this verse beginning with “niyutvantaḥ” is the invitatory verse (yājyā) for the third oblation.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Like men who possess teams of horses and conquer the village, drive away the adversaries and the difficult-to-seize ones" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.13).
"Like men who possess teams of horses and conquer the village, like the Maruts who are the lords and possess water-skins;
when they roar, they cause the spring to flow; they drench the earth with the sweet juice."

Possessing millions, conquerors of the village, like men who are Aryaman-like, the Maruts, carrying water-skins, cause the spring to flow. When the mighty ones roar, they drench the earth with the juice of honey. 8.

The Maruts are "possessors of *niyuts*," meaning they are accompanied by those [horses] known as *niyuts*. They are "conquerors of hosts" (*grāmajit*), that is, those who disperse objects that exist in the form of a multitude. They are "men" (*naraḥ*), meaning they have the form of men or are leaders.
Thus, the Maruts are possessors of *niyuts*.

The word *aśva* here refers to horses in general. Those who possess horses (*aśvavantaḥ*)—that is, those who have conquered villages (*grāmajitaḥ*), meaning winners of a village—become like men (*nara iva*), that is, like human beings;
likewise, they are like the Ādityas, such as Aryaman and others.
The word "blazing" (*dīptāḥ*) is to be supplied [as the subject]. Such *marutaḥ* (winds) become "possessors of water" (*kavandhinaḥ*).
When (*yat*—*yadā*), being "mighty" (*ināsaḥ*) lords, they "swell" (*pinyanti*)—that is, cause to overflow with water—the "spring" (*utsam*), meaning a low-lying place such as a valley or a cloud.

When they resound, when they make a noise, when they moisten the earth with the essence of the sweet water—that is how it happens. Or rather: when they resound, then those who are eager for food swell; then they moisten the earth with that food.
1. [The vowels] *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *yaṃ* are well-purified (*suṣūdatha*).
2. *ta* and *tu* are near (*upa*).
3. *kha* is by this (*anena*).

Sloping downward is this earth for the Maruts; sloping downward does the sky become for those who offer gifts. Sloping downward is the broad earth; sloping downward are the regions of the mid-air. Sloping downward are the mountains, which grant life-giving waters. This earth is sloping downward for the Maruts; the sky becomes sloping downward for those who offer gifts. Sloping downward is the broad earth; sloping downward are the regions of the mid-air. Sloping downward are the mountains, which grant life-giving waters.
This earth is *pravatvatī* for the Maruts, that is, for the sake of the Maruts;
it is such that it possesses *pravantas*—regions that are excellent, extensive, and wide.
It becomes like that.
The meaning is that even the entire earth becomes inclined toward the Maruts;
that is to say, they pervade it all.
Likewise, even the sky becomes possessed of downward slopes for them as they move forward with great speed.
She too is for the movement of the Maruts.

Likewise, those belonging to the intermediate space (*antarikṣyāḥ*), existing in the intermediate space, following the path, and possessing downward slopes (*pravatavatīḥ*) belong to the Maruts by virtue of their sloping nature.
The mountains (*parvatāḥ*), the rocks (*adrayaḥ*), or the clouds are possessed of downward slopes; they are the "quick-givers" (*jīradānavaḥ*), bestowing gifts swiftly upon the Maruts.

O Maruts, you who carry wealth together, O heroes of heaven, when the sun has risen, grant us favor from the sky. Your horses do not falter as they gallop; instantly you reach the end of this journey. yat | marutaḥ | sabharasaḥ | svarnaraḥ | sūrye | udite | mardatha | divaḥ | naḥ | na | vaḥ | aśvāḥ | śrathayanti | ā | sisrataḥ | sadyaḥ | asya | adhvanaḥ | pāram | aśnutha || 10 ||

O Maruts, you who are sharers of the spoils, possessors of strength, sun-like, and leaders of all— when, at the rising of the sun at midday, you rejoice in Soma, O leaders (naras) of heaven (divaḥ)— that is to say, when you desire to drink the Soma—
at that time your horses, as they rush along, do not slacken; they do not falter at all.
"Immediately," that very moment, "you reached the further shore" of this path, the way of the gods;
or rather,
when you exhilarate yourselves with Soma, then your horses do not become slack.
And you have heard of the further shore of the entire path of the three worlds.

Upon your shoulders are seers; on your feet are rings; upon your chests are golden ornaments, O Maruts; on your chariot are splendors; lightnings blazing like fire are in your arms; and golden helmets are spread upon your heads. 11. Upon your shoulders are seers; on your feet are rings; upon your chests are golden ornaments, O Maruts; on your chariot are splendors; lightnings blazing like fire are in your arms; and golden helmets are spread upon your heads. 11.

The Ṛṣis are upon your shoulders; the Khādis are upon your feet; the Rukmas and Maruts are upon your chests; the Śubhas, Agnibhrājas, and Vidyuts are upon your chariot; the Śipras are upon your forearms; and the golden [ornaments] are spread upon your heads. 11.

1. Kha-ca-ṇa is for the movement of wind; jha-bha is for the movement of wind; ta-ra is for the essence of wind; na is for the purpose of the immortals (amara) of wind; śa is for the purpose of wind. 2. Jha-na-bha-ra is the mountains.

O Maruts, you grant wealth with desirable heroes; you protect the seer who is inspired by the Sāman. You bestow a swift horse as booty upon Bharata; you establish a king who is full of power. 14. You... wealth... O Maruts... with desirable heroes... you... the seer... protect... inspired by the Sāman... you... a swift horse... for Bharata... booty... you... establish... a king... full of power. 14.

O Maruts, you bestow wealth—riches accompanied by desirable heroes, that is, sons, servants, and the like. O Maruts, you protect the sage who is a singer of the threefold Sāmans, or rather, the seer whose prayers are accompanied by the Sāmans. O gods, you grant the horse, the prize-winning steed, and food to Bharata, the son of Jyāvāśva, who supports the gods.
O Maruts, you bestow upon him a king who is radiant, a lord, or indeed a son— meaning one who is full of strength and happiness.

I beg that wealth from you, O you who possess helpful succor, by which we may extend ourselves over men like the sun. O Maruts, graciously accept this well-spoken word of mine, through the power of which we may cross over a hundred winters. I beg that wealth from you, O you who possess helpful succor, by which we may extend ourselves over men like the sun. O Maruts, graciously accept this well-spoken word of mine, through the power of which we may cross over a hundred winters.
"ha sacaūtayaḥ": those whose protection is immediate; or, "sadyogamanāḥ," meaning you who approach instantly. To you, we go—that is, we entreat—that wealth and treasure.
With that wealth by which we have overspread our men—our sons, servants, and others—as the sun overspreads the sky with its rays;
O Maruts, do you graciously desire, that is, take pleasure in, this speech of mine, this hymn now being performed.
By the power and strength of that hymnic speech, may we cross over a hundred winters—a hundred in number—that is to say, may we live for a hundred years.
The eleventh hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with “prayajyavaḥ,” is the seerly work of Jyāvāśva; it is addressed to the Maruts.
The tenth verse is a Triṣṭubh, while the remaining verses are Jagatīs. The Anukramaṇikā states: “‘prayajyavaḥ,’ ten [verses], the others [are] Jagatīs.”
In the sixth [offering] for the Ābhilāvika [day], this hymn is to be dedicated to the Maruts in the Āgnimāruta [śastra].
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘prayajyava imaṃ stomam’ constitutes the Āgnimāruta” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.7).

The Maruts, eager to sacrifice, with straight-flying spears and golden breastplates, have assumed great vigor. They move along with swift horses that are easy to control; as they go toward splendor, their chariots follow after them. *Prayajyavaḥ* (eager to sacrifice), *marutaḥ* (the Maruts), *ārjahaṛṣṭayaḥ* (with straight-flying spears), *bṛhat* (great), *vayaḥ* (vigor), *dadhire* (they have assumed), *rukma-vakṣasaḥ* (with golden breastplates), *īyante* (they move), *aśvaiḥ* (with horses), *suyamabhiḥ* (easy to control), *āśubhiḥ* (swift), *śubham* (splendor), *yātām* (of those going), *anu* (after), *rathāḥ* (chariots), *avṛtsata* (they have turned).
1. *kha-ca-ṇa-yācāmi*. 2. *jha-ta-na-ra-kāmayata*.

The *prayajavaḥ*, those who sacrifice excellently; the *ājahvayaḥ*, those with shining weapons; the *marutaḥ* (Maruts) *bṛhat*, abundant—either youth characterized by vigor or abundant food—*vayaḥ*, they *dadhire*, maintain.
With broad chests and adorned with necklaces upon their chests,
those Maruts are reached— that is, attained— by means of swift-moving horses that are easy to control;
they proceed in a beautiful and splendid manner.
Or rather:
the chariots of the great ones who have gone forth toward the water also turn after them; they follow along.
You bestow strength upon yourselves as you know how; great and vast, you shine far and wide.
They have measured out the mid-air with their might; the chariots have followed after them as they go in splendor.

By yourselves, you have bestowed strength; as you know, O great ones, you rule far and wide. And they have measured out the mid-air with their might; as they go forth in splendor, their chariots have rolled along.
O Maruts, you yourselves—without any external assistance—maintain, uphold, or perform; what?
Might, strength, and capability.
O wise ones, as you know—
meaning that your power is unimpeded—
you, O great ones, being vast, shine forth widely.
Furthermore, you pervaded the intermediate space with your *ojas*, that is, with your power;
the phrase beginning with "the auspicious" has already been explained.
Born together, well-formed, and nourished together for glory, these heroes have increased even further;
like the radiant rays of the sun, their chariots followed as they went toward splendor.

Born together, well-formed, they have grown up together; for the sake of glory, these heroes have increased even further. Radiant like the rays of the sun, their chariots have followed as they went toward splendor.
Born together, they arose simultaneously; being "subhvaḥ," meaning well-being or great ones.
Likewise, nourished together as sprinklers and showerers, they have grown exceedingly far and wide for the sake of beauty alone, increasing on every side.
The *naras* are the leaders of actions; *virokinaḥ* means shining brightly, like the rays of the sun—just as the rays of the sun (*sūryasyeva raśmayaḥ*).
The word *śubham* and so forth have already been explained.

O Maruts, your majesty is worthy of being arrayed for battle and worthy of being beheld, like the characteristic mark of the sun. Furthermore, establish us in immortality; the chariots have followed after those who go in splendor.

O Maruts, your greatness is worthy of being adorned and worthy of being beheld, like the visible sign of the sun. And so, establish us in immortality; let the chariots follow after the sound of your march. 4.
O Maruts, your greatness is worthy of being honored— that is, worthy of praise— and moreover,
like the characteristic form of the sun, it is worthy of being beheld; and furthermore,
[you lead] us to immortality, that is, to liberation or heaven.
In this context, "dadhātana" means "hold fast. The rest has been explained.
For the first rice-ball offering at the Kārīrī sacrifice, "udīrayathā" is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*).
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "udīrayathā marutaḥ samudrataḥ; pra vo marutastaviṣā udanvataḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.13).
Rouse yourselves from the ocean, O Maruts; you, rich in moisture, cause the rain to fall.
Your milch-cows, O destroyers of enemies, never fail; as you go forth for glory, your chariots have followed after you.
Rise up, O Maruts, from the ocean! You, rich in moisture, cause the rain to fall. O Dasyus (destroyers), your milch-cows do not fail; as they go forth in splendor, their chariots have followed after.
O Maruts, you "urge forth" (udīrathaya) the rain from the "ocean"—that is, from the source of the ocean—from the intermediate space.
This same meaning is stated again:
O "possessors of water" (purīṣiṇaḥ)!
*Purīṣam* is water, derived from the roots *pṛṇati* (to satisfy) or *prīṇāti* (to please).
O you who possess that [water], you cause rain to fall.
O *dastrāḥ*—those who are beautiful to behold, or those who destroy (*upakṣapayitṛ*) the enemies—your *dhenavaḥ*, the clouds which provide satisfaction, do not *upa-dasyanti*, they do not dry up.

When you have yoked the spotted mares to the necks of your horses and have fastened the golden trappings, O Maruts, you scatter all rivals; as you go forth for glory, your chariots follow in your wake.
When you have yoked the spotted mares to your chariot-poles, O Maruts, and have clothed yourselves in golden mantles, you scatter all enemies. As they go forth in splendor, their chariots follow. 6.
O Maruts, when you have yoked the horses to the poles belonging to the chariot—
what kind of horses? The spotted ones (*pṛṣatīḥ*).
Because it is stated that "the spotted mares belong to the Maruts," the mares are those with spotted bellies;
or alternatively, here the word "aśva" (horse) may refer to the *sāraṅgī* (dappled deer).
"Golden" means golden-colored; "atkān" refers to armor; "prati amṛgdhvam" means you put them on.
Having done this, O Maruts, you scatter—that is, you disperse—all these "viśvā" (all) "spṛdhaḥ" (rivals), meaning all battles.
The word "śubham" and so forth have already been explained.
Neither mountains nor rivers obstruct you where you have resolved to go; thither you travel, O Maruts.
Even heaven and earth you pass around; when you set out for glory, the chariots follow after you.
Neither mountains nor rivers obstruct you where you have resolved to go, O Maruts; even heaven and earth you pass around. As they go forth in splendor, their chariots have rolled along.
1. O Maruts, let neither mountains—masses of rock—nor rivers obstruct you; let them not hinder you.
But go, indeed, to that very place where you know, perceive, or intend to be.
Moreover, you two traverse heaven and earth on all sides for the sake of rain.

O Maruts, whatever merit there is, and whatever is new, and whatever is extolled when you have risen up, O Vasus—of all that you are the knowers, O heroes; as you go toward the auspicious, the chariots have followed after you.

Whatever merit there is, O Maruts, and whatever is new; whatever is offered up, O Vasus, and whatever is praised—of all that you are the partakers, O heroes. As they go forth in splendor, their chariots have followed after them. 8.
O Maruts, whatever ancient deed—meaning that which was performed by the ancients—is mine; and whatever new deed is mine;
and whatever is being raised up, meaning that which is attained or praised.
O Vasus, you who provide dwellings, you become the knowers of all that is praised, of every recitation that is performed, and of everything spoken by the singer of hymns.
O Maruts, do not slay us at our root; extend to us manifold protection.
Take heed of this ladle of praise; as you go forth in splendor, the chariots have turned to follow you.
O Maruts, do not strike us down from our root; extend to us manifold protection. Pay heed to this ladle of praise. As they go forth in splendor, their chariots have followed after them. 9.
O Maruts, protect us;
do not harm us!
Do not slay us with the anger born from his [the enemy's] misdeeds.
But grant us abundant, exceeding protection and happiness;
furthermore, come toward the praise of our hymn and the flow of our libation— meaning, bestow upon us the merit of our hymn and the flow of our libation.
Lead us toward better things, O Maruts, being praised, away from all afflictions;
accept our offering of oblations, O holy ones, and may we be masters of riches.
You, O Maruts, being praised, lead us toward greater prosperity away from all harms; O worshipful ones, enjoy our offering of oblations, and may we be masters of riches. 10.
1. For the purpose of moving through *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*.
2. Since the *vasavaḥ* (the Vasus) are those who cause one to dwell in *ga*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and *ha*; and since the *vasavaḥ* (the Vasus) are those who cause one to dwell in *ra* and *ha*.
3. It is extracted, uttered, and sounded.
4. [The syllables] kha, ca, a, ṇa, bha, ra, he are the Vasus, the dwellers; [the word] "nāsti" (does not exist) is absent. 5. [The syllables] ga, gha, ja, śa belong to the Utkṛṣṭas.
6. [The syllables] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, bha, ra are for the purpose of killing.
O Maruts, "you" lead us "toward"—that is, cause us to attain—"vasyaḥ," meaning wealth consisting of heaven and other such things, or the state [of liberation];
furthermore, being "praised" (gṛṇānāḥ), lead us out from "aṃhatibhyaḥ," that is, from sins.
The agentive suffix occurs in the sense of the object.
"Enjoy"—that is, "serve"—"our" "offering-gift," the sacrifice consisting of the giving of oblations; O "worshipful ones," you who are worthy of worship!
And may we "be masters" of "chariots," that is, of various kinds of wealth.
"O Agni, [protect] the bold one"—this twelve-verse hymn consisting of nine verses is the *ārṣa* of Śyāvāśva, addressed to the Maruts.
The third and seventh verses are *satobṛhatī*s; the remaining verses are *bṛhatī*s.
The *Anukramaṇikā* states: "O Agni, nine [verses]; a *bārhata* [hymn], with the third and seventh being *satobṛhatī*s."

O Agni, I now call hither the defiant host of the Maruts, adorned with bright golden ornaments, from the very light of heaven. O Agni, I now call hither the defiant host, adorned with bright golden ornaments; I call the people of the Maruts down from the very light of heaven.
"O Agni, summon—this is the ellipsis—" the host of Maruts, which is "unyielding," "overpowering its enemies," or "conquering for the sake of the sacrifice.
Of what nature is that host? It is "covered"—meaning endowed with or composed of—"golden ornaments" (*rukma*) and "shining decorations" (*añji*).
"Today, on this day of sacrifice, the 'clans' (viśaḥ)— meaning the hosts— of the 'Maruts,' from the 'luminous' (rocanāt) 'heaven' (divaḥ), the celestial world."
The word *adhi* expresses the sense of the ablative case;
*cit* is a filler particle;
*ava* means "downward" or "toward"; *hvaye* means "I call."

Whatever you intend with your heart, even that has my hopes attained. Those who have come most closely to your sacrificial offerings—strengthen them, O you of terrible aspect. Whatever you intend with your heart, even that has my hopes attained. Those who have come most closely to your sacrificial offerings—strengthen them, O you of terrible aspect.
O Agni, you [know] with your heart how the Maruts think— *cit* is used here for emphasis—
by which manner you recognize them as most highly honored.
The meaning is: "Do you show them respect?

"Therefore, let those very ones go for my sake"—let them go, they who are full of hope, desiring, or striking down enemies. Immediately thereafter, those Maruts, having heard your invocations which are most near, come; strengthen them, who are terrible to behold and incapable of enduring delay, by the offering of oblations.
1. In the manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, and ra, the word "asmaddattam" (given by us) is absent.
