2. In the manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra, and śa, the word "rukmaiḥ" (with gold) is not present.
3. In the manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, and ra, the phrase "cit pūraṇaḥ" (the filler word "cit") is absent; in manuscript śa, "viditi" is the filler word.

Like a bountiful earth struck down, she comes toward us, exulting. O Maruts, your onset is like a bear, like a beast with sharp fangs; it is fierce, like a wild bull, full of dread. mīḍhuṣmatīva pṛthivī parāhatā madantī ety asmāt | ṛkṣo na vo marutaḥ śimīvān amo dudhro gauriva bhīmayuḥ || 3 || Like a bounteous earth struck down, she comes toward us, exulting. O Maruts, your onset is like a bear, possessed of sharp fangs; it is impetuous, like a wild bull, full of dread.

Like the earth (*pṛthivī*)— which is *vīḍahumatī* (endowed with firmness), *prabalasvāmikā* (having a powerful lord), yet *aparāhatā* (unassailable) [in its own state] but *anyair abhibhūtā* (overwhelmed by others)—
here the word "earth" (*pṛthivī*) indicates by secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) the subjects residing upon it.
Just as she approaches her own lord when she is afflicted, so too [is the situation here].
The army of the Maruts, rejoicing and exulting, comes to us in its entirety, in every way, and by way of connection; that is to say, it approaches us. Or rather, "vā" means "or. It comes.

O Maruts, that strength of yours is a troop like a tree; it is vigorous, active, and difficult to restrain, like a bull. It is terrifying, yoked with fearsome bulls, like a bull that is vigorous and active.

They who by their might cause [the waters] to flow down at will, like oxen with difficult yokes; they, by their journeys, cause even the sounding stone, the mountain, the peak, and the hill to tremble. 4.

O Maruts, by your own vigor and innate strength, you indeed scatter and destroy your enemies effortlessly, without exertion, merely by your own movement—like oxen that are difficult to harm, or like horses. Those Maruts [shattered] the mountain Parvata, which resounds with its own voice and possesses waters that fill the world;
for the Nirukta states: "Parvata is called 'pavān' because it fills (*pṛṇāti*) or delights (*prīṇāti*) again and again."
Such a "vgiri" refers to a cloud;
or alternatively, "parvata" is the substantive and "giri" is the qualifier, [the latter] being called "giri" because it swallows (nigirati) water.
They cause it to be moved forward by means of poles for the purpose of discharging the water.

Arise now! To these Maruts, who have been sprinkled with hymns of praise—call forth their most abundant and unprecedented host, like a release of cattle! 5. Arise! Now! Of these! With hymns! Sprinkled! Of the Maruts! Most abundant! Unprecedented! Like a release of cattle! Call forth! 5.
O Maruts, you must rise up; arise!
The singular number is used by way of transposition.
Surely, the praise of those Maruts— who have been sprinkled with or increased by hymns (stomas)—
is [the subject]; or rather,
the connection is that they are being invoked by means of hymns.
I invoke that most abundant and unprecedented host of such Maruts—
unprecedented because no one exists prior to them— and I call upon their assembly, the release of waters, or the well-known herd of cows.
1. *kha*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *am* are the vowels (*amīva*).
2. [The consonants] joined with *ta*.
3. [The consonants] preceded by *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *ha*.
Yoke the two bay steeds to the chariot; yoke the two ruddy steeds to the chariots.
Yoke the two swift bay steeds to the pole to draw; the most excellent at drawing, yoke them to the pole to draw.
Yoke them; indeed, yoke the ruddy mares to the chariot. Yoke the two red steeds to the chariots; yoke the two swift bay horses to the pole to draw, the most capable at the pole to draw.
O Maruts, on your common chariot, yoke the ruddy, shining mares;
likewise, on your chariots, yoke the red, crimson-colored steeds.
Yoke the two bay horses, swift and rapid in their course, to the pole for the purpose of drawing.
The repetition is for the sake of emphasis:
"O most powerful ones, you two horses, best at drawing, are yoked to the pole to carry the burden."
And this vigorous, ruddy steed, resounding through the wide space, has been established here as beautiful to behold.
O Maruts, do not cause delay for us on your journeys; urge him on in your chariots.
And this ruddy steed, loud-neighing and beautiful to behold, has been placed here. O Maruts, let him not cause you delay on your journeys; urge him forward upon your chariots. 7.
Moreover, this vigorous steed is trembling, ruddy, radiant, and loud-sounding—a horse with a powerful roar. By the word "ruddy" (*aruṣa*), "red" (*rohita*) is meant;
as it is fittingly stated: "The red one carries [the oblation]" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 1.39.6).

Now here, being visible and beautiful to behold, he has been placed upon the chariot—*sma* being a filler particle. O Maruts, on your journeys and travels, let that horse not cause long delay; let him not tarry.
"He is yoked to the chariots"—this is the ellipsis.
"Impel him," that is, urge him forward;
impel him in such a way that he does not cause delay.
We now invoke the Marut’s chariot, which seeks renown—
the chariot upon which Rodasī stands together with the Maruts, bringing forth delightful treasures.
Now we invoke the Marut’s chariot, which seeks renown—the chariot upon which Rodasī stands together with the Maruts, bringing forth delightful things. 8.
We, the Ātreyas, now invoke today that Marut chariot which is swift by nature, the chariot belonging to the Maruts, the seeker of glory who desires to follow after us.
Upon that chariot, Rodasī— the wife of Rudra and mother of the Maruts (or alternatively,
Rudra being Vāyu)— bears and sustains the delightful waters.
His wife, the goddess Mādhyamikī, stood together with the Maruts; I invoke her as she has mounted that chariot.
1. Kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, ra—these are repeated again.
2. Kha, ca, ṇa—this is "possessing speed" (vegavān); jha, na, bha, ra—"possessing speed. 3.
Kha, ga, gha, ca, ṇa—these they call "the chariot" (ratha).
I invoke that host of yours, resplendent on chariots, brilliant and worthy of praise—
the host in which the well-born, fortunate, and bountiful goddess rejoices together with the Maruts.
I invoke that host of yours, brilliant on the chariot, impetuous and worthy of praise, in whom the well-born, highly blessed, and bountiful goddess exalts herself together with the Maruts. 9.
O Maruts, I invoke your host—your own force, your troop, resplendent on the chariot, brilliant, radiant, and worthy of praise.
Upon that arrow [of yours] are the well-born, well-grown, fortunate, most exalted, and bountiful ones;
for from such passages as "O most bountiful, O most auspicious," we see that *mīḷhvan* refers to Rudra.
His wife is Mīḷhuṣī.

She is magnified—that is, honored—in the company of the Maruts; I invoke that host. Āpastamba also referred to Rudra’s wife by the name Mīḷhuṣī: "With the next [verse], he invokes Īśāna in the southern [fire]; with common speech, [he invokes] Mīḷhuṣī in the northern [fire]; and Jayanta in the middle" (Āpastamba Gṛhya Sūtra 20.1–3).
In the fifth section (anuvāka), there are sixteen hymns (sūktas).
Among them, the first hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with "ā rudrāsaḥ," is the great hymn of Jyāvāśva;
the seventh and eighth verses are in the Triṣṭubh meter, and the remaining six are in the Jagatī meter.
"‘Ā rudrāso ’ṣṭau dvitriṣṭubantaṃ’—thus says the Anukramaṇikā. The application [of the hymn] is based on its internal characteristics."

O Rudras, accompanied by Indra, acting in harmony, and mounted on golden chariots, come for our well-being! This thought of ours is offered to you; it yearns for you as a spring in the sky yearns for the thirsty one.

O Rudras, accompanied by Indra, acting in harmony, with golden chariots, come for our prosperity! This prayer of ours is offered to you; it yearns for you like a spring of heaven for one parched with thirst. 1.

O Rudras, sons of Rudra, accompanied by Indra—possessing him as your lord—and being in perfect harmony with one another, you whose chariots are made of gold, come hither for the sake of the sacrifice, which is well-traversed by all and serves as a means for easy passage toward prosperity. What is it that is found here? It is said:
this our thought, this hymn of praise, yearns for you.
Therefore, come!

O you who are thirsty for water, whose splendor is in the waters, born of longing—just as springs of flowing water were sent forth by you from the sky, the celestial realm, so too, having come for our sake, grant us what we desire. This is the meaning.
1. [The vowels] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, ma are well-known.
2. [The consonants] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha [are well-known]; [the seventh vowel is] ṛ.
(Ṛgveda Prātiśākhya 2.115)

Armed with axes and spears, wise, possessing excellent bows and arrows, adorned with golden ornaments, you have fine horses and beautiful chariots; O Maruts, sons of Pṛśni, well-armed, come hither for glory! Armed with axes. Armed with spears. Wise. Possessing excellent bows. Having arrows. Adorned with golden ornaments. You have fine horses. You are. With beautiful chariots. Sons of Pṛśni. Well-armed. O Maruts. Come. For glory! 2.

O Maruts, you are armed with *vāśīs*—the *vāśī* being a tool or weapon used for marking; you possess these. You are armed with *ṛṣṭis*—the *ṛṣṭi* being a dagger; you possess these. This should be applied similarly in all cases. You are *manīṣiṇaḥ*: lords of the mind, wise ones. You are *sudhanvānaḥ*: possessing beautiful bows. You are *iṣumantaḥ*: possessing arrows. You are *niṣviṇaḥ*: possessing slings. You are *svaśvāḥ*: you possess beautiful horses. You are *surathāḥ*: possessing beautiful chariots. You are *pṛśnimātaraḥ*: sons of Pṛśni. You are *svāyudhāḥ*: endowed with all weapons such as axes, spears, and so forth. Being thus great-souled, you go on your beautiful chariot toward the auspicious water, proceeding in a manner that is truly splendid and auspicious.

You shake the sky and the mountains for wealth to the donor; the forests bow down before your course out of fear. O you whose mother is Pṛśni, you stir up the earth when you, the fierce ones, have yoked your spotted mares for glory. 3. You shake; the sky; the mountains; for the donor; wealth; down; you; the forests; bow down; from the path; out of fear; you stir up; the earth; O you whose mother is Pṛśni; for glory; when; the fierce ones; the spotted mares; you have yoked. 3.
O Maruts,
you shake the clouds from the mountains excessively for the sake of the donor— the sacrificer who offers oblations— and you bring forth wealth and riches.
At your approach, out of fear, the forests—the multitudes of trees and the like—bow down deeply; that is to say, they tremble violently and bend low on all sides.
O you whose mother is Pṛśni, sons of Pṛśni!
"For the Maruts were born from the milk of Pṛśni" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 2.2.11.4); such is the Vedic revelation.
O Maruts, you cause the earth to tremble; you strike it and agitate it.
O fierce ones, you of formidable strength, when—on account of *śubha*, i.e., for the sake of water—you have harnessed your spotted mares (*pṛṣatīḥ*), then you cause the earth to tremble.

The Maruts, blazing like the wind, born from the rain-clouds, beautiful to behold like twins, well-adorned, with tawny horses and ruddy steeds, stainless, impetuous in their power, and vast in greatness like the sky—4. *Vātatviṣaḥ*, *marutaḥ*, *varṣanirñjaḥ*, *yamā iva*, *susandṛśaḥ*, *supeśasaḥ*, *piśaṅgāśvāḥ*, *aruṇāśvāḥ*, *arepasaḥ*, *pratvakṣasaḥ*, *mahinā*, *dyaur iva*, *uravaḥ*. 4.
1. ma-gha-ca-ja-ṇa-ta-na-ma-yā-thana; jhā-yo-thana; ra-yatha-na | 2. kha-ca-ṇa-ta-na-ma-gac-chata; kṣa-gaccha | 3. kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra-yadā dyām |

4. For the sake of *ma*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, *dha*, and *nā*; and then *ta* and *dhana*. 5. *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *āra*, *yatha*; *jha*, *dhakṣārayatha*; *ra*, *dhakṣāra*; *śa*, *cāthava*. 6.
*kha*, *ga*, *gha*, *ca*, *ja*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *śa*—the phrase "O Marutas" is not present; *ra*, *he*.
7. Kha, jha, arbha, and atipṛṣṭha; na, ma, and atipṛṣṭha.
8. Kha, jha, ta, na, bha, ra—O you who are agitated!
You who are always well-pleased with the three winds, you who are free from all taints, and you who are the purifiers of creation.
Alternatively, *nirṇik* is a name for form (*rūpa*). Those whose forms are rain itself are such [beings]; that is to say, they are "givers of satisfaction" (*tṛppradāḥ*).

Like twins born from the same womb, they are exceedingly similar to one another in strength, form, and other qualities; they are well-formed (*supeśas*), possessing beautiful bodies, and are endowed with tawny-colored horses (*piśaṅgāśva*) as well as ruddy horses (*aruṇāśva*). They are stainless (*arepas*), sinless, and possess great speed (*pravakṣas*), being the destroyers of their enemies. By their greatness (*mahinā*), they are as vast as the sky or the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). The connection with the following verse is that those [beings] possessing such characteristics have attained these names.

Abounding in drops, adorned with ointment, bounteous givers, brilliant in appearance, and of undiminished vigor— well-born by birth, with golden plates upon their breasts, these singers of heaven have attained the name of immortality.

Abounding in drops, adorned with ornaments, bounteous givers, brilliant in appearance, whose gifts never fail, well-born by birth, with golden plates upon their chests—these singers of heaven have attained the name of immortality. 5.

The Maruts—possessing abundant waters (*purudrupsāḥ*), adorned with ornaments (*añjimantaḥ*), givers of excellent gifts (*sudānavaḥ*), brilliant in appearance (*tveṣasaṃdṛśaḥ*), possessing inexhaustible wealth (*anavabhrarādhasaḥ*), nobly born by very birth (*sujātāsaḥ januṣā*), with golden breastplates upon their chests (*rukmavakṣasaḥ*), and worthy of worship (*arkāḥ*)—having come from the heavenly world (*divaḥ*), have obtained (*bhejire*) the immortal (*amṛtam*) substance called water (*nāma*), which is the cause of bowing down, or the oblation of that nature.
Spears are upon your shoulders, O Maruts; together, power and strength are placed in your arms.
Splendor is in your heads, weapons upon your chariots, and all beauty is adorned upon your bodies.

Spears are upon your shoulders, O Maruts; strength and vigor are placed in your arms, and power is established in your hands. Splendor is set upon your heads, weapons upon your chariots, and every beauty is adorned upon your bodies.
O Maruts, upon your shoulders the spears—specific weapons—are placed, that is, they rest there.
The word *hita* (placed) used in the upcoming verse should be understood here as well.
The prefix *adhi-* serves to restate the sense of the locative case.

Likewise, upon his arms is placed power that overcomes enemies; for *ojas* is the eighth constituent element (*dhātu*), and thus strength is beneficially established there. Upon his heads are placed golden headbands and ornaments.
In the chariots, the weapons—the instruments of war—are placed;
your splendor, O heroes, has been fashioned upon and rests within your bodies.
1. Kha, ca, ṇa: *sarvatrapradīpaya*; ga, gha, ja: *sarvadīpraya*; śa: *sarvadeśaprāptadīpaya*. 2. Kha, ca, ṇa, śa: *śobhanajātāḥ*. 3. Na: *dhātuḥ*.

The tissues (*dhātavaḥ*) are chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen; these are the seven tissues. The essence of these is the eighth, which is *ojas*. Furthermore, that splendor (*kānti*) which shines in the mouth is perceived as both *ojas* and strength (*bala*). 4. [The variants] kha, ca, ṇa, bha, śa read "golden" (*hiraṇmayāni*).

O Maruts, grant us wealth consisting of cattle, horses, chariots, and brave sons; bestow upon us a gift as brilliant as the moon. O sons of Rudra, grant us high renown. May I partake of your divine protection. 7. O Maruts, grant us wealth consisting of cattle, horses, chariots, and brave sons; bestow upon us a gift as brilliant as the moon. O sons of Rudra, grant us high renown. May I partake of your divine protection. 7.

O Maruts, grant us wealth consisting of cattle—endowed with many cows; wealth consisting of horses—endowed with many horses; wealth consisting of chariots—endowed with chariots; wealth consisting of fine sons—well-endowed with offspring; and wealth consisting of gold—endowed with gold; bestow upon us this food! Grant it! Grant it!
The singular number is used by way of transposition.
Alternatively, it is the second person plural of the perfect tense (liṭ) used in the sense of the imperative (loṭ).

O Rudriyas, sons of Rudra, Maruts—grant us our praise, that is, prosperity. Perform that for us! May I partake of, that is, enjoy, your own inherent protection (*avasaḥ*), the divine protection of the gods.

Come, O heroes, O Maruts, be gracious to us! You who possess abundant wealth, you immortals, knowers of the cosmic order (*ṛta*), hearers of the truth, sages, youths, whose songs are lofty, and who grow great—[be gracious to us]. 8. Come, O heroes, O Maruts, be gracious to us! You who possess abundant wealth, you immortals, knowers of the cosmic order, hearers of the truth, sages, youths, whose songs are lofty, and who grow great—[be gracious to us]. 8.
O Maruts, leaders of men, have mercy upon us; grant us happiness for our welfare, or rather, become happy [for us].
O you who possess abundant wealth, who are immortal by nature, and who know the *ṛta*—that is, the waters or the sacrifice—you are its makers (the sense being that you are the performers of it).

O you who have heard the truth, renowned for truth and the fruits of truth; O sages, wise, ever-youthful, and possessing vast songs of praise; O you who are greatly nourished by abundant offerings or who pour down water—may you all be gracious!
The second hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with “*namo nūnam*,” is the seerical composition (*ārṣa*) of Śyāvāśva; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and is addressed to the Maruts.
This is stated in the *Anukramaṇikā*: “*tamu*.
The application (*viniyoga*) is determined by indicative marks (*laiṅgika*).

Now I shall indeed praise that powerful host of these most recent Maruts—their excellence—those who, with swift horses, carry [the chariot] like the impetuous wind, and who, as self-radiant lords, rule over immortality. tam | ūm iti | nūnam | tarviṣīmantam | eṣām | stuṣe | guṇam | mārutam | navyasīnām | ye | āśvaśvāḥ | amavat | vahante | uta | īśire | amṛtasya | svarājaḥ || 1 ||
1. In the manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, and ra, the phrase "rathavata... putropetaṃ" is absent. 2.
In the manuscripts kha, ca, ṇa, bha, the plural number is used; in jha, ta, na, and ra, the plural number is used. 3. In ta, tuvi-maghāsaḥ.
4. Served by *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *bha*, *ra*, and *sa*; sprinkled with *śa*.
Now I praise that very host belonging to the Maruts (*māruta*), which was previously praised, which is indeed luminous (*taviṣīmantam*) and radiant (*dīptimantam*).
Of what kind are the Maruts?
Not for those who are not [worthy].
There is a change of gender.
Of these newer ones worthy of praise,
[he praises] this host of Maruts;
the Maruts are the constituent members of the host.
What kind [of Maruts] are they? It is said: those Maruts who, being *āśvathāḥ*—endowed with swift movement—and *amavataḥ*—possessing strength—travel and go in such a manner;
and moreover, they *īśire*, meaning they are lords, *amṛtasya*—of the water—and *svarājaḥ*—self-ruling, having their own power, shining by themselves—I praise their host.

Worship, O sage, those men who are radiant, virtuous, powerful, with grasping hands, impetuous in their vows, masters of magic, and givers of many boons— those who bring delight, who are unbounded in their greatness, and who bestow abundant wealth.

The brilliant host, the powerful one, with grasping hands, whose law is roaring, the master of magic, the giver of boons—those who bring happiness, who are immeasurable in their greatness, the men of abundant bounty; O sage, do thou praise them! 2.

"O wise Hotṛ priest, praise and laud the brilliant, blazing host of Maruts—the powerful, strong ones with rings in their hands, who shake [the earth] as their vow, the wise ones, the givers of wealth—this is the connection. Praise those Maruts who are the bringers of bliss, immeasurable in their greatness and unlimited;
praise those leaders who possess abundant riches."
May your chariots come hither today, you Maruts who impel the rain;
O wise and youthful ones, take pleasure in this Agni who has been kindled.
May your ascending chariots come hither, you Maruts who all together impel the rain; O wise and youthful ones, take pleasure in this Agni who has been kindled. 3.

Those Maruts who, being all-pervading, impel—that is, send forth—the rain; those Maruts, the carriers of water, may they come to you this very day, as they are being officiated over by the priests. Now follows the direct address:
O Maruts, this well-known Agni has been fully kindled; enjoy—serve—this Agni, O wise ones, O youths, eternally young or all-pervading.

O worshipful Maruts, you bring forth for the people a king fashioned by Viśvakarman; from you comes the club-wielder impelled by his arms, and from you come the well-bred horses along with brave heroes.

O worshipful Maruts, you generate for the people a vigorous king, fashioned by your own hands; from you comes the man who strikes with his fist and is impelled by his arms, and from you come those with excellent horses and heroic sons.
1. For these—kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, and ra—the [suffix] *e* does not exist.
2. Those carrying kha, ca, ṇa, and bha go; those carrying jha, ta, na, and ra go; those carrying śa go. 3. You are the winds (marutaḥ) of jha, na, bha, and ma.
4. This [consonant] which is well-known as kha, ga, gha, ca, ja, and ṇa;

O Maruts, you [beget] for the sacrificer a son who is a *rājā*—a lord or one who shines—a driver away (*hyam*) of enemies, a shaker of all; one who is "all-glittering" (*viśvataps*), meaning fashioned by Viśvā, the middlemost of the Ṛbhus, and thus exceedingly beautiful. O Maruts, worthy of worship, produce such a son. From you, O Maruts, the son goes forth. Of what nature? A "slayer with the fist" (*muṣṭihā*); the term "fist-slayer" indicates the arms: a slayer of enemies by the strength of his own arms alone. This is expressed as "one whose arms are impellers" (*bāhūntas*): a son whose arms drive away enemies. Likewise, from you, there is born a son who is "like unto you"—meaning many—and "well-heroic" (*suvīra*), possessing excellent valor. This is the sense of "he is born."
In the Varuṇapraghāsa sacrifice, "arā iva" is the *yājyā* for the *āmikṣā* offering to the Maruts.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: "arāivedacaramā ahevame varuṇa śrudhi" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.17).
It serves as the *yājyā* for the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) specifically in the eleven-animal sacrifice dedicated to the Maruts.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Like spokes, like days, those shelters of yours which exist for the one who exerts himself" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 3.7).
Like days, the last ones have followed the first; they are born forth with their splendors like songs of praise.
The sons of Pṛśni, the most excellent, have attained the highest likeness; through their celestial thought, the Maruts have come together.

Like spokes, they are not the last; like days, they are born one after another. The singers, the sons of the Great One, the most joyous Upamās, have grown with their bright splendors. With their heavenly thought, the Maruts have come together. 5.
Like spokes on a chariot, they are not the last nor are they inferior;
all are equal, for the sake of excellence, as if together with the days themselves. Like days.
The meaning is that all days are equal, consisting of sixty *ghaṭikās* and being endowed with the seven groups (*saptagaṇa*) at their end.
By these two similes, the absence of dissimilarity (*vaisādṛśya*) has been established.
Thus, those characterized as described above are born forth—that is, they manifest pre-eminently—by means of great splendors.
The repetition of the prefix "pra" is according to Pāṇini Sūtra 8.1.6, "ekaḥ prasamupohaḥ pādapūraṇe," and that [repetition] serves for the purpose of filling the verse.
And they are *akavāḥ*, meaning not small;
or rather, it is an epithet of *mahābhiḥ*.
They are *pṛśraiḥ*, meaning those who are like sons of the intermediate speech (*mādhyamikā vāk*), which is of the nature of a cow, or of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

Being "upamāsaḥ," each equal to one another, and "ramiṣṭhāḥ," possessing supreme speed—such are the Maruts of great majesty; by their own "matyā," that is, by their own gracious intention, they "sam mimikṣuḥ," they thoroughly sprinkle with rain.
When you have set forth with your spotted deer as horses, O Maruts, on chariots with strong fellies, the waters are stirred and the forests flow away; let the red bull, the sky, thunder down.

When you have set forth with your spotted deer as horses, O Maruts, on chariots with strong-fellied wheels, the waters surge and the forests give way; let the bull of heaven thunder down upon the earth. 6.
1. *Jha*, *ta*, and *ra* are kings.
2. Only *kha*, *ca*, and *ṇa* possess a state of similarity; only *jha*, *na*, and *bha* possess a state of similarity; *śa* and *ba* possess a state of dissimilarity.
O Maruts, when (*yat*)—that is, whenever (*yadā*)—you set forth (*prāyāsiṣṭa*), you go forth with the *pṛṣatī*s, that is, with horses known by that name, which serve as the means of transport.
In this context, the word *aśva* denotes vehicles in general;
hence it takes the masculine gender.
Likewise elsewhere: "When you yoked the dappled horses to the poles" (*Ṛgveda Saṃhitā* 5.55.6).
The expression "rāṃhidaśva" (having swift horses) and "ajāśva" (having goat-drawn horses) is a case of grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Thus equipped with such horses, you set forth with chariots possessing strong fellies and firm wheel-rims.
Or alternatively:
When you, O Maruts, set forth together with your horses and chariots, then the waters surge and flow;
the forests—the masses of trees—are shattered and destroyed by the force [of your speed].
The *ummriyas* are the dawns and the rays of the sun.
May Parjanya, who is connected with that [cloud], the bull, the showerer of waters, and the shining sky, roar downward—that is, let him sound with his face turned downwards—for the sake of rain.

They have spread out upon their path even the earth; they have placed the embryo within their own womb like a builder. They have harnessed the winds as draft-animals for the yoke, and the sons of Rudra have made sweat rain down.

He has spread out upon his path; even the earth trembles before them. Like a husband, they have placed their own embryo within the swift-moving one. For they have yoked the winds as horses to the pole; the sons of Rudra have made sweat their bull.
At every journey, at every movement of these Maruts, even the earth— the ground— *prathiṣṭa*, that is, she became wide-extending; *cit* is a filler particle.
The meaning is that she became fit for conception.

And those Maruts, like a worldly husband (*bhartṛ*), placed—as a wife places the embryo—upon the earth, their own master, the "embryo" which stands in the place of the embryo, namely the water (*śavas*). For, because they have yoked the winds, the moving horses, to the pole belonging to the chariot, therefore the sons of Rudra (*rudriyāsaḥ*) have made the rain their sweat, acting as if it were perspiration.
Hear us, O Maruts, you heroes! May you be gracious to us—you who possess abundant wealth, are immortal, and know the cosmic order;
you who listen to the truth, are sages, and are youthful, swelling with great vigor and mighty strength.

Hear us, O Maruts! Be gracious to us, you who possess abundant wealth, the immortals who know the cosmic order (*ṛta*), who hear the truth, the sages, the youthful ones, whose songs are lofty and who grow great. 8.
"O men!"—thus the eighth [lunar day] of the bright fortnight has passed.
The third hymn, consisting of eight verses beginning with “pra vaḥ spad,” is the Ṛṣi Śyāvāśva’s composition addressed to the Maruts.
The eighth verse is in the Triṣṭubh meter; the remaining seven are in the Jagatī meter.
The Anukramaṇikā states: “‘pra vaḥ spad’: ending in Triṣṭubh.”
The application is indicated by the mark.
1. The masculine gender names are: kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra, and puṃ.
2. [The forms] na-rathaibhiḥ and rathaiḥ. 3. A complete commentary on this mantra exists in the Kha, Ca, and Ṇa manuscripts.
I sing forth for you a song of praise so that the radiant ones may grant us prosperity; I offer the sacred Law (*ṛta*) to Heaven and to Earth.
They moisten their paths, they hasten through the mid-air, and they spread out their own splendor over the surging floods.

May your spy hasten forth to grant us well-being; sing praise to Heaven and offer the sacred Law (*ṛta*) to Earth. They moisten their paths, they traverse the mid-air, and they spread their own radiance along with the surging floods.
He, the clear Hotṛ-priest, cries out loudly—that is, he praises—for you, who are dying, for the sake of attaining *suvitá* (well-being) and for the giving of the oblation.
Or rather, he cries out for you, for the sake of well-attaining [the goal].
This is the form [of the verb] *krandati* in the *laṅ* tense with the suffix *tip*, derived from the root meaning "to cry out," which has already acquired its object.
O Hotṛ, praise—extol with excellence—the shining one, the god Yuvan; O Ātman, do so!

Likewise, O Maruts, you maintain for the sake of glory upon the earth the most excellent, supreme [ornaments] such as turbans and the like, belonging to the cattle. (This is the ellipsis to be supplied.)
Like the sun, you are like the sun itself. Just as the sun holds its orb—the means of sight—for the emission of light, so do you hold the eye, the illuminating light of all, for the emission of rain.
Like swift horses, being well-established everywhere, possessing great speed, and beautiful to behold, you move along.
O mortals, you who are sacrificers,
just as you know how to seek glory through sacrifice and other rites, even so, O leaders, O Maruts, take heed for our glory!

Who has heard the poetic wisdom of you, the great ones among the great, O Maruts? Who indeed [has heard] your manly deeds? You shake the two worlds like a beam of light when you hasten forth for the sake of granting prosperity and bounty.

Who has heard you, the great ones, with your greatness? Who [has heard] your poetic wisdoms, O Maruts, or who your manly deeds? You shake the two worlds like a particle of dust when you set forth to bestow prosperity and wealth.
O Maruts, among you who are great and worthy of worship, which sacrificer would attain great blessings—that is, reach the highest excellence?
And who, for that purpose, would produce *kāvyā*, poetic hymns related to you, the seers?
Or indeed, who would produce *pauṃsyā*, heroic exploits?
This repetition is for the sake of emphasis:
"O you, indeed, you shake the earth; you move it as if it were a beam of light.
Just as one moves a beam of light for the sake of rain, even so do you cause this earth to tremble."

Because you bring forth— that is, you accomplish— the rain for the sake of bestowing such wealth or the water of rain upon one who is to attain it well (*suvitāya*), meaning for one who is to obtain what is to be obtained. You thus produce the rain in abundance.
The meaning is: because you do thus, therefore he does thus.
Like horses of ruddy hue, kinsmen together; like heroes eager for combat, they have indeed fought forward.
Like well-favored youths, the men have struck down [the darkness]; with their rains, they diminish the eye of the Sun.

Like ruddy horses of one and the same harness, like heroes eager for battle, they have indeed fought forward; like well-grown youths, these men have grown strong; they obscure the eye of the sun with their showers of rain. 5.
O Maruts, you who are like swift-moving steeds, radiant guardians, and kinsmen—
those whose sole common bond (*bandhu*) is Rudra,

who are thus related to one another, or who are full of affection for each other— like heroic warriors, you are combatants; indeed, you have fought and continue to fight pre-eminently against your enemies.

Just as men increase like a boundary, so too do these *naras*, the leaders—both those who are excellent increasers (*suvṛdhas*) or those who are themselves increasing (*vardhamānās*)—themselves increase (*vavṛdhuḥ*).
Thus, these great-souled ones thoroughly pierce (*praminanti*), that is, they strike down or envelop with rains, the eye of the sun—the mass of radiance or its orb.

1. kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra-śa-kaḥ udaśravat | 2. kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra- parākramāṇa | 3. kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra-rejatha | 4. kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra-vṛṣṭyudakāya | 5. kha-jha-na-bha-mahātmanaḥ | Ṛgveda 2.116.122.

They who have no eldest, no youngest, and no middlemost, have grown great by their majesty; well-born by birth, sons of Pṛśni, youths of heaven—come hither toward us! 6. They who have no eldest, no youngest, and no middlemost, have grown great by their majesty; well-born by birth, sons of Pṛśni, youths of heaven—come hither toward us! 6.

Those Maruts—having no eldest, having no youngest (all being equal), breakers-forth of enemies, not middling—that is, equal in every respect—have grown forth, they increase, by their greatness and splendor.
Well-born, perfectly formed from birth, sons of Pṛśni, you who are beneficial to men (maryāḥ)—you [are such].

May Heaven measure out for our sake; may Aditi, the Earth, fashion a favorable expansion. That is to say, may she act accordingly. Of what nature is she? Aditi, the undecaying. Or rather: May Heaven measure out, and may Aditi and the Earth fashion the *sūva* (the place of birth). For what purpose? For enjoyment, for protection, or for procreation. May the Dawns, of wondrous appearance and givers of various lights, extend themselves together. O Bull (*vṛṣan*), by you being praised, may the Maruts—the sons of Rudra—be extolled; they have shaken, or cause to shake, the celestial cask, the cloud, or the water. 24.
‘Īḷe agniṃ mavaṃsam’: this is the fourth hymn, consisting of a Ṛc; it is the seer Śyāvāśva’s composition.
The seventh and eighth verses are Jagatīs, while the remaining six are Triṣṭubhs.
Its deity is either the Maruts or Agni with the Maruts as deities.
"I praise the one whose path is for the twice-born, and the one belonging to Agni"—
this is the application of the hymn based on its indicative mark (*liṅga*).
The first [verse] is used as a *yājyā* in the *kārīrī* sacrifice among the *āghāra-offerings*.
And it is stated in the Mūtrita:
"Out of fear, even the earth itself trembles."
"Even Parvata, though he is a mountain, trembles and shakes.
The second half [of the verse] is presented as a perceptible fact.
The connection with the preceding part is: "those who did not act in this way, their hymn of praise [the poet] has meditated upon."
For the seven-potherd oblation to Māruta at the Kārīrī sacrifice, "parvataścin" is the *yājyā* verse.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "parvataścinmahi vṛddho bibhāya sṛjanti raśmimojasā" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.13). "Even the mountain, though greatly increased, trembled at the roar of the bird from heaven; even the earth shook at its sound."
When you play, O Maruts, armed with spears, you rush along like waters flowing through the middle of a valley.

Even the mountain, though greatly increased in size, trembles; even the ridge of heaven shudders at your roar when you play, O Maruts, armed with spears, rushing along like waters flowing through the middle of a valley. 3. O Maruts, when your roar—that terrifying sound—is heard, even the mountain, though great and vast, is struck with fear;
even the lofty region of the sky, the intermediate space, trembles.
O Maruts, whenever you, armed with spears, sport, then you rush forth like great men plunging into the midst of waters.
Like excellent steeds from the gods, they have adorned their bodies with gold and with their own inherent powers;
for the sake of glory, these most excellent ones have placed splendors upon their chariots and greatnesses upon their persons.

Like excellent steeds from the Raivata mountains, they have adorned their bodies with gold and their own inherent powers. For the sake of glory, these most excellent ones have established their splendors upon their chariots and their persons. 4.

Like brides fit for marriage, or like young men—just as they, being wealthy (raivatāmaḥ), adorn their own bodies (tanvaḥ) with gold (hiraṇyaiḥ), that is, with specific golden ornaments, and with *svadhā* (libations) or waters; even so these Maruts, being wealthy (raivatāmaḥ), have adorned their own bodies (tanvaḥ) with gold-like pure white ornaments and with *svadhā*s.

For the sake of glory—that is, for beauty—the most excellent, the best, the powerful Maruts have truly established their greatness upon their chariots and in their bodies. The meaning is that, endowed with all ornaments and [anointing] waters, they mounted their chariots and maintained splendor within their own persons.

"Among these, none being eldest and none being youngest, the brothers have grown together for good fortune."
You two are the father of these, Khapā Rudra; Pṛśni is well-milking and the days are auspicious for the Maruts.

Neither the eldest nor the youngest—these brothers have grown together for good fortune. You two are their father, the skillful Rudra; Pr̥śni is their well-yielding mother, providing fair days for the Maruts.
Without an eldest and without a youngest—devoid of the state of being elder or younger among one another—they have risen up together, equal in strength.

These great brothers, being mutually brotherly, have grown, indeed they flourish, for the sake of prosperity. Their father is Rudra, eternally youthful and skillful in his deeds; their mother is Pṛśni, the well-milking cow-deity; and for the Maruts, there are auspicious days.
The remainder [of the verse] refers to the Akuru [demons].
Whether you, O Maruts, are in the highest, the middle, or even the lowest heaven, O fortunate ones;
therefore, O Rudras, take notice of us, whether in the presence of men or when we sacrifice with oblation.

Whether you Maruts are in the highest [heaven], or in the middle, or indeed in the lowest, O fortunate ones, you who dwell in heaven—from there, O Rudras, take notice of us now at the beginning of this oblation which we offer. 6.

O Maruts, you who are fortunate (*subhagāsaḥ*), whether you abide in the highest, most excellent, or final heaven (*divi*), or in the middle heaven, or even in the lowest heaven—since these three worlds are threefold, as the Vedic scripture states, "The threefold [worlds] are these: there, of heaven, earth," and so forth; therefore, O Rudras, come from these three places for our sake (*naḥ*). (The word *āgacchata*—"come"—is to be supplied.)
Or rather, indeed, today, if we sacrifice, O Agni, you who are the lord of the sacrifice, may you consume this oblation; recognize this offering.
And since Agni, O all-knowing Maruts, has carried [the oblation] from the high ridges of heaven,
may you, rejoicing, the shakers who ward off harm, bestow wealth upon the sacrificer who presses the soma.

And when you, O Maruts, possessors of all wealth, carry Agni from the higher heaven across the ridges, do you, rejoicing, roaring, and destroyers of enemies, bestow desirable wealth upon the sacrificer who presses the soma.
O Maruts, you who are all-knowing— knowers of everything— or possessors of all wealth, since you and Agni carry yourselves upon the ridges (*snu*) above the higher, most excellent heaven (*divaḥ*),
that is to say, you dwell there; or else, by the word *snu*, horses similar to those ridges are meant.

O Agni, with the Maruts who shine with splendor, drink the Soma, rejoicing with the hymns of praise, together with the glorious hosts, the purifiers, the all-pervading, and the living beings; O Vaiśvānara, hasten hither from of old with your banner of light! 8.

O Agni, rejoicing together with the Maruts, drink the Soma! With what kind of Maruts? With those who are "śubhayadbhiḥ"—shining or making others shine; "arkibhiḥ"—worthy of praise; "gaṇaśribhiḥ"—resorting to the state of a troop; "pāvakaiḥ"—purifying; "viśvamanvebhiḥ"—delighting all through their vision; "āyubhiḥ"—endowed with long life.
O Vaiśvānara, Agni who belongs to all men, joined together with the ancient "ketunā"—the mass of flames—from time immemorial.

The fifth hymn, consisting of nineteen verses, begins with "ke chā naraḥ. According to the Anukramaṇikā: "Ke [is] nineteen [verses]; Gāyatrī; Śyāvāśva is the seer here; he praised Vaidadaśvi, Taranta, Purumīḷha, Dābhya, Rathavīti, and the Maruts; he also praised Dadhuṣṭar, Tudadhvā, and Taranta’s most excellent queen; the fifth verse is an Anuṣṭubh, as is the ninth; [the rest] are Satānuṣṭubhs. Śyāvāśva is the ṛṣi.
The fifth verse is an *anuṣṭubh*, the ninth is a *sato-bṛhatī*, and the remaining verses are *gāyatrīs*.
The first four have the Maruts as their deity.
Of the four beginning with “*manasā*,” the deity is the wife of King Taranta, named Śaśīyasī.
The deity of the verse beginning with “uta meḍarapata” is Purumīḷha Vaidadaśva;
the deity of the verse beginning with “yo me dhenām” is King Taranta Vaidadaśva;
and those beginning with “ya īṃ vahante” belong to the Paṇis and the Maruts.
For this triplet beginning with "etaṃ me," the deity is King Dābhya named Rathavīti;
the application is based on internal indicative marks (liṅga).
Regarding this, those who have mastered the traditional scriptures recount a wonderful event from the past:
that Arcanānas was slain by his own son, Dabhīti Rathavīti.
Chosen for the office of *adhvaryu* at the sacrifice and established in the role of *hotṛ* priest for Vinatā,
he beheld the maiden daughter of Rathavīti in the presence of her father.
Just as he, being intent on giving that daughter to his own son Śyāvāśva, asked his wife, "To whom shall I give her? and she replied, "To whomsoever you wish."
Thus questioned, she spoke again: "How will you give her to him?
Until now, no daughter has ever been given to one who is not a householder."
Having ascertained that it was indeed so, Śyāvāśva rejected the worshiper at the conclusion of the sacrifice; by him, the king was cast out.
Filled with hope for that, the Brahmin performed most severe austerity;
remaining celibate and tranquil, the twice-born wandered about seeking alms.
He begged for the virtuous Mahiṣī, who was most excellent;
she, having approached her husband, said, "A sage has arrived."
Thus addressed by the two kings, she replied, "I shall worship you";
having received their permission, she gave a herd of cows and ornaments.

Having heard the king’s words, "So be it," and being shown the path by his wife,

Beholding him, the Brahmin, filled with fear, bowed with palms joined in reverence; his body’s every limb bristling with thrill, his heart delighted and his mind supremely satisfied, he offered praise with most excellent words.
Then, having fulfilled all his own desires, he, with a joyful heart and self-controlled, [bestowed them] upon the hosts of Maruts.
Then there was also the seer Jyāvāśva, the author of the hymn;
later, having gone to the house of Unnetṛ, he obtained yet another hundred cows.
Urged by the king, Dabhya gave his daughter to the two seers of mantras, Purumīḷha and Turata;
yet their wife was not more praiseworthy.
The two [deities] from whom [the gift came], he whose mouth is the chariot-wind (rathavātyāsya), and those seven hosts of Maruts—
whatever they gave to him, that is indeed described here at the Śrāddha.

Having perceived from signs such as the lashing with whips that they were desirous of departing, he says:

"O heroes (*vīrāsaḥ*), you who incite enemies; O mortals (*maryāsaḥ*), those who are beneficial to mortal men; O you of auspicious birth (*bhadrajānayaḥ*)—those whose birth (*jāniḥ*) or lineage is auspicious (*bhadraḥ*), meaning praiseworthy."
The meaning is "sons of Rudra. Just as those such as Agni and the others, heated by fire, become intensely blazing, so do you become.
Or rather, become like those who, being scorched and their bodies burnt, flee away.

May she win for him horses and cattle, even a hundred sheep; may that arm which she extended for the hero, praised by Iyāvāśva, grant him wealth. (5) May she win for him horses and cattle, even a hundred sheep; may that arm which she extended for the hero, praised by Iyāvāśva, grant him wealth. (5)
She, the daughter of Taranta, bestowed— that is, gave— to me a herd of horses,
meaning either consisting of horses or a collection thereof.

The singular number is used for the genus (*jātāvekavacanam*). Furthermore, "gavyam" means a herd of cattle consisting of a multitude of animals; "śatāvayam" means endowed with many parts. Regarding the word "sanat," he asks: "What is it that is so called? and answers as follows:
She who, for the hero Taranta—who was praised by me, Iyāvāśva—raised up her own arm to embrace him;
she is "sanat" (the giver), because, being the object of her husband's love, she is capable of bestowing great wealth upon him.

And even a woman becomes more constant and better than a man who is godless and ungenerous. 6. And: *uta* | *tvā* | *strī* | *śaśīyasī* | *puṃsaḥ* | *bhavati* | *vasyasī* | *adevatrāt* | *arādhasaḥ* || 6 ||

Moreover, she alone is *śaśīyasī*. *Śaśīyasī* is a name for greatness; she is indeed a woman. Or rather, the particle *uta* has the sense of the restrictive *eva*; the meaning is that she alone is most excellent among women. Because of the rule "In *tva*, *asama*, and *asmin*, the *e* is unaccented," the word *ve* (from *vā*) is unaccented. She alone becomes *vamyasī*—more excellent—than *puṃsaḥ*, i.e., than men. From which man? It is said: from *adevatrāt*. Those by whom one is protected through praise and so forth are *devatrāḥ*; those who are not so are *adevatrāḥ*. From such a person, i.e., from one who is *arādhasaḥ*—devoid of wealth (*rādhaḥ*) or the merit of giving; that is to say, from a miser.

She who discerns the exhausted, the thirsty, and the desirous, turns her mind toward the gods. ||7||
She who is more frequent [or abundant], [she who knows] the one who is exhausted and distressed—
*jamis* being a term for striking or a term for consuming—
she knows him thoroughly.
Likewise, he discerns one who is thirsty;
he discerns one who is lustful and possesses a longing for wealth.
Out of compassion, he has bestowed what is desired upon those standing on the path.

"Among the gods," that is, among the deities, he "makes his mind," that is, he directs it; for the sake of pleasing the gods, he performs an increase in giving—that very [act] is what is referred to as "that" (yā sā) in the preceding connection.

*Uta* means "also" (*api ca*). *Gha* is an expletive (*pūraṇa*). *Nema*: according to the Nirukta (3.20), "the meaning of *svā nema* is [one] half. *Nema* means "half. Because the wife and husband together perform a single task, they constitute a single entity, as per the Smṛti texts such as, "The wife is half of one's body. I say that the man who belongs to the half of the female is "unpraised" (*astutaḥ*). Even though he is praised in many ways, because of the extreme abundance of his qualities, I say he is "as if unpraised. *Paṇiḥ* refers to me, the praiser. And *saḥ* (he) is "crossing over" (*tarantaḥ*) in the matter of the distribution of heroes (*vairadeye*). Heroes (*vīrāḥ*) are those who send forth wealth and are disposed toward giving. That which is to be given by them is "wealth to be given" (*deyam*). In that wealth, he is "equal" (*samaḥ*), meaning he is to be given to all. *It* is an expletive.

And the young woman, joyfully smiling, has come toward me, the dark-hued one, along the path. Her two ruddy horses have drawn [the chariot] for Purumīḷha, the inspired sage of far-reaching fame. What?
The path, the track. Of what sort is it?
It is young.
She who has reached the bloom of youth, rejoicing like a woman among men—
for whom?— for the one of long renown, for the one of abundant command, or for the one of great fame; for the one named Purumīḷha, the possessor of many dwellings, for the inspired sage (vipra).

However, regarding the word *varuṇa*, since the preceding word is considered non-existent according to the rule "an *āmantrita* [vocative] that precedes is as if non-existent," it is logical that this very word [varuṇa], beginning the quarter, should not be *nighāta*-ed.

According to the rule "an address [is treated as] non-existent when it stands in grammatical apposition with a word of general meaning," because *varuṇa* stands in apposition with the address and this [latter] is a word of general meaning, there is no absence of the status of being "as if non-existent"; thus, since it is not at the beginning of a *pāda*, it is appropriate that the following word (*adhārayatam*) receives the *nighāta* accent.

This chariot, adorned with gold (*hiraṇya-nirṇik*), has a golden form (*hiraṇya-rūpa*). *Nirṇik* is a name for appearance or ornament. The pillars, pins, and other parts of that chariot are *vayas*. O Mitra and Varuṇa, by your favor, Parjanya— the cloud— utters, for the sake of rain, a voice that is most excellent, full of nourishment (*irāvatī*), effective in providing food, wonderful (*citrá*) and praiseworthy, and radiant (*tviṣīmatī*). And the Maruts, through their own wisdom (*māyayā*), well clothe the clouds, the vessels of food, with rain.
And you two, together with Parjanya and the Maruts, cause that which is ruddy—of ruddy color, stainless, free from evil, and unimpeded by rain—to rain down.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, wise ones, you guard the sacred laws through the creative power of the Asura by means of Dharma.
By the Eternal Order (*ṛta*), you rule over the entire world; you have placed the sun in heaven and the wondrous chariot in the sky.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who are wise through the Law, you guard the sacred ordinances by the power of the Asura and by Truth; you rule over the entire world. You place the sun in heaven as a wondrous chariot.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, you two wise ones, through *dharma*—the sustaining power characterized by rain and other such functions—you protect and maintain the *vratas*, the ritual acts such as sacrifices. By means of the *māyā* (power) and wisdom of the *asura* Parjanya, the dispeller of clouds, and by means of *ṛta*—whether as water or as sacrifice—you cause the entire world, the whole multitude of beings, to shine forth; that is to say, you make it manifest.
O Sūrya and Sūryā, you two place in the heavenly world the wondrous, worshipful chariot, which has the nature of moving swiftly, for the sake of benefiting the world.
The seventh hymn, beginning with "varuṇa vaḥ," is the eighth [hymn] of the *arcanāna* collection; it is addressed to the Aśvins and Varuṇa (*maitrāvaruṇa*).

O Mitra and Varuṇa, I maintain with a hymn—that is, by means of praise—as something to be given by you both, a wealth that is "upama," measured out in close proximity.

The meaning is that there arises a rivalry regarding the possession of wealth among the wealthy patrons and the praisers.

In that [place], my own pressed Soma—

[is to be drunk] now by those possessing hands (*hastabhiḥ*).

"O leaders, Mitra and Varuna, come hither!

The ninth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with "yaśriketa," is addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa; its seer is Atri Gatahavya.

May he of good deeds speak our praise; may he instruct us in the highest [truth].
And he who is *darśataḥ*, worthy of being seen—Varuṇa, the worthy of being seen, or Mitra (the word *vā* has the sense of "and").
"He accepts—that is, he enjoys—our words, our hymns of praise."
For they are two kings of most excellent luster and most far-famed; they are the lords of the good, increasers of cosmic order, upholders of truth among every people.
For they are two kings of most excellent luster, most far-famed; they are the lords of the virtuous, the increasers of cosmic order (*ṛta*), possessors of *ṛta*, among every people. 2.

Approaching you both for protection, I invoke those ancient ones together;
possessing good horses, may we, through your wisdom, prevail in the winning of spoils.
Approaching you both for protection, I call upon you first with this prayer; accompanied by good horses and through your wise insight, grant us strengths for our advancement.

Knowing you two, who are ancient and primordial, I have approached for protection; coming together, I praise you. We, the Ātreyas, possessing good horses, [praise] you two of beautiful wisdom with excellent insight, directing our hymns toward food and wealth for the sake of your giving—this is the sense.

Mitra wins a path even from distress for a dwelling;
for the favor of Mitra, who overcomes all, belongs to the one who serves him.

The god Mitra releases even from great distress the one who praises him; immediately thereafter, he grants a wide path for a spacious dwelling, that is, for a home or a place of residence.

May we, as sacrificers, abide in the most extensive—that is, the most wide-reaching—protection of the god Mitra, the remover of suffering. O bounteous ones, do not abandon us who possess the oblation; do not forsake even the sons of us, the seers. But rather, protect us in the *gopītha*—that sacrifice wherein the Soma-cow is drunk—and guard us there. 3.
The tenth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “ā cikitāna,” is the seer Rātahavya’s composition; it is in the Anuṣṭubh meter and is dedicated to Mitra and Varuṇa.

It is used as the first [verse] in the Prauga Śastra of the Maitrāvaruṇa on the fourth day of the Daśarātra sacrifice.

O mortal man, take heed of the two gods of wise intellect who destroy the enemy;
let him offer [oblations] for the great enjoyment to Varuṇa, whose form is the cosmic order (ṛta).

O mortal man, take heed! Let the two gods of noble wisdom, who destroy the enemies, be mindful [of you]. To Varuṇa, whose form is the eternal Law (ṛta), let one offer for the sake of great refreshment.

O man, being conscious—that is, knowing—the praise, O giver of oblations (rātahavya)—this is an address to him—[invoke] those two gods of excellent power (sukratū), whose limbs perform beautiful deeds, who are the destroyers of the harmful (riśādasā). [The word] "ā" is understood as "invoke. And having invoked them, [offer] to Varuṇa, who is of true form (ṛtapeśase)—*peśas* is a name for form; *ṛta* is water; to him whose form is water—to such a one, for the sake of refreshment (*prayase*). The possessive suffix (*matup*) is elided. "Vṛṣṭidyāvā": either "those for whom heaven is for the sake of rain," or "those by whom heaven is praised through rain. Or else, "those by whom rain is produced (vṛṣṭi-vipikā) and heaven (dyauḥ) is the intermediate space (antarikṣa). "Rityāpā": *rīti* means attainment; "those whose attainment (*āpā*) is the desired goal (*āsiḥ*)"—such are they. "Iṣaḥ": lords (*patī*) of food (*anna*). Their lordship arises from being the bestowers of rain. "Dānumatyaḥ": possessing giving (*dānavatyaḥ*); that is to say, "possessing the thought of giving"—this is an adjective. Such great-souled ones "āśāte," meaning they pervade or occupy the "bṛhantam" (vast) "gatam" (moving) chariot, for the purpose of sacrifice. || 6 ||
1. kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra-devī;
2. kha-ca-ṇa-stutau; ta-stutyā; 3.
kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra-barhirvā.

4. Kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra—these constitute *āti*; ga, gha, ja, śa—these constitute *apā*. 5. Kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra—[these belong] to the one worthy of giving (*dānamucitā*); ga, gha, ja, śa—[these belong] to the one worthy of the giver (*dātṛpūcitā*).

The hymn consisting of four verses beginning with "trī rocanā" is the thirteenth hymn. The seer (*ṛṣi*) is Uruccakri Ātreya; the metre (*chandaḥ*) is Triṣṭubh; the deities (*devatā*) are Mitra and Varuṇa. And in the Anukramaṇī: "trī rocanā: the group of four [verses] has Uruccakri as the seer. The application (*viniyoga*) is indicated by the internal characteristics of the text.
O Varuṇa, you two uphold the three luminous realms and the three heavens; O Mitra, you maintain the three regions.
Increasing in power, you protect the dominion of the Kṣatriya and his ageless law.
Three bright realms, O Varuṇa, three, O Mitra—you two uphold these three regions. Increasing in strength, you guard the imperishable majesty of the sovereign according to his law.

The connection is as follows: "O Varuṇa, O Mitra, you two sustain the three, yes, the three luminous realms—the worlds of heaven. Furthermore, you also sustain the three young, shining intermediate regions (the atmosphere), and likewise the three dust-laden realms—the worlds of the earth.
What kind of two are you?
Increasing, growing—the *kṣatra*, or power, of a *kṣatriya*;
that indeed belongs to Indra.
Or rather:
this refers to the lack of intelligence (or form) of a sacrificer belonging to the Kṣatriya caste.
They were guarding their physical form, their vows, and their actions—though these were unworthy, undigested, or unrestrained.
O Varuṇa, your two cows are full of nourishment; O Mitra, the rivers yield honeyed milk.
Three bulls stand firm, the bestowers of seed upon the luminous bowls of heaven.
O Varuṇa, the cows rich in milk are yours; O Mitra, the rivers yield your sweet honey. Three bulls have stood as the depositors of seed for the three worlds; they shine forth with splendor.
O Varuṇa, O Mitra, yours—yours both—are the victorious cows, the milch-kine rich in *irā*.
*Irā* here signifies milk; they are characterized by that.

Likewise, the flowing waters (*sindhavaḥ*) yield sweet water from the river; similarly, the three bulls—those who possess three forms, the showerers, the bestowers of seed, the sustainers of water, and the radiant ones—namely Agni, Vāyu, and Āditya, being the lords of the three *dhiṣaṇās*, the three places consisting of the earth, the intermediate space, and the celestial world, stand individually and variously. The meaning is that by your grace, all three gods abide in these three locations.

In the morning I invoke the goddess who rejoices; at midday, when the sun has risen, I call upon you, O Mitra and Varuṇa, for wealth, for our heroes, and for the well-being and peace of our children and descendants.

At dawn I call aloud to the goddess Aditi; at midday, and even at the setting of the sun, O Mitra and Varuṇa, for the sake of wealth and for our complete well-being, grant peace and prosperity to our children and descendants.
1. There is no *chandaḥ* with the syllabic sequence sva-ca-a-ga-ta-na-ma-ra-śa.
2. [The sequence] sva-ca-a-ga-bha-ra-śa is *rocamānāni*; *na-rocanāni* does not mean *rocamānāni*. 3. There is no [sequence] sva-na-ṇa-bha meaning “vāvṛdhānau vardhamānau.”
4. There is no [mention] of the "places... of the worlds" (ma-ca-ṇa); rather, there are the places beginning with a-na-na-ma-ra-śa.
I, Upi, at every dawn—at the time of morning—invoke repeatedly the goddess Aditi, the mother of the gods, who is indivisible and radiant.
Likewise, at midday, at the rising of the sun—that is, at the time of its full emergence—I invoke her repeatedly during the midday libation.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, I praise you both at the sacrifice for the sake of all-encompassing wealth, so that we may attain riches.
For what purpose?
For the welfare of our children, our grandsons, and their sons; for peace as the pacification of misfortune, and for well-being as the attainment of easy passage.
Those laws of yours which are upheld in the bright realm of the mid-air, and those of the celestial and earthly spheres, O divine Adityas—
neither the immortal gods nor others violate these firm decrees of yours, O Mitra and Varuna.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, you who uphold the realm of light within the dustless firmament—both the celestial and the terrestrial—your eternal laws, O immortal gods, are not transgressed by the deities. 4.

"Those two who [are the sustainers] of the shining *rocana*, that is, of the radiant *rajas*—meaning the world known as heaven—and moreover, those two who are the sustainers of the earthly *rajas*; those two divine sons of Aditi, you two who exist in heaven—I praise you. This is how the connection with the preceding verse is made.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, your firm vows—your actions—even the other immortal gods, whose nature is deathlessness, such as Indra and the rest, do not violate;
for they are indeed firm, such is the intended meaning.
The four-verse hymn beginning with “purūraṇā” is the fourteenth hymn; it consists of eleven verses, is in the Gāyatrī meter, and is addressed to Mitra and Varuṇa.
The Anukramaṇikā states: “‘purūraṇā’: [it is] in the Gāyatrī [meter].
This hymn, along with the preceding one, is for the purpose of insertion (āvāpa) during the morning pressing (prātaḥsavana) of both the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava Ṣaḍahas.
It is stated: “One should extract the second [verse] from the four beginning with *pra vo mitrāya*.
On the twenty-fourth day (*cāturviṃśaka*), during the morning pressing (*prātaḥsavana*), at the *mitrāvaruṇa-śastra*, the first verse is designated as the *ṣaḍaha-stotra*.
And it is recorded in the sūtra: “*purūraṇā cid rayasi prati vām mūra udite*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.2).

Even abundant wealth exists; now indeed, O Varuṇa and Mitra, may I obtain your protection and your favor. 1. Even abundant wealth exists; now indeed, O Varuṇa and Mitra, may I obtain your protection and your favor. 1.
O Mitra and Varuṇa, even *purūṇā* [the many] of you two— here, the form *moḥ* is derived from the genitive dual ending by the rule *supāṃ suluk*.
"Purorapi" means much, vast,
or even more so; or alternatively, "puru" and "uru" combined as "purūru," meaning exceedingly superior.
There is indeed, certainly, no protection at all; for "hi" indicates well-known fact,
and "cit" is a filler particle.
O Varuṇa, O Mitra, may I enjoy your *sumati*—your benevolent thought;
the sense is that because such protection exists, I shall therefore enjoy it.

1. "I call upon them. 2. O you two who are held by *jha*, *ta*, *na*, *ra*, and *dhṛ*, may we obtain that food from you in a well-sustained manner for our nourishment. O Rudras, may we be yours. O you two, may we, being well-supported, obtain that food for our sustenance; O Rudras, may we be yours.
O you two who are firm, O you two who are firmly established—those two of you, well-known [as such], we praise you thoroughly; this is the ellipsis.
May we, as singers of praise, obtain and attain *iṣ*, that is, food, for the sake of nourishment, drinking, and eating.
O Rudras, you two who cause misfortunes to flee (*rudrā duḥkhān drāvayitārau*), or who are themselves to be approached with devotion (*rudriḥ* = *dravaṇīyau*), may we be your praisers;
that is, may we be prosperous— this is the ellipsis— or may we belong to you.

Protect us, O Rudras, with your protections; and save us, O excellent deliverers. May we overcome our assailants with our weapons. 3. Protect us, O Rudras, with your protections; and save us, O excellent deliverers. May we overcome our assailants with our weapons. 3.
O Rudras, you two gods of the aforementioned form, protect us with your guardians—that is, with your protections.
Moreover, as excellent saviors (*sutrātrau*), may you rescue and preserve us;
the distinction [between the two verbs] is based on the difference between the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired.
"Protect us from the enemy by means of a deficiency in their hymns of praise and so forth; that is to say, guard us by bringing about what is desired.
And may we, together with our offspring and others—or with our own [strength]—overcome (*turyāma*), meaning we shall harm or cross over, the *dasyus*, the enemies."

O you of wondrous power, may we not, through our own bodies, suffer the affliction of anyone; may we not suffer it through our offspring, nor through our progeny. 4. Mā | kasya | adbhutakratu | yakṣam | bhujema | tanūbhiḥ | mā | śeṣasā | mā | tanasā || 4 ||

O you two of wondrous power (*adbhutakratu*), performers of marvelous deeds (*āścaryakarmāṇau*), may we not—by means of our own bodies, that is, our physical members—enjoy the worshiped wealth of any other whatsoever. The meaning is: through your favor, being prosperous, we shall not nourish our bodies with unasked-for wealth.
Likewise, may we not enjoy [it] together with our offspring (*śeṣasā*).
"May we, along with our sons, grandsons, and others, not eat;
the meaning is that no one at all in our lineage shall eat."
The hymn consisting of three verses beginning with “ā no gantam,” the fifteenth [in the book], is seen by Vāyu; its seer is Ātreya, its meter is Gāyatrī, and its deities are Mitra and Varuṇa.
The Anukramaṇikā states: “‘ā naśca’ [is by] Bāhuvṛkta.
The application of this hymn has been stated.
In the Agniṣṭoma, at the morning libation (prātaḥ-savana), this triplet serves as the *anurūpa* for the Maitrāvaruṇa’s recitation (*śastra*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “*ā no mitrāvaruṇā no gantaṃ riśādasā*” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 5.10).

Come to us, O Varuṇa and Mitra, destroyers of enemies, with your great power, to this delightful sacrifice. 1. Come to us, O Varuṇa and Mitra, destroyers of enemies, with your great power, to this delightful sacrifice. 1.
1. Kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, ra: Rudriḥ. 2. Kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ra: By means of protection (trāṇena); in Ga, gha, ja, and śa, "by means of protection" (trāṇena) is absent.
3. In Ga, gha, ja, "you two should protect" (pālayethām) is absent; in Ta: pālayetām; in Ra: pālayatām; in Śa: protection (pālanam).
4. By means of [the syllables] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra, śa, and ma;

O Varuṇa, O Mitra, O you two destroyers of enemies (ṛśādasā), who impel the foes, come hither (upa ā gantam) to our (naḥ) sacrifice (adhvaram)—which is beautiful (cārum), worthy of being performed, and non-violent (ahiṃsakam). Of what nature are you two?
Exceeding, exceeding, utterly crushing, and slayers of enemies.
For you two, Varuṇa and Mitra, rule over the universe with wisdom;
as lords, cause our prayers to swell with fulfillment.
For you two, O Varuṇa and Mitra, who are all-knowing, rule over the universe; as lords, cause our prayers to swell with fulfillment. || 2 ||

O Mitra, O Varuṇa, you two of supreme wisdom (pracetamā) rule over the universe; indeed, you are the lords of all. O sovereign rulers, may you two cause our thoughts—that is, our ritual actions—to swell with their fruits.
Come to our pressed juice;
by your sacred law you are steadfast in peace, O you who are worthy of sacrifice among men.
Sit down upon the sacrificial grass for the drinking of Soma.
By your vow you are steadfast in security; by your law, O you two who are worthy of sacrifice, sit down upon the sacred grass for the drinking of Soma. 2.

O Mitra and Varuṇa, by virtue of your *dharma*— the law that sustains the world— your *vrata*, your action, and your ritual procedure (*yoga*), you are established in firm security; you remain in an unshakable state,
O you who are worthy of sacrifice.
Those two for whom people, acting as officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), perform sacrifices (*yājayantaḥ*) by engaging them in rituals;
or alternatively, those two for whom people, acting as servants (*bhṛtya*), perform sacrifices while harming their enemies (*yājayantaḥ*);
the rest has been explained.
May Mitra and Varuṇa both graciously accept our sacrifice for the sake of fulfillment; may they sit upon the sacred grass to drink the Soma.
May Mitra and Varuṇa both graciously accept our sacrifice for the sake of the rite; may they sit down upon the sacred grass to drink the Soma. 3.

May both Mitra and Varuṇa enjoy and attend our sacrifice for its fulfillment. Having arrived, may they sit down upon the sacred grass (*barhis*). Here, I call those two who are most pervasive, who bear many wondrous deeds, the seekers of the desirable, the unrestrained; I invoke those most powerful ones for our enjoyment. 2. Here, those two who are most pervasive, who bear many wondrous deeds, the seekers of the desirable, the unrestrained—I invoke those most powerful ones for our enjoyment. 2. Here, those two who are most pervasive, who bear many wondrous deeds, the seekers of the desirable, the unrestrained—I invoke those most powerful ones for our enjoyment.

In this sacrifice, I approach those two who are most abundant in being for many, the most effective promoters of many sacrificers; who bear and maintain manifold wondrous deeds; who are most excellent and desirable;
who are irresistible, their movement unimpeded by others; the most powerful ones, I invoke for my enjoyment and protection.

By a miracle, you have fashioned for your own body another wondrous form; you have guided the wheel of the chariot. Around the other yokes of Nahuṣa, you fly through the great realms. 3. *Īrmā* (by a miracle), *anyat* (another), *vapuṣe* (for your body), *vapuḥ* (wondrous form), *cakram* (the wheel), *rathasya* (of the chariot), *yemathuḥ* (you have guided). *Pari* (around), *anyā* (other), *nāhūṣā* (of Nahuṣa), *yugā* (yokes), *mahā* (great), *rajāṃsi* (realms), *dīyathaḥ* (you fly). 3.
O Aśvins, you two [place] another wheel of your own chariot upon the wave.
The form is "artaḥ īrmā. For the sake of his beauty, for the sake of his splendor, you two have yoked the beautiful, radiant wheel; you two have restrained it.
With another wheel, by means of greatness through your own power, [you have joined] the naves and the yokes.
O Nahuṣas, you are men;
you traverse (*paridīyathaḥ*) the ages (*yugāni*), the times characterized by those ages—such as the periods beginning with morning—or the days and nights, as well as the *rajas* (worlds).
It has been said: "At the summit of the navel, you have guided the wheel of the chariot" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.30.10).

Truly, that deed of yours was well performed by you both, since we shall praise all your deeds. Born separately, yet stainless, you have come together with us to our kinship. *That*, *truly*, *well*, *by you both*, *this deed was done*, *all that* which *we shall praise for you*. *Born separately*, *O stainless ones*, *together*, *with us*, *you have come* to kinship.
With that hymn by which he has praised you both, may it be well accomplished for you two through this recitation;
"u" is a filler particle.
May it be well performed for you two by means of this [hymn].

Born separately and individually, you two who are prosperous and stainless—being free from evil—you have come fully to us; that is, you have brought to us kinship, food, or wealth. You cause these to reach us perfectly;
the meaning is that you bestow them completely.
1. Not by me, the ancient one.

2. Ṛ, Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Bha, Ra: *mā*; Śa: the word *su* is not present. When Sūryā mounted your chariot that moves swiftly upon three feet, your two ruddy birds flew around it; they warded off the burning heat with their brilliance. (5) When Sūryā mounted your chariot that moves swiftly upon three feet, your two ruddy birds flew around it; they warded off the burning heat with their brilliance. (5)
O Aśvins, when Sūryā, your wife, mounted your swift-gliding, rapid-moving chariot, then the ruddy, glowing, radiant, and scorching rays— the birds that are the horses— encompassed you on all sides.
Alternatively, "ātapa" (the sun) is the subject to be qualified:
the winds, which are movers possessing the characteristics previously described, surround the sun, which causes all things to reach their end and is radiant.

O Heroes, Atri is mindful of you both with a benevolent heart, since he stirs for you—the Nāsatyas—the stainless Gharma offering with food. 6. Of you two; Atri; is mindful; O Heroes; with a benevolent; mind; the Gharma; since; for you two; stainless; O Nāsatyas; with food; he stirs. 6.
O leaders, O Aśvins, yours— meaning,

belonging to you both— is Atri, our father, the seer; through *sumna*, that is, through happiness consisting of the alleviation of the burning of fire, and through *hantu*, that is, a healing remedy, he knows [you] with *cetayā*, that is, with a mind full of reverence.
The meaning is that he has offered praise.
Since pleasure is sought when suffering exists, one asks: what occasion for suffering is there? To this, he says:

"O Nāsatyas, because that Gharma—the glowing, burning Agni which the Asura had cast forth for his own destruction—has reached you both through your mouth, through your tongue, and through your hymn of praise; [he has reached] the stainless, sinless, and bliss-bestowing one. Thus he has attained it.
The root *bhuraṇyati* has the sense of "going."

Protection from fire is clearly demonstrated here by such [mantras] as "With cold [we ward off] the fire" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.8) and "You two [protect] the one who is weary and the one who is distressed" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.39.7).

Fierce, towering, and swift-moving, your chariot is heard as it speeds on its journeys with a resonant sound; O Aśvins, O Heroes, when Atri turns you hither by means of your wondrous deeds. ugraḥ | vām | kakuhaḥ | yayiḥ | śṛṇve | yāmeṣu | sa'mutaniḥ | yat | vām | daṃsobhiḥ | aśvinā | atriḥ | narā | ā'vartati || 7 ||

1. In the manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, na, bha, and ra, the word "sadā sarvadā" is absent. 2. In the manuscripts ma, ca, ṇa, bha, and vā, it is "sadā". 3. In the manuscripts kha, ca, jha, ṇa, and śa, it is "ātapanāḥ".
4. One looks at the face of *jha*; one looks at the face of *ta*; one looks at the face of *ra*; one looks at the face of *śa*. 5.
In *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *ma*, and *ra*, the phrase "O Nāsatyas" does not exist. 6. That will be produced from *a* and *ra*; it is not produced by *na*.
Fierce, of fierce strength, O you two—young, lofty, great, swift-moving, far-reaching, and continuous—your chariot is heard, it is renowned, as it goes on its journeys or to the sacrifices.
Indeed, O Aśvins, O heroes, because Agni turns toward us with wondrous deeds (*daṃsobhiḥ*).

The swelling, overflowing [stream] of honey clings to you two, O Rudras, lovers of honey, when you carry across the ocean; they bring you cooked nourishments. 8. Of honey, indeed, well—O lovers of honey, O Rudras, it clings to you, the swelling one, when you carry across the ocean; bringing cooked nourishments for you two. 8.
O you who desire the honey, [that is] the sweet Soma (the Rudras are indeed those who act like honey-seekers;
this is a praise of the breast).
By that flowing [breast], O sons of Rudra, may the hymn—which is well-satiating, swelling with the sweetness of honey—serve and attend upon you both.
When you two, O oceans, reach the oceanic waters and cross beyond the intermediate spaces—
meaning you carry them across— the offerings characterized by oblations, being cooked, are brought to you and presented by the sacrificers.

Truly, O Aśvins, they call you both the bringers of bliss; you who are most swift to hear at our invocation, most gracious in your journey. 9. Truly, indeed, O Aśvins, they call you both the bringers of bliss; you who are most swift to hear at our invocation, most gracious in your journey. 9.
O Aśvins, you two are indeed truly real— *ve* is a verse-filler. Those who know the past have called you the bringers of bliss (*mayobhuvā*), the makers of happiness.
O you two who are renowned for bringing happiness, I call upon you both most earnestly to come to our sacrifice (*yāman*); that is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).
At our sacrifice (*yāman*), or for the sake of coming to us (*asmad-āgamanē*), protect us as those who bring the greatest joy (*mṛḷayattamāu*), that is, as those who cause us exceeding happiness.
The particle *ā* has the sense of "and" (*cārthe*).

May these most auspicious prayers be strengthening for the Aśvins; those which we have fashioned like chariots, we have spoken aloud as a great hymn of praise. 10. May these prayers be strengthening for the two Aśvins; may they be most peaceful. Those which we have fashioned like chariots, we have uttered as a lofty song of praise. 10.

1. *sva-jha-ta-na-bha-ra-yuvām* (O you two, [possessing] your own...). 2. *sva-ca-ṇa-he aśvinā*—O Aśvins, O leaders (*narā*). 3. *ta-drāṇīyā*. 4. *ta-vām yuvām* (you two). 5. *ma-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra-prāpnuyuḥ* (they may attain...). 6. *ma-ma-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra*: the letter *ā* is not used in the sense of "and" (*ca-arthe*). Now he concludes the hymn of praise:
these, these very powerful prayers (*brahmāṇi*) now performed, which are strengthening (*vardhanā*) and capable for the Aśvins, should be considered the most praiseworthy and most blissful.

Whatever we have fashioned and accomplished, as a craftsman fashions chariots—may those [efforts] be fruitful. We have uttered this vast, abundant salutation (*namas*), which bestows manifold rewards.
The second hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "kṛṣṭaḥ," has Paurastyarṣi as its seer.
This is indicated by the Anukramaṇikā [which states], "‘kṛṣṭaḥ’.
However, because of the word "tu" (but/however) in the preceding [entry], this [hymn] is also to be understood as an *ānuṣaṅga* (an appended or supplementary section).

Because it was stated previously that "the *nata* [verse] belongs to the Aśvins," the application (*viniyoga*) of this very hymn for both the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra* has already been declared.

The two gods, O Aśvins, have been praised; O you who possess the wealth of heaven, hear that! O you who possess the wealth of bulls, may Atri cause you to accept the gifts. 1. kūṣṭau | devau | aśvinā | atha | divaḥ | manā vasū iti | tat | śravathaḥ | vṛṣaṇvasū iti vṛṣaṇvasū | atriḥ | vāma | ā | vivāsāti || 1 ||
O two gods, O you who possess wealth through praise, O Aśvins, on this day of sacrifice, having come from the sky—the celestial realm—you have been drawn forth;
standing upon the earth, listen with your minds to that hymn of praise. (Note: The singular form is used by way of grammatical substitution.)
O you two who possess rain-giving wealth, Atri—the son of Atri—seeks to win you over; he serves you on every side.

Alternatively, there is a compound formed by the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) between the particle *kṛt* and the verb *stha*, with the word *saha* [understood]. And its monosyllabic nature is established by the present time [of the rule].

This should be viewed as being like the word *ava* in *arāiva* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.58.5), or like *kṛt* in *kṛcchrajñāyate* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.4.5) and *kṛtsantam* (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 10.93.11), and so forth.
Where do you two abide? The meaning is: Atri praises you; listen to us.

Where are they? Where indeed are those famous ones, the divine Nāsatyas in heaven? Among which people do you exert yourselves? Or who is with you among the rivers? 2. Where? Those two. Where? Indeed. Famous. In heaven. Divine. Nāsatyas. Among which? Toward. Do you exert yourselves? Among the people. Who? For you both. Of the rivers. Together with? 2.
Where, indeed, do those two divine gods, the Nāsatyas, the Aśvins, stay?
Where are they heard of today? Where are they renowned? The ellipsis implies: "They dwell in heaven, in the celestial world. Now, [the following] is addressed directly.
O two gods, to which sacrificing person do you both go? To whom do you come?
