Who among the singers would be a companion to you two, along with the praises of the rivers?
1. There is no delusion regarding *va*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra*.
2. *Ta*, *na*, *ra*, *śa*, *tāma*.
The Fourth Aṣṭaka.

To whom do you go? To whom indeed do you go? Toward whom do you yoke your chariot? Whose sacred hymns (*brahmāṇi*) do you delight in? We desire you both for our sacrifice. To whom? You go. To whom? Indeed. You go. Toward whom? You yoke. The chariot. Whose? Sacred hymns. Do you delight in? We. You both. We desire. For the sacrifice.
O Aśvins, toward which sacrificer or which sacrifice do you two go? You travel by crossing over the path;
toward whom indeed do you proceed?
And having gone, with whom have you met? And toward what do you two strive to reach— that is, you yoke it,
you harness the chariot with horses?
Whose sacred hymns (*brahmāṇi*) do you embrace, that you may take delight in the praises?
We desire you both for the sake of sacrifice—for your coming or for your seeking; therefore, the meaning is that you must not fail to go to the sacrifice of anyone at all.

O Paura, you two indeed quicken the ancient one who has been submerged in the waters; O Paura, you quicken him for the sake of the ancient [Paura], when he was seized for the sake of rejuvenation, like a lion thrust into a cave.
O Paura, from Cyavana the seer—who had grown old and was worn out by age—you two stripped away his ancient form, like a skin or armor, and cast it off.
"He stripped the garment from Cyavana" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.116.10)—such is another mantra.
When you two again make him young— that is, you make him a youth—
then I have obtained the desirable form, the lovely appearance, of the bride, the beautiful woman.

For here indeed is your praiser; we are yours for the sake of glorious beauty. Now, having heard me, come hither with your swift steeds, O you who possess abundant wealth! asti | hi | vām | iha | stotā | smasi | vām | su-darśa | śriye | nu | śrutam | me | ā | gatam | arvadbhiḥ | vājinī-vasū || 6 ||
O Aśvins, your worshiper Paura awaits you; indeed, he remains here.
O two gods, O Sudarśanas, come into our presence upon your most beloved chariot, the showerer of blessings, the carrier of wealth.
The praising seer adorns you both, O Aśvins, with a hymn; O lovers of sweetness, hear my call!
Toward your most beloved, powerful chariot that carries wealth, O Aśvins, the seer Stāta stands ready with his hymn of praise; O lovers of sweetness, hear my call! 1.
Those two are the Aśvins.
One "eka" (one) is a restatement (*anu-vāda*).
The praising seer, desiring aid, adorns—that is, decorates—with a hymn of praise your most beloved chariot.
What kind of chariot? "Vṛṣaṇam" means the showerer of fruits; "vasuvāhanam" means the carrier of riches. The meaning is that he praises the chariot as being such as this, which has arrived.
Therefore, O two sweet ones, you who know the Madhu-vidyā, hear my invocation; listen to my call.
O Aśvins, you who pass beyond all things, I have called upon you from afar;
O Dastṛs, whose paths are golden, who possess beautiful splendor and are borne by the rivers, O lovers of sweetness, hear my invocation!
Come quickly, O Aśvins! Across all things, I [call] upon you, O destroyers, of ancient time, whose paths are golden, most gracious, who carry the rivers—O lovers of sweetness, hear my invocation! 2.
O Aśvins, come hither;
pass by all other sacrificers and come to me,
so that I, the seer, may utterly surpass all those people who oppose me.
Alternatively, there is the Nirukta (Nirukta 3.20): "Or [the word *tiras*] means 'beyond,' as in the phrase *tiraḥ tiraḥ mataḥ*.
The meaning is that all actions pertaining to you have been attained—that they are to be performed.

O eternal (*sanātana*) *dastrā*, destroyers of enemies; O you whose paths are golden (*hiraṇyavartanī*), whose chariots are golden; O most gracious ones (*susumnā*), who cause the rivers to flow (*sindhuvāhamā*) by impelling the rain; O roarers (*nardānāṃ*).
Such as you two are, you have arrived too late.
Bearing treasures for us, O Aśvins, come hither;
you two Rudras who travel on golden paths, enjoying [our offerings], rich in booty and lovers of sweetness, hear my invocation.
O Aśvins, you who bring us treasures, come to us! O Rudras, whose paths are golden, you who possess abundant wealth, who delight in our offerings—O lovers of sweetness, hear my invocation! 3.
1. *kha-ca-ṇa-bha*—"O wise ones! O Aśvins, you two who carry (*bibhratau*) and hold (*dhārayantau*) delightful treasures (*ratnāni*) for us—come to us!

O Rudras, sons of Rudra, or rather, those worthy of praise; O possessors of wealth (*vājinīvasū*), having horses as your riches; O you whose paths are golden and whose chariots are golden, come, being well-disposed and honoring our sacrifice."
The passage beginning with "mādhvī" has already been explained.

O you of excellent praise, O possessors of bovine wealth, songs are placed upon your chariot; and your lofty wild beast makes the food glorious with its wondrous form. O lovers of sweetness, hear my call at the vital moment!

O you of beautiful praise, O possessors of rain-bestowing wealth, the voices are placed upon your chariot. And your lofty wild beast, through its wondrous form, creates nourishment; O lovers of sweetness, hear my earnest call. 4.
O Aśvins, possessors of abundant wealth, givers of riches, or showerers of treasures— may the voices of the well-praising singers, or the Ṛgveda in the form of speech,
[bring you hither]. O Heroes, your mind-yoked horses have speckled coats.
May the steeds carry you hither for the drinking, O Aśvins, with great favors; O lovers of sweetness, hear my invocation.
O Heroes, may the steeds yoked by thought, their coats speckled with spray, bring you both hither for the draught, together with blessings, O Aśvins; O lovers of sweetness, hear my invocation! 6.
O Aśvins, you two who are the leaders of men— may your horses, yoked by thought alone (meaning well-trained),
spotted in appearance, and swift-moving, bring you here for the drinking of Soma.
May they carry you both with great joy—by means of the blisses to be granted to us, or by the instruments of that bliss, or by their splendors.
O Aśvins, come hither; O Nāsatyas, do not disregard me. Even through the obstruction of the one who seeks wealth, come around, O invincible ones; O lovers of sweetness, hear my call.
The Aśvins:
Come hither!
Come today, O lords of beauty, O Aśvins, masters of the waters; come to me, who am praising you—the singer, the praiser, seeking your aid—at this sacrifice, and protect me from all sides.

The Dawn has appeared with her radiant cattle; Agni has been established in his proper season. O Dasyus, O Masters of wealth, your immortal chariot has been yoked. O you who are rich in sweetness, hear my invocation! The Dawn has appeared with her radiant cattle; Agni has been established in his proper season. O Dasyus, O Masters of wealth, your immortal chariot has been yoked. O you who are rich in sweetness, hear my invocation!

The Dawn has shone forth; and Agni, possessing bright cattle—that is, possessing radiant cattle, meaning the oblations have been made manifest—or else "cattle" refers to rays: since he possesses such bright rays, therefore, O two charioteers, O Aśvins, lords of the chariot, come hither today on this day of sacrifice, turning toward us.
Toward whom? [Toward us.]
The swelling one with its own limbs; the preeminent, blazing Gharma, the sacrifice.
Or rather:
the swelling, nourished Soma juice, the form of autumn, [strengthened] by the Vasatīvarī waters.
Alternatively, come hither toward the swelling *gharma*—the *pravargya* vessel—by means of the *ṛta* and so forth;
this is the application (*viniyoga*) of the hymn for the *pravargya*.
The two who travel most readily do not measure out the conditioned; O Aśvins, you are now praised here.
At the arrival of day, you come with help as those who travel most readily; you are the most beneficent ones, turning back toward the donor.

Not [so]; they have fashioned the refined [song]. They two, most ready to come, are surely near at hand. O Aśvins, being praised here, you are most ready to come with your aid at the arrival of day. You are the most beneficent, bringing healing to the donor who turns away from distress. 2.
The Aśvins do not measure out the consecrated *gharma* with intent to harm;

rather, being most swift to come (*gamiṣṭhā*) here at this sacrifice now, they are present in close proximity (*anti*) to the *gharma*. Praised (*upastutā*), the two Aśvins arrive most readily with their protection (*avasā*) at the onset of day (*divābhipitve*), that is, in the morning.
It protects against the occurrence of pairs of opposites;
it is a life of worldly involvement.
The absence of that is *avarti*.
May you two come in such a way that the food is free from those [defects];
and having arrived, may you two become the greatest bringers of well-being (*śambhaviṣṭhā*) to the donor, the sacrificer who gives the oblation.
And come at the time of gathering, at the morning libation, and throughout the day until the rising of the sun;
by day and by night with most auspicious protection, O Aśvins, let not our drinking remain unextended.

And come, O Aśvins, at the gathering of the cattle—at dawn, at midday, when the sun has risen, by day and by night—with your most auspicious protection; let not the drinking now be delayed for you, O Aśvins. 3.
Ah! There are equal divisions twofold, threefold, fivefold, and fifteenfold;
here the fivefold division exists.
Moreover, come hither, do you two arrive!
"When at the *saṃgava*—that is, at the time of *saṃgava*. *Saṃgava* is that time when the cows gather at the place of milking.
For during the latter part of the night, the cows, having grazed on the snowy grasses in the forest, return to the *saṃgava* for the purpose of being milked again."
Likewise, "in the morning" means at the time of dawn;
likewise, "at midday" means at the middle period of the day, at the rising of the sun, at its emergence— that is, at the time when it has fully risen,
meaning during the afternoon (this also implies the evening).
Not only... but also... / Not merely... but...

1. [The syllables] *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra* represent the heat (*gharma*) nourished by the autumnal form. 2. [The syllable] *ta* has arrived at the sacrifice (*yāga*). 3. [The syllables] *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra* represent non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). 4. [The syllables] *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra* represent you two, the most excellent goers (*gantṛtamau*). 5. [The syllables] *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra* mean "be ye" (*bhavatam*). 6. [The syllable] *ta* means "by protection" (*rakṣaṇena*) and "by the unborn" (*ajena*). 7. [The syllable] *ta* means "the two most excellent arrivals" (*āgantṛtamau*); the word "destroying" (*nāśayantau*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Alternatively: 8. In the versions *kha-jha-bha-ra*, the phrase "not... and" (*prati...ca*) is absent; [the meaning is] "destroying poverty" (*na-dāridryaṃ nāśayantau*). 9. In the versions *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra*, the word "be ye" (*bhavatāṃ*) is absent; in *ga-gha-ja-ta*, it is "be ye" (*bhavatam*). 10. In *ta*, it is "in fifteen ways" (*pañcadaśadhā iti-mānā*); in *bha*, it is "in the self consisting of fifteen parts" (*pañcadaśadhātmanā*). 11. In *ga-gha-ja*, the phrase "milking-ground" (*dohabhūmi*) is absent. 12. In *ta*, it is "they shall eat" (*bhakṣyanti*) and "having eaten" (*bhakṣayitvā ca*).
At those very times already mentioned—what then? By day and by night, at all times, come with your most peaceful and most pleasant protection, or with the oblation as the occasion.
For what purpose do you come? He says "no," because it has already been accepted by other gods.
Even now, *vītiḥ*—the drinking of the other gods—does not extend (*ā tanāna*), that is, does not spread, [to you], O Aśvins; the word "having left behind" (*vihāya*) is to be supplied.
For this has been your station from of old, O Aśvins: these are the dwellings, this is the home.
Come to us from the high heaven, from the mountain, bringing nourishment and vigor.

For this, indeed, has been your place from of old, O Aśvins, your vital power; these are the houses, this is our dwelling. From the high heaven, from the mountain, come hither to us, bringing food and strength. 4.

O Aśvins, this place of yours from of old, since ancient times, is indeed your ancient home—a dwelling-place worthy of habitation known as the *uttaravedi*. Now, with reference to the *saumika* altar, he says: "These are the houses," such as the *prācīnavaṃśa* and others.
This is our home, the house for the sacrifice to the gods.
For our sake, come hither from the great heaven, from the mountain, from the cloud, from the atmosphere which is the source of the waters—come like a horse! Why do you tarry?
No; [it means] food and strength, that is, nourishment and power.
The meaning is that food, which is the means of attaining power, is the essential substance.
Carrying such [a state], they two carry it.
May we go forth under the newest, bliss-bestowing protection of the two Aśvins, with their excellent guidance.
O Immortals, bring to us wealth, heroic sons, and all auspicious fortunes.
O Aśvins, may we come to you with your newest protection, which brings happiness and provides excellent guidance. Bring to us wealth, and also heroic sons, and all immortal blessings, O Immortals! 5.

May we come together, may we unite with the Aśvins, through their newest protection—protection that is not made by another, which is bliss-bestowing, which brings about happiness, and which is characterized by excellent guidance and a most auspicious arrival.
Or perhaps these two [terms] are qualifiers of "help" (*avasa*).
May we come together according to the characteristics already described.
Bring wealth to us;
bring also heroic sons and the like. O immortal ones, you who possess the nature of the immortals, bring all auspicious fortunes.

The fifth hymn, consisting of five verses beginning with “*prātaryāvāṇā*,” is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and is dedicated to the Aśvins. This is indicated by the Anukramaṇī: “‘*prātaryāvāṇā*’ [is the hymn]. Its ritual application (*viniyoga*) in the *prātaranuvāka* and the *āśvina-śastra* is stated together with that of the preceding hymn.
In the *asoryāma* sacrifice, when there is an additional *uktha* for Mitra and Varuṇa, this very [hymn] is to be recited.
Thus it is stated in the Sūtra: "O you who travel at dawn, O Lord of the Field, [recite] the honey-sweet *ūrj*" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 9.11).
1. [The text] says "not *sva*, *na*, or *ṇa*"; *jha*, *bha*, *ra*, *ta*, and *nya* are excluded; *na*—"Why then? does not exist. 2.
In *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, "ā" does not exist.
3. In *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, for what purpose is it understood?
4. [In the variants] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, ta, na, bha, ra, śa, the phrase “idaṃ hi” is absent. 5. ta—[The verse reads: “Vibhā vibhā viśvāni.
Worship first those who travel at dawn; let them drink before the ruddy eagles [appear].
For at dawn the Aśvins establish the sacrifice; the sages, receiving their first portion, praise them forth.

In the morning, O you who traverse the distance, as the first ones, drink the oblation before the vulture; for the ruddy ones drink in the morning, for the Aśvins establish the sacrifice in the morning; the sages proclaim them as those who receive the first portion. 1.
"O my officiating priests, worship the Aśvins—the two who travel at dawn, going to the sacrifice early in the morning; the first, and thus preceding all other gods, or the most excellent ones.
For what purpose is this rule for the first sacrifice? It is said:
"From the vulture, [the Aśvins] rescued [him]; the dark one gave [him] before the onset of the Rākṣasa; let them drink first, while they are drinking.
How can that which has not yet arrived be sacrificed to? To this he says:
O Aśvins, the two Aśvins, indeed at dawn they uphold—that is, they maintain and partake in—the sacrifice."
"The ancient ones," meaning those belonging to former times—"the sages" (*kavayaḥ*), "the learned ones" (*anucānāḥ*), "the seers" (*ṛṣayaḥ*)—praise these two only at dawn.
For there is a Vedic citation: "Those who are learned are indeed the sages" (*Ai. Brā. 2.38*).
O Aśvins, urge us toward the morning sacrifice; the evening sacrifice is not pleasing to the gods.
Moreover, another besides us sacrifices, and each preceding sacrificer has been more successful than the one after him.

In the morning, O Aśvins, impel the sacrificer; not in the evening is there one who goes to the gods. What is offered is not pleasing, for another besides us sacrifices, and he prevails; each preceding sacrificer is more worthy of gain.
"O my men, worship—the two Aśvins—at every dawn; praise them!
Send forth the oblations!
At every evening, there is no oblation that goes to the gods; it does not exist."
The meaning is that the gods do not accept it;
it becomes something undesirable and unfit for service.
For the Śruti says: "The forenoon indeed belongs to the gods."
"Moreover, if anyone other than us should sacrifice or offer the Soma, he would satisfy [the gods] with the oblation;
therefore, among both ourselves and others, whichever sacrificer is the first—the one who sacrifices first—he becomes the most worthy of the gods' favor, the one most to be honored."
‘Hiraṇyatvak’ is the invitatory verse (*yājyā*) for the oblation in the animal sacrifice dedicated to the Aśvins.
For it is prescribed in the Sūtra: “‘Hiraṇyatvaḍamaśvavarṇo ghṛtasnuḥ... (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 3.8).
Your chariot, with golden skin, honey-colored, dripping with ghee, and laden with nourishment, rolls forward by its own power;
O Aśvins, swift as thought and possessing rapid speed, it is by this that you reach even the most distant places and all difficulties.
With golden skin, honey-colored, dripping with ghee, full of nourishment—your chariot rolls hither, O Aśvins, swift as thought, with the speed of the wind, wherewith you traverse all difficulties. 3.

1. In the *jha*, *bha*, and *ra* [gaṇas], the *yajñaga* (the *ya* and *ja*) occur at the end. 2. In the *kha*, *ca*, and *ṇa* [gaṇas], the first [syllable] is joined with *yāga* (the *ya* and *ga*); in the *jha* and *na* [gaṇas], the first [syllable] is joined with *vinaya* (the *vi* and *na*).
3. In the *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra* [gaṇas], the word "uta" does not exist.
Your chariot, O two of you, comes toward us, bringing food that is strengthening and immortal.

Of what kind is this chariot? It has a golden surface, covered with gold; it is honey-colored, of enchanting hue; it drips with clarity (ghṛtasnu), meaning it pours forth water; it is swift as thought (manāṃjavas), possessing the speed of the mind; and it has the velocity of the wind (vātaraṃhas).
O Aśvins, with that chariot by which you pass beyond—that is, traverse across—all difficult paths and ways of travel.

He who has served most abundantly for the two Nāsatyas, who gives the sweetest food in the distribution—may he deliver his offspring by means of protections; may he overcome the enemy whose light does not rise upward. He who has served most abundantly for the two Nāsatyas, who gives the sweetest food in the distribution—he shall deliver his offspring by means of protections; let him utterly overcome the enemy whose light does not rise upward.

The sacrificer who, at the sacrifice characterized by the distribution of oblations, performs most abundantly—that is, most excellently—the rite consisting of much food for the sake of the two Nāsatyas, the Aśvins.
(Note: *cana* is a name for food; Nirukta 6.16.
He performs the ritual with abundant food.
Having drunk.
The genitive case is used for the object of an action.
And the sacrificer bestows food; he protects his own offspring, his son, through his ritual acts.
He is one whose splendor is not diminished—or rather, whose light is not surpassed.
Those who offer oblations to the upward-shining [gods]—
may he, being ever present, strike down those who perform sacrifice without fire.

May we go forth together under the new protection of the Aśvins, which is bliss-bestowing and provides excellent guidance. Bring to us wealth, and also heroic sons, and all immortal blessings, O Immortals! 5. sam | aśvinoḥ | avasā | nūtanena | mayaḥ-bhuvā | su-praṇītī | gamema | ā | naḥ | rayim | vahatam | ā | uta | vīrān | ā | viśvāni | amṛtā | saubhagāni || 5 ||
The fifth [chapter], beginning with "samaśvinoḥ," has been completed.
The sixth hymn consists of nine verses beginning with "aśvināveha.

Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "Aśvinau [is the deity]; nine [verses]; Masavādhin Ātreya is the seer; the fourth verse begins with 'udhiṇagā'; it is a Triṣṭubh, while the others are Jagatīs.
Masavādhin, son of Atri, is the ṛṣi.
The first three verses are *uṣṇih*, the fourth is a *triṣṭubh*, and the remaining five are *anuṣṭubhs*.
In the *prātaranuvāka* of the *Āśvina* sacrifice, this initial triplet is employed in the *auṣṇiha* metre during the *Āśvina-śastra*.
This is prescribed in the Sūtra: “‘O Aśvins, come to our dwelling; O Aśvins, come hither’—these two triplets” (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 4.15).
On the third day of the ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*), this triplet dedicated to the Aśvins occurs in the *prauga* recitation.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "O Aśvins, come hither! Come with the waters to the pressed [soma]" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 7.10).
1. Kha, Ca, and Ṇa read *hiraṇyavaditarūpaḥ*; others read *itararūpaḥ*. 2. Ta reads *havirbhāgavati*. 3. Kha, Ca, and Ṇa read *pālayata*; Jha, Ta, Na, and Bha read *pālayata*.
The complete commentary on the mantra located in the Kha-ca-ṇa manuscript is to be found at the end of the seventh section (parva) [vigate].

O Aśvins, come here; O Nāsatyas, do not be indifferent. Fly hither like two swans toward the pressed juices. O Aśvins, come here to this sacrifice. O Nāsatyas, do not be indifferent—*venati* is a verb meaning "to desire"; do not be averse, or rather, do not be devoid of longing or desire. Like two swans flying toward clear water, fly hither, that is, approach the pressed and offered Soma juices.

O Aśvins, like two antelopes, like two white wild oxen following the pasture, fly hither like two swans toward the pressed juices. O Aśvins, like two antelopes, like two white wild oxen—that is, like two white deer—they run after the pasture; even so, come to the Soma like two swans.

O Aśvins, possessors of abundant wealth, may you both take pleasure in our sacrifice for the sake of our desired goal. Fly hither like two swans toward the pressed juices. (3) O Aśvins, possessors of abundant wealth (*vājinīvasū*), may you both enjoy (*juṣethām*) our sacrifice (*yajñam*) for the sake of our desire (*iṣṭaye*). Fly (*patatam*) hither (*ā*) like two swans (*haṃsāv-iva*) toward the pressed soma-juices (*sutān*). (3) O Aśvins, you who are the providers of food (*annasya vāmayitārau*), may you both favor (*sevethām*) our sacrifice for the attainment of what is desired or sought after.

When Atri descended into the glowing pit, he called out to you both like a woman in distress; then, O Aśvins, you came with the swiftness of a hawk, with your most recent and most auspicious aid. Atri: When you two descended into the glowing pit, he called out to you like a woman in distress; then, O Aśvins, you came with the swiftness of a hawk, with your most recent and most auspicious aid.
1. *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ga-yavage dhāsāya*.

Atri, our father, whenever he called upon you both—praising you like a woman in distress who is entreating her husband—he, being cast down, calling out, and descending, made the *ṛbīsa* manifest for the sake of the two heroes (*nṛpā*).
Just as a woman pleases her husband, so did he act. He called out, releasing [the fire] from within.
With the speed of even a hawk, with the velocity of a soaring eagle—
*cit* here having the sense of "even" or "as if"—
or rather, with the fresh, first-born, and most constant speed of a hawk that ever flies, come with our most auspicious chariot to protect us, O Aśvins!
Regarding this, those learned in ancient lore relate the history of Saptavadhi: how, having carefully cast that Ṛṣi into the chest of Ātreyī, they concealed him.
Having made a sign and guarded his own house, he settled them there;
he acted in such a way that his wife would not approach him even at night.
Day after day, having piled up [fuel], they will churn that sage;
thus, remaining for a long time in a chest, he will become miserable and emaciated.
The sage reflected for a long time on a means of departure;
having resolved it in his heart, he, with a joyful mind, summoned the two Aśvins.
Then the Aśvins arrived there and, having opened the chest, quickly extracted that Ṛṣi; they both became eightfold.
Having dallied with his wife, that seer then meditated again;
returning in the morning, he entered the chest as before and remained there.
Then, at the time of opening the chest, he saw the boy.
Open wide, O Lord of the Forest, like the womb for one desiring a son;
hear my call, O Aśvins, and release me from the sevenfold bond.
Move aside, O Lord of the Forest; [be] like the womb of Sūryantī. Hear my call, O Aśvins, and release the seven-horsed chariot. 5.

O Vanaspate, you who are in the form of a chest made from the modification of a tree, open wide; move apart! Be uncovered, just as the womb (*bhaga*) of a woman longing for childbirth opens wide like the sun. Be you likewise uncovered.
For that purpose, O Aśvins, hear—listen to my invocation;
and having heard it, release me, the seer Saptavadhri.
For the terrified Rishi Saptavadhri who was crying out to you,
O Aśvins, you both joined together and then split apart the tree by means of your magical powers.
To the one who was afraid, not to the one who was imploring; for the seer Saptavadhri, O Aśvins, by means of your wondrous powers, you both joined together and then parted the tree. 6.

1. Having cast him out; 2. Kha, Ca, Jha, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Bha, Ra—like a child; 3. Na, Ta—on the eighteenth day; 4. Ta—having acted with illusory power (māyā); 5. Kha, Ca, Bha, Ṇa, Ta, Na, Bha, Ra—likewise.

To the one who was afraid, to the one fearing departure, to the one imploring for liberation, to the one seeking release, to the sage, O Aśvins, O you two Aśvins, by means of your powers (māyābhiḥ), you two approached the tree—a product of wood, a chest—and came together for the sake of my departure. You divided it into three parts?

Just as the wind stirs a lotus pond on every side, so let your embryo stir; let it come forth, ten months old. 7. Just as... the wind... stirs a lotus pond... on every side, so let your embryo stir; let it come forth, ten months old. 7.
These three ṛks constitute the *ūpanipat* for one who has suffered a miscarriage.
By means of these three ṛks, the son of Masravant was restored to heaven;
the seer praised the Aśvins so that the pregnant woman might quickly give birth.
Just as the wind thoroughly agitates and completely stirs a lotus pond, a lake, or the like on all sides, even so let your embryo quiver, tremble, and move here and there.

[The hymn] "darśamāsya ‘mahaṃ no adya’" is the seventh hymn; it consists of ten verses, is the seerly composition (ārṣa) of Satyaśravas Ātreya, is in the Pāṅkta meter, and is intended for the Upasthāna rite.
And it is enumerated thus: "The *maha* [verse] belongs to Daśasatyaśravas, but the *upastha* is *pāṅkta*.
This hymn occurs in the *prātaranuvāka* at the *uṣasya* rite in the *pāṅkta* metre and the *ābhinavala* [recitation].
For it is stated: "'*maha nām ayam*' is *pāṅkta*" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.14).

O Dawn, rich in light, awaken us today to great wealth, even as you have awakened Citra for Satyaśravas Vāyya, O well-born lady, mistress of noble speech. O Dawn, rich in light, awaken us today to great wealth, even as you have awakened Citra for Satyaśravas Vāyya, O well-born lady, mistress of noble speech.

"O Dawn, on this day of sacrifice, you who are radiant, awaken us for the sake of great wealth— that is, enlighten us; for it is through the light of the intellect that material goods can be acquired by means of ritual action."

‘Just as’ (*yathā*)—that is, ‘just as before’ (*yathaiva pūrvaṃ*), ‘you awakened us’ (*abodhayaḥ*) on past days; the meaning is that you awaken us even now. O ‘well-born one’ (*sujāte*), O ‘one of beautiful manifestation,’ O ‘one whose wealth consists of horses’ (*aśvasūnṛte*):
she is one for whom there is praise consisting of beloved truth for the sake of horses.
"O Goddess, O daughter of Vāyu, O Satyaśravasī, please show favor to me"—this is the meaning.

O Daughter of Heaven, you who have shone forth for Sunītha and Śaucadratha—shine forth likewise for Sahīyas, Satyaśravas, Vāyya, Sujāta, and Aśvasūnṛta. 2. O Daughter of Heaven, you who have shone forth for Sunītha and Śaucadratha—shine forth likewise for Sahīyas, Satyaśravas, Vāyya, Sujāta, and Aśvasūnṛta. 2.

"O Daughter of Heaven, daughter of the Sun, you who, O Sunīthā—daughter of Śucadratha—formerly shone forth and dispelled the darkness; as such, shine forth for me, the exceedingly powerful Vāyya, son of Vaya, Satyaśravas, and dispel the darkness!
[The root] *ucch* means 'to dispel';
*vivāsa* means 'removal'."
The rest has been explained.

May she, the bringer of wealth, dawn upon us today, O daughter of heaven! You who have shone forth for Sahīyas, Satyaśravas, Vāyya, Sujāta, and Aśvasūnṛta. 3. May she, the bringer of wealth, dawn upon us today, O daughter of heaven! You who have shone forth for the most powerful Sahīyas, for Satyaśravas, for Vāyya, for the well-born Sujāta, and for Aśvasūnṛta. 3.
1. The sequence *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ma-ra* does not exist in the sense of "beautifully manifested.
2. Regarding the one named by *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ma-ra*: O Daughter of Heaven, O Dawn, you who have brought wealth—being such a renowned one, shine forth for us today on this day; dispel the darkness.
The word *mahīyami* is [an error for] *yā*; the syllable *u* is meaningless. It means:
"O you who shone forth previously, even now [you shine]."

O radiant one, those many who praise you with hymns— those wealthy ones, O bountiful lady, possessing great splendor, liberal givers, and noble gifts— [approach] thee, O well-born one, rich in horses and true blessings.

O radiant one, those many who praise you with hymns—those wealthy ones, O bountiful goddess, who possess great splendor, who are rich in gifts and most liberal—[all these] are well-born, O giver of horses and true blessings. 4.
O night, you are endowed with light.
The suffix *vanip* is applied here because of the word *vibhā*, according to the rule "in the Vedic language, *vanip* and *iṣap*" (*chandasīvanipau*),
or else it is applied to the root *āp* in the sense of the agent (*kartari*).

O Uṣas, those many eager ones—the upholders, the officiating priests, and the singers—praise and extol you with hymns. O wealthy one, through your favor, these singers become possessed of great splendor;
they become worthy of refuge through excellent glory and become endowed with gifts.
They are *surātayaḥ*. *Rāti* means giving;
and they are also those who give well (*sudāna*).
For indeed, these virtues of yours delight us for the sake of bestowing wealth;
they have placed around us boldness as you, O noble-born one, rich in horses and kind, bestow worthy bounty upon the giver.

For indeed, these virtues of yours are displayed for the granting of wealth; even those who are fainthearted have been made to bestow worthy bounty, O well-born one, O you whose nature is horses and abundance! 5.

"O Uṣas, whatever indeed... (the word *yat* is used here as a filler). Those who are your own people there, these groups (*gaṇāḥ*) standing before us, being assembled in a multitude, "invite" (*chadayanti*)—that is, they entreat—for the giving of wealth (*maghattaye*), for the bestowing of riches, or for the possession of wealth; all of them have "surrounded" (*pari dadhuḥ*) us, holding us on every side, "desiring" (*vaṣṭyaḥ*) us alone.
What were they doing?

They were *dadat*, meaning they were sacrificing—that is, offering wealth (*rādhas*) characterized by oblations (*havis*) that was inexhaustible (*ahiyamāṇa*) and which brought about the destruction of impurities (*kṣīṇamala-jāvaha*); or alternatively, they were giving inexhaustibly to those who requested it.
All those who praise you while offering oblations maintain the fruit for our sake alone;
this is the meaning of "they praise.
Alternatively, in the phrase *yaccid dhi*, it should be explained as *yat-pi* (even that which).
In that alternative view, the same [term] should be supplied by ellipsis in the subsequent sentence;
the rest is identical.

O wealthy Dawn, bestow upon these patrons glory accompanied by heroes; for they, our liberal lords, have bestowed gifts upon us according to their merit, O nobly born one, rich in horses and kind favors.
Bestow upon us, O wealthy Dawn, heroic glory among our patrons—those liberal lords who have granted us unceasing gifts, O nobly born one, rich in horses and kind favors! 6.

1. [The substitution of] *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *bha*, and *dha* occurs for *na*; *na*, *ra*, and *dha* occur for *da*; and *śa* occurs for *ta*. 2. [The substitution of] *jha*, *bha*, and *ya* occurs for *dyat* in this context; *na* occurs for *cit* in the phrase *yaccit*; and *ra* occurs for *yat* in the phrase *yadyat*. 5. 1. 4. 6. 79. ] The Fourth Aṣṭaka, 97.

O Goddess Uṣas, O bountiful one, O generous lady, let that glory which consists of heroes come to us, your praisers; bestow upon us food accompanied by heroic sons and the like, or indeed that glory itself.
Bring it! Bestow it! Those wealthy patrons who are our masters have granted—indeed, they have bestowed—unfailing riches and gifts upon us, their praisers. This is the meaning.
O wealthy Uṣas, bring hither from among them for us, O noble-born one, rich in horses and blessings, those liberal patrons who, as wise lords, bestow upon us secret and desirable riches.

From them—[grant] *yuṣmad* (you)—O Bṛhatī, O Uṣas, O Maghonī, bring hither great glory! May those wise patrons, who win for us secret riches, shine forth, O well-born one, O you who are rich in horses! 7.
O generous Uṣas, bring to those sacrificers that shining wealth consisting of gold and other riches, great glory—that is, great fame—or vast renown.
May the wise donors, who are intent upon us, bestow upon us riches joined with horses, secret treasures joined with cattle, and herds of cows and herds of horses; may they grant these to us.
And bring us nourishments rich in cattle, O Daughter of Heaven;
let us not be harmed by the rays of the Sun, O well-born one, you who are gracious with horses!
And, O Daughter of Heaven, bring us food consisting of cattle, together with the rays of the sun—with bright, glowing beams—O well-born one, rich in horses! 8.
And furthermore, O Dawn, daughter of heaven, bring to us food consisting of cattle, accompanied by cows;
when will you come together with the rays of the sun, with glowing, shining, bright, and stainless flames, and with the splendors of fire?
The meaning is: at the time of sunrise and at the time of adding fuel to the fire.
Depart, O daughter of heaven; do not delay in spreading your waters, lest the sun scorch you with his flame like a thief or an enemy, O well-born one, O bringer of horses and bounty!
Shine forth, O daughter of heaven; do not delay in spreading out your waters. Let not the sun’s flame consume you like a thief or an enemy, O well-born one, rich in horses! 9.
1. The syllables *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *śa* do not occur [in this context].
2. The manuscripts *sa*, *ca*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *ra* divide [the word] as *neti*; *ga*, *ya*, *ja*, and *śa* divide it as *bhajantaḥ*; and *jha* divides it as *ceti*.
O Daughter of Heaven, O Dawn, shine forth; make thy own light manifest.

"Do not delay for long regarding our work; do not cause it to be postponed. Just as a king or other authority torments a thief who steals from him, so shall the Sun (Sūra) heat you with this very radiance (arcis).
[This is said] so that you may rise quickly."
This much you have granted; you ought to grant more.
O well-born Dawn, rich in horses and gifts, who shines forth for your worshippers and never perishes!
This much, O Uṣas, or even more than this, you ought to grant—O radiant one, who do not fail those who praise you as you shine forth, O well-born one, rich in horses and blessings! 10.
"O Uṣas, do you [grant] this to us, or whatever else is desired—only this much?
The particle *eva* has the sense of "only" (*icchacchat*).
The meaning is: "It is precisely that which has been prayed for in this hymn."
Alternatively, "abhūyaḥ" means "you ought to give even more," or "even though it was not requested"; or rather, the meaning is: "give me all that I am."
"O radiant Dawn, you who shine forth for the sake of the worshippers—dispelling the darkness so that they may engage in worldly and Vedic affairs—you do not perish; you do not destroy them.
The meaning is: 'You do not cause harm.
Therefore, it is right that you should grant [us blessings]."
From the root *mīñ* in the sense of "to injure," this [suffix] *iyan* is applied with the substitution of *vya* for *śram*.
"dyutadyāmānam" is the eighth hymn, consisting of six verses.
Regarding this, the Anukramaṇikā states: "dyutadyāmānam, six [verses].
Samyaśravas is the seer (ṛṣi).
Because it consists of *anuṣṭubh* verses, it is [classified as] a *triṣṭubh*.
Since it is stated [in the ritual manuals], "But the lap," the deity is Uṣas.
This hymn is used in the *prātaranuvāka*, in the *upastha* rite, in the *traiṣṭubha* meter, and in the *āśvina-śastra*.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The shining one, the dawn, with vigor" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.14).

The wise singers praise with their hymns the goddess Uṣas, who shines with great splendor through the eternal Law, who is rich in the waters of dawn, who is radiant, and who brings forth the light of heaven.

The wise ones praise with their hymns the goddess Uṣas, who illumines the sky with her splendor, who is vast, who is true by the Eternal Law, whose waters are ruddy, who shines forth, and who brings the light of heaven. || 1 ||

The wise, inspired priests praise with their hymns of praise that Uṣas who is shining, whose chariot is a gift, who is vast and great, who is true to the cosmic order (ṛta) through intoxicating drink or sacrifice, who possesses the nature of ṛta, whose waters are ruddy, who shines forth, who is radiant, the goddess, who brings forth the light of heaven, and who goes toward the sun— Uṣas of such great majesty they celebrate.
1. In the versions *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *jha*, *ta*, *ra*, and *śa*, the phrase "mā kṛthāḥ" (do not do) is absent.
2. In *kha*, *ca*, *ṇa*, and *na*, it reads "kim etāvad iti"; in *jha*, *ta*, *bha*, and *ra*, it reads "kim etāvat he yadi".
3. In *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *jha*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, and *śa*, the deity is Uṣas.
4. Toward that Dawn. 5. [The variants] kha, ca, ṇa, and ta do not contain the word "prati.
She, the beautiful one, awakening the people, making the paths easy to travel, goes at the forefront.
O Bṛhadrathā, Bṛhatī, and Viśvaminvā, Dawn bestows light at the beginning of the days.
This one, beautiful to behold, awakening the people, making the paths easy to travel, goes at the head; the great, lofty Dawn, who stirs all things, bestows light at the beginning of the days. 2.
This Dawn, beautiful to behold and worthy of being seen, awakens the people. Whom? The people.
The meaning is "having awakened.

Making the paths easy to traverse (*sugān*), she goes—meaning she moves—before the sun, in the east. Of what nature is Uṣas? She possesses a great chariot (*bṛhadrathā*), being abundant; she is great (*bṛhatī*) and all-pervading (*viśvaminvā*), either encompassing the universe or satisfying it.
Such is Dawn that bestows light and splendor at the beginning of the days.
Yoking her ruddy kine, this goddess drives away want and bestows wealth; carving out paths for easy passage, she shines forth, praised by many, possessing all boons.
Yoking her ruddy cows, this goddess—driving away poverty, never failing, opening paths for prosperity—shines forth, praised by many, possessing all boons. || 3 ||
This Dawn, yoking her chariot with ruddy, red-hued oxen— driving it forth, never failing, or rather,
never wasting away— has made wealth and riches immovable, so that they do not depart.
What is she doing?
She is rending—that is, revealing—the paths, the ways.
For what purpose?
The Goddess, shining brightly, praised by many, possessing all desirable things and worthy of praise by all, shines forth and makes light for the sake of reaching a good state and proceeding well.
This woman becomes a braid-wearer, doubly-braided, manifesting her body in front;
she follows the path of *ṛta* correctly, as if knowing it well, and does not confuse the directions.
This one becomes two-colored, possessing two forms; manifesting her body in front, she follows the path of *ṛta* correctly. Like one who knows, she does not miss the directions. 4.

This Dawn becomes variegated; she becomes especially white, possessing two wings—that is, she is sovereign over the two positions, the first and the middle. Afterwards, making her own body manifest, revealing her form—where?
In the east, in the eastern direction.
Furthermore, she follows correctly and perfectly the path of Ṛta, that is, the path of Āditya.
Moreover, she makes everything known as if she were fully conscious;
the particle *iva* is used here in the sense of *saṃpra* (complete engagement).
She does not measure out the directions, nor does she destroy them;
on the contrary, she illuminates the directions.
Or rather, as if knowing—understanding with excellence that "this is what must be followed"—she follows the path of *ṛta*.
1. The [consonants] *ga*, *gha*, *ja*, *śa*, and *ṣṭhāna* do not exist [here]. 2. *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *na*, *bha*, and *ava* appear as if they were present. (Ṛgveda-prātiśākhya 2.123)
This bright one has stood visible to us, conscious of her own body, like a woman bathing in the waters;
driving away hatred and the darknesses, Uṣas, the daughter of Heaven, has come with her light.
This one, bright, conscious of her own body, has stood up for us to be seen like one bathing; driving away hatred and the darkness, Uṣas, the daughter of Heaven, has come with her light. 5.

Like a radiant woman, bright-hued and stainless, well-adorned, revealing her slender limbs, Uṣas stands—performing her bath, appearing as if rising high as she follows through the act of bathing—for our sake, before us, visible for all to see; she has arisen in the eastern quarter.
What does she do?
Driving away hateful darknesses, Uṣas, the daughter of Heaven, comes with light and splendor.
This daughter of heaven comes hitherward; like one unveiling her breast, she reveals her auspicious form.
Disclosing precious boons to the donor, the youthful maiden has once again created light as of old.
This daughter of Heaven comes hitherward; like a beautiful maiden, she strips off her garment. Revealing precious treasures for the donor, the youthful maiden has once again created light as of old.

This Dawn, facing toward us as the daughter of Heaven, like a beautiful woman in auspicious attire, unveils her form for all living beings. Moreover, bestowing desirable wealth upon the donor who offers oblations, she, the eternally youthful maiden who mingles with all, once again creates light even now, just as she did of old.
The ninth hymn, consisting of five verses, begins with "yuñjate manaḥ.
Regarding this, the *Anukramaṇī* states: "yuñjate pañca; [the seer is] Iyāvāśva; it is addressed to Savitṛ and is in the Jagatī meter. The seer is Iyāvāśva by name, a descendant of Atri.
The meter is Jagatī;
the deity is Savitṛ.
This [verse] is the Sāvitra containing the Nivid, to be recited in the Vaiśvadeva Śastra on the first day of both the Pṛṣṭhya and Abhiplava Ṣaḍahas.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "The four verses beginning with 'yuñjate mana iheha va' [are used]" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 7.5).
The first [verse] is also used in the Prasthāna-stotra.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "'yuñjate mana uta yuñjate dhiyaḥ' and 'ā tū na indra kṣumantam'" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 5.12).

The inspired poets harness their minds and harness their thoughts for the sake of the great, inspired, and wise one. He alone, the knower of all ways, ordains the priestly functions; vast indeed is the praise of the divine Savitṛ.

The inspired poets yoke their mind, and they yoke their thoughts—the inspired ones of the great inspired one, the seers of sacred hymns. He alone, the finder of the way, ordains the priestly offices; great indeed is the praise of the divine Savitṛ. 1.
1. [The vowels] kha, ca, jha, ṇa, bha, and ma arise; [the consonants] ga, gha, ja, ra, śa, and ṣa arise.
2. kha, ca, jha, ṇa, bha, ma, ra, and kica are the things to be avoided.
The wise—the intelligent priests and sacrificers—yoke their own minds to all ritual acts.
The meaning is that they form their intentions after having abandoned [all other] thoughts of the Sun (Savitṛ).
Moreover, they also apply themselves to, or attain, their mental activities (dhiyaḥ karmāṇi). By whose permission? It is said: [by his].
"By the permission of the wise, great, and learned *vipra*—that is, the praiseworthy and knowledgeable *Savitṛ*.
For the Śruti says: "Savitṛ indeed is the lord of all impellings" (*Ai. Brā.* 7.16).
That very Savitṛ is the knower of the ways (*vayunāvit*) of the sacrificial oblations (*hotrāḥ*), that is, the appropriate rites of the *hotṛ*.
"Vayuna" is a name for wisdom (*prajñā*).
He, the sole knower of the wisdom regarding each respective object of performance, alone indeed ordains—that is, he acts;
he determines each thing individually.
Furthermore, the praise (*paridhuti*) of that god Savitṛ is great (*mahī*), meaning vast or exceedingly abundant; the sense is that it lies beyond the range of ordinary praise.
When the *havirdhāna* shedder rolls forward while being covered, the verse beginning with “*viśvā rūpāṇi*” is to be recited.
And it is stated in the Sūtra: “‘*viśvā rūpāṇi prati muñcate kaviḥ*’ [is used] in the case of the fixed position.
That God, the *etaśa*—of swift color and resplendent—measures out and defines by his own greatness (*mahitvana*) the worlds, such as the earth and others.
The word "shines" (*rājate*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
In expressions such as *yuvaśā tākaṇotana* (RV 1.161.7), the addition of the letter *śa* in *etaśa* and so forth is a Vedic archaism (*chāndasa*).
And you go, O Savitṛ, to the three luminous realms; you unite with the rays of the sun.
And you encompass the night on both sides; and by your laws, O God, you become Mitra.
And you go, O Savitṛ, to the three luminous realms; and you are united with the rays of the sun. And you traverse the night on both sides; and by your divine laws, O God, you become Mitra. 4.
O divine Savitṛ, you go to and traverse the three shining luminous realms, the worlds of heaven—
thus it is said in "tisro divaḥ pṛthivīḥ" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 4.53.5).
Moreover, you unite with and join yourself to the rays of the sun.
This is a form derived from the root *uc* in the sense of "to assemble."

The one who exists prior to the rising is Savitṛ, while the one who abides during both the rising and the setting is Sūrya. Moreover, O God Savitṛ, you traverse—meaning you encompass on both sides—the night. Furthermore, O God Savitṛ, through your *dharmas*—actions that sustain the world—you become Mitra; you become the deity known as Mitra.
Or rather, by providing light and other benefits, you are the friend of all the worlds.
You alone are the one who impels procreation, and you, O God, become Pūṣan through your journeys.
You rule over this entire world; Śyāvāśva has offered this hymn of praise to you, O Savitṛ.

And you alone indeed rule over procreation; and, O God, you become Pūṣan through your journeys. And you shine forth over this entire world. Śyāvāśva has brought this hymn of praise to you, O Savitṛ. 5.

O Savitṛ, you alone—you being truly one—rule over, that is, are capable of granting permission for, all actions consisting of procreation. You alone have the power to authorize all those who perform worldly acts such as walking and so forth, as well as Vedic acts such as the Agnihotra and so forth. Moreover, O God, you are Pūṣan, the nourisher, by means of your journeys.
Moreover, you rule over and are the master of this entire world—the multitude of beings—to sustain it.
Since you possess such great majesty, O Savitar, the seer Śyāvāśva has attained, that is, performs, a hymn of praise for you.
Thus, he speaks while referring to himself in the third person.

The tenth hymn, consisting of nine verses beginning with "tatsavitur," is the seerly composition (ārṣam) of Śyāvāśva. Regarding this, the index (anukramaṇikā) states: "tatsavitur nava; Gāyatra; the first is Anuṣṭubh. Thus, the first verse is an Anuṣṭubh, and the remaining ones are Gāyatrīs.
Because it is stated, "But [the verse] addressed to Savitṛ," it is *sāvitra*.

"O God Savitṛ, impel for us today auspicious fortune accompanied by progeny; drive away evil dreams! (4) O God Savitṛ, impel (*sāvīḥ*) for us today—on this day of sacrifice—auspicious fortune (*saubhāgyam*) endowed with progeny (*prajāvata*), such as sons and the like. Drive away (*parā suva*) evil dreams (*duḥsvapnyam*), that is, the misery of bad dreams and poverty.

O God Savitar, drive away all difficulties. Send forth to us that which is auspicious. (5) O God Savitar, drive away all difficulties. Send forth to us that which is auspicious—that is, progeny, cattle, houses, and so forth—and impel it toward us. For the Śruti declares: "Progeny indeed is auspicious; cattle are auspicious; a house is auspicious. (25)
Sinless, under the impulse of the god Savitṛ for Aditi, may we obtain all desirable things.
To the sinless one;
to Aditi;
to the god.
At the impulse of Savitṛ, all.
We meditate upon the noble deeds.
Being sinless under the impulse (*save*)—that is, with the permission—of the god Savitṛ, the impeller, may we be sinless and free from offense toward Aditi, the indivisible goddess;
for it is upon the earth that sins arise.
When our offenses have departed, may we hold fast to all desirable riches (*vāmāni*).
In the Vaiśvadeva section of the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, for the offering of the twelve-potherd cake to Savitṛ, "ā viśvadeva" is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "ā viśvadevaṃ sapatiṃ vāmamadya savitaḥ" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 2.16).
This same verse serves as the invitatory verse for Savitṛ at the Prāyaṇīya sacrifice.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Ā viśvadevaṃ sapatiṃ ya imā viśvā jātāni" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.3). This very verse is the invitatory mantra (*anuvākyā*) for the oblations of the *devasū* sacrifice. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "Ā viśvadevaṃ sapatiṃ na pramiye saviturdaivyasya tat" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 4.11).
We choose with well-spoken hymns Savitṛ, the Lord of Truth, who belongs to all the gods. (7) We choose with well-spoken hymns Savitṛ, the Lord of Truth, who belongs to all the gods. (7)
1. *Kha-ca-jha-ṇa-bha-ra-preraya*: impel the subjects, cattle, the home, and so forth; *ta-preraya*: impel the subjects, cattle, the home, and so forth.
*Viśvadeva*:
one under whose control all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*) abide—such [a one].
For he is the Self of all, according to such scriptural texts as, "They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.164.46), since all others are his manifestations.

We worship—that is, we honor and celebrate with hymns—the god Savitṛ on this day of sacrifice: the true one, the protector of those who perform righteous deeds, whose impulse is truth, and whose permission is truth.
He who goes before these two days, never failing—
the wise god Savitṛ.
He who, with good intentions, goes before both these days, day and night, without faltering—the god Savitṛ. 8.

The connection is as follows: we choose that Savitṛ, the god who is well-disposed—meaning possessing beautiful meditation—or who performs good deeds, who goes before these two days—the night and the day—unfailing and without negligence.
At the *prāyaṇīya* [offering], "ya imā viśvā" is the *yājyā* for Savitṛ. And it is stated in the Sūtra: "ya imā viśvā jātāni... sutrāmāṇaṃ pṛthivīṃ dyāmedhasam" (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 4.3).
In the Aśvamedha, after releasing the horse, a sacrifice to Savitṛ (*sāvitrīṣṭi*) should be performed at each pressing (*anusavana*).
This is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*) for that midday pressing (*mādhyandina-savana*).
And it is stated in the Sūtra: "May that god Savitṛ, the possessor of excellent jewels, come to all these created beings" (*Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra* 10.6).
Savitṛ, who makes all these created beings hear with his song, impels them forward.
He who makes all these creatures hear by means of his song, and impels them forth—Savitar. ||9||
The deity who makes all these beings— meaning all these creatures that have been born and produced—
he causes them to hear [his name] through this verse of glory.
The meaning is that everyone hears his praise.
Alternatively, being on the verge of rain, he makes all these beings hear [his voice] by means of the sound of thundering.
Furthermore, Savitṛ impels and urges them forth; him we choose.
The eleventh hymn, consisting of ten verses beginning with "acchā vada," has Bhauma Ātreya as its seer.
The index (anukramaṇikā) states: "Accha daśa: Ātreya [composed] a hymn to Parjanya; three are Jagatī, and the penultimate is Anuṣṭubh.
Thus, the ninth verse, "yat parjanya," is an Anuṣṭubh, while the three beginning with "vi vṛkṣān" are Jagatīs.
The remaining six verses are *triṣṭubh*s;
Parjanya is the deity.
By means of this hymn, one should worship the quarters of the sky verse by verse.

And it is stated in the Sūtra: "When [the fire] has been established, one should worship all the directions with the four verses beginning 'Speak auspiciously to us with these songs' (RV 10.141.1–4), verse by verse, or with the entire hymn" (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.13).
Speak clearly with these songs to the powerful one; praise Parjanya and invite him with homage. Bellowing like a bull, he of swift bounty shall deposit his seed as a germ within the plants.

Well! Speak! With these songs praise the powerful one; laud Parjanya with homage and win him over. Bellowing like a bull, the one of quickening gifts, may he place seed as a germ within the plants. 1.

1. In manuscripts ga, gha, and ja, the word ‘ca’ is absent. 2. In manuscripts ga, gha, and ja, it says “iti”; here ‘ca’ is for the purpose of completing the meter. 3. [The reading] is “sūktena sūktena.
O singer, pray with your hymn toward the powerful Parjanya.

Regarding the word *parjanya*, Yāska has provided various etymological explanations: “*Parjanya* is derived from the root *tap* with its initial and final syllables transposed; he is the one who satisfies (*tarpayitā*), the one who belongs to the people (*janyaḥ*), the supreme conqueror (*paro jetā*), or the progenitor (*janayitā*) of essences (*rasānām*)” (Nirukta 10.10).
Praise him with these words of praise, these "cows";
worship him on every side with reverence and with oblations characterized by the sacrificial axle.
Praise that Parjanya, the bull, the showerer of waters, the swift-giver who, thundering with a roar, places the seed—water acting as the embryo—within the plants. Praise him!

He strikes down the trees and he slays the demons; the entire world trembles before his great weapon. Even the innocent man flees from the one possessed of such virile power, when Parjanya, thundering, smites the evildoers. He strikes down the trees, and he slays the demons; the whole world fears him because of his mighty weapon. Even the sinless man flees from the one endowed with such strength, when Parjanya, roaring, destroys the wicked.
This mantra has been clearly explained in the Nirukta;

it is written here as follows: “Parjanya strikes down the trees and strikes down all the Rākṣasas; all beings are afraid of him because of his great weapon, for his weapon is mighty. Even one who is innocent flees in fear from him who, possessing the power of rain, strikes the evildoers while thundering” (Nirukta 10.11).

Like a charioteer lashing his horses with a whip, he makes manifest his vigorous messengers for the sake of the serpent. From afar, the roars of the lion rise up when Parjanya displays his virile power in the sky. Like a charioteer, lashing his horses with a whip, he makes manifest his vigorous messengers for the sake of the serpent. From afar, the thunders of the lion rise up when Parjanya displays his virile power in the sky.
Like a charioteer, that is, like the master of a chariot;

just as he makes his messengers—the soldiers—manifest by lashing the horses with a whip, so too does this Parjanya, lashing—that is, impelling—the horses, which are the clouds, manifest—that is, make visible—the "vapya" clouds, which are like messengers, namely the rain-inducing clouds or the Maruts.
The word *aha* is a filler (*pūraṇa*).
This being so, the word *siṃha* (lion) is derived from the root *sah* or *hiṣ*, meaning "to sound.
From afar, the *stanathas*—the thundering sounds—of the cloud, which is the showerer or the utterer of sound due to its non-raining, arise or emerge. When? [At the time of the rain.]
Whenever Parjanya makes the sky—the intermediate space—fertile, that is, endowed with rain, at that time.
The verse beginning with “pra vātā” is the *yājyā* for the fourth *caru* offering to Parjanya.
This is also stated in the Sūtra: “‘pra vātā vānti patayanti vidyutaḥ’ and so forth, starting from the fire-installation ceremony” (Āśvalāyana Śrautasūtra 2.15).

1. [The reading] kha-ca-ṇa is by way of the characteristic of the oblation (havir-lakṣaṇena). 2. [The reading] ta is "parjanya-stapa," with the beginning and end reversed. 3. [The reading] ta is "vānti. 4. [The reading] kha-ca-ṇa is "pārjanyasya."

The winds blow forth; lightnings fly; the plants rise up; the sky swells. Refreshing food is born for every living being when Parjanya protects the earth with his seed. 4. The winds blow forth; lightnings fly; the plants rise up; the sky swells. Refreshing food is born for every living being when Parjanya protects the earth with his seed. 4.
The winds blow for the sake of rain;
the lightnings fly, go, and move about on all sides;
the plants—the herbs—spring up, rise upward, and flourish.
He causes the heaven to swell; he flows into the intermediate space.
The earth is born—that is, it becomes capable—for the sake of the entire world, for the welfare of the whole universe. When is this so? [At the time of the sacrifice.]
Whenever the god Parjanya protects, nourishes, or approaches the earth with his seed—namely, water—it becomes thus.

At whose command the earth bows down deeply; at whose command that which has hooves leaps about; at whose command the plants of every form flourish—O Parjanya, grant us great protection. 5. At whose command the earth bows down deeply; at whose command that which has hooves leaps about; at whose command the plants of every form flourish—O Parjanya, grant us great protection. 5.
At whose command—the rite of Parjanya—the earth bows down, bending low and becoming the lowest of all;
at whose command the hoofed creatures, such as cows and others, quiver, are supported, filled, or move about;
at whose command the plants become manifold in form, possessing various shapes—O Parjanya, you who are great, grant us, to us, great protection and happiness.

O Maruts, bestow rain upon us from heaven; let the streams of the showering cloud swell forth. With this thundering voice, pouring down the waters hitherward, may the Asura, our Father, come near. divaḥ | naḥ | vṛṣṭim | marutaḥ | rarīdhvam | pra | pinvat | vṛṣṇaḥ | arśvasya | dhārāḥ | arvāṅ | etena | stanayitnunā | ā | iha | apaḥ | ni'siñcan | asuraḥ | pitā | naḥ || 6 ||
O Maruts, you, from the sky and from the intermediate space, bestow rain upon us for our sake;
let the streams—the torrents of water belonging to the vigorous, pervasive, raining cloud—swell forth and flow out. O...!
1. They blow forth; thus they are called "winds" (vātāḥ). 2. He protects; thus [he is called] "protector" (rakṣitṛ). Ṛgveda 2.124.
O Parjanya, with this thundering, roaring cloud, come toward us, come hither!
What are you doing?
Pouring down waters. That god, the Vasu—the bestower of water—though he is the one who releases it, is our father and our protector.
Roar out! Thunder! Place the embryo within! Fly around with your water-laden chariot!
Tear asunder the well-aimed bolt; let the heights be leveled and the lowlands raised! Let the Nipādas be brought low!
Roar forth! Thunder! Deposit the germ! Fly around with your water-laden chariot! Draw down the well-aimed thunderbolt! Let the plains and the heights become level; let the lowlands be filled up! 7.
Roar toward the earth; that is, utter a sound. This is stated again for the sake of firmness:
thunder, that is, roar.
Place the embryo—the water that occupies the position of an embryo—within the plants.
For that purpose, go all around with a watery chariot.
Draw down well for the sake of rain the cloud that holds water like a leather bag, which is specially bound and directed downward.
Alternatively:
*viṣitam* means "with its bonds loosened"—draw it [the furrow] thus.

When this has been done, let the high places (*ūrdhvavantaḥ*)—that is, elevated regions—and the low places (*nipādāḥ*), meaning those with downward-turned feet or depressed regions, become level (*samāḥ*), that is, uniform; the meaning is that they shall become filled with water.
Draw up the great reservoir and pour it forth; let the canals flow, released from the front.
Drench heaven and earth with clarified butter; let there be a good drinking-place for the cows.
Draw up the great treasure; pour it down. Let the canals flow forth, well-dispersed before us. Drench heaven and earth with clarified butter; let there be a good place of drinking for the cows. 8.
O Parjanya, you have caused that great, fully grown vessel— the cloud, which serves as a receptacle— to rise upward;
having done so, pour it down, let it flow downward.
O clanswomen, rivers, well-established and widely renowned, let them flow, let them stream forward toward the east;
for generally, rivers flow toward the east.
With clarified water, drench—moisten excessively—heaven and earth.
From the cows that bear the yoke, may there be excellent water—water that is very good and most excellently fit to be drunk.

1. *ta-kuru*. 2. Regions with depressions and elevations caused by stones, gravel, and the like: *kha-ca-ṇa*; regions with depressions and elevations: *jha-na-ra*; regions with depressions and elevations caused by stones and the like: *bha-pāṣāṇādi-nimnonnatāḥ pradeśāḥ*. 3.
*kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra-śa* denote the most excellent [regions].
4. From the East: When you roar with the forefinger, thundering and striking down the evildoers, then all this world rejoices, whatever exists upon the earth.
When Parjanya thunders with a roar and strikes down the evildoers, then all this world rejoices, whatever exists upon the earth.

O Parjanya, when you, thundering and crying out excessively, strike and rend the clouds that do evil—that is, the clouds that commit sin—then this entire world rejoices. The "entire world" is further specified:
whatever exists upon the earth, established on the ground, consisting of both the moving and the unmoving—all this universe rejoices and exults.
It is well known that rain is the cause of joy for the entire world.
It rained, it rained; seize it well! Draw it near; let the cow that follows come hither. You have generated the plants for the sake of food, and you have bestowed wisdom upon your creatures.

The rainless season has passed; let there be rain! Now, O singer, grasp it well. He has caused the rivers to flow across the desert wastes. He has generated the plants for our nourishment, and he has bestowed wisdom upon all living beings.

This [verse] is for the release of excessive rain. O Parjanya, you who have not rained before, you have now rained. "Varṣam ud u pū gṛbhāya": take up the rain, take it up excellently and well; that is to say, withhold it. You have made the deserts—regions devoid of water—possessing water. For what purpose? "Atyetavai u": so that they may pass beyond [the drought]. You have generated the plants, you have brought them forth. For what purpose? "Bhojanāya dhanāya": for food, for wealth, or for enjoyment. The word *kam* here is a verse-filler, as in "śiśiraṃ jīvanaya kam" (Nirukta 1.10). Moreover, "uta api ca": from among the creatures, you have found—that is, you have received—the *manīṣā*, the hymn of praise. 28.
The hymn beginning with "balisthā" consists of three verses; it is the twelfth hymn, composed by Atri, addressed to Bhauma (the Earth), and is in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
It is cataloged thus: "balisthā [consists of] three verses, addressed to Pārthiva (the Earth), in the Anuṣṭubh meter.
The application of this hymn is determined by its internal characteristics (liṅga).
"The first among the gods, the nourisher of the earth"—this is the invitatory verse (*anuvākyā*).
For it is stated in the Sūtra: "'She who is the foundation of the mountains, who is firm even among the lords of the forest' (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 6.14).
And in the *Bhūmistoma*, this verse serves as the opening hymn (*sūktamukhīyā*) for the *Marutvatīya* Śastra (Āśvalāyana Śrauta Sūtra 9.5).
O Earth, you truly bear the cleft of the mountains;
you, the mighty one, who extend far, quicken the vast expanse with your greatness.
Truly, O Earth, you bear the burden of the mountains; you who, being vast and mighty, spread out the ground and cause it to flourish. || 1 ||
1. [A verse] with the syllables *jha*, *ta*, *bha*, and *ra* is "excellent" (*udutkṛṣṭam*).
2. [A verse] possessing the syllables *kha*, *ca*, *jha*, *ṇa*, *ta*, *na*, *bha*, *ra*, *ja*, and *la* [describes] deserts (*dhanvāni*), regions devoid of water (*nirudakapradeśān*).
This earth is of two natures, and she is also a perceptible deity.
The deity described here as being situated in the center is explained by means of awakening.

O Earth, you who extend far and wide, O deity dwelling in the intermediate space! You indeed bear and maintain in that manner, there in the atmosphere, the piercing—the crushing or breaking—of the mountains or the clouds.
O Great One, O Mighty One, O you who possess excellence or who possess flowing waters, you who with your greatness or your great waters intensely gladden the manifest earth.
The hymns of praise, moving in various ways, respond to you with chants and verses;
O straight-moving one, you rush toward the prize like a neighing steed, as you pierce through the swelling mass of the enemy.
The hymns of praise, O far-reaching one, celebrate you with their recitations—you who, O bright one, send forth the swelling flood like a neighing steed toward the prize.

O discerning Earth, O Goddess of manifold movements, the singers praise you with hymns—those songs characterized by movement—and celebrate you with their recitations. Furthermore, O bright-colored one, O goddess of swift motion, you cast forth the swelling cloud that fills all things, like a neighing horse that bestows booty.
"devānāṃ haviḥ pu dṛlhā cit" is the *yājyā* for the Earth;
this very verse is also the *sūktamukhyā* in the *niṣkevalya* of the *bhūmistoma*.
The *sūtra*, however, has already been cited previously.
With your power, you shatter even the firm trees of the forest with your might, when the rains of the cloud and lightning fall from heaven.
Even the firm trees you have shattered upon the earth with your might, when the rains of the cloud and the lightnings of heaven pour down for you. 3.
O Earth, you who are firm—here the third case ending is replaced by *ākāra* according to the rule *supāṃ suluk*;
with that firm patience, the ground, you sustain (*dardharṣi*) the trees, the lords of the forest, by means of your power and strength.
Alternatively, "firm" (*dṛḍhā*) may be understood as an attribute of the object to be enjoined.

The meaning is that you support the trees by making them firm. Those rains belonging to you— namely, the rain-bearing clouds and lightnings— rain down from the cloud (the genitive case used in the sense of the ablative), from the sky or the atmosphere which carries the waters, or from the sun.
Or rather, those showers of water-masses from your cloud—that is, from the raining cloud—fall, descending from the sky as it flashes with lightning.

1. Even though the deity is not directly perceived (*ra-pratyakṣadevatā*). 2. *ta*—it is addressed (*saṃbodhyate*). 3. *ta*—the goddess Earth (*pṛthivīdevi*). 4. *kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-jha-ṇa-na-bha-śa*—they praise (*abhistuvanti*). 5. *ta*—O Goddess Earth (*pṛthivi devi*). 6. *ta*—"O strong one" (*dṛlheti*). 7. *ta*—of her (*asyāḥ*). 8. *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-na-bha-ra*—from heaven, the shining one (*divo dyotamānāt*). 9. *kha-ca-jha-ṇa-ta-na-bha-ra*—lower than heaven (*divaḥ nīcaiḥ*).

10. *kha-ga-gha-ca-ja-jha-ṇa-na-bha*—"Or else... they fall" (*patanti*) is absent. "In the battle" (*pra samnāje*) is the thirteenth hymn, consisting of eight verses; it is in the *triṣṭubh* meter and dedicated to Varuṇa.
And it is enumerated: "At the *pra-samnāja*, eight [verses] dedicated to Varuṇa.
The application is based on indicative marks (*liṅga*).
Sing forth a lofty and profound prayer, dear to the renowned Varuṇa,
he who has spread out the earth for the sun like a butcher spreading out a hide.
Sing forth a lofty, profound, and beloved prayer to Varuṇa, the renowned sovereign; he who, like a butcher spreading out a hide, has spread out the earth as a covering for the sun.
Here, addressing himself, he says:

"O you, O *atra*—to *samnāje*, the one who shines perfectly as the Lord; to *śrutāya*, the one heard everywhere; to *varuṇāya*, the god so named who is the warder-off of calamity and the restrainer of men—*pra arca* (praise) *bṛhat* (the vast), *gabhīram* (the profound and difficult to fathom), *bandhathopetam* (endowed with bonds), *priyam* (the beloved), *brahma* (the sacred work in the form of a hymn).
The meaning is: utter it aloud."
"Varuṇa, who—like a *śamitṛ*, a preparer who slaughters the hide for the sake of stretching it out—[stretched] the earth, that is, the vast intermediate space (*antarikṣa*)."
According to the Vedic scripture, "On the third earth" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.12.1), even the intermediate space (antarikṣa) is denoted by the word "earth."
"For Sūrya," for the sake of "Sūrya's" "upastara," that is, for his spreading out; he "vi-jaghāna," meaning he spread it out.
For that which is spread out becomes fit for practical use (*vyavahāra*); therefore, he spread out the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) for the sake of practical activity.
This is consistent with the statement: "For King Varuṇa has made it wide" (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.24.8).

Varuṇa has spread the intermediate space through the forests, speed through the horses, and milk through the cows; he has placed wisdom in hearts, fire in the waters, the sun in heaven, and Soma on the mountain.

He has spread the atmosphere across the forests; he has placed strength in the coursers, milk in the cows, mental power in the hearts, Varuṇa has placed fire in the waters, Sūrya in the sky, and Soma upon the mountain.
This Varuṇa has stretched out the intermediate space within the forests—that is, among the tops of the trees.

Thus says the Vājasaneyaka: "For in these forests, among the tops of the trees, the intermediate space is stretched out; therefore he says, 'He has stretched out the intermediate space within the forests.
He has also stretched out strength (vāja) among the coursers—that is, among the horses.

"Milky juice" (*payaḥ*) means "milk" (*kṣīram*) in the "cows" (*usriyāsu*); *usriyā* is a name for cows, derived from the fact that "enjoyments flow forth from her"—this is its etymology. [He places it] "in the hearts," that is, in the hearts (*hṛdayeṣu*), as "intention" (*kratum*), meaning the resolve for action.
If one meditates with the mind, one performs that action with the body;
[one places] Agni—whether of lightning or of the earth—within the waters, that is, within the liquid elements.
The connection is that he has spread it everywhere.
Furthermore: "In heaven, in the celestial world, he placed the sun;
and the Soma, too, he placed upon the mountain."
1. kha-ca-jha-ṇa-bha-ra—here;
2. kha-ca-ṇa-ra—kṣatrajña; jha-na-bha—kṣetrajña; 3.
kha-ca-ṇa—priyarūpam.

4. *kha-ca-ṇa-pa* is the one who performs the driving away of the sacrificial animal (*paśu-vivāsana-kartā*); *ga-gha-ja-pa* is the one who performs the killing of the sacrificial animal (*paśu-viyāsana-kartā*); *śa-pa* is the one who performs the cutting of the omentum (*vapā-samāna-kartā*). 5. *ta* [is the one who acts] on the second and third [days].
6. *jha-ta-na-bha-ra*: here, the etymological explanation (*nirukta*) is given.
7. Kha-ca-ṇa-bha meditates; he speaks that with his voice.
Varuṇa has cast down the waterless well toward the earth, the two worlds, and the intermediate space.
With it, the king of the entire world moistens the ground as rain moistens the barley.

Varuṇa has released the water-skin with its opening turned downward; it has poured forth across the two worlds and the mid-air. With that, the King of the entire universe drenches the earth, as rain does the barley. 3.
He released— that is, he fashioned— the *kavandha*, which has its opening facing downward like a vessel turned upside down.
*Kavanda* means water; that in which it is held is *kavandha*, namely, a cloud. He made him into such [a cloud].
Alternatively, *kavandha* means water.
He made that water *nīcīnavāram*, meaning it had an outlet flowing downwards;
the sense is that he split open the cloud and caused the water to flow face-downward.
With reference to what is it said? It refers to *rodasī*, meaning heaven and earth, and the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*);
the meaning is "for the benefit of the three worlds."
With that water, Varuṇa, the king and lord of the entire world—that is, of all created beings—moistens the earth; he drenches the ground.
Just as a man who sprinkles, such as a sower, spreads barley everywhere for its growth, so too does he moisten the earth on all sides.
Alternatively, the connection may be "the rain [is] Varuṇa."
*Varṣakaḥ* means *parjanya* (the rain-god).
In this interpretation, the word *puruṣa* must be supplied [to complete the sense], as in "like a man [drinking] barley.
In this regard, the *Nirukta* passage beginning with "Varuṇa [holds] the cloud, the vessel turned downward" (*Nirukta* 10.4) should be consulted.
He moistens the earth, the ground, and the sky when Varuṇa desires the milk to be poured out;
the mountains dwell together with the ocean, and the heroes, exerting their power, relax their tension.

He moistens the earth, the broad ground, and also the sky. When Varuṇa desires that which has been milked, then indeed the mountains clothe themselves in clouds; the heroes, exerting their strength, relax [their tension]. 4.
Varuṇa spreads out the earth, the broad mid-region—
wherein it was previously stated that even the mid-region is denoted by the word "earth"—
and furthermore, he moistens the sky, the world of heaven.
When he desires or longs for milk filled with water—
or rather, milk-water—
thereby the effects thereof, such as medicinal herbs and so forth, are indicated.
When he desires, "May the plants and the rest flourish," immediately thereafter, they clothe him—that is, they cover him.
Who? The mountains; that is, the rocky peaks.
By what?
By the cloud, by the rain-mass.
And furthermore, what are they? Those desiring strength (*taviṣīyantaḥ*).
The heroic Maruts, the special impellers of rain, loosen—that is, they cause to burst open—the clouds.
I shall proclaim this great cosmic artifice of the wise Asura Varuṇa:
he who, as if standing in the mid-air with a measuring rod, has measured out the earth with the sun.
This great illusion of the son of Asura Śruta, Varuṇa’s, I shall proclaim: standing as if upon a measuring rod in the mid-air, he measured out the earth with the sun. 5.
1. The mountains Kha, Ca, and Ṇa; the mountain Jha-Bha.
[The term] *āsura* means belonging to the Asuras.
The relationship between the Asuras and this [mountain] is that of the slain and the slayer.
The meaning is "the slayer of the Asuras. Alternatively, *asura* means a cloud.

Because it bestows life, I proclaim—that is, I declare—this great (*mahīm*) and vast (*mahatīm*) *māyā*, which is wisdom (*prajñā*), belonging to that [cloud] which is renowned (*viśrutasya*). I speak forth this.

What is this that is called "illusion" (māyā)? It is this: Varuṇa, who stands in the intermediate space, measures out and defines the earth and the intermediate space by means of the sun, as if with a measuring rod; this is his illusion.
Who indeed can withstand this great creative power of the god?
For the many dark rivers, flowing toward him, fill the single ocean.
This—*ū~*—indeed! Who has ever dared to withstand this great power of the god? When he alone, like a bull, [roars].

Whatever we have done as enemies in play, or whatever indeed was true, or what we do not know—all that, O God, loosen like something slack; then, O Varuṇa, may we be dear to you. 8. Whatever we have done as enemies in play, or whatever indeed was true, or what we do not know—all that, O God, loosen like something slack; then, O Varuṇa, may we be dear to you. 8.
The *kitavāsaḥ* are gamblers, those who play at dice. A *kitavaḥ* is so called because he says, "What stake have you with me? What have I won?
Just as they smear [the blame] upon the opponent during the gambling match—that is, in the game of dice—they cast aspersions on us, saying, "O hater, you have committed this sin against me."
In this context, the *nakāra* occurring before the prefix is used in the sense of comparison (*upamārthīya*). The word *vā* means "or," and *gha* is a filler (*pūraṇa*).
Whatever sin we have committed through falsehood or even through deception,
and whatever sin we have done that we do not know or perceive— release all those very sins as if they were loosened, like fruits with loose bonds.
He was created for the sake of liberation.
O God, hereafter, may we be dear to you—may we become beloved.

The fourteenth hymn, consisting of six verses beginning with “indrāgnī yam,” is addressed to Indra and Agni; it is composed in the Anuṣṭubh meter, except for the sixth verse, which is a Virāj-pūrvā, because it is defined by the rule: “The first two [feet] have ten syllables, and the others have eight” (Anuvāka 9.11).
And thus it has been listed in the Anukramaṇī: “‘indrāgnī pālendra’ is in the Ānuṣṭubh metre, ending with Virāj.
The application [of the mantra] is determined by its indicative marks (liṅga).

O Indra and Agni, you both protect the mortal man in battles; he indeed shatters even the firm things, as Trita [shatters] the splendors like reeds. 1. O Indra and Agni, whom you two protect in battles, that mortal man indeed shatters even the firm things, as Trita [shatters] the splendors like reeds. 1.
O both of you, Indra and Agni, when separated from one another, you two protect—that is, guard—the mortal man.
In battles, that mortal man shatters—even those things that are *dṛlhā*, firm—and even the *yumnā*, shining riches belonging to the enemy.
Trita, the seer, [shatters them] like the words of opposing disputants.

Let the mountain-born hymns—those thoughts and praises produced through speech—go forth, let them proceed! To whom? To you (*vaḥ*), though there is a transposition of the case-ending; [they go] to Viṣṇu, to Vyāsa, or to Indra accompanied by the Maruts (*marutvat*). Whose praises are these? It is said: of the seer named Evayāmarut (the genitive ending is elided). Alternatively, this [seer] is the progenitor of the mountain-born praise. In the latter half [of the verse], there is a praise of the Maruts. Furthermore, let the praises go forth. To whom? To the host (*śardha*), the powerful company of the Maruts. Everything else is an epithet of that power: to the one who is to be sacrificed to preeminently (*paryajyu*), to the one possessing beautiful ornaments (*sukhādi*), to the one with lovely adornments (*su-ābharaṇa*). *Khādi* is a specific type of ornament, as seen in the Śruti: “And the *khādi* in their hands” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 1.168.3) and “the *khādayaḥ* among the cattle” (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā 5.54.11). Herein, the Venerable Vasubandhu, having already refuted the self as it is conceived by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), now intends to refute the self as it is conceived by the Śrāvakas. Therefore, he says: "If the aggregates were the self, there would be no self at all. This means that if one were to say, "The aggregates themselves are the self," then because the aggregates are multiple and momentary, the self would likewise be multiple and momentary; thus, the self would not exist as a single, permanent entity. Furthermore, since the aggregates are impermanent, the self would also be impermanent. Moreover, because the aggregates are distinct from one another, the self would also be distinct. Consequently, the self would be subject to arising and ceasing, and would lack the characteristics of permanence, unity, and independence. For these reasons, the self does not exist. Furthermore, if the aggregates were the self, then because the aggregates are many, the self would also be many. Because the aggregates are momentary, the self would also be momentary. Because the aggregates are mutually distinct, the self would also be distinct.
